title: The Minnesota Water Campaign, July and August 2026
what: On 26 and 27 July 2026 a coordinated cyber attack disrupted controllers at more than thirty water and wastewater systems in Minnesota, shutting down one town's well and treatment plant for about two hours; by mid-August open-source analysis put the campaign at about one hundred facilities in at least twelve states. The attackers reconfigured internet-exposed controllers, many on cellular links, to lock operators out. An Iran-aligned group claimed responsibility; no official body has attributed the attacks, and the investigation is open.
tier: Not military action: three of the four characteristics are present and the fourth is absent, placing it at the upper bound of the adversarial tier.

findings.title: Indication integrity is absent from the design basis.
findings.text: At another victim of the campaign, displays showed normal values while protection was disabled.

findings.title: The defense-in-depth principle lacks a common-substrate test.
findings.text: Protection and indication were defeated through one controller project file.

findings.title: The engineering workstation, vendor engineering software, and controller project file are not design basis objects.
findings.text: Legitimate engineering tools were used from outside.

findings.title: The threat actor taxonomy does not accommodate capability proliferation.
findings.text: The techniques spread to many affiliated groups.

findings.title: The applicability determination trigger now fires without discrimination.
findings.text: A small interior town was struck.

findings.title: The scope threshold excludes a population that is materially exposed.
findings.text: The town struck serves fewer people than the framework's scope.

findings.title: The framework depends on a single cyber reference event.
findings.text: Oldsmar had carried the whole cyber reference load.

findings.title: Common third-party configuration is an unaddressed sector-level common substrate.
findings.text: Configuration shared by contractors could let one success repeat.

annex.p: This annex is for drinking water and wastewater utilities of every size, especially small and rural systems without dedicated operational technology staff, and for the integrators and contractors who configure their controllers. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known

Before the questions below: have you listed every controller and remote station that talks to the outside world, with the network it does so through (your own, a cellular carrier’s, or a vendor’s or integrator’s remote-support path) and the address it actually uses?
You cannot look at an exposure you have not listed, and a search of your own addresses can come back clean while equipment at someone else’s is open. A.3.4.
Can any of your controllers, including those at towers, wells, and lift stations on cellular links, be reached from the public internet?
Anyone scanning can reach your process. A.3.1.
Could someone with a copy of your controller’s credential or software change its configuration, and would the controller know the change was not yours?
An attacker locks you out of your own plant. A.3.1.
Would you know if engineering software was being run against your controllers from outside your organization, outside a maintenance window?
A legitimate tool is used against you unseen. A.3.2.
Do your safety shutdowns and alarms stand on something other than the controller project file, so that one changed file could not defeat both?
The controller runs the process and has stopped protecting it. A.3.2.
Would you know if your displays were showing false values, and could your operators check the process another way?
Does a contractor supply the same configuration to you and to other utilities, so that one success could be repeated across many?
An attack on one utility is an attack on all its contractor’s clients. A.3.3.
Could you switch to manual operation, and do you know what a loss of pressure would mean for your water’s safety?
Pressure loss lets untreated groundwater into the pipes. A.3.3.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Take Control Technology Off the Internet

annex.p: On 30 July 2026 the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency advised operators to remove water control technology from the public internet, and its announcement of that day gave explicit attention to end-of-life hardware and noted that impact depends on a utility’s capability to switch to manual operations. Its advisory AA26-097A documented the exploitation of internet-exposed programmable logic controllers. No step of this instrument’s is added here.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Make Indication and Protection Independent of the Controller

annex.p: The announcement records that modified project files were found by noticing ladder logic discrepancies across several sites. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-1, F-2, and F-3: give operators a way to check the process that does not pass through the controller’s own displays; keep safety shutdowns and alarms on a substrate the controller project file cannot change; and treat the engineering workstation, vendor engineering software, and controller project files as protected assets, watching for their use from outside the organization.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Count Shared Configuration, and Plan the Manual Fallback

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-6 and F-8. Know whether a third party supplies a common configuration across you and other utilities, and treat that as a shared exposure; and make sure even the smallest system can run by hand and knows what a pressure loss means for its water.

annex.h3: A.3.4 List What Talks to the Outside, Then Look as an Attacker Would

annex.p: List first, then look. The inventory comes first because exposed equipment often sits outside your own address space: this campaign reached controllers at towers, wells, and lift stations on cellular links, and a cellular modem usually takes its address from the carrier’s pool, so a search of the utility’s own blocks can come back clean while the controller is open. Then look at each address on the list as an attacker would, by any of three routes, each its provider’s. Shodan and Censys each offer a search of the devices they have found answering on the internet, and a search limited to your own address blocks and the addresses on your list shows you what it would show anyone. In the United States, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency offers Cyber Hygiene Vulnerability Scanning, which scans the internet-facing assets an organization names and reports weekly, at no cost to governments and critical infrastructure organizations (cisa.gov, Cyber Hygiene Services). Your integrator and vendors can tell you what they can reach remotely, if you ask them. Whatever the look finds that is not on your list goes on it, and whatever need not talk to the outside should stop. The inventory and the look are a standing item in every annex whose event turned on equipment reachable from the internet, on the author’s direction of 15 November 2026; here they rest on element A-1 and Section 6.2.

On 26 and 27 July 2026 a coordinated cyber attack disrupted controllers at more than thirty community water and wastewater systems across Minnesota; in Braham the attack shut down the well and treatment plant for about two hours, and Plymouth ran towers and lift stations by hand. By mid-August open-source analysis put the campaign at about one hundred facilities in at least twelve states, and near Atlanta a utility serving about 300,000 people issued a precautionary boil water advisory after cyber activity dropped its pressure. Officials said drinking water quality was not affected in the Minnesota cases. The attackers reached controllers exposed to the internet, many on cellular links and some past their support, and reconfigured them to lock operators out. The federal government had already reported, at another victim of the same campaign, a changed project file that disabled safety shutdowns and alarms while displays showed normal values. An Iran-aligned group claimed responsibility; no official body has attributed the attacks, and the investigation is open. The lessons are that control technology must come off the internet, that operators need a way to see the process that does not depend on the controller, and that protection must not stand on the same file as control. Any water utility has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this utility does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Oldsmar Water Treatment Incident, February 2021
what: On 5 February 2021 an operator at the Oldsmar, Florida, water treatment plant saw a workstation's cursor move without local input as the sodium hydroxide setpoint was raised from about 100 to about 11,100 parts per million, and set it back at once. The workstation was reachable through shared remote-support software, with shared credentials, on an unsupported operating system. Its description as an external cyberattack was later disputed by an official in office at the time and was not confirmed by the federal investigation.
tier: Not military action: intentionality is indeterminate, persistence and denial are absent, and precision is low.

findings.title: The design basis reading is independent of the contested attribution.
findings.text: The access path is the hazard whoever used it.

findings.title: Oldsmar does not satisfy the military-action characteristics; the extension rests on a constructed analog.
findings.text: The framework's military-action reading of the event is a construction, not the event.

findings.title: The detection-independence lesson was drawn from a case where detection succeeded and indication was true.
findings.text: The operator saw a true display.

findings.title: The access vector, shared remote-support tooling and an unsupported host, is only implicitly addressed.
findings.text: The common case in small systems is not named.

findings.title: The sole effective barrier was human observation under favorable physics.
findings.text: Harm was averted because someone happened to be watching.

annex.p: This annex is for drinking water utilities, especially small systems, whose operators reach treatment controls through remote-access software, and for the staff who manage their credentials and workstations. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

Before the questions below: have you listed every workstation and controller in the treatment process that talks to the outside world, with the network it does so through (your own, a cellular carrier’s, or a vendor’s or integrator’s remote-support path) and the address it actually uses?
You cannot look at an exposure you have not listed, and a search of your own addresses can come back clean while equipment at someone else’s is open. A.3.3.
Can your supervisory workstations be reached through remote-support software from outside the plant?
Anyone with the software and the password can reach your controls. A.3.1.
Are the credentials for that access shared among staff, or held individually and protected by multifactor authentication?
There is no telling an intruder from an operator. A.3.1.
Do your control workstations run an operating system your vendor still supports?
Known weaknesses stay open on the machines that run your plant. A.3.1.
Could a chemical dosing setpoint be changed to a dangerous value through the normal interface, with nothing but an operator’s eye to stop it?
Only luck stands between the change and the tap. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Govern Remote Access, Credentials, and the Host

annex.p: The advisory of February 2021, AA21-042A, directed attention to remote-access hygiene, credential practice, and operating-system currency in the sector. This step adds the instrument’s own, from F-4: name the specific access surface of this event, shared remote-support tooling, shared credentials, and an unsupported host, in the utility’s own controls, since it is the common case in small systems.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Put an Engineered Limit Behind the Operator

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1, F-3, and F-5. Treat the path from a control action to a physical consequence as the hazard, whoever’s hand is on the interface; and give a consequence-bearing setpoint an engineered limit or independent check, so that harm is not averted only because someone happened to be watching.

annex.h3: A.3.3 List What Talks to the Outside, Then Look as an Attacker Would

annex.p: List first, then look. The inventory comes first because exposed equipment often sits outside your own address space: the path in this event was remote-support software, which commonly connects out through its vendor’s relay service, so a search of the plant’s own addresses may not show it. List every remote-support tool installed on a process workstation, and remove any that is not needed. Then look at each address on the list as an attacker would, by any of three routes, each its provider’s. Shodan and Censys each offer a search of the devices they have found answering on the internet, and a search limited to your own address blocks and the addresses on your list shows you what it would show anyone. In the United States, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency offers Cyber Hygiene Vulnerability Scanning, which scans the internet-facing assets an organization names and reports weekly, at no cost to governments and critical infrastructure organizations (cisa.gov, Cyber Hygiene Services). Your integrator and vendors can tell you what they can reach remotely, if you ask them. Whatever the look finds that is not on your list goes on it, and whatever need not talk to the outside should stop. The inventory and the look are a standing item in every annex whose event turned on equipment reachable from the internet, on the author’s direction of 15 November 2026; here they rest on element A-1 and F-4.

On the afternoon of 5 February 2021, an operator at the water treatment plant in Oldsmar, Florida, serving about fifteen thousand people, saw the cursor on a supervisory workstation move without local input, and the sodium hydroxide setpoint changed from about 100 to about 11,100 parts per million. The operator set it back at once; officials said the change would have taken a day or more to reach customers and that other monitoring would have caught it. The workstation was reachable through remote-support software, with credentials shared among staff, on an operating system past its vendor’s support. At the time it was described as a cyberattack, and a federal advisory treated it as one; later, an official in office at the time disputed that account, and the federal investigation did not confirm it. This instrument does not resolve the dispute, and its findings do not depend on it. The lessons are that the path from a control to a physical consequence is the hazard whoever is at the interface, that shared credentials erase the difference between an intruder and an operator, and that harm averted by someone happening to watch is not protection. Any utility reaching its controls remotely has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this utility does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: Hacktivist Attacks on Small Water Systems, 2024 to 2026
what: From January 2024, groups presenting as hacktivists attacked small water systems in Texas, Pennsylvania, Denmark, Poland, and Spain, overflowing a tank in Muleshoe, Texas, and in Tureby Alkestrup, Denmark, dropping pressure to zero and then bursting pipe by overpressure. Denmark and Poland state that the groups act for the Russian state; that is their attribution. No supply was lost for longer than a day.
tier: A state-attributed campaign below the military-action threshold: no incident met the four characteristics.

findings.title: The taxonomy has no place for a state acting through a hacktivist persona.
findings.text: Two governments say the groups act for a state, with the skill of hacktivists.

findings.title: A state-attributed campaign below the threshold is a design-basis condition.
findings.text: The campaign was attributed to a state while no incident met the threshold.

findings.title: Commanded hydraulic consequences belong in the cyber category.
findings.text: Remote commands drove pressure to zero and then burst pipe.

findings.title: The coordination threshold waits for a confirmation the campaign is built to deny.
findings.text: The campaign was recognized only when governments aggregated the record.

findings.title: The adversary's own publication is an indicator.
findings.text: The groups published claims and video of their attacks.

annex.p: This annex is for the owner of a water or wastewater system, and especially a small one, and for the engineers who advise owners. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to a plant. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an owner answers about the owner’s own system (A.2); the actions the authorities have published, each stated as theirs, with this instrument’s own additions marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an owner can give a board or council (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one system. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the owner; it is that system’s finding, and the place to start. The questions fit within an AWWA J100 or America’s Water Infrastructure Act risk and resilience assessment and can be worked as a walkdown of the plant and its remote stations.

table: If the answer is no, or not known

Before the questions below: have you listed every operator screen, controller, and remote station that talks to the outside world, with the network it does so through (your own, a cellular carrier’s, or a vendor’s or integrator’s remote-support path) and the address it actually uses?
You cannot look at an exposure you have not listed, and a search of your own addresses can come back clean while equipment at someone else’s is open. A.3.7.

Can any operator screen, remote-desktop or remote-screen connection to the control system be reached from the internet, including through a cellular modem at a remote station? Has anyone checked from outside?
The system is in the population this campaign scans. Start with A.3.1.
Does every controller and operator account have its own password, changed from the maker’s and of sufficient length and complexity, and is remote sign-in protected by a second factor?
The Tureby and Polish route is open. A.3.2.
From the operator screen, can someone set a pressure setpoint to zero, start a pump against a closed valve, fill a tank past its overflow, or silence an alarm?
The screen is the limit, and an attacker holding the screen holds the limit. A.3.3.

If every pump were run at full speed, what is the most pressure they could produce, and is it below what the weakest pipe can take as it is today? If not, what in the field stops them: a speed limit in the drive, a high-pressure trip, relief? What stops a tank overfilling or a chemical feed running away? Can any of these be changed from the screen?
Nothing bounds the consequence but the attacker’s restraint. A.3.4.
Would the operator know? Is there a reading of pressure, level or flow that does not pass through the control system that could have been altered?
A changed or silenced alarm would go unseen, as it did for four hours at Bremanger. A.3.4.
If the screens were lost tonight, who would run the system by hand, how, for how long could they keep it up, and when did they last practice?
Recovery depends on skill not yet tested. A.3.5.
If a group posted video claiming it had struck the utility, could the utility’s own records show what the control system did? Who would answer, and to whom?
A false claim cannot be refuted and a true one cannot be scoped. A.3.6.
Does the loss of distribution pressure leave a fire district with no other supply?
The fire consequence of Section 6.6 applies; tell the district. A.3.4.
Can a valve be closed, or a pump stopped, from the screen fast enough to cause water hammer? Is closing speed limited in the actuator, and is there transient protection where it matters?
An attacker can choose where a pressure wave breaks pipe (Section 4.1). A.3.4.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Take the Screens Off the Internet

annex.p: The joint advisory tells operators to reduce the exposure of operational technology to the public internet; its account of method shows that the groups find operator interfaces by scanning for remote-screen connections and log in to whatever answers. ABW names direct internet exposure as one of the two routes into Poland’s plants. A remote-screen or remote-desktop connection that answers from the internet should be removed, or placed behind a private network with individually assigned, multi-factor sign-in. A cellular modem at a remote station is a route of its own.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Change Every Default and Weak Password

annex.p: The joint advisory calls for robust authentication on operational assets; ABW names weak password policy as the other route. A controller on its maker’s password, or on a four-digit PIN like Tureby’s, should be changed now to one of sufficient length and complexity, and the change recorded. When buying a controller, its support for individual accounts and strong authentication is a purchasing criterion; Tureby’s committee bought on price.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Know What Can Be Reached and What It Can Command

annex.p: The joint advisory calls for asset management that maps data flows and access points. The owner should know which screens can be reached from where, and what each can command. Network maps and asset-condition records belong in the same inventory: in an attacker’s hands they show where a pipe is weak, and they should be held where the control-system attacker cannot reach them, which is this instrument’s reading from Section 4.1. A limit the operator interface can override is not a limit against an attacker; that reading is this instrument’s, from F-3.

annex.h3: A.3.4 Put the Last Protection in the Field

annex.p: No authority on this record has published this action; it is this instrument’s, from F-3, and it is the one step that bounds the consequence whatever the attacker holds. It differs by mechanism (Section 4.1). Against sustained overpressure, the strongest protection is pumps whose pressure at full speed stays below what the weakest pipe can carry as it is today, so that no command can break it; where that is not so, a speed limit set in the drive, a high-pressure trip at the pump and relief sized for steady flow. Against water hammer, closing-speed limits set in the valve actuators, controlled pump stopping, and transient protection such as anticipator valves or air chambers where the network needs it; relief sized for steady pressure may be too slow for a pressure wave. Against overfilling, a hardwired high-level cutoff on each tank; against a runaway chemical feed, limits at the pump. Each acts on its own measurement, and a local gauge or level indication the network cannot alter gives the operator a reading to trust. The step is to confirm that none of these can be changed from the screen, and that their settings reflect the condition of what they protect: an old or corroded main bursts at a pressure a new one carries, so protection set for the network as designed may not hold the network as it is. Asset condition remains a factor in whether anything fails, engineering controls or not, and belongs in the same walkdown.

annex.h3: A.3.5 Keep the Hands-On Skill

annex.p: Where control was lost on this record, the utility restored service by hand, and Hale Center ran by hand while its system was disconnected. Framework §5.2 asks for a manual procedure for every control function and practice in it. The procedure should say how long the system can be run by hand with the staff the utility actually has, around the clock, before people, chemicals or fuel run out; an outage of hours is one problem and an outage of weeks is another.

annex.h3: A.3.6 Report, and Verify Before Answering a Claim

annex.p: Report an unexplained control change to the state primacy agency, to CISA and the FBI, and to WaterISAC, and say whether a campaign was known to be active. If a group claims an attack on the utility, check the control system’s records before confirming or denying it; the groups publish true and false claims alike. That step is this instrument’s, from F-5.

annex.h3: A.3.7 List What Talks to the Outside, Then Look as an Attacker Would

annex.p: List first, then look. The inventory comes first because exposed equipment often sits outside your own address space: the groups on this record found operator screens by scanning for remote-screen connections, and a screen behind a cellular modem at a remote station answers at the carrier’s address, not the utility’s. Then look at each address on the list as an attacker would, by any of three routes, each its provider’s. Shodan and Censys each offer a search of the devices they have found answering on the internet, and a search limited to your own address blocks and the addresses on your list shows you what it would show anyone. In the United States, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency offers Cyber Hygiene Vulnerability Scanning, which scans the internet-facing assets an organization names and reports weekly, at no cost to governments and critical infrastructure organizations (cisa.gov, Cyber Hygiene Services). Your integrator and vendors can tell you what they can reach remotely, if you ask them. Whatever the look finds that is not on your list goes on it, and whatever need not talk to the outside should stop. The inventory and the look are a standing item in every annex whose event turned on equipment reachable from the internet, on the author’s direction of 15 November 2026; here they rest on element A-1.

Between 2024 and 2026, groups calling themselves pro-Russia hacktivists, which the governments of Denmark and Poland say act for the Russian state, broke into the control systems of small water utilities in the United States and Europe. They did not pick their targets; they took whatever they could reach from the internet, usually through a remote screen with a weak or factory password. In Texas a tank overflowed. In Denmark about 450 homes lost water when the pumps were switched off, and pipes burst the next day when they were switched to full speed. No one was hurt, and each utility recovered by hand or with its supplier’s help. A utility of any size whose control screens can be reached from the internet, or whose passwords are weak, is in the population these groups scan; size and location do not protect it. Most of the protection costs little: taking the screens off the internet, changing passwords, and practicing manual operation. The protection that matters most, equipment in the field that stops a pump or a tank from being driven past safe limits whatever the screen says, may already be in place and needs only to be checked. The self-check in this annex tells management where the utility stands.

title: The Baltic Sea Cable Incidents, 2023 and 2024
date: 7 and 8 October 2023, 17 and 18 November 2024, and 25 December 2024
date_full: 7 and 8 October 2023, 17 and 18 November 2024, and 25 December 2024
what: In three incidents in the Baltic Sea, commercial ships, each dragging an anchor along the seabed on the investigators' accounts, were associated with damage to subsea telecommunications cables, the Balticconnector gas pipeline, and the Estlink 2 power cable. Each ship damaged several assets of different owners and countries in one voyage. Communications held because traffic rerouted over the region's many paths; the gas pipeline and the power link were each out for about six months.
tier: Not established as military action: no investigator has found whether any anchor was dragged deliberately, and governments' statements differ, each stated as its own. It is a sequence of unattributed cable faults by dragged anchors, the pattern the design basis takes as its model of deniable attack. The legal record is open.

findings.title: The surviving paths held.
findings.text: Traffic rerouted over the paths that remained, and no loss of service to end users was reported.

findings.title: One drag reaches every path across the track.
findings.text: One ship damaged several cables of different owners in one voyage, so exposure is counted against a ship's track, not a single corridor.

findings.title: The shared corridor is shared in exposure, not in repair.
findings.text: The same drags took energy links that were out for months, while the cables were repaired in days to weeks.

findings.title: The repair record sets the repair time, and one ship set it here.
findings.text: One repair ship, sent from France each time, mended the main cable three times in four months.

findings.title: The investigation is part of the repair time.
findings.text: A cut that may be a crime is also evidence, and repair and investigation share the site and the time.

findings.title: The explanation delays attribution, not repair.
findings.text: Detection, rerouting, and repair were quick; attribution and the legal response were not.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its correction of the facility class's account of the event was taken in by the class.

annex.p: This annex is for the owners and operators of subsea cables and their landing stations, and for the carriers, governments, and enterprises whose international traffic rides on them. It is also for any owner, in any sector, of a pipeline, power cable, or other asset that lies across a shipping lane. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Which of your cables, or the cables your traffic depends on, lie across shipping lanes in water shallow enough for an anchor to reach the seabed?
The exposure is unknown until a ship drags across it. A.3.1.
Could one ship dragging its anchor along its track reach more than one of the paths you count as independent, even where those paths do not share a corridor?
Paths counted as separate are lost together to one voyage. A.3.1.
If your cables were cut, would your traffic reroute automatically over paths that remain, and has that been tested?
Service holds only by luck, not by design. A.3.1.
Do your telecommunications paths share a seabed corridor with power cables or pipelines whose repair would take months?
The corridor is shared in exposure but not in repair. A.3.2.
Do you have an arrangement for repair, with a named ship or consortium and a stated response time, and do several of your cables depend on the same ship?
Repair waits for a ship that must come from outside the sea, or from another job. A.3.2.
If a cut were treated as a possible crime, does your repair arrangement provide for preserving evidence with the investigating authority so that repair and investigation do not contend?
The repair waits on the investigation, or the evidence is lost to the repair. A.3.3.
Does your plan respond to a cut on its detection, without waiting to learn its cause?
The response waits on an attribution that may never come. A.3.3.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Count Paths Against a Ship, Not a Place

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1 and F-2. Count as exposed to one drag every path that lies across a shipping lane within the reach of one ship’s voyage, whether or not the paths share a corridor, and count a cable’s length along a lane as exposure to more than one drag. Keep enough paths that share none of that exposure for the traffic that matters, and test that traffic reroutes over them.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Plan Repair Against the Ships Available

annex.p: The European Union’s Action Plan on Cable Security of 21 February 2025 found repair vessels “a major bottleneck for the capacity to recover from an incident” and proposed a reserve fleet of cable vessels. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-3 and F-4: hold a repair arrangement with a named ship or consortium and a stated response time; count cuts that would call on the same ship as sharing a repair dependency; and where your paths share a corridor with power cables or pipelines, plan for that corridor’s energy links to take months to repair.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Respond on Detection, and Preserve the Evidence

annex.p: NATO launched Baltic Sentry on 14 January 2025. These steps are this instrument’s, from F-5 and F-6: trigger rerouting, priority, and repair on detection, without waiting on the cause; agree in advance with the investigating authorities how evidence will be preserved during repair, and count any hold for evidence in your repair time; and do not count prosecution or the legal regime for cables as protection.

In October 2023 and November and December 2024, three commercial ships, each dragging an anchor along the seabed of the Baltic Sea on the investigators’ accounts, were associated with damage to subsea telecommunications cables, a gas pipeline, and a power cable between Finland, Estonia, Sweden, Lithuania, and Germany. Each ship damaged several cables of different owners and countries in a single voyage. The region’s communications held, because it had many paths and traffic rerouted; the gas pipeline and the power link were out for about six months each. One repair ship, sent from France each time, mended the main telecommunications cable three times in four months. Governments have differed on whether any of the drags was deliberate, no investigator has found that any was, and the courts are still deciding. The lessons are that one ship can cut several paths you count as separate, that repair is set by the ships available, and that the response must start when a cut is detected, not when its cause is known. Any operation whose traffic or energy crosses the seabed under shipping lanes has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Red Sea Cable Cuts, February 2024
what: On 24 February 2024, three subsea cable systems in the southern Red Sea were cut, most likely by the dragged anchor of a cargo ship that a Houthi missile had disabled six days earlier and its crew had abandoned. Traffic rerouted, and no country is reported to have lost its international connection, though some providers lost transit routes and saw added delay. The repair took about five months, almost all of it waiting on permits from two rival authorities, insurance, and security for the crew.
tier: Collateral severance under military action: the cables were cut in the course of a missile campaign against shipping, but the damage to them is not shown to have been intended, and their repair was denied for months by the conditions of the war. The accounts of the campaign and of who may have targeted the cables are each the speaker's own.

findings.title: The surviving paths held, without designed priority.
findings.text: Eleven of fourteen systems remained and carried the traffic, by commercial redundancy rather than design.

findings.title: A corridor at war is shared by the paths that survive in it.
findings.text: The paths that survived lay in the same sea and the same war.

findings.title: A ship disabled by war is an initiating event.
findings.text: A ship disabled by a missile and abandoned cut the cables, and its wreck then stood in the way of repair.

findings.title: Repair time was set by permission, not by the ship.
findings.text: A repair needing days of ship work waited about five months.

findings.title: Repair can be denied by authority without force.
findings.text: Rival permit authorities and the terms of insurance and security delayed the repair without any attack on the repair ship.

findings.title: Repair capacity in a war is one firm and one ship.
findings.text: One contractor and one ship repaired all three systems in turn.

findings.title: The permits for a shared repair are coordinated.
findings.text: The three systems shared a contractor, a ship, and a permitting problem, and their permits should be coordinated.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its correction of the facility class's account of the event was taken in by the class.

annex.p: This annex is for the owners and operators of subsea cables, the carriers and consortia that share them, and the enterprises and governments whose international traffic depends on a corridor that runs through a region at war. It is also for any owner, in any sector, whose links pass through waters where conflict may disable ships. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Does your traffic depend on cables that run through a sea where a war is being fought, and would the paths that survive a cut lie in the same sea?
The surviving paths share the war. A.3.1.
How many of the systems in your corridor could one drag from one ship reach?
Several systems are lost together. A.3.1.
If cables in that corridor were cut, would your traffic reroute automatically over paths inside and outside it, and at what cost in latency and transit?
Customers lose transit providers and see delays you did not plan for. A.3.1.
Could a ship disabled or abandoned in a conflict drift across your cables, and would its wreck stand in the way of repair?
An event no one aimed at the cable cuts it anyway. A.3.2.
If a repair needed permits from more than one authority in contested waters, insurance for a crew in a war zone, and security for the ship, how long would that take, and who would arrange it?
The ship is ready in days and the repair waits months. A.3.2.
Do you and the other carriers in your corridor depend on the same contractor and ship, and do you coordinate your permits?
Each repair waits in line behind the last. A.3.3.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Count the Corridor at War as One Place

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1 and F-2. Against conflict, count a corridor in which a war is being fought as one place for every path that runs through it, and keep paths outside it for the traffic that matters; test rerouting, and know its cost in latency and transit.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Plan for Repair That Is Denied by Permission

annex.p: On 28 February 2024, the International Cable Protection Committee urged governments to expedite repair permits and to protect the vessels doing the work. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-3, F-4, and F-5: count a ship disabled, abandoned, or sunk in a conflict near your corridor, and its wreck, as a cause of cuts and a hazard to repair; and plan in advance for the permits, insurance, and security a repair in contested waters needs, since in the Red Sea a repair that took days of ship work waited about five months.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Coordinate Repair Among Those Who Share It

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-6 and F-7. Know which contractor and ship your repair depends on and whether others depend on the same one, and coordinate permits and repair ships with the other carriers in your corridor and with the coastal authorities.

On 24 February 2024, three subsea cable systems in the southern Red Sea, which carries most of the communications between Europe and Asia, were cut, most likely by the dragged anchor of a cargo ship that a missile had disabled six days earlier and its crew had abandoned. Traffic rerouted over other cables and overland, and no country is reported to have lost its international connection, though some providers lost transit routes and saw added delay. The repair needed a week to reach the cables and about two days of work on each, but it took about five months, waiting on permits from two rival authorities, a dispute over a consortium member, and insurance and security for a crew in a war zone. One contractor and one ship repaired all three systems in turn. The lessons are that paths that survive in the same war are not independent, that a ship disabled in a conflict can cut cables no one aimed at, and that repair in contested waters is set by permission, not by the ship. Any operation whose links run through waters at war has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Tonga Isolation, January 2022
what: On 15 January 2022, the eruption of the submarine volcano Hunga Tonga–Hunga Ha'apai sent currents of debris along the seabed that broke both of Tonga's cables: its single international cable and the domestic cable to its northern islands. The main island was on limited satellite links for thirty-eight days, the northern islands waited eighteen months for their cable, and banks, exports, and remittances stopped. The repair ship came from nearly 5,000 kilometers away, and spare cable had to be borrowed.
tier: Not a deliberate act: a natural-hazard event, a volcanic eruption that cut both of a region's paths at once, below the threshold for the military-action tier.

findings.title: A natural hazard is sized by its reach and the length it destroys.
findings.text: The eruption's currents ran more than 100 kilometers on the seabed and destroyed more than 89 kilometers of cable.

findings.title: Repair time and repair capacity are set by the ship's position and the cable in stock.
findings.text: The ship's distance and a shortage of spare cable set the thirty-eight days and the eighteen months.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Merged into F-2.

findings.title: The surviving service is held in reserve, not bought after.
findings.text: Satellite capacity met about an eighth of demand, and new paths came only after the cable was restored.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its substance is recorded as context and was taken in by the class.

findings.title: A nation's path count is counted island by island.
findings.text: The northern islands had one cable to their capital and were cut off for eighteen months.

findings.title: A sole path lost once is a residual realized.
findings.text: Tonga lost its sole international path in 2019 and again in 2022, and a second cable came only in 2026.

findings.title: A second path is counted from the dependents and against the hazard.
findings.text: A second cable credits only the places its dependents are, and only against hazards it does not share.

findings.title: Emergency communications without the backbone are in place before the event.
findings.text: The government's first statement took three days, and equipment flown in was quarantined.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its correction of the facility class's account of the event was taken in by the class.

annex.p: This annex is for island states and remote regions, the operators of their cables and satellite links, and the governments, banks, and emergency services that depend on them. It is also for any owner, in any sector, whose connection to the outside world rests on one path. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
How many independent paths connect you to the outside world, and how many connect each of your populated places to the places they depend on, your own capital among them?
One break isolates you, or isolates part of you from the rest. A.3.1.
Have you sized your exposure to a natural hazard by its reach on the seabed and the length of cable it could destroy, not only by how many paths it would cut?
One event destroys more than the spares can replace. A.3.1.
Where is the nearest repair ship, how long would it take to reach you, and do you hold enough spare cable of each type you use?
Repair takes weeks for the international link and more than a year for the domestic one. A.3.2.
If your cable were cut, what share of normal demand could your standby satellite capacity carry, and is it in place, licensed, and tested before the event?
The surviving service is bought after the event, too late and too small. A.3.3.
If you have lost your sole path before, has a second path been built, and does it reach your dependents without crossing the same hazard?
The same loss happens again. A.3.1.

Are emergency communications that do not need the backbone, such as satellite telephones and high-frequency radio, already in the country, licensed, and practiced, and would arriving equipment be held at the border?
The government cannot speak for days, and help waits in quarantine. A.3.3.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Count Your Paths Island by Island, and Against the Hazard

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1, F-6, F-7, and F-8. Count your paths to the outside world and from each populated place to those it depends on; size your exposure to a natural hazard by its reach and the length of cable it could destroy; credit a second path only for the places its dependents are, and only against hazards it does not share; and where you have lost a sole path once, record the basis on which you accept a path count of one.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Know Your Repair Ship and Your Spares

annex.p: This step is this instrument’s, from F-2. Know where your repair ship is and how long it would take to reach you, and hold spare cable of every type you use in the lengths a major event could destroy; in 2022 the ship came from nearly 5,000 kilometers away, and the operator borrowed spare cable held for another customer.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Hold the Surviving Service, and Emergency Communications, Before the Event

annex.p: No authority has published an action for owners from this event; after it, Tonga’s operators agreed a satellite backhaul and a standby terminal, and a second international cable was switched on in 2026. These steps are this instrument’s, from F-4 and F-9: hold standby capacity in reserve, licensed and tested, sized to the traffic that matters, including payments and the coordination of a disaster response; and keep emergency communications that do not depend on the backbone in the country, licensed and practiced, with arrangements so that equipment sent in is not held at the border.

On 15 January 2022, the eruption of the submarine volcano Hunga Tonga–Hunga Ha’apai broke both of the Kingdom of Tonga’s cables: the single international cable that joined it to the world, and the domestic cable that joined its capital to its northern islands. Currents of volcanic debris ran along the seabed for more than 100 kilometers and destroyed more than 89 kilometers of the international cable. The main island was on limited satellite links for thirty-eight days, the government’s first statement came three days after the eruption, and banks, exports, and remittances stopped. The repair ship came from nearly 5,000 kilometers away, and the operator had to borrow spare cable; the northern islands waited eighteen months for their cable. Both cables had been cut before, in 2019, and the domestic cable was cut again in 2024. The lessons are that a sole path will be lost, more than once, and that the service that survives it must be in place before the event, not bought after it. Any place whose connection to the outside world rests on one path has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Nashville Bombing, December 2020
what: Early on Christmas morning 2020, a vehicle bomb exploded in the street in front of AT&T's central office in downtown Nashville. The building stood, but the blast cut its commercial power and disabled its generators, and its staff were kept out for about twelve hours while the scene was secured. The batteries ran out after about four to five hours, and telephone, wireless, internet, and 911 service failed across parts of Tennessee, Kentucky, and Alabama for days.
tier: A deliberate act by an individual, not military action: the Federal Bureau of Investigation found that the bomber acted alone and that the act was not terrorism, and the record does not show the building was chosen for what it carried.

findings.title: The building stood; its power plant did not.
findings.text: The structure and equipment survived, but the power connection and generators were lost from outside.

findings.title: Endurance must outlast the exclusion.
findings.text: The batteries lasted about five hours, and staff were kept out for about twelve.

findings.title: A central office's endurance against its own loss is its battery.
findings.text: With its generators gone, the building's endurance was its batteries alone.

findings.title: One building's reach is counted in the map.
findings.text: The building carried other carriers' traffic, public-safety networks, and customers' backup paths, far beyond its own service.

findings.title: Diversity is shown line by line and by test.
findings.text: Lines that 911 authorities believed independent ran through the same building.

findings.title: Warning comes while the batteries run, on a path the failure does not cut.
findings.text: For hours before the failure, the 911 centers that depended on the building received no warning.

findings.title: FirstNet and radio are second paths only where they are.
findings.text: Paths that shared nothing with the building carried; the public-safety network that shared its power did not.

findings.title: The analog is a building chosen for what it carries.
findings.text: The design basis should consider a building chosen for the service it concentrates.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its correction of the facility class's account of the event went to the class as an erratum.

annex.p: This annex is for the operators of telephone central offices, data centers, and other buildings that concentrate network service, and for the 911 centers, hospitals, airports, and agencies that depend on them. It is also for any owner, in any sector, whose service depends on one building’s power. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Could an event in the street outside your building cut its commercial power and disable its generators without entering it?
The building stands and its service fails. A.3.1.
How long can your equipment run on batteries alone, and is that longer than the time your staff could be kept from the building after an incident?
The batteries run out while your people wait at the perimeter. A.3.1.
Do you know everything your building carries: other carriers’ traffic, public-safety networks, your customers’ backup paths, and what each depends on you as its only path for?
One building takes out far more than you counted. A.3.2.
For 911 and other critical customers, have their paths been shown diverse line by line and by test, not by contract or belief?
Two vendors’ lines meet at one choke point in your building. A.3.2.
While your building runs on batteries that you know will fail, how would you warn the 911 centers and others who depend on it, by a path the failure would not cut?
Dependents learn of the failure when their phones go silent. A.3.3.
Which second paths would carry your critical customers if your building failed, and do any of them share its power or its walls?
The backup fails with the building it backs up. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Make Endurance Outlast the Exclusion

annex.p: After the event the operator said it would extend its batteries at that building from about five hours to twelve or twenty-four and pursue access protocols with the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the Federal Communications Commission. These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1, F-2, and F-3: protect a building’s power connection and generators against loss from outside it; size its endurance to outlast the time staff could be kept out after an incident, not only the time to start a generator; and agree in advance with law enforcement how you would enter, or act remotely, to preserve power at a damaged building that is a crime scene.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Know What One Building Carries, and Show Diversity by Test

annex.p: Tennessee afterward required two physically diverse connections and a wireless connection for each 911 center. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-4, F-5, and F-7: map everything each building carries and for whom it is the only path; show the diversity of critical customers’ paths line by line and by test; and credit a second path, such as a public-safety network, only where it shares nothing with the building, its power included.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Warn While the Batteries Run

annex.p: This step is this instrument’s, from F-6. When a building is running on batteries it cannot recharge, warn the 911 centers and other critical dependents at once, by a path the failure would not cut, so that they can move to their alternatives before the service fails.

Early on Christmas morning 2020, a vehicle bomb exploded in the street in front of AT&T’s central office in downtown Nashville. The building stood and its equipment kept working on batteries, but the blast cut its commercial power and disabled its generators, and its staff were kept out for about twelve hours while the scene was secured. The batteries ran out after about four to five hours, and telephone, wireless, internet, and 911 service failed across parts of Tennessee, Kentucky, and Alabama; flights at Nashville stopped, and hospitals and payments were affected. Many 911 centers had no warning, and some found that lines they believed independent ran through the same building. The Federal Bureau of Investigation found that the bomber acted alone and that the act was not terrorism. The lessons are that a building that survives can still lose its service, that its backup power must outlast the time its staff can be kept out, and that one building may carry far more than its owner has counted. Any operation that concentrates service in one building has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: Hurricane Maria, September 2017
what: Hurricane Maria crossed Puerto Rico on 20 September 2017 as a high-end Category 4 storm, knocking down most of the island's utility poles and all its transmission lines. The day after landfall about 95 percent of reported cell sites were out, and sites then ran on generators for months while the grid was rebuilt, on fuel that was scarce and sometimes stolen. Broadcasting was largely off the air, 911 centers answered without full caller location, and it took six months for the cell sites to return to about 4 percent out.
tier: Not a deliberate act: a natural-hazard event, a major hurricane that took down the communications network and the grid beneath it together, below the threshold for the military-action tier.

findings.title: The storm and the grid were one event.
findings.text: Damage and the loss of power took the sites together, power's share growing as the weeks went on.

findings.title: The design outage of a major hurricane can be months.
findings.text: The grid was down for months, and the network's restoration took six.

findings.title: Endurance was the fuel that could be delivered and defended.
findings.text: Sites ran on generators for months, and their endurance was the fuel that could reach them and be kept from theft.

findings.title: Surviving coverage is stated with its base and its population.
findings.text: The share of sites out was reported on a moving base, and did not say how many people were served.

findings.title: Backhaul on the grid's poles fails with the grid.
findings.text: The fiber connecting sites hung on the utility's poles and came down with them.

findings.title: The grid's restoration must hold the network's priorities and protect its plant.
findings.text: The utility's crews, without the carriers' priorities, removed newly installed fiber as debris.

findings.title: The 911 centers answered, without the location the access network delivers.
findings.text: Calls were answered without full caller location and call-back numbers.

findings.title: Broadcasting carried the area, and did not report its own state.
findings.text: Most stations were off the air, and the regulator learned their state by scanning the spectrum.

findings.title: The network could not report its own state.
findings.text: Providers could not report because their communications were down, and the response worked without knowing what was up.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its correction of the facility class's account of the event went to the class.

annex.p: This annex is for the operators of cell sites, wireline and cable networks, broadcasters, and 911 centers in places exposed to major storms, and for the governments that coordinate their restoration. It is also for any owner, in any sector, whose sites depend on a grid that a storm could take down for months. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
If a major storm took both your sites and the grid at once, would your plan treat them as one event, or as two that happen one after the other?
The plan for each fails because the other is assumed to hold. A.3.1.
How long could your sites run without the grid, and is that set against an outage of months rather than days?
Sites fail weeks before power returns. A.3.1.
How would fuel reach your generators if ports were closed, roads blocked, and fuel supplies controlled by others, and how would you protect fuel and generators from theft?
Endurance ends when the fuel stops coming. A.3.2.
Does your backhaul hang on the grid’s poles, and what path would carry your sites’ traffic if those poles came down?
Sites with power have nothing to connect to. A.3.2.
Is your restoration coordinated with the electric utility’s, so that its crews know your priorities and do not remove your newly restored plant?
Fiber you just restored is cleared away as debris. A.3.3.
Do your critical customers, 911 centers first, keep the caller’s location and call-back number when your network is degraded?
Calls are answered without knowing where they come from. A.3.3.
If your network were down, how would you report your state to the regulator and the response, and would broadcasters report theirs?
The response works without knowing what is up and what is down. A.3.3.
Do you count your surviving coverage by people served, with a stable base, or only by the share of sites up?
The numbers look better or worse than the service people actually have. A.3.3.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Plan for the Storm and the Grid as One Event, Lasting Months

annex.p: No authority has published an action for owners that this instrument reads; the Federal Communications Commission’s report and the Government Accountability Office’s analysis are its record. These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1 and F-2: treat a major hurricane and the loss of the grid as one event, and size your sites’ endurance and your restoration plan to a grid outage of months; on Puerto Rico’s main island most of the grid was down for about two months, and the cell sites took six months to return to about 4 percent out.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Secure the Fuel and the Backhaul

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-3 and F-5. Plan how fuel will reach your generators when ports and roads are closed and others control the supply, and how both will be protected from theft; and know which of your backhaul runs on the grid’s poles, with a path, such as satellite, that does not.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Coordinate Restoration and Report Your State

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-4, F-6, F-7, F-8, and F-9. Agree your restoration priorities with the electric utility before the storm, and protect your restored plant from its crews; keep 911 location and call-back working when the network is degraded; keep a way to report your network’s state that does not depend on the network, and expect broadcasters to report theirs; and count surviving coverage by people served, against a stable base.

Hurricane Maria crossed Puerto Rico on 20 September 2017 as a high-end Category 4 storm, two weeks after Hurricane Irma. It knocked down most of the island’s utility poles and all its transmission lines, and with them the fiber that connected cell sites. The day after landfall about 95 percent of reported cell sites were out of service, and in nearly two-thirds of the island’s municipalities every site was out. Most of the main island’s grid stayed down for about two months, and the sites ran on generators fed by fuel that was scarce, stolen, and at times controlled by others. The utility’s crews, working without the carriers’ priorities, removed newly installed fiber as debris. Broadcasting was largely off the air, the 911 centers answered without full caller location, and providers could not even report their own state. It took six months for the cell sites to return to about 4 percent out. The lessons are that a major storm and the loss of the grid are one event, lasting months, and that the network’s endurance is the fuel that can be delivered and defended. Any operation exposed to major storms has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The KA-SAT Attack, February 2022
what: At the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022, an attacker who had entered the management network of the KA-SAT satellite broadband service the evening before used legitimate management commands to overwrite the memory of tens of thousands of customer modems in about forty-five minutes. Customers in Ukraine and across Europe lost service, and about 5,800 wind turbines in central Europe lost remote monitoring and control for weeks while continuing to run. Malicious traffic attacked the restoration for weeks.
tier: Military action: a cyber attack through the management plane of a satellite network at the onset of an armed conflict. The European Union and the governments of the United Kingdom, the United States, Canada, Australia, and Estonia attributed it to Russia, each in its own words; this instrument makes no finding of attribution.

findings.title: The reach was set by the management partition.
findings.text: One set of commands reached every terminal in one partition across a continent.

findings.title: The way in was the operators' remote access.
findings.text: The attacker came in through the operators' own remote access, not an unknown vulnerability.

findings.title: Legitimate commands need a structural limit.
findings.text: The commands were legitimate in form, so only a structural limit on what one command can reach would have held.

findings.title: Restoring a terminal fleet takes weeks.
findings.text: Disabled terminals were updated, reset, or replaced over about eight weeks.

findings.title: The adversary attacked the restoration.
findings.text: Malicious traffic was renewed in new forms for weeks to keep terminals offline.

findings.title: Dependents reached through distributors are not on the operator's map.

findings.title: The dependent kept working; its second path must share no management.
findings.text: The turbines ran on, but many wind farms had no backup link for monitoring.

findings.title: The act reached beyond its aim.
findings.text: An attack aimed at Ukraine reached consumers in at least six other countries.

annex.p: This annex is for the operators of satellite and other access networks that manage large fleets of customer terminals remotely, for the distributors that sell their service, and for the enterprises, such as wind-farm operators, whose equipment depends on those terminals. It is also for any owner, in any sector, whose devices can all be reached by one management system. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known

Before the questions below: have you listed every entry point to your management network that talks to the outside world, with the network it does so through (your own, a cellular carrier’s, or a vendor’s or integrator’s remote-support path) and the address it actually uses?
You cannot look at an exposure you have not listed, and a search of your own addresses can come back clean while equipment at someone else’s is open. A.3.5.
How do your operators reach your management network remotely, and is that access protected by more than one factor, least privilege, and monitoring of unusual logins?
The way in is the operators’ own door. A.3.1.
Could someone who reached your management network move within hours to the system that distributes software or commands to your terminals?
One foothold reaches the whole fleet. A.3.1.
Could one set of legitimate management commands disable your terminals in large numbers at once, or is there a structural limit on how many one command can reach?
Tens of thousands of terminals are lost in minutes. A.3.2.
If your terminals were disabled, how long would it take to update, reset, or replace them, and do you or your customers hold spares?
Could an attacker keep restoring terminals offline after the first strike, and how would you respond?
The restoration itself is attacked. A.3.3.
Do you know which critical dependents use your service through distributors, and do those dependents have a second path that shares no management with yours?
Turbines, sensors, or sites lose monitoring, and you do not know they were yours. A.3.4.
Could an attack aimed at one country reach your terminals in others because they share the same management?
A conflict elsewhere reaches your customers at peace. A.3.4.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Guard the Way Into the Management Plane

annex.p: The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and the Federal Bureau of Investigation, in advisory AA22-076A of 17 March 2022, recommended that satellite communications providers use multifactor authentication, least privilege, the removal of unnecessary trust relationships, and the monitoring of unusual login attempts. This step adds the instrument’s own, from F-2: treat the remote access by which your operators reach the management plane as the door an attacker will use, and keep the system that distributes software to terminals separate from it.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Put a Structural Limit on What One Command Can Reach

annex.p: This step is this instrument’s, from F-1 and F-3. Divide your terminal fleet so that no one set of management commands can reach more of it than you can afford to lose, and make the distribution system structurally unable to push a change to more than that, however legitimate the command appears.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Plan to Restore a Fleet Under Attack

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-4 and F-5. Plan to restore disabled terminals by update, reset, and replacement over weeks, with spares held by you or your critical customers; and plan for an adversary who attacks the restoration as well as the network.

annex.h3: A.3.4 Know Your Dependents, Wherever They Are

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-6, F-7, and F-8. Know which critical dependents reach your service through distributors; for dependents, keep a second path that shares no management with the first; and treat terminals far from a conflict as within its reach if they share management with terminals in it.

annex.h3: A.3.5 List What Talks to the Outside, Then Look as an Attacker Would

annex.p: List first, then look. The inventory comes first because exposed equipment often sits outside your own address space: the way in on this record was the remote access by which operators reach the management network, and the device that answers it is easily left off the list of the network it guards. Then look at each address on the list as an attacker would, by any of three routes, each its provider’s. Shodan and Censys each offer a search of the devices they have found answering on the internet, and a search limited to your own address blocks and the addresses on your list shows you what it would show anyone. In the United States, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency offers Cyber Hygiene Vulnerability Scanning, which scans the internet-facing assets an organization names and reports weekly, at no cost to governments and critical infrastructure organizations (cisa.gov, Cyber Hygiene Services). Your integrator and vendors can tell you what they can reach remotely, if you ask them. Whatever the look finds that is not on your list goes on it, and whatever need not talk to the outside should stop. The inventory and the look are a standing item in every annex whose event turned on equipment reachable from the internet, on the author’s direction of 15 November 2026; here they rest on element I-1 and F-2.

At the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022, an attacker who had entered the management network of the KA-SAT satellite broadband service the evening before used legitimate management commands to overwrite the memory of tens of thousands of customer modems in about forty-five minutes. The European Union and the governments of the United Kingdom, the United States, Canada, Australia, and Estonia, each in its own words, attributed the attack to Russia, the European Union stating that it facilitated the military aggression. The attack also reached customers across Europe, and about 5,800 wind turbines in central Europe lost remote monitoring and control for weeks, though they kept running. Malicious traffic attacked the restoration for weeks. The attacker came in through the operators’ own remote access, and from there reached the system that sends commands to every terminal. The lessons are that the management plane is the way to an entire fleet, that one command should never be able to reach more than you can afford to lose, and that an attack on one country can reach customers far from the conflict. Any operation whose devices are all managed from one place has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The AT&T Mobility Outage, February 2024
what: Early on 22 February 2024, during routine maintenance, an AT&T employee placed a misconfigured network element into production without the peer review the company's procedures required, and an automated protective response disconnected all of the network's voice and 5G processing three minutes later. More than 125 million devices lost service in every state, and more than 25,000 calls to 911 were blocked. The rollback took about two hours, but the surge of devices reconnecting stretched full restoration past twelve hours.
tier: Not a deliberate act: the Federal Communications Commission found error and procedures not followed, and the company said it was not a cyberattack. It is a faulty configuration change, below the threshold for the military-action tier.

findings.title: The governed act is enforced where the change is loaded.
findings.text: A change that had not passed review could still be loaded.

findings.title: A protective response has a reach.
findings.text: An automated protective response took the whole network off the air.

findings.title: Restoration time includes the load of recovery.
findings.text: Every device reconnecting at once took more than ten hours to clear.

findings.title: During a core loss, emergency calls reach another network.
findings.text: Phones held on AT&T's network could not reach 911, while phones on other networks could.

findings.title: A separate core one change reaches is not independent.
findings.text: The public-safety network's separate core recovered faster, but the same change took it down.

findings.title: Public-safety users are told while it matters.
findings.text: Public-safety users were first told of the outage after their service was back.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its completion of the facility class's account of the event went to the class.

annex.p: This annex is for the operators of mobile and other core networks, the public-safety networks that ride on them, and the 911 centers and other critical customers that depend on them. It is also for any owner, in any sector, whose whole system can be reached by one configuration change. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from.
