A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Can a change that fails your review, testing, or approval criteria still be loaded into your production network, or does the loading mechanism itself refuse it?
A change no one approved reaches the whole network. A.3.1.
Do your downstream elements have controls specific to the errors a change could carry, so that one error does not pass through them?
The error spreads further than the change. A.3.1.
What could your automated protective responses disconnect, and could one of them take your whole network off the air?
The protection causes the outage. A.3.2.
When you roll a change back, can your registration and signaling systems handle every device reconnecting at once?
Recovery takes many times longer than the rollback. A.3.2.
When your core cannot serve 911, are phones released to other networks for emergency calls, or held on yours?
Emergency calls fail while other networks could carry them. A.3.3.
Is your public-safety network’s core truly separate, so that no single change can reach both it and your commercial core, and are its users told of an outage while it matters?
The separate core fails with the same change, and its users learn of it afterward. A.3.3.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Enforce Approval Where the Change Is Loaded

annex.p: The Federal Communications Commission found that the operator’s required peer review was not done and its testing was inadequate, and recommended that it should not be possible to load a change that fails the criteria. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-1 and F-2: make the mechanism that loads a change refuse one that has not passed review, testing, and approval; and give downstream elements controls specific to the errors a change could carry.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Bound What Protection and Recovery Can Do

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-2 and F-3. Know what each automated protective response can disconnect, and bound it so that it cannot take the whole network down; and prepare your registration and signaling systems for the load of recovery, with 911 and priority services restored first.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Keep Emergency Calls Moving and Tell Public Safety in Time

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-4, F-5, and F-6. When your core cannot serve 911, release phones to other networks for emergency calls; make sure no single change can reach both your commercial core and the core that carries 911 and public-safety traffic; and tell public-safety users and 911 centers of an outage while it is happening.

At 2:42 in the morning of 22 February 2024, during routine overnight maintenance, an AT&T employee placed a misconfigured network element into the production network, without the peer review the company’s own procedures required. Three minutes later an automated protective response disconnected all of the network’s voice and 5G processing from its towers. More than 125 million devices lost service in every state, more than 92 million calls were blocked, and more than 25,000 calls to 911 were prevented. Rolling the change back took about two hours, but when every device tried to reconnect at once the network was overwhelmed, and full restoration took more than twelve hours. The public-safety network AT&T runs recovered faster on its separate core, but the same change had taken it down too, and its users were told only after it was back. The Federal Communications Commission found error and procedures not followed, and the company said it was not a cyberattack. The lessons are that a change no one approved must be impossible to load, that protection and recovery can do more harm than the error, and that emergency calls must have somewhere else to go. Any operation whose whole system can be reached by one change has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Rogers Outage, July 2022
what: Early on 8 July 2022, a maintenance change at Rogers Communications removed a routing filter, and the core routers it protected were overwhelmed and failed within minutes. Because wireless and wireline service shared one core, more than twelve million customers across Canada lost both for about a day. 911 calling failed, emergency alerts went undelivered, and Interac debit failed nationwide because both its primary and backup connections ran through Rogers.
tier: Not a deliberate act: the independent review found error in the change and in a process that waived its scrutiny. It is a faulty change realized through a routing flood, below the threshold for the military-action tier.

findings.title: The assessment of reach is part of the governed act.
findings.text: A change first rated high risk was lowered to low by an algorithm and went in unexamined.

findings.title: The limit at the receiver stands without the filter at the sender.
findings.text: The core routers had no protection of their own when the filter was removed.

findings.title: Reach is counted across every service a core carries.
findings.text: Every service on the shared core failed together.

findings.title: A dependent's redundancy through one carrier is one path.
findings.text: Interac's primary and backup connections ran through the same carrier's core.

findings.title: The restorers' path carries visibility as well as control.
findings.text: The staff restoring the core could not reach or see it, because their own tools ran on it.

findings.title: Alerting runs through the core.
findings.text: Emergency alerts failed with the core, along with 911.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its completion of the facility class's account of the event went to the class.

annex.p: This annex is for the operators of communications cores that carry several services, and for the banks, payment networks, hospitals, governments, and alerting authorities that depend on them. It is also for any owner, in any sector, whose backup runs through the same provider as its primary. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Can your change-risk process lower a change from high risk to low without further scrutiny, approval, or laboratory testing?
A risky change goes in unexamined. A.3.1.
Do your core routers have limits of their own against overload, so that the removal of one filter elsewhere cannot overwhelm them?
One maintenance step floods the core. A.3.1.
Do several of your services, wireless, wireline, and your own internal communications among them, share one core?
If you are a critical customer, do your primary and backup connections run through the same carrier’s core?
Your redundancy is one path. A.3.2.
If your core failed, could your staff still reach your equipment, see its logs, and talk to each other, by means that do not depend on it?
Restoration waits while the restorers are blind. A.3.3.
Does the delivery of emergency alerts and 911 depend on the core that could fail?
Warnings and emergency calls fail with the core. A.3.3.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Keep Risky Changes Examined, and Limits at the Receiver

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1 and F-2. Do not let a risk algorithm lower a change’s rating without the scrutiny and testing its first rating required; and give your core routers limits of their own against overload that no single change elsewhere can remove.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Count Every Service a Core Carries, and Every Dependent’s Real Paths

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-3 and F-4. Count the reach of an act on a core as every service it carries, and separate the services whose combined loss you cannot afford; and if you are a critical customer, count connections that share one carrier’s core as one path, however many circuits they use. After the outage, Interac added a second carrier and a third link.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Keep the Restorers’ Path and the Alerts Off the Failed Core

annex.p: Canada’s Minister of Industry gave the carriers sixty days to agree on emergency roaming, mutual assistance, and a communications protocol, and the agreement took effect on 9 September 2022; Telecom Decision CRTC 2025-225, in effect from 4 November 2025, requires notice of a major outage within two hours. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-5 and F-6: keep the management network, operations center connectivity, and staff communications on paths that do not depend on the core they restore; and hold 911 and the delivery of emergency alerts on core sites independent of each other.

On the morning of 8 July 2022, a maintenance change at Rogers Communications removed a routing filter, and one router sent the core more than 900,000 routes where about 10,000 were normal. The core routers had no protection of their own, and they failed within minutes. Because wireless and wireline service shared one core, more than twelve million customers across Canada lost both, for about a day. 911 calling failed, emergency alerts in Saskatchewan were not delivered, and Interac debit and e-Transfer failed nationwide because both its primary and its backup connections ran through Rogers. Restoration was slowed because the company’s management network, operations center, and staff phones all depended on the core that had failed. The change had been rated high risk and then lowered to low by an algorithm, skipping the scrutiny and testing it would otherwise have had. The independent review found error, not an attack. The lessons are that a risky change must not be waved through, that every service on one core fails together, and that a backup through the same provider is not a backup. Any operation that depends on one provider’s core for its primary and backup has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Attack on Kyivstar, December 2023
what: On 12 December 2023, an adversary that had been inside the network of Kyivstar, Ukraine's largest mobile operator, for months destroyed systems on which its core ran and was managed, and some twenty-four million subscribers lost mobile and internet service. National roaming did not work because the lost core could not pass subscriber information to the other networks, and air-raid alerts and payment terminals failed in some regions. With vendor help, service came back in stages over about eight days.
tier: Military action: the Security Service of Ukraine attributes the attack to Sandworm, which it identifies as a unit of Russia's military intelligence service, and that attribution is stated as its own. The adversary was inside for months and chose its moment against the country's largest carrier.

findings.title: The core's management does not share the enterprise's identity.
findings.text: Entry came through a compromised employee account, and the core's management should be reachable only by separate identities.

findings.title: The virtualization layer is a surface.
findings.text: What was destroyed was the platform the core ran on, whose loss takes every function it hosts.

findings.title: Isolating the core is a planned act.
findings.text: The network was shut down to limit the damage, and that decision should be planned in advance.

findings.title: Vendor help is part of the means of restoration.
findings.text: About a thousand people and three vendors restored the core in about eight days.

findings.title: A fallback among networks is designed for the lost core.
findings.text: National roaming failed because it depended on the core that was lost.

findings.title: Alerting and payments fail with a carrier's core.
findings.text: Air-raid alerts and payment terminals failed where they depended on the carrier.

findings.title: The residual the class cites is worse than Kyivstar.
findings.text: The core was restored from means that survived, so Kyivstar shows the edge of the worst case, not its limit.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its correction of the facility class's account of the event was taken in by the class.

findings.title: No block reaches emergency calls.
findings.text: Roaming was blocked to protect other networks, and the record does not show whether subscribers could still reach emergency services.

annex.p: This annex is for the operators of mobile and other core networks, the governments and regulators that arrange fallbacks among them, and the alerting authorities, banks, and other dependents that rely on one carrier. It is also for any owner, in any sector, whose operational core is reached through the same identities as its office systems. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Can your core network’s management be reached through the same identities and administrative paths as your enterprise systems, such as an employee’s office account?
One compromised office account opens the core. A.3.1.
Would you see an adversary who had been inside your network for months, and how?
The adversary chooses the day. A.3.1.
Does your core run on a virtualization or cloud platform whose loss would take every function it hosts, and is that platform counted in the independence of your core sites?
One platform’s destruction takes the whole core. A.3.2.
If you had to isolate your core to stop an attack, is that decision planned, with who may take it and when the security services join, and by means that do not depend on the core?
The shutdown is improvised in the middle of the attack. A.3.2.
If your core were lost, could your subscribers roam onto other networks, and could they still reach emergency services, even if roaming were blocked to protect the others?
The fallback fails with the core, and emergency calls may go with it. A.3.3.
Do alerting systems, payment terminals, or other critical dependents rely on your core alone?
Air-raid alerts and payments fail with one carrier. A.3.3.
Would your vendors’ help in restoring the core be available, by channels the adversary had not reached, and is it part of your restoration plan?
Restoration waits on help that was never arranged. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Separate the Core’s Management From the Enterprise

annex.p: No authority has published an action for owners that this instrument reads; the Security Service of Ukraine’s account and the carrier’s are its record. These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1: reach the core’s management only through identities and administrative paths that the enterprise systems do not share, and watch those paths for an adversary who has been inside for months.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Plan the Isolation and the Restoration

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-2, F-3, F-4, and F-7. Count the virtualization and cloud platform under your core as one surface whose loss takes every function it hosts; make the isolation of the core a planned act, with its authority and the security services’ part stated in advance and its means off the core; and make your vendors’ help part of the means of restoration, by channels the adversary cannot reach. Kyivstar restored service in about eight days with about a thousand people and three vendors.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Design the Fallback for the Lost Core

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-5, F-6, and F-9. Design any fallback among networks, national roaming among them, to work when the home core is lost; make sure no block placed on that fallback to protect the other networks reaches emergency calls; and do not let alerting or payments depend on one carrier’s core.

On 12 December 2023, an adversary that had been inside the network of Kyivstar, Ukraine’s largest mobile operator, for months destroyed systems on which its core ran and was managed, and some twenty-four million subscribers lost mobile and internet service. The Security Service of Ukraine attributed the attack to Sandworm, which it identifies as a unit of Russia’s military intelligence service; that attribution is its own. The carrier and the security services shut the whole network down to limit the damage. National roaming, meant to let subscribers use other networks, did not work, because the lost core could not pass subscriber information to them, and air-raid alerts and payment terminals failed in some regions. With about a thousand people and the help of three vendors, service came back in stages over about eight days. On the carrier’s account, the way in was a compromised employee account. The lessons are that the core must not share identities with the office, that its isolation and restoration must be planned before the day, and that a fallback among networks must work when the home core is gone. Any operation whose core can be reached through its office systems has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The GPS Timing Error, January 2016
what: For about thirteen and a half hours on 25 and 26 January 2016, fifteen GPS satellites broadcast incorrect parameters for converting GPS time into the world's standard time, after a fault in the ground software surfaced when the oldest satellite was retired. Navigation was unaffected, but timing receivers that applied the parameters were off by about 13 microseconds, disrupting telecommunications timing, digital broadcasting, and some public-safety radio. Receivers that checked the data's age refused it; the system's operators learned of the error from users.
tier: Not a deliberate act: an upstream error in the ground control of a satellite constellation, below the threshold for the military-action tier.

findings.title: The error's reach was set by the receivers.
findings.text: Receivers that tested the data refused it; those that did not took the error.

findings.title: The broadcast carried its own validity test.
findings.text: The bad data carried an expiry nearly two years past, which receivers could have checked.

findings.title: Holdover carried, for a duration set by the source's detection.
findings.text: Clocks held time on their own while the error lasted, and that time is set by how fast the source's operator finds the fault.

findings.title: The independent source is counted by its root.
findings.text: A backup source is independent only if its time comes from a different root.

findings.title: A refusal set alike across a fleet is a common-cause loss.
findings.text: Receivers set alike dropped out together, and some downstream equipment ran free without alarms.

findings.title: The source's operator learned from its users.
findings.text: Users' equipment found the error within the hour; the operator verified it about eight hours after it began.

findings.title: The alarms outlasted the error.
findings.text: Operators logged thousands of alarms, which took hours to days to clear.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its correction of the facility class's account of the event went to the class.

annex.p: This annex is for the operators of telecommunications networks, power grids, broadcasters, public-safety radio systems, and financial systems that take their time from satellite navigation receivers. It is also for any owner, in any sector, whose equipment depends on time from a source it does not control. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Do your timing receivers test the data they receive for validity, its age and fit interval, and compare it across satellites, before applying it?
An error that carried its own warning is applied anyway. A.3.1.
If your receivers refused bad time, how long could your clocks hold time on their own, and is that longer than the time the source’s operator might take to find and fix an error?
Holdover runs out before the source is corrected. A.3.2.
Do you have a second source of time, and is it traceable to a root other than the same satellite system?
The backup takes its time from the same place. A.3.2.
Are all your receivers set to refuse bad time in the same way, so that they could all drop out together, and would downstream equipment run free without telling you?
Every unit goes offline at once, some silently. A.3.3.
If the source were wrong, would you find out from your own monitoring, and would you tell others, or wait for the source’s operator?
Everyone waits for an operator who learns of the error from its users. A.3.3.
Could a general timing error raise thousands of alarms at once, and are they grouped by cause so that staff can act on them?
The alarms bury the response for days. A.3.3.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Test the Data Before You Use It

annex.p: The technical paper on the event recommends automated checks of the data before it is uploaded to the satellites, an action for the constellation’s operator. For owners of timing equipment, these steps are this instrument’s, from F-1 and F-2: configure receivers to refuse data whose age or fit interval says it is not valid, and to compare the data broadcast by different satellites before applying it.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Hold Time on Your Own Long Enough, From a Different Root

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-3 and F-4. Size your holdover to the time the source’s operator might take to detect and correct an error, about eight hours to verification in 2016, plus the time to requalify your inputs; and count a second source as independent only if its time is traceable to a different root.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Vary the Refusal, Watch the Source, and Group the Alarms

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-5, F-6, and F-7. Do not set every receiver to drop out in the same way at the same moment, and make sure downstream equipment alarms when it runs free; detect a bad source by your own monitoring and pass the warning on; and group alarms for suspect time by cause so that staff can act on them.

For about thirteen and a half hours on 25 and 26 January 2016, fifteen satellites of the Global Positioning System broadcast incorrect parameters for converting GPS time into the world’s standard time, after the oldest satellite was removed from service and a latent fault in the ground software surfaced. Navigation was unaffected, but timing receivers that applied the parameters were off by about 13 microseconds, enough to disqualify GPS in telecommunications networks, disrupt digital broadcasting, and take some public-safety radio receivers offline together. The data carried its own warning, an expiry nearly two years past, and receivers that checked it refused it; many did not. The system’s operators learned of the error from users, about eight hours after it began, and some operators took days to clear the alarms. The lessons are that time from a source you do not control must be tested before it is trusted, that your clocks must hold time on their own longer than the source may take to be fixed, and that every receiver set to fail the same way will fail together. Any operation that depends on satellite time has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Galileo Outage, July 2019
what: From 11 July 2019, the European Union's Galileo satellite navigation system stopped renewing the data its satellites broadcast, after a failure in its ground infrastructure during an upgrade, while its backup was temporarily limited. The satellites kept transmitting aging data, and receivers that checked its age excluded Galileo and, where they could, went on using other systems. Service returned with instability after about six days and fully after about eleven and a half.
tier: Not a deliberate act: a failure of a constellation's ground segment during an upgrade, below the threshold for the military-action tier.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its correction of the facility class's account of the event went to the class.

findings.title: A constellation's loss arrives as aging data under flags that did not at first mark it.
findings.text: The data aged while the satellites still reported themselves healthy, and only receivers that checked the age refused it.

findings.title: The second constellation was independent against this failure.
findings.text: Receivers that combined Galileo with other systems kept working.

findings.title: Redundancy out for maintenance is not redundancy.
findings.text: The failure came while the backup was limited for an upgrade.

findings.title: The receiver design basis should carry what decided the event.
findings.text: Receivers should use several constellations and refuse data past its validity.

findings.title: About six days is a point on the record.
findings.text: The outage gives a measured duration for the loss of a constellation.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its substance is carried by DBA-COMM-RE-10, The GPS Timing Error.

findings.title: A foreign constellation is outside every series.
findings.text: A system run by another government lies outside anything this design basis can protect.

annex.p: This annex is for the operators of telecommunications networks, power grids, broadcasters, and other systems that use satellite navigation for position or time, and for the makers and integrators of their receivers. It is also for any owner, in any sector, who relies on a service operated by another government. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
If one satellite navigation system stopped renewing its data, would your receivers notice that the data was aging and refuse it, even while the satellites still reported themselves healthy?
Receivers use stale data and give wrong answers. A.3.1.
Are receivers that can use several constellations actually configured to use them, so that the loss of one does not stop them?
A receiver restricted to one system has no answer when it fails. A.3.1.

Is your second source of position or time independent of the failure you are planning for, such as another constellation for a constellation failure, and not only another signal a jammer would also take?
The second source fails with the first. A.3.1.
When a source, receiver, or holdover clock is out for maintenance or upgrade, do you count it as absent?
The redundancy you counted is not there when it is needed. A.3.2.
Could you ride through a week or more without one constellation, and would you detect its loss yourselves rather than wait for the operator’s notice?
You learn of the outage a day after it starts. A.3.2.
Do you rely on a constellation operated by another government, and is that reliance counted as a dependency you cannot protect?
A failure you cannot see into, investigated in a report you cannot read. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Refuse Aged Data, and Use More Than One Constellation

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-2, F-3, and F-5. Configure every receiver of consequence to refuse navigation data beyond its validity period, and to exclude a constellation whose data has aged, whatever its health flags say; configure receivers that can use several constellations to use them; and count another constellation as a second source against a constellation failure, but not against a jammer that covers both.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Count Maintenance as Absence, and Plan for a Week

annex.p: The Inquiry Board set up by the European Commission recommended, on the Commission’s account, among other things, prompt and structured communication with users. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-4, F-6, and F-8: count anything out of service for maintenance or upgrade as absent from your redundancy; plan to ride through about six days without a constellation, and about eleven and a half of degraded service; detect the loss by your own monitoring; and count reliance on a constellation operated by another government as a dependency no series of the design basis protects.

From the early hours of 11 July 2019, the European Union’s satellite navigation system, Galileo, stopped renewing the orbit and clock data its satellites broadcast, after a failure in its ground infrastructure during an upgrade, at a time when the backup was temporarily limited. The satellites kept transmitting, but their data aged, and for days their health flags did not mark it as bad. Receivers that checked the data’s age excluded Galileo, and those that could use GPS or other systems went on working; a receiver restricted to Galileo had no fix, and a research receiver that skipped the age check was off by 500 meters or more. Service returned with instability after about six days, and fully after about eleven and a half. The operator’s first notice came about fourteen hours after the outage began, and the full inquiry report has not been published. No source suggests the failure was deliberate. The lessons are that a receiver must refuse data that has aged, that a second constellation protects against the failure of one, and that redundancy out for maintenance is not redundancy. Any operation that depends on satellite navigation has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: Satellite-Navigation Interference in the Baltic Region, from 2023
date: from 2023, continuing on the record of 30 September 2026
date_full: from 2023, continuing on the record of 30 September 2026
what: Since 2023, satellite navigation signals over the Baltic Sea and surrounding countries have been jammed and spoofed, taking signals away from aircraft, ships, and drones and giving some of them false positions and false time. On the six states' data, more than 120,000 flights were affected in four months of 2025, and an airline suspended a route for a month because its approach needed satellite navigation. Ground timing held where networks kept time without satellites, as Finland's regulator requires.
tier: Read as a gray-zone effect of military electronic warfare: the affected governments and international bodies place the transmitters in Russian territory, deliberately on their accounts, and Russia has denied wrongdoing, as reported. It is persistent and imprecise, and not shown to be aimed at the networks this sector protects. The record is open.

findings.title: Interference is an initiating event whatever its aim.
findings.text: The design basis must operate through jamming and spoofing whoever causes it and why.

findings.title: The denial is measured in years.
findings.text: The interference has gone on for more than three years and continues.

findings.title: Exposure is set by height and horizon, and measured at the antenna.
findings.text: Aircraft and ships felt it most; ground networks largely did not.

findings.title: A regulator in the region already requires two weeks without satellites.
findings.text: Finland requires its mobile networks to keep time for two weeks without satellite synchronization, and they were not affected.

findings.title: Spoofed time reached aircraft, and the class does not say when time is accepted again.
findings.text: False time reached aircraft systems, and the design basis should say when satellite time may be trusted again.

findings.title: Authentication is a check, not a second source.
findings.text: Signal authentication helps against spoofing but does nothing against jamming.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its findings on effects in other sectors are routed to those sectors' series.

findings.title: A regulator's published picture of interference is the warning channel.
findings.text: Regulators' published reports were the region's warning, and should reach timing users too.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its correction of the facility class's account of the event went to the class.

annex.p: This annex is for the operators of telecommunications networks, power grids, and other systems that take time or position from satellite navigation, and for airports, airlines, ports, and shipping in regions where satellite signals are jammed or spoofed. It is also for any owner, in any sector, near a border where electronic warfare is a standing condition. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Does your design treat jamming and spoofing of satellite navigation as a standing condition you must operate through, whoever causes it and whatever its aim?
You plan for an attack that may never be aimed at you, and miss the condition you are already in. A.3.1.
How long could your timing hold without satellite signals, and is that set against a denial lasting years, not hours?
Holdover is sized for an outage, not for a region. A.3.1.
Do you know which of your receivers can see a transmitter across the border, given their height and the horizon, and do you measure interference at the antenna?
Exposure is assumed, not measured. A.3.2.
If your receivers were given false time or position, would they detect it, and do you know when it is safe to accept satellite time again after interference?
False time is believed, or good time is refused too long. A.3.2.
Do you have terrestrial sources of time and position that do not depend on satellites, and are they kept in service?
The fallback has been retired. A.3.1.
Do you use navigation-message authentication where it is available, knowing that it detects spoofing but does nothing against jamming?
Authentication is counted as a second source. A.3.2.
Do you receive the regulators’ published warnings of interference, and would you pass a warning of suspect time to others?
You learn of the interference from your own failures. A.3.3.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Plan to Operate Through Years of Denial

annex.p: Finland’s regulator, Traficom, requires in regulation 54 C/2021 M that the time and phase synchronization of mobile networks using time-division duplexing work for at least two weeks without satellite synchronization, and the region’s answer in aviation and at sea has been terrestrial: keeping instrument landing systems, distance-measuring equipment, and VOR beacons, a minimum operational air-navigation network, and the terrestrial ranging service R-Mode Baltic. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-1, F-2, and F-4: treat interference as a standing condition to design through, whatever its aim; size holdover and terrestrial sources against a denial measured in years; and keep terrestrial sources in service.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Measure Exposure at the Antenna, and Check the Signal

annex.p: The European Union Aviation Safety Agency has told crews to compare satellite time with other sources, and with the International Air Transport Association has asked for faster recovery of receivers after interference; Galileo’s navigation-message authentication was declared operational as an initial service on 24 July 2025. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-3, F-5, and F-6: measure interference at your antennas, knowing that height and the horizon set exposure; state when satellite time is accepted again after interference; and use authentication as a check against spoofing, not as a second source against jamming.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Read the Regulators’ Warnings, and Pass Yours On

annex.p: This step is this instrument’s, from F-8. Treat the regulators’ published picture of interference as a warning channel, and pass warnings of suspect time on to the networks, grid operators, and financial systems that share your exposure.

Since 2023, satellite navigation signals over the Baltic Sea and the countries around it have been jammed and spoofed, taking signals away from aircraft, ships, and drones and giving some of them false positions and false time. The affected governments and international bodies place the transmitters in Russian territory, deliberately on their accounts; the Kremlin has denied wrongdoing, as reported, and its purpose is contested. On the six states’ data, more than 120,000 flights were affected in four months of 2025, and an airline suspended flights to one Estonian airport for a month because its approach needed satellite navigation. Ground timing held: Finland’s mobile networks, which its regulator requires to keep time for two weeks without satellites, were not affected. On the record of September 2026 the interference was continuing, more than three years on. The lessons are that interference is a condition to design through whoever causes it, that it can last years, and that the defense is time and position that do not depend on satellites, kept in service and measured. Any operation near a region of electronic warfare has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The CenturyLink Outage, December 2018
what: On 27 December 2018, a switching module in CenturyLink's fiber transport network generated four malformed management packets that passed a filter screening only by size and were rebroadcast through a vendor management channel the carrier did not use, until the network's nodes could no longer carry traffic. Service was disrupted for almost thirty-seven hours, and about seventeen million customers in twenty-nine states lacked reliable access to 911. Engineers had to travel to nodes they could not reach remotely.
tier: Not a deliberate act: the packets arose spontaneously in the equipment, and the carrier and the Federal Communications Commission found no external cause. It is below the threshold for the military-action tier.

findings.title: An unused function in the equipment counts in reach.
findings.text: A vendor channel the carrier never used carried the failure across the network.

findings.title: Isolation is counted in processing as well as path.
findings.text: Management traffic consumed the processing that forwarding depended on.

findings.title: A storm that sustains itself is stopped at every node.
findings.text: The storm went on for hours after its source was removed.

findings.title: A center that cannot see its network has lost it.
findings.text: The carrier could not reach its nodes and restored them by sending people.

findings.title: Other providers' 911 counts in reach.
findings.text: Much of the 911 loss was in other providers' services riding the network, including one whose four diverse links all did.

findings.title: A notification not recorded cannot be shown.
findings.text: The carrier said it notified 911 centers; a state commission found it notified none of fifteen.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its correction of the facility class's account of the event went to the class.

annex.p: This annex is for the operators of fiber transport networks and other networks built from vendors’ equipment, for the providers whose services ride on them, and for the 911 centers and processors that depend on them. It is also for any owner, in any sector, whose equipment carries functions it does not use. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Does your equipment carry vendor functions, such as management channels, that are enabled by default but that you have neither configured nor used?
A function no one knew was on carries the failure across the network. A.3.1.
Do your filters allow only the traffic you expect, or do they block only some traffic by a simple rule such as size?
Malformed traffic passes the filter. A.3.1.
Could management traffic consume the processing on which your network’s forwarding depends, and does your monitoring alarm on processor and memory load?
The nodes stop carrying traffic and you do not see why. A.3.2.
If a storm of traffic sustained itself after its source was removed, could you stop it at every node by a path the storm does not take?
The storm outlives its cause by hours. A.3.2.
If you could not reach your nodes remotely, could you restore the network by people at the nodes, and how long would that take?
Restoration waits on engineers traveling to every site. A.3.3.
Do your 911 and other critical customers know whether their diverse paths all ride on your network, and would you notify them, on the record, when it fails?
Four diverse links fail together, and no one is told. A.3.3.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Turn Off What You Do Not Use, and Filter for What You Expect

annex.p: The Federal Communications Commission’s report on the outage drew lessons that features not in use should be turned off and that catch-all filters should allow only expected traffic; the vendor disabled the channel on new equipment and updated its manual to recommend disabling it where unused. This step adds the instrument’s own, from F-1: count in the reach of your network every function by which one element can reach others without a governed act, including vendor functions you do not use.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Protect Forwarding From Management, and Be Able to Stop a Storm

annex.p: The Commission’s report also drew the lesson that monitoring should include processor and memory alarms that are regularly audited. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-2 and F-3: isolate management from forwarding in processing as well as in path; and keep a means to stop a self-sustaining storm at every element by a path the storm does not take.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Plan to Restore Blind, and Notify on the Record

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-4, F-5, and F-6. Plan to restore the network by people at the nodes when the operations center cannot see it; count other providers’ 911 traffic on your network in its reach, and tell those providers whether their diverse paths share your network; and notify 911 centers of an outage on detection, and record that you did.

Early on 27 December 2018, a switching module in one node of CenturyLink’s fiber transport network in Denver generated four malformed management packets, for a reason neither the carrier nor its vendor could find. They passed a filter that screened only by size, entered a vendor management channel that was enabled by default and that the carrier did not use, and were rebroadcast from node to node until the nodes could no longer carry traffic. Service was disrupted for almost thirty-seven hours for as many as twenty-two million customers in thirty-nine states, about seventeen million of them in twenty-nine states without reliable 911, and at least 886 calls to 911 were not delivered. The overloaded nodes could not be reached remotely, so engineers were sent to them, and the storm went on for hours after its source was removed. The Federal Communications Commission found no external cause. The lessons are that functions you do not use can carry a failure across the whole network, that filters must allow only what is expected, and that you must be able to restore a network you cannot see. Any operation built from equipment with functions it does not use has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Salt Typhoon Intrusion, Disclosed 2024
date: disclosed from September 2024; activity since at least 2019 on the United States government's account
date_full: disclosed from September 2024; activity since at least 2019 on the United States government's account
what: In September 2024 it became public that actors had compromised at least nine United States telecommunications carriers, taking call records, the communications of a limited number of people in government and politics, and information about court-ordered law-enforcement requests. They entered through publicly known flaws in routers and other network devices, changed those devices to stay, and were inside for one to two years or more on officials' accounts. Federal agencies advised senior officials to use end-to-end encrypted communications.
tier: State espionage, not military action: the United States government attributes the intrusion to actors sponsored by the government of the People's Republic of China, and that attribution is its own. The purpose was espionage, and no service was taken away. The record is open.

findings.title: The network's own devices are a door to the operations layer.
findings.text: The actors came in through known flaws in routers and edge devices.

findings.title: Administering intercept systems is an operations function.
findings.text: The systems built to answer lawful-intercept requests were reached and should be governed as operations.

findings.title: Eviction is shown on evidence the adversary could not reach.
findings.text: Carriers said the actors were gone, but the logs had been erased and the assessments were not provided when asked for.

findings.title: The commons is protected against being read.
findings.text: Officials were told to assume their mobile communications could be read and to use end-to-end encryption.

findings.title: For a compromise, hunting is prepared in advance.
findings.text: The response was improvised, and its federal review ended before it reported.

findings.title: The presence is measured, not the purpose.
findings.text: Access held for espionage is access available for disruption.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its correction of the facility class's account of the event went to the class.

annex.p: This annex is for telecommunications carriers and the operators of other networks whose routers and edge devices are reachable from outside, for the systems they keep to answer lawful-intercept requests, and for officials and others whose communications may be read. It is also for any owner, in any sector, whose network devices could hold an adversary for years. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known

Before the questions below: have you listed every router, firewall, and edge device that talks to the outside world, with the network it does so through (your own, a cellular carrier’s, or a vendor’s or integrator’s remote-support path) and the address it actually uses?
You cannot look at an exposure you have not listed, and a search of your own addresses can come back clean while equipment at someone else’s is open. A.3.4.
Are your routers, firewalls, and other edge devices patched against publicly known flaws, some of them years old, and are their management interfaces reachable only from where they must be?
An adversary walks in through a flaw you knew about. A.3.1.
Would you detect changes made to your devices’ configuration to keep an intruder in, and do you watch the connections from other providers’ networks?
The adversary stays by changing your own equipment. A.3.1.
Could an adversary stay inside for a year or more, erase your logs, and leave no evidence you could find?
You learn of the presence from others, years later. A.3.2.
Are the systems you use to answer court-ordered intercept requests protected and administered as an operations function, with their own controls?
The systems built for lawful access become the adversary’s. A.3.1.
If you said an intruder was gone, could you show it on evidence the intruder could not have reached or altered?
Eviction is claimed and cannot be shown. A.3.2.
Do the people whose communications matter most use end-to-end encryption, so that a compromised network cannot read them?
Whoever holds the network holds their conversations. A.3.3.
Is hunting for an intruder across many carriers prepared in advance, with the parties, tools, and evidence agreed before it is needed?
The response is improvised, and its review may never finish. A.3.3.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Close the Known Doors, and Protect the Intercept Systems

annex.p: On 3 December 2024 the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, the National Security Agency, and the Federal Bureau of Investigation, with the cyber agencies of Australia, Canada, and New Zealand, issued hardening guidance to the defenders of communications infrastructure, and a joint advisory lists publicly known flaws in network devices that the actors used. On 15 January 2025 the Federal Communications Commission ruled that section 105 of the Communications Assistance for Law Enforcement Act requires carriers to secure their networks against unlawful access and interception; that binding interpretation was later withdrawn in favor of voluntary commitments. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-1 and F-2: treat the management interfaces of your own routers and edge devices as a door into your operations, and administer the systems that answer lawful-intercept requests as an operations function with controls of their own.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Measure the Presence, and Show the Eviction

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-3 and F-6. Design your detection for an adversary who stays for years and erases logs, and measure the presence, not its purpose, since access held for espionage is access available for disruption; and show that an intruder is gone on evidence the intruder could not have reached.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Protect What Is Said, and Prepare the Hunt

annex.p: On 18 December 2024 the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency told highly targeted individuals in senior government and political positions to assume their mobile communications were at risk of interception or manipulation and to use only end-to-end encrypted communications. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-4 and F-5: protect the communications that matter against being read on a compromised network; and prepare in advance, with other carriers and the authorities, how a compromise across many networks will be hunted.

annex.h3: A.3.4 List What Talks to the Outside, Then Look as an Attacker Would

annex.p: List first, then look. The inventory comes first because exposed equipment often sits outside your own address space: the doors on this record were the management interfaces of routers and edge devices, which are easily left off the inventory of the network they run. Then look at each address on the list as an attacker would, by any of three routes, each its provider’s. Shodan and Censys each offer a search of the devices they have found answering on the internet, and a search limited to your own address blocks and the addresses on your list shows you what it would show anyone. In the United States, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency offers Cyber Hygiene Vulnerability Scanning, which scans the internet-facing assets an organization names and reports weekly, at no cost to governments and critical infrastructure organizations (cisa.gov, Cyber Hygiene Services). Your integrator and vendors can tell you what they can reach remotely, if you ask them. Whatever the look finds that is not on your list goes on it, and whatever need not talk to the outside should stop. The inventory and the look are a standing item in every annex whose event turned on equipment reachable from the internet, on the author’s direction of 15 November 2026; here they rest on element I-1 and F-1.

In September 2024 it became public that actors the United States government says were sponsored by the government of the People’s Republic of China had compromised at least nine United States telecommunications carriers, an intrusion known as Salt Typhoon. On the government’s account they took call records, the communications of a limited number of people in government and politics, and copies of information about court-ordered law-enforcement requests. They entered through publicly known flaws in routers and other network devices, one disclosed in 2018, changed the devices to stay, erased logs, and were inside for one to two years or more on officials’ accounts. The purpose was espionage, and no service was taken away. Federal agencies told senior officials to assume their mobile communications could be read and to use end-to-end encryption. Three carriers said the actors were gone, but in 2026 their security assessments had not been provided to the congressional member who asked for them. The lessons are that a network’s own devices are a door into its operations, that presence held for spying is presence available for disruption, and that an eviction must be shown, not claimed. Any operation whose network devices face the outside has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The NotPetya Attack on Maersk's Terminals, June 2017
what: On 27 June 2017, destructive malware reached the shipping company A.P. Moller-Maersk through an update to a Ukrainian tax program used in one of its offices, spread across the company's single global network, and destroyed the systems it reached. The company shut its systems down to contain it, and container terminals run by its terminal company on five continents closed or slowed, some for days, working by hand where they could while neighbors and partners took cargo. All affected terminals were reported open by 5 July, after the company rebuilt its computing in about ten days.
tier: An adversarial cyber attack, attributed to the Russian military by the United Kingdom and the United States, each stating that attribution as its own, and described by them as aimed at Ukraine. The terminals were not shown to be the target: they were reached because the company's network connected them to an office in Ukraine. This instrument makes no finding of attribution.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its correction of the facility class's account of the event went to the class as an erratum.

findings.title: The shared platform was the operator's own network.
findings.text: Every terminal shared one corporate network and identity domain, entered through software no terminal ran, and the terminals' own systems should be separated from it.

findings.title: The shutdown is a decision on every node at once.
findings.text: Isolating a shared network to contain an attack stops every site that depends on it, so its holders and its scope should be planned in advance.

findings.title: The manual fallback rate, observed, is many rates.
findings.text: Terminals ranged from no working at all to reduced productivity, so the rate by hand should be stated for each function, not once per site.

findings.title: Diversion capacity needs its own information.
findings.text: Neighbors could take cargo only where the information to handle it reached them without the lost network.

findings.title: Restoration rested on chance.
findings.text: The rebuild depended, on one published account, on a single copy of the company's network directory kept offline by a power cut, and restoration from protected copies should be required and exercised.

findings.title: The node lost what it knew.
findings.text: Records were destroyed rather than altered, and those kept for working by hand should be current to a stated interval.

findings.title: A node reached as the collateral of an attack aimed elsewhere.
findings.text: On the attributing governments' accounts the terminals were collateral of an attack on another country, a form the design basis should name.

findings.title: The regulatory record has changed since the event.
findings.text: The Coast Guard's 2025 rule answers this event's path in controls but sets no fallback rate, restoration time, or limit on stranded flow.

annex.p: This annex is for the operators of container terminals, ports, airports, rail yards, and other transportation nodes whose terminal operating systems, gates, and equipment controls run on a network the operator shares with the rest of its business. It is also for any owner, in any sector, whose operating sites share one corporate network and one set of credentials with offices elsewhere. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known

Does software from suppliers that have nothing to do with your operations, such as accounting, tax, or payroll programs, run anywhere on the network your operating systems use, and do its updates arrive without your checking them?
A supplier you never think of has a path to your terminals. A.3.1.

If one stolen password or one unpatched file-sharing service were used against an office in another country, could the attack reach your terminal operating system, your gates, and your equipment controls? Do they sit in an identity domain of their own?
Every site carries the exposure of the weakest office. A.3.1.
If you had to shut down your corporate network to stop a spreading attack, which of your sites would stop with it? Who decides, and who decides if that person cannot be reached?
The containment decision stops every site at once, made on the day by whoever is there. A.3.2.
At each site, what rate can each function, gate, berth, yard, rail, imports, and exports, sustain by hand, and for how long?
The site’s week after a loss is unknown until it happens. A.3.3.

If your systems were lost, could neighboring terminals and your carriers receive what they need to take your cargo, what each container is, where it goes, and who may release it, by a means that does not use your network?
Diversion capacity exists on paper only. A.3.3.
Are the records you would work from by hand current to within hours, so that you could say where every container is at the hour of the loss?
Cargo is lost track of, and trucks arrive for containers no one can find. A.3.3.
Could you rebuild your identity domain and operating systems from copies that nothing on your network could reach or alter, and how long would it take? When was that last tested end to end?
Recovery rests on luck, as it did here. A.3.4.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Separate the Operating Systems From the Business Network

annex.p: The Coast Guard’s rule on cybersecurity in the marine transportation system, in force since 16 July 2025, requires the owners and operators it covers to apply cybersecurity controls and to have cybersecurity plans in place by 16 July 2027 (33 CFR 101.650); for those owners, those are the published actions. This step is this instrument’s, from F-2: keep the terminal operating system, the gates, and the equipment controls on a network and an identity domain of their own, so that the loss of the business network does not take them, show that separation as built, and know which suppliers’ software shares the network they run on.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Decide the Shutdown Before You Need It

annex.p: This step is this instrument’s, from F-3. Isolating a shared network to stop an attack may be the right decision, and it stops every site that depends on that network at once. Name in advance who holds that decision and to whom it passes when that person cannot be reached, plan the isolation so that it takes out the fewest sites the containment allows, and count the time it holds the sites down in their recovery time.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Work by Hand, and Hand Off Without the Network

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-4, F-5, and F-7. State for each site and each function the rate it can sustain by hand and for how long, and measure it in exercises. Keep the records you would work from current to a stated interval. Agree in advance with your carriers and neighboring terminals how load lists, bay plans, and release information would reach them without your network, as the carriers in this event had to find on the day.

annex.h3: A.3.4 Keep a Copy No Attacker Can Reach

annex.p: The Coast Guard’s rule requires the owners and operators it covers to keep protected and frequently tested backups (33 CFR 101.650(g)). This step is this instrument’s, from F-6: make the systems your sites depend on, the identity domain among them, restorable from copies that no system an attacker could reach can alter or destroy, within a stated restoration time that is exercised end to end.

On 27 June 2017, destructive malware, which the governments of the United Kingdom and the United States attributed to the Russian military and described as aimed at Ukraine, reached the shipping company A.P. Moller-Maersk through an update to a Ukrainian tax program used in one of its offices. It spread across the company’s single global network, and the company shut its systems down to contain it. Container terminals run by its terminal company on five continents closed or slowed, some for days, and worked by hand where they could; neighbors and partners took cargo where they could get the information to handle it. The company rebuilt thousands of servers and computers in about ten days, and that rebuild, on one published account, rested on a single copy of its network directory that a power cut had happened to keep offline. The terminals were not the target. They stopped because they shared a network and a set of passwords with an office in another country. Any operation whose sites share one network and one set of credentials with the rest of the business has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Ransomware Attack on the Port of Nagoya, July 2023
what: On 4 July 2023, a ransomware attack encrypted every server of the one terminal operating system that runs all five container terminals and the central gate at the Port of Nagoya, Japan's first port by total cargo. The gate was shut for about three days; on the government committee's account the ships were worked by hand, while the operator's report says work stopped at every terminal. The system was restored from backups that themselves held the malware, and after the restored records were checked against the yard, the terminals restarted on 6 July.
tier: Not a state act on the record: a criminal ransomware attack, which press and government accounts attribute to a criminal group, each as its own statement. It took the one platform the port's terminals shared, below the threshold for the military-action tier.

findings.title: No fallback at the gate, two accounts at the ship.
findings.text: The gate had no way to work by hand, so the fallback should be stated for each interface through which flow passes.

findings.title: The fallback rested on people who remembered the work.
findings.text: Working by hand was possible only because staff who knew the work before the system were still there.

findings.title: One platform for a port, owned by none of its users.
findings.text: Where several terminals share one system, who owns it and who holds its backups, access, and fallback should be settled by contract.

findings.title: Backups that held the compromise.
findings.text: The backups were too short to reach back before the infection and covered only part of the system, so they carried the attack back in.

findings.title: The channel the postulated event names and the requirement does not.
findings.text: The attackers likely entered through a maintenance connection reachable from anywhere with a password, and such channels should be restricted, protected, logged, and closed when not in use.

findings.title: Restore first, a decision the class does not place.
findings.text: Who decides between restoring quickly and preserving evidence, and on whose advice, should be named in advance.

findings.title: The records reconciled with the yard before work resumed.
findings.text: Checking restored records against the physical yard worked, and its method and duration belong in recovery planning.

findings.title: Stranded flow, counted at the ship and the gate, and the dependent facility.
findings.text: Stranded flow should be measured at each interface so that dependents such as a manufacturer's packing lines can plan on real numbers.

findings.title: The gap the class fills, partly closed elsewhere for the platform.
findings.text: Japan's later measures govern the security of terminal systems but set no fallback rate or limit on stranded flow.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its correction of the facility class's account of the event went to the class as an erratum.

annex.p: This annex is for the operators of ports, container terminals, and other transportation nodes where several terminals or several companies work on one shared operating system, and for anyone who maintains such a system from outside. It is also for any owner, in any sector, whose sites share one system that a contractor maintains remotely. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known

Before the questions below: have you listed every system and maintenance channel serving your terminals that talks to the outside world, with the network it does so through (your own, a cellular carrier’s, or a vendor’s or integrator’s remote-support path) and the address it actually uses?
You cannot look at an exposure you have not listed, and a search of your own addresses can come back clean while equipment at someone else’s is open. A.3.5.
Do several of your terminals, or several companies at your site, run on one operating system? Who owns it, and who is responsible, by contract, for its backups, its remote access, and its fallback?
No one holds the requirements of the system everyone depends on. A.3.1.

Can the channel used to maintain your systems be reached from any internet address with a username and password? Is it patched, protected by more than one factor, logged somewhere other than the system it reaches, and closed when not in use?
One password opens every terminal. A.3.2.
How far back do your backups reach, do they cover every environment needed to rebuild the system, are they kept apart from it, and do you show them clean before restoring from them?
The backup carries the attack back in. A.3.3.
If your system stopped, what could each interface, the ship and the gate at least, do by hand, and for how long?
One interface keeps working and the other strands its flow for the whole of the loss. A.3.4.
Who on your staff can do the work by hand, and how many of them will still be here in five years?
The fallback retires with the people who remember the work. A.3.4.
Who decides between restoring the system quickly and preserving it for investigation, and on whose advice? Is a cybersecurity specialist named?
The choice is made in the moment, and both the evidence and a clean restart may be lost. A.3.4.
Before restarting, how would you check restored records against what is physically in your yard, and how long would that take?
Work resumes on records no one has confirmed. A.3.4.
Do you know which customers depend on you as their only path, and would you know how much flow was stranded at each interface?
Dependents learn of it when their own lines stop. A.3.4.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Know Who Owns the Shared System

annex.p: This step is this instrument’s, from F-3. Where several terminals or companies share one system, name its owner and maintainer, and record by contract who holds its backups, its external access, its fallback procedures, and their exercise.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Close the Maintenance Door

annex.p: The committee that Japan’s Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism set up after the event set emergency measures for every terminal operating system, among them authentication by more than one factor for external access. This step adds the instrument’s own, from F-5: restrict any remote-access channel to known sources, patch it on a stated interval, log it outside the system it reaches, and open it only while it is in use.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Keep Backups That Reach Back Before the Attack

annex.p: The committee’s emergency measures include backups in several generations, kept apart from the system. This step adds the instrument’s own, from F-4: keep backups that reach back beyond the longest time an intrusion might go undetected, that cover every environment needed to rebuild the system, and that are shown clean before anything is restored from them.

annex.h3: A.3.4 Plan for the System’s Failure, Not Only for Disaster

annex.p: The committee’s emergency measures include a plan for system failure that covers manual working; in this event the operator had a plan for disasters and none for a system failure. These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1, F-2, F-6, F-7, and F-8: state the rate each interface can sustain by hand and for how long, train staff in it so that it does not rest on those who worked before the system, name in advance who decides between restoration and preservation and on whose advice, time the check of restored records against the yard, and record the flow stranded at each interface after any loss.

annex.h3: A.3.5 List What Talks to the Outside, Then Look as an Attacker Would

annex.p: List first, then look. The inventory comes first because exposed equipment often sits outside your own address space: the door on this record was the channel used to maintain the system, reachable from any internet address, and a maintenance contractor’s equipment may sit at the contractor’s address rather than the operator’s. Then look at each address on the list as an attacker would, by any of three routes, each its provider’s. Shodan and Censys each offer a search of the devices they have found answering on the internet, and a search limited to your own address blocks and the addresses on your list shows you what it would show anyone. In the United States, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency offers Cyber Hygiene Vulnerability Scanning, which scans the internet-facing assets an organization names and reports weekly, at no cost to governments and critical infrastructure organizations (cisa.gov, Cyber Hygiene Services). Your integrator and vendors can tell you what they can reach remotely, if you ask them. Whatever the look finds that is not on your list goes on it, and whatever need not talk to the outside should stop. The inventory and the look are a standing item in every annex whose event turned on equipment reachable from the internet, on the author’s direction of 15 November 2026; here they rest on element I-2 and F-5.

On 4 July 2023, a ransomware attack stopped the one computer system that runs all five container terminals and the central gate at the Port of Nagoya, the busiest port in Japan by total cargo. On the reading of the government’s committee, the attackers came in through a maintenance connection that anyone on the internet with the right username and password could reach. Every server was encrypted, and the backups held only three days of data and carried the malware back in when the system was restored. The gate was shut for about three days. On the committee’s account the ships were still worked by hand, because people were on staff who had done the work before the system existed; the operator’s own report says work stopped at every terminal. About 20,000 containers were affected, and a major manufacturer stopped export packing lines. No government has attributed the attack to a state; press and government accounts name a criminal ransomware group. The lesson does not depend on who did it. One system served everyone, one door reached it, and the backup could not be trusted. Any operation where several sites or companies share one system maintained from outside has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Power Outage at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, December 2017
what: On the afternoon of 17 December 2017, the electric utility's switchgear failed and caught fire in a tunnel beneath the airport's concourses, where the cables of the airport's two supplies and the switch between them ran together. The terminals lost power shortly after one o'clock, flights were stopped, and the people inside were held for about five hours without public address or escalators before being evacuated. Power returned to all concourses around midnight, and more than a thousand flights were cancelled.
tier: Not a deliberate act: the city's joint investigation found no evidence of foul play. It is an accidental failure of utility equipment inside the airport's fence, below the threshold for the military-action tier.

findings.title: Separate at the source, shared on the way.
findings.text: The two supplies came from separate substations but met in one place, so independence must be shown along the whole route to the load.

findings.title: The switchover time when the transfer is lost.
findings.text: With the switch itself destroyed there was no switchover, only repair, and the design basis should state that time too.
