findings.title: The node's power, owned by the utility inside the fence.
findings.text: The airport did not hold the design of the utility equipment inside its own fence, and that knowledge should be exchanged both ways, in writing.

findings.title: Public address and vertical circulation at the point of use.
findings.text: Backup power lit the halls but did not carry the public address or the means of moving people who cannot use stairs.

findings.title: Held before cleared, by several holders.
findings.text: The people inside were held for hours before being cleared, so the design basis should state how long a full node may hold its occupants and who decides to clear it.

findings.title: The channel to the people the node holds.
findings.text: The airport judged its means of reaching passengers insufficient, and a channel that shares nothing with normal power and networks should be required.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its finding that recovery runs to the return of traffic, not of power, is carried by DBA-TRAN-RE-4, The Closure of Heathrow Airport.

findings.title: The adversary need choose only the place where supplies meet.
findings.text: The design basis should treat the point where supplies converge, not only each supply, as the place to protect.

findings.title: The gap the class fills, confirmed in the United States.
findings.text: No federal requirement obliges backup power for the passenger areas of an airport.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its correction of the facility class's account of the event went to the class as an erratum.

annex.p: This annex is for the operators of airports, stations, terminals, and other transportation nodes that hold many people and take their power from a utility, above all where the utility owns or designs power equipment inside the node’s fence. It is also for any owner, in any sector, of a large building whose occupants depend on its power to be directed or moved. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known

Follow each of your power supplies from its substation to the loads that matter. Is there any place, a tunnel, room, vault, or duct, where two supplies, or a supply and the switch between them, run together?
One fire can take both supplies and the means of switching between them. A.3.1.
Is any of the power equipment inside your fence owned or designed by someone else? Do you hold, in writing, its routes, its switching, and how it is maintained?
You cannot show the independence of what you cannot see. A.3.1.
If both supplies and the transfer were lost, how long would it take to restore power by repair, counting the time before anyone could safely reach the damaged equipment?
The design has no number for its worst day. A.3.2.
What do your backup generators carry? The public address, the elevators, and the means of moving people who cannot use stairs, as well as the emergency lighting?
People are held in the dark without a voice to direct them. A.3.3.
How long can you safely hold a full building in place with its normal systems degraded before you must clear it, and who decides to hold or to clear when several organizations act at your site?
The hold runs on until someone decides, and no one is sure who that is. A.3.3.
How would you reach the people inside if your public address, your power, and your networks were all lost?
Occupants learn what is happening from rumor and social media. A.3.4.
Does your recovery plan run to the return of normal traffic, not only the return of power?
The plan ends a day before the disruption does. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Trace Every Supply to the Load

annex.p: This step is this instrument’s, from F-1 and F-3. Walk each supply’s whole route from its source to the critical loads, including any length another party owns inside your fence, and show separately each place where two routes, or a route and the transfer between them, come together. Exchange with the utility, in writing, the routes and switching it runs inside your fence and the critical loads you need it to know.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Plan for the Day Both Supplies Are Lost

annex.p: This step is this instrument’s, from F-2. State how long the site would be without power if a supply were lost together with its transfer equipment, as a time to restore by repair, counting the hours before the damaged equipment can be reached through fire, smoke, and fumes; at Atlanta those were nearly four, and power took about six hours to the first concourse and about eleven to the rest.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Power the Voice and the Way Out

annex.p: No authority has published an action for owners from this event; the Government Accountability Office found in 2023 that the Federal Aviation Administration does not require backup power for the areas of an airport serving travelers, and the remedy at Atlanta, permanent backup generation for every terminal and concourse, came by settlement. These steps are this instrument’s, from F-4 and F-5: carry the public address and the means of moving people who cannot use stairs on point-of-use supplies, as well as the emergency lighting; state how long the building can hold its occupants in place; and name in advance who decides to hold or to clear it.

annex.h3: A.3.4 Reach the People You Hold

annex.p: This step is this instrument’s, from F-6. Keep a means of reaching the people inside that shares nothing with the building’s normal power and networks, and bring the utility and any company that operates your terminals into the site’s common plan.

On the afternoon of 17 December 2017, electrical equipment owned by the local utility failed and caught fire in a tunnel beneath the concourses of Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport. The airport’s two supplies came from separate substations, but their cables and the switch between them ran together at that point in the tunnel, and the fire took them all. The terminals went dark shortly after one o’clock. Emergency lights came on, but the public address, the escalators, and security screening did not; the people inside were held for about five hours and then evacuated, and more than a thousand flights were cancelled. Utility crews could not reach the equipment for nearly four hours because of the fire and fumes, and power did not return to all the concourses until about midnight. Investigators found no evidence of foul play. The lesson does not depend on the cause. Two supplies from separate sources are only two if they stay separate all the way to the load, including the parts someone else owns, and backup power that lights the halls but cannot speak to the people in them leaves them waiting in the dark. Any building that holds many people and depends on its power to direct them has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Closure of Heathrow Airport, March 2025
what: Just before midnight on 20 March 2025, a transformer failed and caught fire at the North Hyde substation in west London, and the fire took the substation's other supplies with it, cutting off one of the three points from which Heathrow Airport takes its power. The other two points kept their power, but each fed a separate part of the airport, and moving the lost load onto them took manual switching through most of the next day. The airport closed for most of 21 March, about 1,300 flights were cancelled, and full operation returned on 22 March.
tier: Not a deliberate act: the police found no evidence that the incident was suspicious, and the review found the cause most likely to be moisture in a failed transformer component. It is an accidental equipment failure outside the airport's fence, below the threshold for the military-action tier.

findings.title: Independent supplies that could not stand in for each other.
findings.text: Redundancy requires both that supplies share nothing and that each can carry the others' critical loads in time.

findings.title: The switchover time, measured.
findings.text: The switchover took about eleven hours to the terminals and fourteen and a half to the whole network, and had never been exercised.

findings.title: Power restored is not flow restored.
findings.text: Full operation came about twenty-eight hours after the loss, so recovery should be counted to the return of traffic.

findings.title: The backup was built for safety, not for the switchover.
findings.text: Backup supplies would have run down before the switchover was done, and should be sized to it.

findings.title: Knowledge at the utility is necessary, and buys no priority.
findings.text: The utility did not know the airport's internal arrangements, and even if it had, rules on equal treatment mean the airport must ride through on its own.

findings.title: The decision to close held by the operator.
findings.text: The decision to close was rightly the airport's, and its holders, their succession, and reopening by part should be planned in advance.

findings.title: Coordination with the utility was not prepared, and the scenario was not exercised.
findings.text: There was no agreed way to bring the parties together, and the slowest switchover should be exercised with the utility taking part.

findings.title: The adversary need choose only the supply point slowest to switch.
findings.text: The design basis should be tested against the loss of the supply point that takes longest to switch over, and should not credit a supply as continuous on a judgment of how likely its loss is.

findings.title: The gap the class fills, confirmed.
findings.text: The United Kingdom has no cross-sector requirement that critical operators keep operating through a loss of power.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its correction of the facility class's account of the event went to the class as an erratum.

annex.p: This annex is for the operators of airports, ports, stations, and other transportation nodes fed from more than one supply point, where each supply point feeds a separate part of the site. It is also for any owner, in any sector, whose site takes its power from several points that are not normally connected. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
If you lost your largest supply point, could your other supplies carry its critical loads? How, automatically, remotely, or by switching by hand, and how long would it take?
Independent supplies that cannot stand in for each other are not redundancy. A.3.1.
Has that switchover been exercised end to end, from the loss to the last critical system back in service, with the people who would do it?
The switchover time is an estimate, not a measurement. A.3.1.
How long do your backup supplies last, and is that longer than both the time to clear the site and the switchover time?
The backup runs down before the switchover is done. A.3.2.
Who decides to close the site, and who decides if that person cannot be reached? Who decides to reopen, and can you reopen part of the site while the rest waits?
The decision waits on the right person, and the whole site waits on its slowest part. A.3.3.
Does your recovery plan count the restart of systems and the return of vehicles and crews, not only the return of power?
The plan ends a day before the disruption does. A.3.3.

Does your electric utility know, in writing, your supply points, the critical loads on each, and your switchover time, and do you both mean the same thing by a resilient supply? Is there a way, agreed in advance, to bring the utility and your other parties together?
The utility restores you in its order, not yours, and the parties meet only after the event. A.3.4.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Make Sure Your Supplies Can Carry Each Other

annex.p: The review by the National Energy System Operator recommends, in its eighth recommendation, that critical sites be able to switch load quickly between their supply points. These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1 and F-2: show that the critical loads of any one supply point can be carried by the others within a stated switchover time, by automatic transfer acting on the loss of voltage at the site where you can, and exercise that switchover end to end, from the loss to the last critical system restored. At Heathrow the plan estimated ten to twelve hours and the measured time was about eleven hours to the terminals and fourteen and a half to the whole network.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Size Backup Power to the Switchover

annex.p: This step is this instrument’s, from F-4. Size the backup supplies of life-safety systems, and of the systems needed to hold people safely in place, to the longer of the time to clear the site and the switchover time.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Name Who Closes and Who Reopens, and Count to Full Flow

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-3 and F-6. Name in advance the holders of the decisions to close and to reopen and to whom each passes when a holder cannot be reached; where your supply is divided, plan to reopen by part as each part’s supply and systems allow; and count recovery to the return of full traffic, including vehicles and crews out of position, not only to the return of power.

annex.h3: A.3.4 Plan With Your Utility

annex.p: The review recommends, in its seventh recommendation, that critical sites plan for the loss of energy with a mechanism to bring the parties together. It also found that network operators’ license conditions generally prohibit treating one customer ahead of another in restoration, so a site must ride through the loss of any supply point on its own. This step adds the instrument’s own, from F-5 and F-7: exchange with the utility, in writing, your supply points, the critical loads on each, your switchover time, and what each of you means by a resilient supply, renewed on change, and exercise the slowest switchover with the utility taking part.

Just before midnight on 20 March 2025, a transformer caught fire at an electricity substation in west London. The fire took the substation’s other transformers with it, and with them one of the three points from which Heathrow Airport takes its power. The other two points kept their power, but each fed a separate part of the airport, and moving the lost point’s load onto them took manual switching through most of the next day. The airport closed for most of 21 March; about 1,300 flights were cancelled and some 200,000 to 300,000 passengers were disrupted, and full operation returned on 22 March, about twenty-eight hours after the loss. The review found the cause most likely to be moisture in a failed transformer component, and the police found no evidence that the incident was suspicious. The lesson does not depend on the cause. Three independent supplies are not redundancy unless each can carry the others’ critical loads in the time that matters, and that time is not known until it has been practiced. Any site fed from several points that each serve a separate part has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Bombings at Brussels Airport and Maalbeek Station, March 2016
what: On the morning of 22 March 2016, two bombs exploded in the public departure hall of Brussels Airport, before any screening, and about an hour later a third exploded in a metro train at Maalbeek station. Thirty-two people were killed and 340 injured on the parliamentary commission's count a week later. Between the two attacks the government decided to close the metro, but the decision reached the transport company only after the second explosion. The airport reopened in stages over the following three months, and the metro by station over the following month.
tier: A terrorist attack by a non-state group, claimed for the Islamic State, as the group's claim; adversarial but not military action, since no state stood behind it on any account in the record. A Belgian court reached its verdicts in 2023.

findings.title: The crowd outside the protected area, including the crowd the response makes.
findings.text: The attacks fell where crowds gathered before screening, and the reopening's screening outside the building formed new crowds in the open.

findings.title: An attack on one node is a warning to the next.
findings.text: The decision to close the metro took thirty-one minutes to reach its operator, and the time from an outside decision to the start of clearance should be stated and measured.

findings.title: The public authority closes the node, and the operator does not wait.
findings.text: Several public authorities can close a station, and the operator's plan should name each one and act without waiting on them.

findings.title: The attack case, with the responders' way in, belongs in the node's plan.
findings.text: The airport's emergency plan had no part for an attack.

findings.title: A separate channel that saturated.
findings.text: The emergency radio network saturated under load, so a backup channel must be sized and exercised for the event it is meant for.

findings.title: An occupancy event strands flow, and the reopening regime sets the rate.
findings.text: The airport reopened at about a fifth of its capacity, and recovery runs to the end of the security regime it reopens under.

findings.title: The adversary's sequence: the next node, during the response.
findings.text: The design basis should consider attacks on several nodes in sequence, and on the response itself.

findings.title: The record measures no clearance time.
findings.text: The event confirms the need to clear crowds but supplies no measured time to do it.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its correction of the facility class's account of the event went to the class as an erratum.

annex.p: This annex is for the operators of airports, rail and metro stations, bus terminals, and other passenger nodes, and for the public authorities that may close them. It is also for any owner, in any sector, of a public space where crowds gather before any screening. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Where do your processes gather crowds outside any protected area, and how large do those crowds get at your busiest hour?
The largest crowd stands where nothing screens it. A.3.1.
If you moved screening outward after an incident, where would the new queue form, how large would it be, and for how long?
Your own response builds a new crowd outside the building. A.3.1.

If a public authority decided to close your site, by what channel would that decision reach you, is the channel direct and acknowledged, and how long would it take from that decision to the start of your clearance?
The decision is made and does not reach the people who must act on it. A.3.2.

Which public authorities can order your site closed? Does your plan name each one, the channel by which its order arrives, and what you do on receipt, and would you act on your own judgment without waiting?
Two parties each wait on the other while the site stays open. A.3.2.
Does your emergency plan include an attack, with routes for responders in and the injured out while the site is clearing? Has it been exercised?
The plan stops short of the case that comes. A.3.3.
Has your emergency radio channel been exercised at the load of a major incident, with the discipline of its use part of the exercise?
The separate channel saturates when it is needed most. A.3.3.
Do you know your occupancy at the busiest hour and how long it takes to clear, measured and not estimated?
No one knows how long it takes to get everyone out. A.3.3.
If you reopened under a heavier security regime, what rate could you sustain, and for how long?
The reopening sets your capacity for months without a plan behind it. A.3.4.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Know Where Your Crowds Form, Including the Ones Your Response Makes

annex.p: This step is this instrument’s, from F-1. State where your processes gather crowds outside protected areas and hold them below a stated size by design. Before relying on a new security measure, state the crowd it forms, where, and for how long; on reopening, Brussels Airport’s screening before the building made queues of two to three hours outside it.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Make the Decision to Close Reach You Directly

annex.p: The Belgian parliamentary commission of inquiry recommended that the federal Crisis Center’s management cell communicate its decisions directly to every service concerned, and that the rules on closing public transport say who decides and how the decision is communicated directly; the Brussels transport company’s plan now provides for direct notice. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-2 and F-3: measure the time from an outside authority’s decision to close to the start of your clearance, and keep it, with your clearance time, inside the interval your plan allows; name in your plan every authority that may close the site; and act on your own judgment without waiting for that order.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Plan and Exercise the Attack Case

annex.p: The commission asked that the airport’s emergency and intervention plan be given a part on terrorism, with traffic management so that responders could reach and leave the scene, and that its evacuation plans be updated and exercised. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-4, F-5, and F-8: size and exercise your emergency channels at the load of the event, with the discipline of their use part of the exercise; treat your first information to responders as unverified until it is confirmed; and measure your clearance time in exercises.

annex.h3: A.3.4 Plan the Reopening

annex.p: This step is this instrument’s, from F-6. State the rate you could sustain under the security regime you would impose after an attack, measure it in exercises, and count recovery to the end of that regime; Brussels Airport reopened at about a fifth of its capacity and was fully operational only in June.

On the morning of 22 March 2016, two bombs exploded in the public departure hall of Brussels Airport, before any security screening, and about an hour later a third exploded in a metro train at Maalbeek station in central Brussels. Thirty-two people were killed and 340 injured on the parliamentary commission’s count a week later. The attacks were claimed for the Islamic State. Between the two explosions the government decided to close the metro, but the decision reached the transport company only after the second; the company had already begun stopping trains on its own. The airport’s emergency plan had no part for an attack, and the emergency radio network saturated. When the airport reopened, screening outside the building made long queues in the open, a new crowd outside any protection. The lessons for an operator are not about the attackers. Crowds gather where nothing protects them, including the crowds our own security measures create; a decision to close is only as fast as the channel that carries it; and a plan that has not imagined the case will not hold when it comes. Any site where the public gathers has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Congestion of the San Pedro Bay Ports, 2020 to 2022
what: From October 2020, a surge in imports outran what the Ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach and the trucks, chassis, rail, and warehouses behind them could clear, and container ships queued offshore for twenty-five months. The ports moved record volumes in 2021 while ships waited two weeks or more, and the queue peaked at 109 vessels on 9 January 2022. In the crowded anchorage, a storm dragged two ships' anchors over an oil pipeline that later ruptured; the backlog cleared as demand eased and cargo moved to other coasts.
tier: Not a deliberate act, and nothing was broken: a surge of demand beyond the clearing capacity of the gateway for about 40 percent of the country's containers, below the threshold for the military-action tier.

findings.title: Flow delayed at a node that never stopped.
findings.text: The ports set records while ships waited, so the design basis should count delay as well as lost flow.

findings.title: The clearing capacity was set beyond the gate.
findings.text: What bound the ports was how fast trucks, chassis, rail, and warehouses took containers away.

findings.title: The queue held beyond the fence was a hazard there.
findings.text: The full anchorage put ships over a pipeline, and the queue length that would fill the anchorages should be stated.

findings.title: The queue was managed by an arrangement made nine months after the anchorages filled.
findings.text: The order and place of a queue should be agreed before it forms.

findings.title: Diversion was counted once, because the surge struck every path.
findings.text: The other ports queued too, so diversion capacity cannot be counted twice.

findings.title: The backlog cleared in months, on the timetable of demand.
findings.text: The backlog fell over about ten and a half months from its peak, because demand fell, not because capacity rose.

findings.title: The levers on a queue were unstated and unmeasured.
findings.text: Extended hours, fees, and queue rules did little, and none had been measured in advance.

findings.title: A node at its limit, and a full anchorage, are what the adversary would choose.
findings.text: The design basis should be tested with the port and its alternatives already at surged flow.

findings.title: The gap the class fills, confirmed.
findings.text: No rule sets how long a ship may wait off a port or how full its anchorage may be.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its correction of the facility class's account of the event went to the class as an erratum.

annex.p: This annex is for port authorities, terminal operators, and the operators of other transportation nodes whose flow can, for weeks or months, exceed what they and the chains behind them can clear. It is also for any owner, in any sector, whose site can keep working at full pace while the work waiting for it grows. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Do you measure delay, the vessel-days and container-days of waiting beyond your normal wait, as well as throughput, so that you would know when you are working but not clearing?
Record volumes hide a site that has stopped clearing. A.3.1.

What sets your clearing rate: the least of your berth rate, your yard capacity, and the rate at which trucks, chassis, rail, and warehouses take flow away? Do you watch dwell time against its normal value?
The limit that binds lies beyond the gate, and no one is watching it. A.3.1.
How long a queue would fill the anchorages or holding areas your traffic uses at safe spacing, and what lies beneath or beside them?
The queue becomes a hazard to the ships and to the pipelines and cables below. A.3.2.
Is the order in which waiting vessels are worked, where they wait, and who decides, agreed in advance with the vessel traffic service and the parties at the port?
The arrangement is made months after the anchorages fill. A.3.2.
If you were full, where would your flow go, and could those places take it at their own surged flow?
Diversion capacity is counted twice, and the alternatives queue in turn. A.3.3.
What would you do to clear a backlog, such as extended hours, dwell charges, or queue rules, and do you know their effect from measurement?
The levers are pulled and do little. A.3.3.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Measure Delay, and Know What Sets Your Clearing Rate

annex.p: This step is this instrument’s, from F-1 and F-2. Count waiting, at anchor and on the terminal, beyond your normal wait, beside your throughput; state your clearing rate as the least of your berth rate, your yard capacity, and the rate at which the chains beyond your gate take flow away, with what you count on of trucks, chassis, rail, and storage; and watch dwell time against its normal value as the sign that the limit is near.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Plan the Queue and Where It Waits

annex.p: The National Transportation Safety Board found the probable cause of the anchor strike on the San Pedro Bay Pipeline to be the proximity of established anchorage positions to the pipeline, recommended that the Coast Guard restructure the anchorages, and recommended an alarm in the vessel traffic service’s monitoring system for such an encroachment. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-3 and F-4: state the length of queue that would fill the places your traffic waits at the spacing their safe use requires, and fix in advance, with the vessel traffic service and the parties at the port, the order in which waiting vessels are worked, where they wait, and who decides.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Count Diversion Honestly and Measure Your Levers

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-5, F-6, and F-7. Credit diversion only for what the other ports can take at their own surged flow, since a surge in demand reaches them all; state the measures you would take when flow exceeds your clearing rate, the parties beyond the gate each depends on, and their expected effect; and credit none whose effect has not been measured.

From October 2020 to November 2022, container ships queued off the Ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach, the point of entry for about 40 percent of the containers coming into the United States on the White House’s figure. Demand surged beyond what the ports and the trucks, chassis, rail, and warehouses behind them could clear. The ports moved record volumes in 2021, yet ships waited two weeks or more, and at the peak, on 9 January 2022, 109 vessels were in the queue. In the crowded anchorage a storm dragged two ships’ anchors across an oil pipeline, which ruptured months later. Extended hours, a threatened fee, and a new queuing system did little; the backlog cleared when demand fell and cargo moved to other coasts, whose ports then queued in turn. Nothing broke, and no one attacked. The lesson is that a site can be working at a record pace and still be failing, if the measure is volume and not delay, and that the limit that binds may lie beyond the gate. Any operation whose flow can outrun what it and its partners can clear has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Collapse of the Francis Scott Key Bridge, March 2024
what: In the early morning of 26 March 2024, the containership Dali lost power and steering about four minutes from the Francis Scott Key Bridge in Baltimore and struck one of its piers, bringing down the central spans. A call from the ship's pilot let police stop traffic about 48 seconds before the strike, but six members of a highway maintenance crew on the bridge were not warned and were killed. The channel beneath reopened in stages and was fully restored after seventy-six days; the replacement bridge is still being procured.
tier: Not a deliberate act: the National Transportation Safety Board found the cause to be a loose wire aboard the ship, and officials saw no evidence of terrorism. It is an accidental vessel strike on a span over navigable water, below the threshold for the military-action tier.

findings.title: The spans at risk must first be found.
findings.text: The bridge's risk of collapse from a ship strike was almost thirty times the criterion, and it had never been assessed.

findings.title: Pier protection is credited by what it intercepts.
findings.text: The protection was rated in place and working, but the ship struck where it was not.

findings.title: The assessment is renewed when the vessels change.
findings.text: Ships had grown about tenfold since the bridge's protection last stopped one.

findings.title: The warning time begins at the loss of control, and its path is named.
findings.text: Traffic was stopped by a chain of calls with seconds to spare, and the path from ship to closure should be named and fast.

findings.title: The workers on the span are reached apart from the closure.
findings.text: The six workers who died were not warned, and reaching people on a span must be a separate, exercised step.

findings.title: The channel's repair is counted in stages, and its capacity is stated.
findings.text: The channel reopened in stages, and the salvage capacity it depended on should be known in advance.

findings.title: Replacement time is the time to build the bridge current standards require.
findings.text: The replacement's estimate more than doubled once it was designed to current standards.

findings.title: An alternative absorbs only what it admits.
findings.text: The harbor tunnels could not take hazardous materials, which had no crossing at all.

findings.title: In the deliberate case no one calls.
findings.text: The warning here came from the ship itself, which a design basis for a deliberate strike cannot count on.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its correction of the facility class's account of the event went to the class as an erratum.

annex.p: This annex is for the owners of bridges over navigable water and of other critical spans, for the port and channel authorities beneath them, and for the pilots and vessel traffic services whose word may be the first warning. It is also for any owner, in any sector, of a structure that large moving vessels or vehicles pass close to. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Has each of your spans over navigable water been assessed for vessel collision against the ships that use the channel now, and what is its annual frequency of collapse against the criterion?
The risk is unknown, and may be many times what the standard allows. A.3.1.
Is your pier protection shown to intercept and stop the paths an aberrant ship would take, for today’s ships, or only rated as in place?
Protection stands where the ship will not go. A.3.1.
When did the size or number of the ships using your channel last change, and was the assessment renewed then?
The assessment is for ships that no longer sail. A.3.1.
If a ship lost power approaching your span, by what path would the warning reach the people who can close it, and how long would it take? Can the first person warned close the span?
Clearance depends on a chain of calls reaching the right person in time. A.3.2.
How would you reach the workers, contractors, and inspectors on the span, separately from closing the lanes, and has that been exercised?
The people on the span are not told. A.3.2.
If a fallen span blocked the channel, what salvage and heavy-lift capacity could reach you, from where, and how fast?
The channel stays shut while help is found. A.3.3.
Do you know how long a replacement built to today’s standards, with its protection, would take and cost?
The first estimate is for a bridge that will not be built. A.3.3.
Which cargo has no other crossing if your span is lost, such as hazardous materials barred from the tunnels?
One class of freight has no way across at all. A.3.3.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Find and Assess the Spans at Risk

annex.p: The American Association of State Highway and Transportation Officials recommends a vessel-collision vulnerability assessment of such bridges, and the National Transportation Safety Board, in its report MIR-25-10, named 68 bridges held by 30 owners that had no recent assessment and asked their owners to make one. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-1, F-2, and F-3: credit pier protection only for what it is shown to intercept and stop, as built and for the ships that use the channel now, and renew the assessment whenever the size, displacement, or number of those ships changes, and at a stated interval in any case.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Warn and Clear Everyone on the Span

annex.p: The Board recommended motorist warning systems on such bridges (H-25-28 to H-25-30) and emergency communications for the workers on them (H-25-31). These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-4 and F-5: name every link of the path by which a warning reaches the means of closing the span, starting from the loss of control aboard; let the first party to receive the warning close the span; and clear the people on the span as a step separate from closing the lanes, staffed so that neither waits on the other, exercised and timed.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Know Your Recovery Before You Need It

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-6, F-7, and F-8. State the salvage, heavy-lift, and wreck-removal capacity your channel would need, where it would come from, and how long it would take to arrive; estimate in advance the time and cost of a replacement built to today’s standards; and know which cargo, by class, has no other crossing.

In the early morning of 26 March 2024, the containership Dali lost electrical power and steering about four minutes from the Francis Scott Key Bridge in Baltimore and struck one of its piers. The pier and the central spans collapsed. A call from the ship’s pilot let police stop traffic about 48 seconds before the strike, but six members of a highway maintenance crew on the bridge were never warned and were killed. The National Transportation Safety Board found that the bridge had never been assessed for the risk of a ship strike, that its annual risk of collapse was almost thirty times the accepted criterion, and that its pier protection was not where the ship hit; ships using the channel had grown about tenfold since a smaller one was stopped by that protection in 1980. The Board found the cause to be a loose wire aboard the ship, and officials saw no sign of an attack. The channel took seventy-six days to reopen fully, and the replacement is now estimated at more than twice the first estimate, with no final schedule. The lessons are that a structure built for the ships of its day must be reassessed for the ships of today, and that the people on it must be warned by a path that does not depend on a phone call reaching the right person in time. Any owner whose structure stands near large moving vessels or vehicles has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Fracture in the Hernando de Soto Bridge, May 2021
what: On 11 May 2021, inspectors working on the Hernando de Soto Bridge, which carries Interstate 40 over the Mississippi River at Memphis, saw a fracture in one of its main steel tie girders and called 911. The highway was closed for eighty-three days and the river beneath it for about three. The crack had grown from welding defects made when the bridge was fabricated and, on the state's account, was visible in earlier images, though the bridge had been inspected every year. Testing found twelve more cracked welds on the bridge, and federal regulators ordered such members tested nationwide.
tier: Not a deliberate act: a fabrication defect, on the forensic analyst's account, found before the span fell. It is an accidental structural fracture, below the threshold for the military-action tier.

findings.title: An inspection is credited for what it is shown to have reached.
findings.text: The span was inspected every year and the crack was missed for years.

findings.title: The postulated failure names the fabrication defect, and its population.
findings.text: The crack grew from welding defects, so finding one should open a review of every member that shares them.

findings.title: What a span already records is read for its critical members.
findings.text: A drone video and sensor data held the evidence and were not read for it.

findings.title: A critical finding reaches the closure by a named path.
findings.text: The finding reached the closure by a 911 call from inspectors working outside their scope.

findings.title: The channel beneath a span in doubt reopens on a stated basis.
findings.text: The river reopened on modeling before the span was stabilized, and the basis for reopening should be written down.

findings.title: A repair time includes the search for the defect elsewhere on the span.
findings.text: The repair ran to the eighty-third day because more cracked welds were found and fixed.

findings.title: The alternative is counted with the hazard it shares.
findings.text: The one other nearby crossing shares the region's earthquake hazard.

findings.title: The nonredundant tension member is a target, and its record a reading.
findings.text: The design basis should protect such members and the records on which decisions to close or reopen rest.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its correction of the facility class's account of the event went to the class as an erratum.

annex.p: This annex is for the owners and inspectors of bridges with nonredundant steel tension members, those whose failure may bring down part or all of a span, and for the consultants who work on such bridges whatever their scope. It is also for any owner, in any sector, of a structure whose integrity rests on single members. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known

For each nonredundant member, does your inspection record show which faces and welds were reached by hand, at arm’s length? Do your inspectors rotate in practice, and does an engineer independent of the team review the work?
The inspection is credited for a visit, not for what it saw. A.3.1.
Do you have members of T-1 steel, or members fabricated without a fracture control plan, and have their butt welds been tested by nondestructive methods?
A defect built in at fabrication waits inside the member. A.3.1.
Is every federal advisory on a kind of member recorded against each of your structures that has one, and closed out?
A warning given decades ago is still open. A.3.1.
Are the drone images, sensor data, and records you already hold read for your critical members, whatever they were taken for?
The evidence sits unread in your own files. A.3.2.
If anyone on your structure, a contractor working on something else included, saw a critical defect, how would it reach the person who can close the structure, and how fast?
The finding reaches the closure by a 911 call. A.3.2.

If the channel beneath a span in doubt had to reopen, what basis would you give the Coast Guard: the damaged state analyzed, the margin, the monitoring while vessels pass, and what would close it again?
The channel reopens on a basis no one wrote down. A.3.3.
Does your alternative crossing share the same hazard, such as the same earthquake, and does your repair time include searching for the same defect elsewhere on the span?
The detour and the repair are both longer than planned. A.3.3.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Inspect for What You Reach, and Find the Defect’s Population

annex.p: The Federal Highway Administration required the States in December 2021 to identify fracture critical members of T-1 steel fabricated without a fracture control plan, to test their butt welds in tension by nondestructive methods by 31 March 2024, and to treat rejectable indications as critical findings. The National Bridge Inspection Standards of 2022 set the interval for a nonredundant steel tension member at not more than 24 months and define its inspection as hands-on, within arm’s length of the member. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-1 and F-2: credit an inspection only for the faces and welds its record shows were reached by hand; rotate inspectors in practice and have the work reviewed independently; and record every federal advisory on a kind of member against each of your structures that has one until it is answered.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Read What You Already Hold, and Name the Path to Closure

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-3 and F-4. Read the images, sensor data, and records your structures already hold for their critical members, whatever they were taken for, and keep any instrumentation maintained and reviewed for structural change; and let anyone you admit to a critical structure report a critical finding directly to the person who can close it, and to the Captain of the Port where it crosses navigable water, by a named path that does not wait on review.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Plan the Reopening and the Repair

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-5, F-6, and F-7. Write in advance the basis on which you would ask that the channel beneath a span in doubt be reopened; state the repair time as stabilization, repair of the member, and the search for the same defect elsewhere on the span; and credit an alternative crossing only for the events that would not reach it too.

On 11 May 2021, inspectors working on the Hernando de Soto Bridge, which carries Interstate 40 over the Mississippi River at Memphis, saw a fracture in one of its main steel tie girders, a member whose failure could bring down part of the bridge. They were inspecting other parts of the bridge and called 911. The highway was closed for eighty-three days and the river beneath for about three, with more than a thousand barges waiting. The crack had grown from welding defects made when the bridge was fabricated, and the state said it was visible in a 2019 drone video and in a 2016 photograph. The bridge had been inspected every year, but the state said the face where the crack lay had not been inspected by hand. Testing then found twelve more cracked welds on the same bridge, and federal regulators ordered such members tested nationwide. No one was hurt, and no one suggests the fracture was intended. The lessons are that an inspection is worth what it actually reached, not the fact that it was done, and that the evidence already in our own files must be read. Any owner whose structures rest on single members has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Closure of the Red Sea and the Strait of Hormuz, from November 2023
date: from 19 November 2023, open on the record of 9 October 2026
date_full: from 19 November 2023, open on the record of 9 October 2026
what: From November 2023, Houthi forces attacked merchant ships in the southern Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden, seizing one and sinking four, and most shipping lines diverted around the Cape of Good Hope. After the strikes on Iran of 28 February 2026, the Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed to most shipping by the threat of attack and the withdrawal of insurance, and thousands of seafarers and hundreds of ships were held inside the Gulf. The main pipeline around the strait delivered into the Red Sea, where Saudi shipping was blockaded and the pipeline was struck; neither passage had recovered on the record of October 2026.
tier: Military action, on the accounts of the actors and governments concerned: an armed campaign against shipping by the Houthi forces, and the closure of a strait in armed conflict, declared by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Each attribution is stated as the government's or actor's own, and this instrument makes no finding of its own. The record is open.

findings.title: A passage closed by threat may reopen obstructed.
findings.text: Wrecks and reported mines mean that a passage's closure runs past the end of the threat.

findings.title: Severance time runs to the return of the ships, and it relapses.
findings.text: Traffic stayed far below normal long after a halt, and both passages relapsed after partial reopenings.

findings.title: A passage is closed to some ships, and the country counts its own.
findings.text: Both passages were closed to ships chosen by association, so exposure should be counted for the ships a country depends on.

findings.title: The military-mobility flow stops at the first attack on the flag.
findings.text: The carrier of United States government cargo suspended its Red Sea transits at the first such attack.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its finding on ships and seafarers held inside a closed sea is referred to the classes that hold them.

findings.title: An alternative through the other passage is not independent.
findings.text: The bypass around one passage delivered into the other, which the same conflict reached.

findings.title: The stranded flow states what it counts.
findings.text: Counts differed by an order of magnitude, so each must say what it measures and how.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its finding on dependent sectors' stocks is referred to those sectors' series.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its finding on navigation interference and radio orders at the chokepoint is referred to the communications series and the control class.
