annex.p: This annex is for the operators of ports, shipping lines, and other transportation nodes and corridors, and for the importers and dependent sectors, energy, fertilizer, and manufacturing among them, whose goods move through a foreign chokepoint. It is also for any owner, in any sector, whose supply depends on a passage it does not control. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known

Which of your supplies pass through a foreign chokepoint such as the Red Sea, the Suez Canal, or the Strait of Hormuz, and do you know the flags, owners, and destinations of the ships that carry them?
You count the passage as open while it is closed to your ships. A.3.1.
Do you measure your exposure in the units you need, barrels, tons, or containers, and not in ship counts or a passage’s average traffic?
The numbers say the passage is moving while your cargo is not. A.3.1.
If one passage closed, would your alternative route or bypass run into another passage that the same conflict can reach?
The alternative fails with the first. A.3.2.
Do you know the added time and cost of the long way around, as measured, and the ships that would carry it?
The detour is counted as free. A.3.2.
How long could your stocks carry you, and is that set against a closure lasting months or years, with relapses after a ceasefire, rather than against the ceasefire itself?
Stocks are sized for a disruption far shorter than the one that comes. A.3.3.
Could your ships, crews, or cargo be held inside a closed sea, and what would that do to your operations?
The ships you count on are trapped on the far side. A.3.3.
Does your plan assume that once a passage reopens it is clear, or does it allow for mines, wrecks, and the return of insurers and shipping lines?
Recovery is planned from a ceasefire that does not end the closure. A.3.3.
If your ships received orders by radio, or their satellite navigation were jammed or spoofed near a chokepoint, would they and you know?
False positions and orders are believed. A.3.4.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Count Your Own Ships, in Your Own Units

annex.p: This step is this instrument’s, from F-3 and F-7. Count your exposure for the ships you depend on, by flag, ownership, cargo, and destination, and treat the passage as closed to them where an adversary has named their flag or associations, whatever share of its traffic still moves. State that exposure in barrels, tons, or containers, with the source, period, and baseline of every count, and know when a count rests on ships’ own position broadcasts.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Check That Your Alternative Is Independent

annex.p: This step is this instrument’s, from F-6. Do not count as independent an alternative that delivers into another chokepoint or that the same campaign can reach; the main bypass around the Strait of Hormuz delivered into the Red Sea, which was then closed to Saudi shipping. State the alternative’s capacity with the fleet that would carry it, and its added time and cost as measured.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Plan for a Long Closure That Relapses

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1 and F-2, with the substance of F-5 and F-8, which are referred to the classes and series that hold them. Plan for a closure that runs from the first threat to the return of shipping lines and insurers at a stated share of normal traffic, not to a ceasefire, with relapses counted and the clearance of mines and wrecks after the threat ends; Suez traffic was still 39 percent below its pre-crisis level ten months after the Houthi forces halted their attacks. Size stocks of every commodity a passage carries against that duration, and plan for ships and crews that may be held on the far side.

annex.h3: A.3.4 Treat Positions and Radio Orders as Possibly False

annex.p: On 28 February 2026, the Joint Maritime Information Center advised that radio hails from Iranian Revolutionary Guard elements indicating transit restrictions did not constitute a legally recognized suspension of transit passage under international maritime law; ship operators follow the maritime security advisories in force. This step is this instrument’s, from the substance of F-9, which is referred to the communications series and to the control class: treat satellite positions and orders received over open channels near a chokepoint as indications that can be false, and know how your ships and your own staff would detect it.

Since November 2023, the Houthi forces have attacked merchant ships in the southern Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden, seizing one and sinking four, and most shipping lines have sent their ships the long way around Africa, about ten days longer between Asia and Europe. After the strikes on Iran of 28 February 2026, the Strait of Hormuz, which carried nearly a fifth of the world’s oil supply on the Energy Information Administration’s account, was effectively closed to most shipping, by the threat of attack and the withdrawal of insurance rather than by any physical blockage. Thousands of seafarers and hundreds of ships were held inside the Gulf. The pipeline that was meant to carry Saudi oil around the strait delivers into the Red Sea, where Saudi shipping was then blockaded and the pipeline itself was struck. On the record of October 2026, neither passage had recovered, and each had relapsed after a partial reopening. The lessons are that a passage closed to the ships you depend on is closed, whatever its average traffic; that an alternative which runs through another passage the same conflict can reach is no alternative; and that closures of this kind are measured in years, not weeks. Any operation that depends on goods moving through a passage it does not control has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Boeing 737 MAX Accidents and Grounding, 2018 to 2020
date: 29 October 2018, 10 March 2019, and the grounding to November 2020 and after
date_full: 29 October 2018, 10 March 2019, and the grounding to November 2020 and after
what: Lion Air Flight 610 on 29 October 2018 and Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302 on 10 March 2019 crashed shortly after takeoff, killing 346 people. In each, a flight-control function called MCAS acted repeatedly on a false reading from one angle-of-attack sensor and pushed the nose down, on a design whose pilots had not been told of the function. Regulators grounded the type worldwide over three days in March 2019; the United States returned it to service in November 2020 after a fix requiring both sensors, and other countries followed later.
tier: Not a deliberate act: the investigating boards found the causes in the design, its certification, the documentation, maintenance, and the sensors, and no one suggests either crash was intended. It is an accidental fleet-wide design defect, below the threshold for the military-action tier.

findings.title: The fleet shared the response to a fault, not the fault.
findings.text: The two sensor failures differed; what every airplane shared was the design, the missing alert, and manuals that did not name the function.

findings.title: The crew was the design's second indication.
findings.text: The design relied on pilots to catch an error from a function they had not been told existed.

findings.title: The range shown safe rested on the crew.
findings.text: A function shown safe only by counting on a human recovery has not been shown safe on its own.

findings.title: The function grew before there was a fleet.
findings.text: The function was enlarged during development and not reassessed as a whole.

findings.title: Fleet unavailability is counted by authority, and past delivery.
findings.text: The grounding ran longer and wider than the twenty months and 390 airplanes usually cited.

findings.title: The decision to ground was held by many regulators on different bases.
findings.text: Each authority grounded and returned the type on its own basis, and each should record that basis.

annex.p: This annex is for the operators and maintainers of fleets whose units share automatic control functions, airlines first, and for the manufacturers and repair stations that supply them. It is also for any owner, in any sector, whose equipment acts on its own on a sensor’s reading. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Does any automatic function on your fleet command a control on a single sensor or indication? What does it do if that indication is wrong?
One bad sensor commands the vehicle. A.3.1.
Do your crews’ manuals and training name every automatic function that can move a control, and are the alerts that would tell them an indication is wrong enabled on every unit?
Crews are expected to catch the failure of something they were never told existed. A.3.1.
Where safety rests on a person catching an automatic function’s error, have the response time and the indications assumed been shown in the conditions the failure creates?
The safety case counts on a recovery no one has shown can be made. A.3.1.
When a manufacturer changes how much authority a control function has, or the conditions in which it acts, is the whole function reassessed?
A function grows in development and is certified as it was. A.3.2.
Do you know where your sensors are repaired and how a repaired sensor is tested on installation, and do defects reported by one crew reach maintenance and the next crew?
A fault found on one flight is flown again on the next. A.3.2.
After one serious event on a type, on what basis would you keep it in service or ground it, and who decides?
The second event comes while the first is still being understood. A.3.3.
If a whole type in your fleet were grounded, how many units, for how long, and what work would stop, counted by every authority that would ground it and including units not yet delivered?
The grounding is longer and wider than the plan assumes. A.3.3.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Know What Your Automatic Functions Trust

annex.p: For operators of the 737 MAX, the Federal Aviation Administration’s Airworthiness Directive 2020-24-02 requires, for each airplane, new flight-control and display software under which the function needs both angle-of-attack sensors to activate and acts only once per event, revised procedures, rerouted wiring, a sensor test, and a readiness flight, with the disagreement alert always enabled; and section 501 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023, requires further safety enhancements, among them a synthetic angle-of-attack system on the agency’s notice. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-1, F-2, and F-3, for any fleet: know which automatic functions command a control on one indication; name every such function in manuals and training; enable on every unit the alerts that would show an indication is wrong; and where safety rests on a person catching an error, show the time and indications assumed in the conditions the failure creates.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Watch Changes to Functions and the Parts That Feed Them

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-2 and F-4. Ask that any change in development that enlarges a control function’s authority, or the conditions in which it acts, be reassessed as a whole function; know where the sensors that feed such functions are repaired and how they are tested on installation; and make sure that defects one crew reports reach maintenance and the next crew.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Ground on a Stated Basis, and Count the Whole Fleet

annex.p: After the first accident, the agency issued an emergency directive requiring a revised crew procedure and kept the type in service; after the second, authorities grounded it over three days, each on its own basis. These steps are this instrument’s, from F-5 and F-6: state in advance the basis on which you would keep a type in service or ground it after a serious event, and who decides; and count a grounding by every authority that would ground your fleet, to the last unit returned and including units held from delivery.

On 29 October 2018 and 10 March 2019, two new Boeing 737 MAX airliners crashed shortly after takeoff, in Indonesia and Ethiopia, killing 346 people. In each, a flight-control function called MCAS acted repeatedly on a false reading from a single angle-of-attack sensor and pushed the nose down. The pilots had not been told the function existed, and on most of the airplanes the alert that would have shown the two sensors disagreeing did not work. After the first crash the type stayed in service on a revised crew procedure; after the second, regulators around the world grounded it over three days, each on its own basis. The fix, which made the function use both sensors and act only once, took twenty months to certify in the United States, each airplane then needed its own modification, and other countries returned the type later still. The investigators found the causes in the design, its certification, the documentation, maintenance, and the sensors, and no one suggests either crash was intended. The lessons are that an automatic function that trusts one indication, and a safety case that counts on people catching an error they cannot see, will fail in every unit at once, and that the decision to keep a fleet in service after one accident must rest on a stated basis. Any fleet whose units share automatic functions has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Lac-Mégantic Runaway and Derailment, July 2013
what: Late on 5 July 2013, a freight train of seventy-two tank cars of crude oil was left unattended on a descending main line at Nantes, Quebec, held by seven hand brakes and by air from one running locomotive. After a fire, the locomotive was shut down, its air leaked away too slowly to set off the automatic brakes, and the train ran 7.2 miles downhill and derailed at 65 miles an hour in the center of Lac-Mégantic. The crude oil burned, and forty-seven people were killed.
tier: Not a deliberate act: the Transportation Safety Board of Canada found no evidence of unauthorized entry to the train. It is an accidental loss of securement of an unattended train, below the threshold for the military-action tier.

findings.title: The securement margin is a margin of force.
findings.text: The hand brakes gave about a third of the force needed because they were counted as brakes, not as force.

findings.title: The test of securement is an indication.
findings.text: Securement was tested with other brakes applied, and the report built on that test was believed.

findings.title: The automatic air brake is not fail-safe on a slow loss.
findings.text: The air leaked too slowly to set off the brakes, which were assumed to apply whenever air is lost.

findings.title: The independent means, by where a runaway would go.
findings.text: The train was left with no derail or other independent defense, above a town.

findings.title: An emergency act on a locomotive is an act on the train's securement.
findings.text: Shutting down the burning locomotive removed the air that partly held the train.

findings.title: The runaway's margin begins at its first movement, and no one knew.
findings.text: The train ran for about seventeen minutes with nothing to stop it and no one aware it had gone.

findings.title: A fleet shares configurations and practices, and may be answered by schedule.
findings.text: Retrofits and crew practices were shared across the fleet, and the tank cars were phased out by schedule rather than grounded.

findings.title: The unattended train is a conveyance that can be taken.
findings.text: A train left unattended with an open cab should be protected as a vehicle that could be misused.

findings.title: The line with the Chemical series and the crew question hold.
findings.text: The design basis divides the vehicle from its cargo correctly, and the Board could not conclude whether a one-person crew contributed.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its correction of the facility class's account of the event went to the class as an erratum.

annex.p: This annex is for railroads and the shippers of hazardous cargo by rail, and for the communities and responders along their lines. It is also for any owner, in any sector, of heavy vehicles or equipment left unattended where gravity can move them. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known

When you leave a train unattended, is its securement counted as the force the hand brakes actually give, against the force the grade and weight require, without any brake that depends on air or a running engine?
The train is held by brakes counted wrongly. A.3.1.
Is securement tested with every air brake released, and does the report of securement say how the test was made?
A report of securement rests on a test that proves nothing. A.3.1.
Where do you leave hazardous trains unattended, and where would a runaway go from there? Is each place protected by a derail or another independent means?
A runaway has a clear path to a town. A.3.2.
Would your trains’ brakes apply on a slow loss of air, or on movement, by a means that no shutdown, breaker, or setting can defeat?
The fail-safe brake waits for a fall in pressure that never comes. A.3.2.
Do the retrofitted protective functions on your locomotives, such as reset safety controls, actually act when tested, on every unit?
A defense counted on paper is absent on the track. A.3.1.
If firefighters or anyone else shut down a locomotive on which securement partly depends, who would know, and who qualified would come to restore securement before they left?
The act that ends one emergency starts the next. A.3.3.
If an unattended train began to move, would it detect that, stop itself, and warn anyone in its path?
No one knows the train has gone until it arrives. A.3.3.
Are unattended cabs locked, with their reversers removed?
Anyone passing can reach the controls. A.3.3.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Count and Test Securement as Force

annex.p: The Federal Railroad Administration’s rule of 2015 requires hand brakes sufficient to hold the train with the air brakes released, applied and verified, and Transport Canada’s strengthened Rule 112 has required additional physical means of securement since 15 October 2015. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-1, F-2, and F-7: count securement as the force each applied brake gives, at its measured ratio and at the torque people actually apply, and credit a brake not shown working at nothing; release every air brake for the test and say in the report how the test was made; and inspect retrofitted protective functions for what they do, not for whether they are fitted.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Leave Trains Where a Runaway Cannot Reach a Town

annex.p: Transport Canada’s emergency directive of 23 July 2013 prohibited leaving a locomotive coupled to loaded dangerous-goods tank cars unattended on a main track, and the Federal Railroad Administration’s rule requires a plan for where hazardous trains may be left unattended outside a yard. In March 2026 the Transportation Safety Board of Canada found that “a residual risk remains for uncontrolled movements in areas where derails do not protect the mainline.” These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-3 and F-4: choose where a hazardous train may be left by where a runaway from there would go, preferring a place protected by a derail and using an independent means where there is none; and fit brakes that apply on a slow loss of air or on movement, by a means no shutdown, breaker, or setting can defeat.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Treat Any Emergency Act as an Act on Securement, and Know When a Train Moves

annex.p: Transport Canada’s directive required unattended controlling locomotives to be protected against entry with their reversers removed, and the Federal Railroad Administration’s rule requires a locked cab and a qualified person to verify securement after emergency responders have been on the equipment. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-5, F-6, and F-8: tell responders what shutting down a locomotive takes away, and send someone qualified to restore securement before they leave; and make an unattended train detect its own movement, stop itself, report it, and warn what lies in its path.

Late on 5 July 2013, a freight train of seventy-two tank cars of crude oil was left for the night on a descending main line at Nantes, Quebec, held by seven hand brakes and by air from one running locomotive that was already giving trouble. The locomotive caught fire, and firefighters shut it down, as instructed; with it went the air. The hand brakes gave about a third of the force needed, and as the air leaked away, too slowly to set off the automatic brakes, the train began to roll. It ran 7.2 miles downhill, reached 65 miles an hour, and derailed in the center of Lac-Mégantic. The crude oil burned, and forty-seven people were killed. The railway did not know its train had gone until the police called. The Transportation Safety Board of Canada found that the securement relied on the running locomotive, that the brakes were counted and tested wrongly, and that no physical defense stood in the way; it found no evidence that anyone had entered the train. The lessons are that what holds a heavy vehicle on a grade must be counted as force and tested in the condition it is relied on, that a fail-safe brake must act on a slow loss as well as a fast one, and that any act on a vehicle in an emergency is an act on what holds it in place. Any operation that leaves heavy equipment where gravity can move it has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Midair Collision over the Potomac, January 2025
what: On the night of 29 January 2025, a regional airliner circling to land at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport collided with an Army helicopter flying a published route over the Potomac River, and all sixty-seven people aboard the two aircraft were killed. The helicopter's route ran beneath the approach with about 75 feet of margin, one controller was working both aircraft on two frequencies, and the helicopter crew was twice approved to keep itself clear on reporting the airliner in sight. The National Transportation Safety Board found the cause in the route's placement, the failure to review it, and the reliance on pilots seeing each other to keep traffic flowing.
tier: Not a deliberate act: the Board and the Army found the cause in the route, its review, the reliance on visual separation, the tower's workload, and the helicopter's altimetry. It is an accidental wrong grant of movement made by people, below the threshold for the military-action tier.

findings.title: The wrong grant was a composition of permitted grants.
findings.text: Each permission was within the rules; the conflict lay in their combination.

findings.title: The published route worked as a standing grant.
findings.text: The helicopter route gave permission in advance, guarded only by each crew's altimeter.

findings.title: A review whose proposals are not answered is lost.
findings.text: Proposals to move the route went unanswered for years.

findings.title: The basis of visual separation was the receiving crew's report.
findings.text: Separation rested on a pilot's report that the controller could not check.

findings.title: The conflict alert acts through the person who granted.
findings.text: The alerts that were independent of the controller were in the aircraft, and the airliner lacked one that could have warned it.

findings.title: The positions were combined by choice.
findings.text: Two control positions were combined without a recorded reason, with staffing the Board found adequate.

findings.title: Throughput became risk at the offload.
findings.text: Moving arrivals to another runway to keep traffic flowing was where efficiency turned into exposure.

findings.title: The air-ground channel lost instructions without saying so.
findings.text: Key instructions were lost on the radio while every circuit worked, and no one knew.

findings.title: The margin lay across a boundary that does not hold for military aircraft.
findings.text: The route's margin was smaller than the altimeter error the military helicopter was allowed.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its correction of the facility class's account of the event went to the class as an erratum.

A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known

Does any published route, procedure, or letter of agreement in your airspace bring aircraft within a few hundred feet of each other by design, and has its margin been set against the altimeter error the aircraft using it are allowed?
The margin is smaller than the error. A.3.1.
Are the reviews of your routes documented, are proximity data analyzed, and are proposals from controllers and operators answered on the record?
The warning is given and never answered. A.3.1.
Do you routinely absorb traffic that the facility upstream did not meter, by offloading to other runways or otherwise, and is that counted as risk as well as recovered flow?
Throughput becomes risk at the point no one measures. A.3.2.
When control positions are combined, is the reason recorded and assessed against the traffic, and can every crew sharing the airspace hear the others?
One person works two frequencies, and neither crew hears the other. A.3.2.
Where separation rests on a pilot’s report that traffic is in sight, can the controller check that report, and is it relied on where traffic makes it routine?
Separation rests on a report no one can verify. A.3.3.
Would you know if an instruction on which separation depends was not received, was stepped on, or was lost in a gap in radio coverage?
The instruction is lost and no one knows. A.3.3.
Are there collision-alerting layers that do not run through the controller who made the grants, and are your aircraft equipped with them, ADS-B In among them?
The last alert depends on the person already overloaded. A.3.4.
Which aircraft in your airspace are exempt from broadcasting their position, and what do you rely on in its place?
Some traffic is invisible to the systems built to see it. A.3.4.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Design Routes Net of Error, and Answer Your Reviews

annex.p: On the National Transportation Safety Board’s urgent recommendation, the Federal Aviation Administration removed the segment of Helicopter Route 4 beneath the approach in March 2025, and its interim final rule of 23 January 2026 limits the corridor to essential operations. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-2, F-3, and F-9: design every route’s separation from an approach or departure path net of the altimeter error the aircraft that fly it are allowed, with military operators declaring theirs; document every review; set proximity measures that trigger a review out of cycle; and answer on the record the proposals of the controllers and operators who use a route.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Count Throughput as Risk, and Record Why Positions Combine

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1, F-6, and F-7. Count routine offloading and other ways of absorbing unmetered traffic as exposure to collision, not only as recovered flow; treat a combination of permitted grants as a grant to be judged in its own right; and record the reason and time of every combination of positions, on an assessment of the traffic at that moment.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Do Not Rest Separation on What You Cannot Check

annex.p: On 18 March 2026 the agency announced a general notice suspending visual separation between airplanes and helicopters in Class B and Class C airspace and terminal radar service areas where helicopters cross arrival and departure paths. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-4 and F-8: where the consequence is a collision, confirm a crew’s report against your own surveillance or separate by radar; deliver an instruction on which separation depends only on confirmed receipt; and know each frequency’s coverage of the airspace it serves.

annex.h3: A.3.4 Keep a Layer That Does Not Run Through the Controller

annex.p: The Board found that ADS-B In could have alerted the airliner fifty-nine seconds before the collision, and named among the contributing factors the agency’s failure to implement earlier recommendations, ADS-B In among them. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-5 and F-9: count airborne collision avoidance and ADS-B In as the layer independent of the controller, with their inhibit heights and equipage stated against your routes; and state which aircraft you control are exempt from broadcasting their position and what you rely on in its place.

On the night of 29 January 2025, a regional airliner circling to land at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport collided with an Army helicopter flying a published route over the Potomac River, and all sixty-seven people aboard the two aircraft were killed. Each aircraft was where it had been permitted to be, or within the error it was allowed: the helicopter on a route that ran beneath the approach with about 75 feet of margin, and the airliner on a runway change made to keep traffic moving. The helicopter crew twice reported the airliner in sight and was approved to keep itself clear; the Safety Board found it likely saw a different aircraft. One controller was working both aircraft on two frequencies, so neither crew could hear the other, and the instruction to pass behind the airliner was cut off by a brief radio transmission. Flight data had shown thousands of close encounters near the airport for years, and earlier proposals to move the route had not been acted on. The Board found the cause in the route’s placement, the failure to review it, and the reliance on pilots seeing each other to keep traffic flowing, and no one suggests any of it was intended. The lessons are that permissions each within the rules can combine into one that is not, and that a margin smaller than the error allowed is no margin. Any operation where people grant movement in shared space has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Losses of Radar and Communications at the Philadelphia Approach Control Facility, 2025 to 2026
what: Since July 2024, the controllers who guide aircraft into Newark have worked from the Philadelphia approach control facility, while the system that processes their radar stayed in New York, linked by telecommunications circuits. Twice in the spring of 2025 those links failed for about ninety seconds, and controllers lost radar and radio contact with the aircraft they were guiding; Newark's operations have been limited since. On 21 September 2026 a primary circuit failed and its backup was found cut, ground stops held five airports in the region for most of a day, and about 7,000 flights were affected.
tier: Not a deliberate act. It is a series of accidental losses of a control facility's links, through old equipment and an accidental cut, below the threshold for the military-action tier.

findings.title: The derating beside the outages (cut to a note).
findings.text: Newark's limits, set on the agency's stated basis of staffing, should be recorded beside the outages they followed, with the stress of a loss of the links named among their possible causes.

findings.title: The independence that failed was in time.
findings.text: The backup's loss was found only on switching to it, so independence between primary and backup must include how soon a lost backup becomes known.

findings.title: The transfer of airspace created the dependence.
findings.text: Moving the controllers away from their radar processing should have shown, before it took effect, that every path they would depend on was independent.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Merged into F-5.

findings.title: What the record does not show: how restoration ended and how the aircraft were reached.
findings.text: The record does not say when both paths were restored or how contact with the aircraft was regained, and restoration should be counted to all three of its end points.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its correction went to the facility class as an erratum.

annex.p: This annex is for the operators of control facilities whose people see and speak through circuits they do not own: approach and enroute control in aviation and, in the other modes the class covers, rail dispatch and train control, vessel traffic services, and transit control centers. It is also for any owner, in any sector, whose operators sit in one place while the systems they watch are processed in another. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known

Do your operators work in one place while the systems that process what they see run in another, so that their picture arrives over lines between the two? If you have moved work between sites, was that dependence examined before the move?
The move created a dependence no one measured. A.3.3.
Do you know the age and condition of each circuit that carries your control data, and is each one’s replacement scheduled ahead of its failure?
The oldest line sets the reliability of the room. A.3.1.
Are your primary and backup paths on separate routes and separate equipment, and has that been shown as built rather than as ordered?
One cut, failure, or carrier can take both. A.3.1.
If your backup failed today, how soon would you know: by the carrier’s report, by your own monitoring, or only when you switched to it?
The backup’s loss is found on the day it is needed. A.3.2.
If anyone planned to dig near the routes of your circuits, would you hear of it before the work began?
Someone else’s work can take a path without warning. A.3.1.
If your operators lost their screens and radios for ninety seconds, how would they reach everyone in motion, over something that shares nothing with those links? When was that last practiced?
The people moving are out of reach when they most need direction. A.3.4.
After a loss like that, can the people on watch be relieved, and is there staff to cover them?
The loss’s effect on people becomes a loss of capacity that outlasts it. A.3.4.
When you recover, do you record when the stop ended, when you returned to full capacity, and when both paths were back, and any reduced operation that followed, with its reason?
Recovery is declared at the first end point and the rest is not counted. A.3.4.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Know Your Paths as Built

annex.p: The agency’s own steps after the losses of 2025 are its published actions: on 7 May 2025 it announced new high-bandwidth links between the cities, the replacement of copper with fiber, a temporary backup system, and a radar-processing hub at Philadelphia, and on 3 July 2025 it said it had moved to a new fiber network with two separate communications paths, keeping the temporary satellite system in place for now. On 21 September 2026 the primary failed and the backup was found cut on the same morning, so two paths announced were not two paths that held. This step is this instrument’s, from F-2: for each control site, list the route, the carrier, and the equipment of every path its data and radios use, mark what the paths share, and confirm the separation as built. Know the age of each circuit and replace the oldest ahead of failure, and arrange to learn of work planned near the routes before it begins.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Know When the Backup Is Gone

annex.p: The agency’s order on facility operations already provides an alert for the loss of redundancy (FAA Order JO 1900.47G, ¶3-2). This step is this instrument’s, from F-2: set a time within which you learn that a backup has been lost, whether by the carrier’s report or by your own monitoring, and treat that loss as an event in its own right, acted on when it happens rather than found when the primary fails.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Check the Links Before You Move the Work

annex.p: This step is this instrument’s, from F-3. The transfer of July 2024 was made for staffing, and it moved the controllers away from the system that processes their radar. Before any move of work between sites, or of territory between control centers, show the independence of every path on which the moved work will depend, and record a move made without that showing as a reduction in your margin.

annex.h3: A.3.4 Practice Without the Links, and Count the Whole Recovery

annex.p: This step is this instrument’s, from F-5, with the note of F-1. Practice the case where screens and radios are lost with movements in progress, and after any real loss, record how everyone in motion was reached and how long it took. Count recovery to its last end point: the end of the stop, the return to full capacity, and the restoration of both paths. If operations run reduced afterward, record that beside the loss with its stated reason, and plan for the people on watch: on 5 May 2025 the agency said that some of the facility’s controllers had taken time off to recover from the stress of the outages.

Since July 2024, the controllers who guide aircraft into Newark have worked from Philadelphia, while the system that processes their radar stayed in New York, so that their picture of the sky arrives over telecommunications lines between the two cities. In April and May 2025 those lines failed twice, for about ninety seconds each time, and controllers lost radar and radio contact with the aircraft they were guiding; some took leave afterward, and Newark has operated under limits since. On 21 September 2026 an aging circuit failed, and its backup, which had been cut that morning, was found cut when the system switched to it. Five airports in the region stopped traffic for most of a day, and about 7,000 flights were affected. No one suggests an attack; the record speaks of old equipment and an accidental cut. The lesson does not depend on the cause. A control room is only as good as the lines that feed it, two paths are only two if they are separate in route and in time, and a backup that is lost without anyone knowing is not a backup. Any operation whose people sit in one place and whose systems run in another has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Chatsworth Collision, September 2008
what: On 12 September 2008, a Metrolink commuter train left Chatsworth station in Los Angeles, passed a red signal, and ran head-on into a Union Pacific freight train on single track; twenty-five people were killed. The signal system worked as designed and held the stop, but nothing stopped the train once its engineer, distracted by text messaging against company rules on the Board's finding, passed the signal. Congress required positive train control five weeks later, and it was in operation on every required route mile by the end of 2020.
tier: Not a deliberate act: a person's passage of a stop correctly given, in territory with no enforcement, below the threshold for the military-action tier. The probable cause is the National Transportation Safety Board's.

findings.title: The control plane granted the stop and held it.
findings.text: The signals and control logic did their job; the stop was correctly given and enforced in the field.

findings.title: Chatsworth is a limit passed, not a proceed granted.
findings.text: No one gave the train permission to move; it passed the limit of the permission it had, a case that can be stopped only at the movement.

findings.title: The enforcement the class requires is the enforcement the event needed.
findings.text: Positive train control would have stopped the train before it passed the signal.

findings.title: The duration is a braking distance, not the time to the conflict.
findings.text: Enforcement must act before the point from which a train can no longer stop, not after the signal is passed.

findings.title: Enforcement independence has two parts.
findings.text: Enforcement must be independent both of the person and of the signal system whose knowledge it enforces.

findings.title: A check by a person or a rule is not a layer independent of the person.
findings.text: Every check on the engineer was another person or a rule, and none could stop the train.

findings.title: The enforcement can still be absent, exempt, or cut out.
findings.text: Places and modes without active enforcement remain, and each should be treated as an accepted risk.

findings.title: The indication must be legible where the person decides.
findings.text: The red signal could not reliably be read from the station where the train departed.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its correction of the facility class's account of the event went to the class as an erratum.

annex.p: This annex is for railroads, passenger and freight, and their dispatch centers, and for transit systems whose trains are governed by signals a person must obey. It is also for any owner, in any sector, whose operation relies on a person stopping where a signal says to stop. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
On every track you run, is there enforcement that stops a train short of a red signal or a misaligned switch without depending on the crew? Where is it absent, exempt, or switched off?
A person who errs is held by nothing. A.3.1.
Does your enforcement act on a prediction of braking, so that it stops the train short of the limit rather than after the train has passed it?
Enforcement acts when it is already too late to stop. A.3.1.
When positive train control is suspended, or fails while a train is enroute, how is the return to active enforcement made, and at what speed may the train continue meanwhile?
The train runs as Chatsworth’s did, with nothing behind the crew. A.3.1.

Which of your checks on the person at the controls depend on another person or a rule, such as repeat-back, operating rules, device bans, efficiency tests, or recordings reviewed afterward, and are any of them counted as a layer that would stop a train?
A rule is counted as a barrier. A.3.2.
Can the signal that governs a departure be read from where trains stop to depart, or is the crew shown the governing indication in the cab?
Crews leave on a signal they cannot see. A.3.2.
Does your enforcement know where trains are from a source other than the signal system it enforces?
The enforcement would carry out a false clear faithfully. A.3.3.
Can responders rapidly enter your locomotive cabs after a collision?
Rescue is slowed at the cab door. A.3.3.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Enforce the Stop Where People Can Fail

annex.p: The Rail Safety Improvement Act of 2008 requires positive train control on the main lines it names (49 U.S.C. 20157); the Federal Railroad Administration’s rule requires each system to prevent train-to-train collisions and movement through a misaligned switch (49 CFR 236.1005), and the Administration announced it in operation on every required route mile on 29 December 2020. In 2023 the National Transportation Safety Board found limits that remain: terminal exceptions, limits in knowing where trains are during restricted-speed operation, and switching-mode software that can disable signal enforcement near a switching operation. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-3, F-4, and F-7: make enforcement stop the train short of the limit, acting on its braking distance; treat every place and mode without active enforcement as a risk you have accepted on the record; make the return to active enforcement after a suspension an engineering control, as the Board recommended; and set the speed of a train running without enforcement by how far ahead its crew can read its signals.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Do Not Count People and Rules as Barriers

annex.p: The Federal Railroad Administration restricted on-duty use of electronic devices by emergency order in October 2008 and by rule in 2010, and its rule of 12 October 2023 requires image recorders on passenger locomotives by 12 October 2027. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-6 and F-8: count repeat-backs, operating rules, device bans, efficiency tests, and recordings as monitoring, not as a layer that would stop a train; and make the indication a crew decides on legible where the decision is made, by an in-cab display or by signals shown to be readable from where trains stop.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Know What Your Enforcement Knows

annex.p: This step is this instrument’s, from F-1 and F-5, with the note on cab entry that F-9 sends to Conveyances and Fleet. Know whether your enforcement learns where trains are only from the signal system it enforces, and credit it as independent of that system only to the extent it knows occupancy from another source; and make sure responders can enter your locomotive cabs quickly after a collision.

On the afternoon of 12 September 2008, a Metrolink commuter train left Chatsworth station in Los Angeles, accelerated past a red signal, and ran head-on into a Union Pacific freight train on single track. Twenty-five people were killed. The signal system had done its job: the signal was red, and the control logic would not have let it show anything else. The National Transportation Safety Board found that the engineer, distracted by text messaging against company rules, did not respond to it, and that positive train control would have stopped the train. Every check on him was another person or a rule; the signal could not reliably be seen from the station, and nothing could stop the train once he passed it. Congress required positive train control five weeks later, and it was in operation on every required route mile by the end of 2020; in 2023 the Board found that gaps remain, in places it does not cover, in modes that switch it off, and in knowing where trains are. The lesson is that where a person can fail, only a layer that does not depend on that person will stop the movement, and every place where that layer is absent or switched off is a place where this can happen again. Any operation that relies on a person stopping where a signal says to stop has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Fort Totten Collision, June 2009
what: On 22 June 2009, two Washington Metrorail trains collided on the Red Line near Fort Totten station, and nine people were killed. A track circuit had begun to report its section clear with a train in it, because of a spurious signal inside the equipment, so the stopped train became invisible to the automatic train control, which told the following train to proceed at 55 miles an hour. The same kind of failure had nearly caused collisions near Rosslyn in 2005, and Metrorail ran its trains by hand for about fifteen years after the collision.
tier: Not a deliberate act: the National Transportation Safety Board found no indication of tampering or vandalism. It is an accidental wrong grant of movement by automation, made on a false report that a section of track was clear, below the threshold for the military-action tier.

findings.title: The failure was one the system could not see.
findings.text: The track circuit reported clear with a train in it, and the system had no way to know the report was wrong.

findings.title: Independence can be built from memory, and must act on the grant.
findings.text: A check that remembered where trains had been could have caught the error, but only if it acted on the movement rather than only alerting someone.

findings.title: The test as installed, and the field change that defeated it.
findings.text: The circuit passed a test that did not exercise its failure, after a routine field change made the failure constant.

findings.title: A near-loss of separation by automation is the event realized short of collision.
findings.text: The near-misses at Rosslyn in 2005 should have been treated as the event itself and fixed everywhere.

findings.title: The indication of a lost train was made ordinary.
findings.text: Thousands of minor, self-cancelling alarms a week hid the warning that a train had vanished.

findings.title: The transit regime answers this event, and the withdrawal of automation is a derating.
findings.text: Federal transit safety oversight followed this event, and running by hand for fifteen years was a loss of capacity.

findings.title: The supplier owed a statement of wrong-side failures, and the module was a common mode.
findings.text: Suppliers should declare how their equipment can fail unsafely, and a failure in one unit should be presumed in all units of its kind.

findings.title: A falsified vacancy is a falsified proceed.
findings.text: In an automated system, a false report that track is clear is a permission to move, and should be protected as one.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its finding on protecting passengers in a collision is referred to the class that holds the vehicles.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its correction of the facility class's account of the event went to the class as an erratum.

annex.p: This annex is for transit systems and railroads whose trains are kept apart by automatic train control resting on track circuits or other detection, and for the suppliers of that equipment. It is also for any owner, in any sector, whose automated system grants movement on what a sensor reports. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Could your train detection report a section of track clear with a train in it, and would your system know that it was wrong?
The system grants a proceed into an occupied section. A.3.1.
Does your grant logic check a new vacancy against where trains were a moment before, and does any check with that memory act on the grant itself, automatically, rather than only alerting someone?
The knowledge that could stop the collision only reports it afterward. A.3.1.

Are your track circuits tested across their whole length for the failure modes your safety analysis names, at installation, after every change, and at a stated interval? Is a circuit ever returned to service with an unexplained fault?
The test passes while the failure waits in the middle of the circuit. A.3.2.
When a near-miss shows a failure your design did not consider, is it reported as such, entered in the safety analysis, and verified fixed at every unit of the same kind within a stated time?
The warning becomes a bulletin no one uses. A.3.2.

Has your supplier declared how its detection equipment can fail in the permissive direction and how to test for it, and is a failure found in one unit presumed in every unit of that model until each is tested?
One faulty module is fixed and its siblings wait. A.3.2.
How many detection alarms does your control center see in a week, are any of them self-cancelling, and do operators report unexplained losses of speed commands?
The alarm that matters is buried among thousands. A.3.3.
If you had to withdraw automatic operation pending assurance, how long would it take to restore it on a shown basis?
Capacity is lost for years without a plan to restore it. A.3.3.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Catch a Clear That Cannot Be True

annex.p: The National Transportation Safety Board recommended real-time evaluation of track occupancy that would automatically generate alerts and stop or restrict trains (R-09-6 and R-09-7). These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-1, F-2, and F-8: make the system treat a train that disappears from the circuits without appearing beyond them, or a section that clears with a train tracked into it, as occupied, and stop or restrict the movement behind it; count a check as protection only where it acts on the grant automatically within the time it has; and protect the indications from which the system computes a proceed as carefully as any command channel.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Test for the Failure That Hides, and Act on the Near-Miss

annex.p: The failure mode found at Fort Totten was advised to every transit operator using such circuits. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-3, F-4, and F-7: test detection across the whole circuit for the failure modes your safety analysis names, at installation, after every change, and at a stated interval, and do not return a circuit to service with an unexplained fault; report a near-loss of separation as the event itself realized short of collision, enter its failure mode in the safety analysis, and verify the fix at every unit of the same kind within a stated time; and ask suppliers to declare how their equipment can fail in the permissive direction and how to test for it.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Keep the Critical Alarm Critical

annex.p: The Federal Transit Administration’s Safety Directive 15-1 of 2015 required the Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority to sort its control-center alarms into critical and non-critical. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-5 and F-6: treat the loss of detection under a tracked train as critical, presented until acknowledged and acted on and never self-cancelling, with false alarms held to a rate operators can still act on; have operators report losses of speed commands that the movement ahead does not explain; and count the withdrawal of automatic operation as a loss of capacity with a plan to restore it on a shown basis.

On the afternoon of 22 June 2009, two Washington Metrorail trains collided on the Red Line near Fort Totten station, and nine people were killed. A track circuit, the equipment that tells the system a section of track is occupied, had begun to report its section clear with a train in it, because of a spurious electrical signal inside the equipment. A train stopped in that section became invisible to the system, which then told the following train, running automatically, to proceed at 55 miles an hour; its operator applied the emergency brake when the stopped train came into view, too late. The same kind of failure had nearly caused collisions near Rosslyn four years earlier, the fix devised then was not in general use, and the control center was receiving thousands of minor alarms a week that hid the warning. The National Transportation Safety Board found no sign of tampering. Metrorail ran its trains by hand for about fifteen years afterward. The lesson is that an automated system can be wrong without knowing it, and that before it grants movement it must check what its sensors report against what it already knows. Any operation whose automation grants movement on what a sensor reports has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Unauthorized Radio-Stop Broadcasts on the Polish Railways, August 2023
what: On the evening of 25 August 2023, someone without authority broadcast the emergency stop signal over the Polish railway's analog train radio near Szczecin, and every equipped train in range braked automatically. About twenty trains were delayed or halted and freight was stopped for hours; no one was hurt, and no source identifies the sender. Similar broadcasts followed across Poland over the next few days, and the railway records hundreds of unauthorized uses of the signal a year.
tier: A deliberate, unauthorized act, but not military action on the record: no authority has stated that the broadcast near Szczecin was a state's act. It is an injected command on an unauthenticated channel that could carry only a stop.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its correction of the facility class's account of the event went to the class as an erratum.

findings.title: A stop-only channel is abused at a rate.
findings.text: Unauthorized stops numbered hundreds a year, so the channel's risk should be judged at that rate, not for one event.

findings.title: A stop is not harmless everywhere.
findings.text: A sudden stop is safe in most places but not for a heavy train on a grade or a train on a bridge.

findings.title: Migration is not closure.
findings.text: The replacement digital system is years late, and the old channel stays open where it is not yet in service.

findings.title: The proceed after the stop travels on the same channel.
findings.text: The instruction to restart is given by voice on the same open radio, and should be protected.

findings.title: The reach is the network's, and closing it is not the railway's alone.
findings.text: The same design runs on every line, and finding a transmitter depends on the spectrum regulator and the police.

annex.p: This annex is for railways and other operators whose vehicles can be commanded over a radio channel, above all analog train radio with an emergency stop function, and for the spectrum regulators and police who can find a transmitter. It is also for any owner, in any sector, whose safety function can be triggered by anyone with a transmitter. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Can a radio or other channel that commands your vehicles be reached by a transmitter that is not yours? Does it authenticate its commands, or can it carry only a stop?
Anyone in range can command your vehicles. A.3.1.
How many unauthorized uses of that channel do you see in a year, and how much traffic do they stop?
The abuse is treated as an incident when it is a rate. A.3.1.
Where along your lines would a sudden stop carry consequences beyond delay, such as heavy trains on grades or trains stopped on bridges?
A stop that is safe in most places is dangerous in a few. A.3.2.
After an unauthorized stop, how is the instruction to proceed delivered, and could the same outsider send it?
The restart travels on the same open channel. A.3.2.
Is the equipment that could send such a command on general sale, and who can find and stop an unauthorized transmitter, and how fast: your own staff, the spectrum regulator, or the police?
The sender is never found. A.3.3.
If you are moving to an authenticated system, how much of your network does it cover today, and is the old channel closed to outside transmitters where the new one runs?
Migration is counted as closure while the old door stays open. A.3.3.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Know Who Can Command Your Vehicles, and How Often They Do

annex.p: This step is this instrument’s, from F-2 and F-6. Know every channel by which a command reaches your vehicles and whether anyone outside can use it; count its unauthorized uses as a rate, in traffic stopped a year, not only as incidents; and count the exposure across every line that shares the same design.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Plan for the Stop Where It Hurts, and Protect the Restart

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-3 and F-5. Name the places and loads at which a sudden stop carries consequence beyond delay, and judge the channel’s risk for them; and deliver the instruction to proceed after an injected stop over an authenticated channel, or confirm it by a means the sender cannot reach.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Close the Old Channel, Not Just Build the New One

annex.p: Poland’s Ministry of Infrastructure has stated that each case is reported to the Office of Electronic Communications, the Railway Protection Service, and the police, who try to locate the transmitter; that dual-system radios at the traffic posts allow the signal to be coded; and that a modified alarm signal harder to imitate is to be studied and deployed after tests. PKP Polskie Linie Kolejowe accelerated the replacement of analog train radios with dual-system radios. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-4 and F-6: measure migration as the share of your network on which the old channel is closed to outside transmitters, not the share on which the new one exists; credit a modified signal only once it is shown to authenticate; and agree in advance with the spectrum regulator and the police how a transmitter will be found.

On the evening of 25 August 2023, someone without authority broadcast the emergency stop signal over the Polish railway’s analog train radio near Szczecin, and every equipped train in range braked automatically. About twenty trains were delayed or halted and freight was stopped for hours; no one was hurt, and no source identifies the sender. Similar broadcasts followed across Poland over the next few days. The old radio system lets anyone with a transmitter on general sale send the stop, and the railway has recorded hundreds of such uses a year, more than a thousand in 2024 on its count as reported. Because the channel could carry only a stop, the worst an outsider could do was halt trains, not send them into danger, which is why no one was hurt. But a sudden stop is not harmless everywhere, the instruction to restart travels by voice on the same open channel, and the replacement digital system is years late and, on the railway’s own list, does not yet cover the lines involved. No authority has stated that the broadcast near Szczecin was a state’s act. The lessons are that a channel anyone can reach will be used at a rate, not once, and that building a new system does not close the old one. Any operation whose vehicles can be commanded over a channel outsiders can reach has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: Nationwide Ground Stop of 13 November 2026
what: On the afternoon of 13 November 2026, the network that carries radar and communications data to the Federal Aviation Administration's air traffic control facilities became unstable, and the agency stopped every departure in the United States for about four hours and twenty minutes. On the Secretary of Transportation's account, a router being installed during routine maintenance at one remote site flooded other routers with connection attempts, and within about forty-five minutes 17 of the 22 enroute centers were affected. About 4,000 aircraft already in the air landed, nearly 5,000 flights were cancelled that day, and officials said there was no sign of a cyberattack; the investigation continues.
tier: Not a deliberate act on the record. It is an accidental loss of the links of most of the country's enroute centers at once, below the threshold for the military-action tier. The determination is provisional, because no official cause has been published and the investigation has not ruled out an attack.

findings.title: Independence across facilities.
findings.text: One network carried every center's links, so when it failed no center was left to take over another's airspace.

findings.title: The governed change stops one layer too high.
findings.text: Changes to the network that many facilities share, including maintenance, modernization, and security patches, are not governed the way changes to shared information systems already are.

findings.title: The reach of the protective stop.
findings.text: Stopping every departure was the right call, but the design basis does not bound how much of the nation's movement one loss of confidence may stop, or for how long.

findings.title: What the record does not show: contact with the aircraft aloft.
findings.text: The record does not yet show how controllers kept contact with the aircraft in the air or handed them between centers.

annex.p: This annex is for the operators of control facilities and of the networks that connect them, in aviation and in the other modes the class covers: rail dispatch and train control, vessel traffic services and transit control centers. It is also for any owner whose sites share one network, in any sector. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Do all of your control sites, and the sites that would take over from them, reach their radios, surveillance and data over one network?
One event can take every site and every backup together. A.3.1.
Can one software, configuration or security-patch change to that network be applied to every site at the same time? Who approves it, and is it tried on some sites first?
The change pathway is a single point of failure. A.3.2.
If the network’s equipment began giving inconsistent data, would you know before your people did, and is there a reading that does not pass through it?
The loss of confidence is found by the operators, late. A.3.2.

If every site lost the network at once, could your sites still talk to each other, and to the people moving, over something that shares nothing with it? When was that last practiced with the network assumed lost?
Coordination depends on the thing that failed. A.3.3.
If you had to stop movement, could you stop only the part affected, or only all of it?
Every partial loss becomes a total stop. A.3.4.
If your whole operation had to stop, how long could it stay stopped before safety itself began to suffer: crews out of hours, people stranded, time-critical loads at risk?
The restoration time has not been set against the safety consequence. A.3.4.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Know What Your Sites Share

annex.p: No authority has yet published an action from this event; this step is this instrument’s, from F-1. List, for each control site and for its backup site, the network, the carrier and the equipment by which its radios, surveillance and data arrive, and mark what every site has in common. Whatever is on every line is what one event can take from all of them.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Govern Changes to the Shared Network

annex.p: This step is this instrument’s, from F-2. A change to a network that carries more than one site’s links should be approved as a change to every site it reaches, tried on a part of the network first, held there long enough to show it works, and only then spread, with a way back. Maintenance and modernization are such changes, and so is a patch: on the Transportation Secretary’s account, a router installed during routine maintenance at one site unsettled 17 of 22 enroute centers on 13 November 2026. The agency’s own rule for its notice system after January 2023, which the class records at §4.3, is the model; this event suggests that it applies one layer down.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Practice Without the Network

annex.p: The class’s communications requirements ask that sites be able to speak to the people moving and to each other over means that share nothing with the primary network, and that this be exercised with the network assumed lost (CDB-3, CDB-4, CDB-5, CDB-7). Practice the case where every site loses the network at once, not only where one does.

annex.h3: A.3.4 Design How Much You Will Have to Stop

annex.p: This step is this instrument’s, from F-3. The agency’s stop was the safe choice, and an operator should make the same choice when its data cannot be trusted. When the question is safety, cost does not enter the decision on the day. Cost belongs in the design, before the day: look for a cost-effective way to be just as safe, so that a loss confined to part of the network can be met by a stop confined to part of the operation, safely, and not the whole of it.

On the afternoon of 13 November 2026, the network that connects the country’s air traffic control centers failed. Officials said that a router being installed during routine maintenance at one remote site flooded the network with connection attempts, and older routers began giving inconsistent data; 17 of the 22 high-altitude centers were affected. The agency did the safe thing: it stopped every departure in the country rather than move aircraft on information it could not trust, and about 4,000 aircraft already in the air landed safely. The stop lasted over four hours and nearly 5,000 flights were cancelled. Officials said there was no sign of a cyberattack, and the investigation continues. The lesson does not depend on the cause. Every center depended on the same network, so when it failed there was no center left to take over, and one change to that network, made to improve it, reached most of them at once. Any operation whose sites share one network has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Aliso Canyon Gas Release, October 2015 to February 2016
what: On 23 October 2015 gas began leaking from well SS-25 at the Southern California Gas Company's Aliso Canyon storage field beside Porter Ranch, Los Angeles, after its production casing, the only barrier between the stored gas and the surface, ruptured from external corrosion. Seven surface kills failed, and the release lasted about sixteen weeks until a relief well sealed it in February 2016. Thousands of households were relocated, and the field, about two-thirds of the company's storage capacity, returned in 2017 only at reduced capacity.
tier: Not an attack: a well integrity failure and blowout with no actor.

findings.title: Well control is bounded by the relief well where the casing is the only barrier.
findings.text: Surface kills failed for two months, and only the relief well stopped the release.

findings.title: The first consequence of a storage blowout falls beside the field.
findings.text: Thousands of households left their homes for months.

findings.title: A return to service may be a permanent derating.
findings.text: The field has never returned to its former capacity.

findings.title: A field's share of its region sets the cascade, whatever removes it.
findings.text: Its loss raised the risk of gas shortages to power plants.

annex.p: This annex is for operators of underground natural gas storage, in depleted reservoirs, aquifers, and salt caverns, for the utilities and power plants that depend on their sendout, and for the communities beside them. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Do you know the condition of every well’s casing, including corrosion from outside it, and have earlier casing leaks been investigated?
A casing fails that you had reason to suspect. A.3.1.
Does any well flow through both its tubing and its casing, so that the casing is the only barrier between the stored gas and the surface?
One failure releases the field’s gas. A.3.1.
Do your wells have real-time pressure monitoring?
A leak is found only when it reaches the surface. A.3.1.
If a surface kill failed, how long would a relief well take, and is that time in your plan?
The release lasts months while the relief well is drilled. A.3.2.
Have you planned with the neighboring community for a release that lasts months?
Thousands of households leave their homes without a plan. A.3.2.
How much of your region’s storage and sendout does your field carry, and what happens to power plants and customers if it is lost or derated for years?
The field’s loss becomes the region’s shortage. A.3.3.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Remove the Single Barrier, and Monitor the Wells

annex.p: The federal task force made 44 recommendations in October 2016, among them phasing out designs in which a single point of failure stands between the stored gas and the surface. The Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration issued an interim final rule on 19 December 2016, under the PIPES Act of 2016, incorporating the American Petroleum Institute’s recommended practices 1170 and 1171 for storage in salt caverns and in depleted reservoirs and aquifers, and California’s Division adopted emergency regulations for every storage well in the state. On return to service the field’s remaining wells were fitted with tubing and packers and real-time pressure monitoring. No step of this instrument’s is added here.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Plan Well Control to the Relief Well, and Plan With the Community

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1 and F-2. Where the casing is the only barrier, bound well control by the time to drill a relief well, not by surface kills; and plan with the neighboring community for a release that lasts months, since the first consequence falls beside the field.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Plan for Derating, and State the Field’s Share

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-3 and F-4. Plan for a return to service that may be a permanent derating; and state the field’s share of its region’s storage and sendout, which sets the cascade whatever removes the field.
