On 23 October 2015, the Southern California Gas Company found gas leaking from well SS-25 at its Aliso Canyon storage field, beside the Porter Ranch community of Los Angeles. The root-cause analysis found the well’s production casing had ruptured, thinned by corrosion from groundwater outside it; gas flowed through the casing as well as the tubing, so the casing was the only barrier, there was no real-time pressure monitoring, and more than sixty earlier casing leaks had not been investigated. Seven attempts to kill the well from the surface failed, and the release lasted about sixteen weeks until a relief well sealed it in February 2016. Thousands of households were relocated and a state of emergency proclaimed. The field held about two-thirds of the company’s storage capacity; its loss raised the risk of gas shortages to power plants, and it returned in 2017 only at reduced capacity, and has never returned to its former size. No one attacked anything. A federal task force and the pipeline safety regulator then required wells to have more than one barrier and be monitored. The lessons are that a well with a single barrier is a field with a single failure, that well control is bounded by the time to drill a relief well, and that a field’s loss may be permanent. Any storage operator has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this field does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Attack on the Metcalf Transmission Substation, near San Jose, California, 16 April 2013
date_full: 16 April 2013 (record open as to the investigation)
what: In the early hours of 16 April 2013 AT&T's and Level 3's cables were cut in two vaults near the Pacific Gas and Electric Company's 500 kV Metcalf substation, and from about 1:37 a.m. gunfire from outside the perimeter struck seventeen transformers for about nineteen minutes, draining their cooling oil; police arrived at 1:51 with the attackers gone. Telephone service in nearby towns was lost for about a day and 911 calls in the Gilroy area for a couple of hours; the utility's own SCADA held. Power was rerouted, there were no outages, and the station was back in service after 27 days. The attack led to the CIP-014 physical-security standard.
tier: Deliberate adversarial, below the tier: intentionality and precision established, persistence and denial not established.

findings.title: The class's account is corrected.
findings.text: Metcalf is a 500 kV station, the nine-substation analysis is an unreleased staff study reported in the press, the attack began with a cut to the area's communications, and the station was back in 27 days.

findings.title: A transformer's cooling is repaired in weeks.
findings.text: Damage to cooling made the transformers inoperative and was repaired in 27 days; the class's two-year figure belongs to destroyed transformers, not to this event.

findings.title: Persistence is read from the adversary.
findings.text: The attackers stayed about nineteen minutes, and the record shows no return; a transformer's lead time is how long a consequence lasts, not a characteristic of the attacker.

findings.title: An attack can begin with the area's communications.
findings.text: Two carriers' cables were cut in vaults within sight of each other; the alarms came through on a backup path the attacker missed, and the carriers' outages were never joined to the attack across sectors.

findings.title: Protection is measured in minutes.
findings.text: Police arrived fourteen minutes after the fence alarm, which came among alarms the wind had been setting off; a perimeter alarm that wind can trip cannot tell anyone that a person is at the fence.

annex.p: This annex is for owners and operators of transmission substations, the transmission operators and reliability coordinators who operate the system around them, and the law enforcement agencies and telecommunications carriers on whom a station’s protection depends. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to an owner. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an owner answers about its own stations (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an owner can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one station. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the station; it is that station’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
If the telecommunications cables near one of your stations were cut, every carrier’s along the same route, would its alarms still reach your security monitoring and law enforcement?
An attack begins with no one able to report it. A.3.2.
How long would an attack on a station’s transformers from outside its fence run before it was detected and answered, and has that been tested?
The attack is over before anyone arrives. A.3.2.
Has your CIP-014 security plan assessed whether the transformers’ cooling and other exposed equipment can be struck from outside the perimeter, and what shields them?
A few minutes’ attack takes transformers out of service. A.3.1.
If a station’s transformers were made inoperative but not destroyed, do you hold the spare parts, oil, and crews to return them in weeks, and do you know what damage would mean replacement instead?
A repairable outage becomes a long one. A.3.2.
Could the system around each critical station carry its load for a month while it is repaired?
The loss of one station becomes an outage for the load it serves. A.3.1.
Do your security staff know your alarms, and is every alarm that sounds acted on and reviewed?
An intrusion goes unnoticed while the alarms sound. A.3.2.
Do your station’s alarms have a backup path that shares no route with the primary paths, and has anyone checked what an outsider could see of it?
An attacker who finds every path can silence the station. A.3.2.
If a carrier’s cables were cut at a vault near one of your stations, would you hear of it while it was happening, and from whom?
The first move of an attack is seen by another sector and never reaches you. A.3.2.
Can your perimeter alarms tell weather from a person, and what do operators do when they cannot?
The alarm that matters arrives among alarms people have learned to dismiss. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: After the attack NERC’s Electricity Sector Information Sharing and Analysis Center issued an alert to the industry on steps to mitigate and protect against such attacks, and the Department of Energy and the Department of Homeland Security, with the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Commission, and NERC, briefed utilities, states, and law enforcement on the attack in thirteen cities. The Commission’s order of 7 March 2014 and its Order No. 802 of 20 November 2014 put CIP-014 in place: owners and operators of the most critical facilities identify them, assess the threats and vulnerabilities to them, and put security plans in place that are independently reviewed, and the standard has since been revised. The Spare Transformer Equipment Program, launched by the Edison Electric Institute in 2006, has its participants maintain spare transformers to share after a triggering event (Congressional Research Service). The utility’s own program after the attack, of perimeter barriers, equipment shielding, cameras, and vegetation clearing, is its own account. Each is its author’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Keep the Alarm Path Off the Local Lines, Measure the Response, and Plan the Repair

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-2, F-4, and F-5. Give a station’s alarms at least two physically separate routes to its security monitoring and law enforcement, counting routes and not carriers, keep a backup path that shares no route with them, and test them with the local routes out, on the assumption that an attacker will look for every path; arrange with the carriers, or through the sectors’ information sharing centers, to learn of an outage near a station while it is happening; make perimeter detection tell weather from a person, so that nuisance alarms are reduced at their source rather than silenced; measure the station’s protection by how quickly an attack is detected and answered, and test that too; and plan the repair of damage to transformers’ cooling in weeks, with the spares and crews it needs, as a case separate from the replacement of a destroyed transformer.

In the early hours of 16 April 2013, someone cut two carriers’ telecommunications cables in vaults near the Metcalf substation, a 500 kilovolt station of the Pacific Gas and Electric Company south of San Jose. Shortly afterwards, gunfire from outside the fence struck seventeen transformers for about nineteen minutes, draining their cooling oil, and the attackers were gone before police arrived fourteen minutes after the fence alarm. Telephone and internet service in nearby towns was lost for about a day, and 911 calls in the Gilroy area failed for a couple of hours. Grid operators rerouted power and asked the public to conserve, no customer lost power, and the station was back in service after 27 days. The station’s alarms reached the control center over a backup path the attackers did not account for, but they arrived among alarms the wind had been setting off all night, and the carriers’ outages were never joined to the attack outside the two sectors that saw them. No arrest has been reported. The attack led federal regulators to require a physical-security standard for the most critical stations. The lessons are that an attack on a station can begin by cutting the communications of its area, and two carriers cut at one place are one path, not two, that a station’s alarms need a path an attacker cannot see and must be able to tell a person from the wind, that protection is measured by how fast an attack is detected and answered, and that a month’s repair is a different problem from losing a transformer for two years. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own stations, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The BP Texas City Refinery Explosion, Texas City, Texas, 23 March 2005
date_full: 23 March 2005 (record open as to one recommendation)
what: During the startup of the isomerization unit at BP's Texas City refinery, operators overfilled a distillation tower for more than three hours while its level gauge showed the level falling and a backup alarm stayed silent. Relief valves discharged into a drum and stack open to the air, the liquid thrown out formed a vapor cloud, and its ignition killed fifteen workers, all in or near trailers sited near the unit, and injured about 180. 43,000 people sheltered in place. The refinery's later long outage followed Hurricane Rita and an overhaul.
tier: Non-adversarial process-safety event: none of the four characteristics present.

findings.title: The class's account is corrected.
findings.text: All fifteen died in or near trailers, the damage reached buildings and tanks around the unit, and the refinery's long outage followed Hurricane Rita and an overhaul.

findings.title: The consequence is set by where people are.
findings.text: Every one of the fifteen dead was in or near a trailer close to the unit; the class counts units and production, not people.

findings.title: Operators were misled by their own instruments.
findings.text: The level gauge read falling as the tower filled and the backup alarm stayed silent, with no adversary present; the class treats false data only as an attacker's work.

findings.title: Startup is where the case lives.
findings.text: The explosion came in a startup run by fatigued operators with no supervisor present; the class names neither startup nor staffing.

findings.title: Relief to the open air becomes a release.
findings.text: The relief valves emptied into a stack open to the air, and the liquid it threw out became the vapor cloud; the class does not name relief systems.

annex.p: This annex is for owners and operators of petroleum refineries and of other plants that start up process units after turnarounds, the contractors who work beside those units, and the communities beside the plants. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to a refinery. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions a refinery answers about its own refinery (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account a refinery can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one refinery. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the refinery; it is that refinery’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Are any trailers or other portable buildings occupied within reach of a process unit’s blast, especially during startups and turnarounds?
People are where an explosion will reach them. A.3.1.
Before a unit starts up, are its level, pressure, and flow instruments and its alarms proved to work, and are faults reported during the turnaround repaired first?
Operators start up without knowing what the unit is doing. A.3.2.
Have readings beyond range, alarms, and relief-valve lifts in earlier startups been investigated?
A known near miss is repeated. A.3.2.
Do any relief valves discharge flammable material to a drum or stack open to the atmosphere?
A relief becomes a vapor cloud. A.3.1.
During a startup, is a technically qualified supervisor present throughout, and are operators’ consecutive shifts limited?
A startup runs on tired people with no one to ask. A.3.1.
Are vehicles and other ignition sources kept away from a unit while it starts up?
A vapor cloud finds an ignition source. A.3.1.
When you change staffing, budgets, or ownership, do you assess the effect on process safety?
Safety erodes without anyone deciding that it should. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: On the Board’s recommendations, the American Petroleum Institute issued RP 753 on the siting of portable buildings, which bars lightweight wooden trailers from hazardous areas and limits nonessential occupants of portable buildings nearby; RP 754 on process safety performance indicators; RP 755 on fatigue, which limits work hours and consecutive days; and the sixth edition of RP 521, which requires inherently safer alternatives to atmospheric blowdown where a vapor cloud explosion is a risk. OSHA’s Process Safety Management standard (29 CFR 1910.119) governs refineries, and the agency ran a national emphasis program for refineries on the Board’s recommendation. The Panel’s ten recommendations to the company address process safety leadership, expertise, accountability, performance indicators, and board monitoring. Each is its author’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Prove the Instruments Before Startup, and Assess Organizational Change

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-3 and F-4; the second follows the Board’s one open recommendation. Repair known instrument faults and prove the alarms before a unit starts up, and investigate earlier readings beyond range; and assess any change in staffing, budget, or ownership for its effect on process safety, whether or not a regulation yet requires it.

On 23 March 2005, at the BP refinery in Texas City, operators starting up the isomerization unit after maintenance filled a tall distillation tower with flammable liquid for more than three hours. Its level gauge showed the level falling while it rose, and a backup alarm did not sound. The rising pressure opened relief valves into a drum and stack open to the air; liquid erupted from the stack, the vapor was ignited, most likely by an idling pickup truck, and the explosion killed fifteen workers, all of them in or near trailers placed close to the unit, and injured about 180. Forty-three thousand people sheltered indoors. Investigators found instruments whose repair had been put off, years of overfilled startups that no one had investigated, fatigued crews, and a decision in 2002 not to connect the drum to a flare. No one intended any of it. The lessons are that people must not be placed where an explosion can reach them, that instruments must be proved before a startup, and that relief systems must not send flammable material into the open air. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own refinery, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The 911 Outages After the Derecho of June 2012
what: On the night of 29 June 2012 a derecho cut power across the Mid-Atlantic, and generators failed at two Verizon central offices in Northern Virginia, one of them untested under load for years. Fairfax County's 911 center, on its own generators, received no completed 911 call for seven hours, and nearly 1,900 calls were never routed to it. Across six states seventy-seven 911 centers serving more than 3.6 million people lost some service, and centers learned of it by the silence of their phones.
tier: Not a deliberate act: a windstorm's loss of commercial power outlasting backup, and the failure of call delivery upstream of the centers, below the threshold for the military-action tier.

findings.title: Detection of a silent failure must survive the loss of the power it watches.
findings.text: The carrier's own monitoring failed with the power, and centers found the outage themselves.

findings.title: Backup power is credited only when it has been shown to run.
findings.text: Generators that had not been load-tested failed to start or carry the load.

findings.title: Diversity is verified against the physical route.
findings.text: Circuits had single points of failure the records did not show.

findings.title: The degraded states between silence and service are planned.
findings.text: Calls returned without the caller's number or location, and backup numbers failed too.

findings.title: The area holds its own evidence of what lies upstream.
findings.text: 911 authorities should keep their own evidence of providers' measures, not rely only on certification.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its correction of the facility class's account of the event was taken in by the class.

annex.p: This annex is for 911 centers and the authorities that run them, and for the carriers and providers whose central offices, circuits, and monitoring deliver their calls. It is also for any owner, in any sector, whose critical service depends on equipment upstream that it does not own. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Has the backup power at your center, and at the carrier offices that deliver your calls, been shown to run under load, recently?
The generator does not start when the grid goes. A.3.1.
Have you checked the diversity of your 911 circuits and location links against their physical route, not only the carrier’s records?
Circuits recorded as diverse share one office. A.3.2.
Would the carrier’s monitoring of your service survive the loss of power it watches, and would you or the carrier detect that calls had stopped arriving?
Your phones go quiet, and no one notices for hours. A.3.3.
If your 911 calls stopped, how would you reach the carrier, by a channel that does not depend on the network that failed?
You learn of the outage before the carrier does, and cannot tell it. A.3.3.
Have you planned for calls that arrive without the caller’s number or location, and for telling the public how to reach you when 911 fails?
Calls come in that you cannot locate, and the backup number fails too. A.3.3.
Do you hold your own evidence of what your providers have done upstream, rather than relying only on their certification?
You find out what was upstream when it fails. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Know Your Backup Power Will Run

annex.p: In December 2013 the Federal Communications Commission required covered 911 service providers to take reasonable measures for the diversity of 911 circuits, backup power at the central offices that directly serve 911 centers, and diverse network monitoring, and to certify them each year; in June 2026 it decided to replace the annual certification with a one-time certification updated on material change. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-2: credit backup power, at your center and upstream, only when it has been shown to run under load, recently.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Check Diversity on the Ground, and Hold Your Own Evidence

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-3 and F-5. Verify that circuits recorded as diverse take different physical routes, and keep your own evidence of what your providers have done upstream, all the more now that certification is to be made once and updated on change.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Detect Silence, Reach the Carrier, and Plan the Degraded States

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1 and F-4. Make sure the detection of failed call delivery survives the loss of the power it watches; keep a way to reach your providers that does not depend on the failed network; and plan for calls arriving without number or location, and for an alternate number for the public that does not fail with your 911 lines.

On the night of 29 June 2012 a fast-moving windstorm, a derecho, cut power across the Mid-Atlantic. In Northern Virginia, generators failed at two of Verizon’s central offices, one because it had not been tested under load in years, and 911 calls stopped reaching the county centers they served. Fairfax County’s 911 center, operating on its own generators, received no completed 911 call for seven hours, and nearly 1,900 calls were never routed to it. Neighboring centers found out by the silence of their phones and told the carrier, which had lost its own monitoring. Across six states seventy-seven 911 centers serving more than 3.6 million people lost some service. The Federal Communications Commission then required providers to keep diverse circuits, backup power, and monitoring. The lessons are that backup power counts only if it has been shown to run, that diversity must be checked on the ground, and that a center must be able to detect, and report, the silence of its own phones. Any operation whose critical service depends on equipment upstream that it does not own has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Multistate 911 Outage of April 2014
what: On the night of 9 and 10 April 2014, a routing component at a 911 service provider reached the preset maximum of a counter it used to number calls, and stopped routing them. For about six hours more than 6,600 calls to 911 failed to reach a center, in 81 centers across seven states. A second routing center could have taken the calls at any moment, but no one recognized the failure, because the component's alarms were all rated minor.
tier: Not a deliberate act: a failure of call delivery upstream of the centers, in a shared routing function, below the threshold for the military-action tier.

findings.title: The transfer time was all recognition time.
findings.text: Switching to the backup took moments; recognizing the need took six hours.

findings.title: One element's side of the boundary is set by contract.
findings.text: Who answers for a routing function depends on the contract under which a center buys its 911 service.

findings.title: Detection belongs where the failure is visible, and is rated by consequence.
findings.text: The failure was visible at the routing function and rated minor.

findings.title: Redundancy that needs a person is not transfer, and failover is an action.
findings.text: A backup only a person can invoke does nothing until the failure is recognized.

findings.title: An alternate must not share the primary's design.
findings.text: The backup center carried a counter of the same kind.

findings.title: The class has no measure of concentration.
findings.text: One routing function failed for more than eleven million people across seven states.

findings.title: Notification requirements are right and hard to meet by procedure.
findings.text: Many centers were never told, and notification failed again in 2020.

findings.title: Silent exhaustion of an upstream resource is an attack route.
findings.text: A finite limit upstream can stop calls silently, and the design basis should guard against it.

annex.p: This annex is for 911 centers and the authorities that contract for their service, and for the providers that route and deliver 911 calls across many centers. It is also for any owner, in any sector, whose critical service runs through a function shared with many others. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Does any element upstream of your center have a finite resource, a counter, table, or license limit, that could run out and stop your calls without anyone being told?
Calls stop silently when a limit is reached. A.3.1.
Would the failure of call completion upstream be detected where it is visible, and rated by its consequence rather than by the state of a device?
Thousands of minor alarms, and no one acts for hours. A.3.1.
If your primary routing failed, would your calls move to the alternate on their own, or only when a person recognized the failure and invoked it?
The alternate stands ready for hours while no one knows to use it. A.3.2.
Does your alternate share the design of your primary, so that the same fault could stop both?
The backup fails for the same reason. A.3.2.
How many centers and people depend on the single routing function that serves you, and who is responsible for it under your contract?
One element fails for millions across states, and no one is clearly accountable to you. A.3.3.
If your provider’s service failed, would you be told promptly, at a current address, by someone who can say what is wrong?
You are not told, or told wrongly, and wait on hold. A.3.3.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Find the Limits Upstream, and Rate Alarms by Consequence

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-3 and F-8. Ask each provider in your call path what finite resources could stop your calls if exhausted, and how close they run to their limits; and require that the failure of call completion be detected where it is visible and rated by its consequence, so that a failure stopping 911 is never a minor alarm.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Make Failover Automatic, and the Alternate Different

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1, F-4, and F-5. Count the time to recognize a failure in your transfer time; require that transfer to an alternate happen without waiting for a person where the failure is upstream; and make sure the alternate does not share the primary’s design.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Know Your Concentration, Your Contract, and Your Notice

annex.p: After the outage, consent decrees of 2015 required the providers involved to keep current contact information for 911 centers and to notify them promptly; in 2020 a further outage at the same provider was again notified late or incompletely. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-2, F-6, and F-7: know how many centers and people depend on each element that serves you; make clear in your contract who answers for each function in your call path; and test notification, since procedure and contract alone have not made it reliable.

On the night of 9 and 10 April 2014, a routing component at a 911 service provider in Colorado reached the preset maximum of a counter it used to number calls, and stopped routing them. For about six hours more than 6,600 calls to 911 failed to reach a center, in 81 centers across seven states; more than 11 million people were potentially unable to reach help, and every county in Washington State was affected. A second routing center in Florida could have taken the calls at any moment, and switching to it restored service almost at once, but no one recognized what had failed: the component issued thousands of alarms, all rated minor. Many centers were never told, and some were told wrongly. The Federal Communications Commission found that the move to centralized 911 routing had concentrated the risk. The lessons are that a finite limit upstream can stop calls silently, that a backup only a person can invoke does nothing until the failure is recognized, and that the more centers depend on one function, the more one failure costs. Any operation whose critical service runs through a function shared with many others has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The 911 Call Flood of October 2016
what: In late October 2016 a link posted to social media made iPhones dial 911 again and again without their users meaning to. One 911 center west of Phoenix received more than a hundred hang-up calls within minutes and was said to be in immediate danger of losing service, and calls reached centers in at least a dozen states. The flood eased when the page and the account were taken down at the police's request, and the phone's maker closed the route five months later.
tier: A deliberate act, not established in its intent and not military action: a flood of calls beyond a center's capacity, induced through ordinary phones.

findings.title: The flood began at a device that could call without its user, and was closed there.
findings.text: The defense lay where the call begins, outside the 911 system.

findings.title: A generated flood is recognized by behavior, not identity.
findings.text: The calls came from many real phones and could be told apart only by how they behaved.

findings.title: Stopping the source is part of the design duration, and belongs to others.
findings.text: The flood lasted until a hosting company and a platform acted.

findings.title: An induced flood is measured by its distribution.
findings.text: The flood's reach was the link's audience, not a number of devices.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its correction of the facility class's account of the event went to the class as an erratum.

findings.title: A human act at the point of origin is a safeguard common to two events.
findings.text: Like the false alert in Hawaii, the remedy was a confirmation before the act.

annex.p: This annex is for 911 centers and the authorities that run them, and for the makers of phones and the platforms whose links can cause devices to call. It is also for any owner, in any sector, whose service must answer every request and cannot refuse one. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Could a flood of calls to your center be started by devices that call without their users meaning to, and who would be able to close that route?
You cannot stop the flood at your own edge. A.3.1.
Would you recognize a generated flood by the behavior of the calls, short, silent, hang-up, immediate redial, rather than by the numbers they come from?
A flood from many real phones looks like many real callers. A.3.2.
Since you may not refuse a call, how many calls can you take before you are in danger of losing service, and what would you do then?
The center is overwhelmed with no plan for the moment. A.3.2.
Do you know who could take down the source of a flood, a hosting company, a platform, a device maker, and how fast you could reach them?
The flood lasts as long as it takes to find who can stop it. A.3.3.
Would you know where the people being induced to call are concentrated, so that you and your neighbors could prepare?
The flood lands wherever the audience is dense. A.3.3.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Defend Where the Call Begins

annex.p: No authority has published an action for 911 centers from this event; the route was closed at the handset by its maker five months later. This step is this instrument’s, from F-1 and F-6: the most effective defense against a generated flood lies where the call begins, in a device that asks its user before placing a call from a link, and 911 authorities should press for that safeguard, as they did for the confirmation of alerts after the false alert in Hawaii.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Recognize the Flood by Behavior

annex.p: This step is this instrument’s, from F-2. Train and equip your center to recognize a generated flood by the behavior of the calls rather than their numbers, and plan what you will do when calls approach the level at which you would lose service, since you may not refuse them.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Know Who Can Stop the Source, and Watch the Distribution

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-3 and F-4. Know in advance which hosting companies, platforms, and device makers could stop a source, and how to reach them quickly; and count the reach of an induced flood by the reach of whatever is inducing it, so that centers where its audience is dense can prepare.

In late October 2016 a link was posted to social media that made iPhones dial 911 again and again without their users meaning to. On the night of 25 October the 911 center of the Surprise Police Department, west of Phoenix, received more than a hundred hang-up calls within minutes, and the Maricopa County Sheriff’s Office said the center was in immediate danger of losing service; calls reached centers in at least a dozen states. No center could stop the flood: a 911 center cannot refuse a call, and the calls came from real phones. The flood eased when, at the police’s request, the hosting company removed the page and the account was shut down, and the route was closed at the handset by its maker five months later. The lessons are that a flood can be started by devices calling on their own, that it is recognized by its behavior rather than its numbers, and that the defense lies where the call begins. Any service that must answer every request has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Ransomware Attack on Baltimore's Computer-Aided Dispatch, March 2018
what: In March 2018, while troubleshooting another problem, Baltimore's technology staff changed a firewall and left a port on the city's computer-aided dispatch server open to the internet for about a day, and attackers running automated scans found it and installed ransomware. City and vendor staff took the server offline, and for seventeen to twenty-two hours units were dispatched by hand and by voice. 911 calls were still answered, because answering and radio did not depend on the dispatch server.
tier: A deliberate criminal attack, not military action: nothing in the record points to a state actor, and on the city's account the attackers did not choose dispatch but found an open door.

findings.title: A change to dispatch's protection is a governed act, even at one center.
findings.text: A firewall change made while troubleshooting left the dispatch server exposed.

findings.title: Answering survived because it did not depend on dispatch.
findings.text: 911 answering and radio kept working when dispatch was lost.

findings.title: The decision to take dispatch offline is prepared.
findings.text: Taking the server offline contained the attack, and who may decide it should be named in advance.

findings.title: The cost of dispatch by hand is measured, and the record is kept.
findings.text: Manual dispatch worked, but no one measured how long it took.

findings.title: An attacker need not choose dispatch to take it out.
findings.text: Dispatch exposed to the internet is found by attackers looking for anything.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its correction of the facility class's account of the event went to the class as an erratum.

annex.p: This annex is for 911 centers and the city and county technology teams that run their computer-aided dispatch, call handling, and radio systems. It is also for any owner, in any sector, whose operational system sits on a network its own staff can open to the internet. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known

Before the questions below: have you listed every dispatch, call-handling, and radio system, and every remote-access path to them that talks to the outside world, with the network it does so through (your own, a cellular carrier’s, or a vendor’s or integrator’s remote-support path) and the address it actually uses?
You cannot look at an exposure you have not listed, and a search of your own addresses can come back clean while equipment at someone else’s is open. A.3.3.

Can a change to the protection of your dispatch, call-handling, or radio systems, a firewall rule, a remote-access path, an exception made while troubleshooting, be made without authorization, a check, and an expiry?
A port is left open to the internet, and someone finds it. A.3.1.
Is your dispatch system reachable from the internet at all, so that attackers scanning for anything could find it?
Dispatch is taken out by an attacker who was not even looking for it. A.3.1.
If dispatch were lost, would 911 answering and radio keep working because they do not depend on it?
Losing dispatch takes answering with it. A.3.2.
Who may take dispatch offline on suspicion of compromise, on what indication, and how is the center told?
The decision waits on the right person while the attack spreads. A.3.2.
Have you practiced dispatch by hand and by voice for a full day, and do you measure how long calls and dispatches take while you do?
Manual operation is assumed to work, and its cost is never known. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Govern Every Change to Dispatch’s Protection

annex.p: No authority has published an action for owners that this instrument reads; the city’s account is its record. These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1 and F-5: treat any change to the protection of a dispatch, call-handling, or radio system, including an exception made while troubleshooting, as a governed act with authorization, a check, and an expiry; and keep dispatch off the internet, since attackers scanning for anything will find it.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Keep Answering Separate, Prepare the Shutdown, and Measure Manual Work

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-2, F-3, and F-4. Keep 911 answering and radio independent of dispatch by design, as Baltimore’s were; name in advance who may take dispatch offline on suspicion of compromise and how the center is told; and during manual operation, measure how long call handling and dispatch take, and keep the record.

annex.h3: A.3.3 List What Talks to the Outside, Then Look as an Attacker Would

annex.p: List first, then look. The inventory comes first because exposed equipment often sits outside your own address space: the opening on this record was a change made while troubleshooting, which no list drawn up before the change would show. List what answers now, not what was designed to, and look again after every change. Then look at each address on the list as an attacker would, by any of three routes, each its provider’s. Shodan and Censys each offer a search of the devices they have found answering on the internet, and a search limited to your own address blocks and the addresses on your list shows you what it would show anyone. In the United States, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency offers Cyber Hygiene Vulnerability Scanning, which scans the internet-facing assets an organization names and reports weekly, at no cost to governments and critical infrastructure organizations (cisa.gov, Cyber Hygiene Services). Your integrator and vendors can tell you what they can reach remotely, if you ask them. Whatever the look finds that is not on your list goes on it, and whatever need not talk to the outside should stop. The inventory and the look are a standing item in every annex whose event turned on equipment reachable from the internet, on the author’s direction of 15 November 2026; here they rest on elements I-1 and I-2, F-1, and F-5.

In March 2018, while troubleshooting another problem, Baltimore’s technology staff changed a firewall and left a port on the server running the city’s computer-aided dispatch open to the internet for about a day. Attackers running automated scans found it and installed ransomware. Staff detected the breach at 8:30 a.m. on Sunday 25 March, and city and vendor staff took the server offline. For seventeen to twenty-two hours, 911 calls were still answered, because answering and radio did not depend on the dispatch server, but units were dispatched by hand and by voice, and no one has measured what that cost in time. On the city’s account the attackers did not choose dispatch; they found an open door. The lessons are that every change to the protection of a dispatch system must be governed, however temporary, that answering must not depend on dispatch, and that manual operation must be practiced and measured. Any operation whose staff can open its systems to the internet has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Ransomware Attack on the City of Dallas, May 2023
what: Early on 3 May 2023, ransomware launched across the City of Dallas's network took its computer-aided dispatch and the systems around it out of service, after the attackers had entered about four weeks earlier through a service account in the city's domain and taken about 1.169 terabytes of data. 911 calls were still answered, but dispatchers relayed calls by radio from handwritten notes, and units lost mobile data, station alerting, maps, and address history. Dispatch returned to full automation on 11 May, eight days later.
tier: A deliberate criminal attack, not military action: the attackers were a criminal group seeking extortion, and dispatch was lost along with the city's other systems rather than chosen.

findings.title: Separation of dispatch includes identity and administration.
findings.text: The attackers reached dispatch through the city's shared domain and remote-management tools.

findings.title: Answering survived, again.
findings.text: 911 answering kept working when dispatch was lost.

findings.title: Dispatch by hand covers what is lost with the software.
findings.text: Manual dispatch did not replace station alerting, mobile data, maps, or address history.

findings.title: The cost of dispatch by hand is measured.
findings.text: The city and the unions gave different accounts of the effect, and no one measured it.

findings.title: After a city-wide attack, plan for a week.
findings.text: Dispatch took eight days to return to full automation.

findings.title: Data taken from the city is information about the response.
findings.text: The data taken included records bearing on the city's public-safety response.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its completion of the facility class's account of the event went to the class as an erratum.

annex.p: This annex is for 911 centers and the city and county technology teams that run computer-aided dispatch and the systems around it, mobile data, station alerting, maps, and records. It is also for any owner, in any sector, whose operational system shares an identity domain with the rest of its organization. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Can your dispatch systems be reached through the same identity domain, service accounts, and remote-management tools as the rest of your organization?
One ordinary account leads to dispatch. A.3.1.
Would you detect an intruder who had been inside your network for weeks before acting?
You learn of the intruder when dispatch goes down. A.3.1.
If dispatch were lost, would 911 answering keep working?
Losing dispatch takes answering with it. A.3.2.
Does your manual mode cover everything lost with dispatch: station alerting, updates to units, maps, records, and the history of an address?
Officers go into a call without knowing what happened there before. A.3.2.
Have you measured how long calls and dispatches take by hand, and could you sustain it for a week or more?
Manual operation runs for days with no idea of its cost. A.3.2.
Do you treat data taken from your network as information an attacker could use about your response?
The response plan leaves with the stolen files. A.3.1.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Separate Dispatch by Identity, and Treat Taken Data as Exposure

annex.p: No authority has published an action for owners that this instrument reads; the city’s report is its record. These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1 and F-6: separate dispatch from the rest of the organization by identity domain and administrative tools as well as by network; watch for an intruder who stays for weeks; and treat data taken from a network that holds public-safety records as information about the response.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Keep Answering Separate, Cover Every Lost Function, and Plan for a Week

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-2, F-3, F-4, and F-5. Keep 911 answering independent of dispatch; make the manual mode cover each function lost with dispatch, station alerting, unit updates, maps, records, and address history; measure the times of manual call handling and dispatch; and plan for about a week without automated dispatch after a city-wide attack, as Dallas needed eight days.

Early on 3 May 2023, ransomware launched across the City of Dallas’s network took its computer-aided dispatch and the systems around it out of service. On the city’s report, the attackers had entered about four weeks earlier through a basic service account in the city’s domain, moved through the network with legitimate remote-management tools, and taken an estimated 1.169 terabytes of data. 911 calls were still answered, but dispatchers relayed calls by radio from handwritten notes, and units lost mobile data, station alerting, maps, and the history of the addresses they were sent to. The city said the disruption was minimal; the unions said calls slipped through and units went to wrong locations; no one measured it. Dispatch returned to full automation eight days later. The attackers were a criminal group, not a state. The lessons are that dispatch must be separated from the rest of the city by identity as well as network, that manual operation must cover everything the software did, and that its cost must be measured. Any operation whose critical system shares accounts with the rest of the organization has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The False Ballistic Missile Alert in Hawaii, January 2018
what: At 8:07 on the morning of 13 January 2018, the Hawaii Emergency Management Agency sent a false alert to every phone, television, and radio in the state warning of an incoming ballistic missile. A drill had been started by a recorded call over the live warning path in the words of a real warning, and an officer sent a live alert through software in which live and test messages shared one menu. The correction that told people the alert was false came thirty-eight minutes later, and 911 centers received about 7,755 calls in an hour.
tier: Not an attack: no one intended the false alert to reach the public, and the event was an error in running a drill.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its first part is held as the instrument's attribution posture, and its correction of the facility class's account went to the class as an erratum.

findings.title: A counterfeit warning source is a route to a false alert that needs no compromise.
findings.text: A call in the words of a real warning was enough to start the alert.

findings.title: Drill isolation must cover the input as well as the output.
findings.text: The drill came over the live warning path.

findings.title: A second person is not a second holder.
findings.text: A second person reading the same screen would not have been independent of the operator.

findings.title: The time to authorize must fit inside the warning time.
findings.text: An authorization for a real missile warning must be obtainable in minutes.

findings.title: A cancellation is not a correction, and a prepared correction needs a stated trigger.
findings.text: Stopping the alert took five minutes; telling people it was false took thirty-eight.

findings.title: A wrong act loads the answering class and the networks that must undo it.
findings.text: The alert flooded 911 centers and saturated wireless networks.

annex.p: This annex is for the emergency management agencies that warn the public, the operators of their alerting software, and the warning points that receive notice of attack. It is also for any owner, in any sector, who can send a message or take an action with wide reach from one screen. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Could a drill’s trigger be mistaken for a real one, because it comes over the live warning path or uses the words of a live warning?
An officer acts on a drill as if it were real. A.3.1.
Are live and test alerts sent from the same interface, under the same login, behind the same confirmation, without showing the message?
One click sends the wrong alert to everyone. A.3.1.
Can one person compose and send an alert with the widest reach you have, with no independent holder authorizing it?
A single error reaches every phone in the state. A.3.2.
Could your authorization be obtained within the warning time, at every hour?
Either the authorization delays a real warning, or it is skipped. A.3.2.
If you sent a false alert, is a correction prepared for every template, and do you know who may send it and how fast?
The false alert stands for half an hour while people believe it. A.3.3.
Would your staff and the 911 centers be able to work through the call surge and network saturation a false alert creates, using priority services?
The officials correcting the alert cannot reach each other. A.3.3.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Separate Drill From Real, and Test From Live

annex.p: The Federal Communications Commission noted that industry practice separates the test environment from the live one by a distinct login domain or a separate application, with watermarks, color, and naming that make the two impossible to confuse. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-2 and F-3: make a drill’s trigger distinguishable from a live one by more than words, never in the language of a live warning, and never over the live warning path; and treat a counterfeit of the warning source’s notice as a route to a false alert that needs no compromise.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Require an Independent Holder, Within the Warning Time

annex.p: The agency’s own corrective action added a second person; this instrument’s F-4 notes that a second person reading the same screen is not an independent holder. These steps are this instrument’s, from F-4 and F-5: require that an alert of the widest reach be authorized by a named holder distinct from the operator, on a basis that holder can check, and make sure that authorization can be obtained within the warning time at every hour.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Prepare the Correction, and the Priority Access

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-6 and F-7. Distinguish a cancellation, which only stops retransmission, from a correction, which tells people the alert was false; prepare a correction for every template, sent through the same channels, with a stated trigger; and make sure your staff use priority telecommunications services when an alert has saturated the networks.

At 8:07 on the morning of Saturday 13 January 2018, the Hawaii Emergency Management Agency sent a false alert to every phone, television, and radio in the state warning of an incoming ballistic missile and saying this was not a drill. A drill had been started by a recorded call that simulated the military’s notice over the live warning path, using the words of a real warning, and an officer sent a live alert through software in which live and test messages shared one menu and one confirmation that did not show the text. The agency knew within minutes that the alert was false, but its cancellation only stopped retransmission; the correction that told people it was false came thirty-eight minutes after the alert. 911 centers received about 7,755 calls in an hour, and wireless networks were saturated. No one intended it. The lessons are that a drill must never look or sound like the real thing, that an alert of the widest reach needs an independent holder to authorize it, and that a correction must be prepared before it is needed. Any operation that can reach everyone from one screen has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Failure of Coordination in Hurricane Katrina, 2005
what: Hurricane Katrina made landfall on 29 August 2005, after a warning found adequate days in advance, and its surge breached the levees and floodwalls of New Orleans. The storm flooded the city's operations center, the police headquarters, and the National Guard's headquarters, and some parishes could not reach the state for eleven days. Breaches were reported from the morning of landfall, but that evening the federal picture said the levees had not been breached, and the federal government ran three commands.
tier: Not an attack: the hazard was a hurricane and the failure of engineered flood defenses, though the storm took out operations centers and the links between them as an adversary might aim to.

findings.title: For a forecast hazard, the point of unified command is keyed to the forecast.
findings.text: The full federal response was engaged the day after landfall, on requests the storm had cut off.

findings.title: Each part of an action has one holder, named before the incident.
findings.text: Three federal commands ran at once, and the Guard and the police each said the other had the lead.

findings.title: A fused picture carries disagreement on a catastrophic fact.
findings.text: Breach reports were overridden by a reassuring account.

findings.title: For a regional hazard, the backup stands outside the footprint and each tier can act alone.
findings.text: The city's centers were lost to one flood, while a neighboring parish's hardened center held.

findings.title: Qualification is shown by exercise against the catastrophic case, and its lessons are closed.
findings.text: The city's office had three staff, and the lessons of an exercise for this storm were incompletely implemented.

findings.title: Who holds military support tasks under each status is settled in the map.
findings.text: Command of military forces in the state was settled during the incident.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its corrections of two facility classes' accounts of the event went to those classes as errata.

annex.p: This annex is for emergency management agencies at every tier, the operations centers they run, and the police, National Guard, and other forces that must act together in a disaster. It is also for any owner, in any sector, whose response depends on coordination among organizations that may lose contact with each other. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
For a forecast hazard, is the point at which unified command is established keyed to the forecast, or does it wait on a request the event may prevent?
The full response waits for a request that cannot be sent. A.3.1.
Is your operations center, and its backup, outside the footprint of the regional hazard you plan for?
The center and its backup flood together. A.3.2.
Could each tier, city, parish or county, and state, act on its own if it lost contact with the others for days?
Communities wait for direction that cannot reach them. A.3.2.
Is each part of the response held by one named organization before the incident, so that no two claim the same command?
Two commands each think the other has the lead. A.3.1.
Does your shared picture carry disagreement on a catastrophic fact, such as a levee breach, until it is resolved, rather than reporting the reassuring account?
The picture says all is well while the city floods. A.3.3.
Is your staff deep enough for a catastrophic event, trained in your command system before it happens, and have your exercise lessons been closed?
The command system is taught after the storm arrives. A.3.3.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Key Unified Command to the Forecast, and Name Each Holder

annex.p: The House committee found that the federal Incident of National Significance should have been declared no later than 27 August 2005, two days before landfall, and that the Catastrophic Incident Annex, which would have let federal agencies move resources without waiting for requests, should have been invoked. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-1, F-2, and F-6: key unified command to the forecast of a catastrophic hazard; name one holder for each part of the response before the incident; and settle in advance who authorizes the tasks of military forces under each status in which they may serve.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Place the Backup Outside the Footprint, and Let Each Tier Act Alone

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-4. For a regional hazard, place the backup operations center outside the event’s footprint, harden the primary, as Jefferson Parish’s held, and prepare each tier to act on its own when it cannot reach the others.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Carry Disagreement in the Picture, and Exercise Against the Catastrophe

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-3 and F-5. Carry contradicting reports of a catastrophic fact in the shared picture until they are resolved; size staff to the catastrophic duration, qualify them by exercise against that event, and close the lessons of each exercise.

Hurricane Katrina made landfall on 29 August 2005, after a warning the House committee found adequate fifty-six hours before. Its surge breached the levees and floodwalls of New Orleans, and most of the city flooded. The storm took the centers from which coordination was to be run: the city’s operations center, the police headquarters, and the National Guard’s headquarters were all flooded and abandoned, while the hardened center of a neighboring parish held. Some parishes could not reach the state for eleven days. Breaches were reported from the morning of landfall, but that evening the federal picture said the levees had not been breached. At the Superdome the Guard and the police each said the other had the lead, and the federal government ran three commands. Congressional committees found that the federal response waited on declarations and requests the storm had cut off. The lessons are that command for a forecast catastrophe must be set by the forecast, that backup centers must stand outside the hazard’s footprint, and that every part of the response must have one holder named before the event. Any operation that depends on many organizations acting together has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: Air-Raid Alerting in Ukraine, 2022 to 2026
what: Since the full-scale Russian invasion of 24 February 2022, Ukraine has warned its population of air attack many thousands of times, by sirens, broadcast, messaging channels, a public application, and cell broadcast. The Air Force declares the threat and regional and district authorities warn their areas, and the signal between them was cut from minutes to seconds. When an attack on the largest mobile carrier took the alert system out in some areas in December 2023, the authorities said so and police and rescuers warned people by loudspeaker.
tier: Military action by a state against a country, sustained for more than four years; the warning held under attack.

findings.title: The signal from the authority that detects is part of the warning time.
findings.text: The signal from the Air Force to the regions took minutes until 2025.

findings.title: A true alert that reaches too far costs response.
findings.text: Region-wide alerts for threats to a district wore down people's response.

findings.title: The independence of a channel reaches its trigger.
findings.text: The alert system went out where it depended on the carrier that was attacked.

findings.title: The authority knew the channel was down, and said so.
findings.text: Authorities announced the outage and named the channel that replaced it.

findings.title: Grade the instruction by kind of threat, and re-validate it against the adversary.
findings.text: Ukraine introduced separate alerts for drones and for missiles in 2026.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its substance on campaign duration is carried by DBA-ESS-RE-12 F-6.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its correction of the facility class's account of the event went to the class as an erratum.

annex.p: This annex is for the authorities that warn the public of attack or other hazard, and for the operators of sirens, broadcast, cell broadcast, and alerting applications. It is also for any owner, in any sector, whose warnings must keep reaching people while power and networks are under attack. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
How long does the signal take from the authority that detects a threat to the authority that warns the public, and is that counted in the warning time?
Minutes of warning are spent passing the word. A.3.1.
Is the reach of each warning matched to the area actually threatened, so that people are not warned so often for threats elsewhere that they stop responding?
People ignore the warning that matters. A.3.1.
Do your warning channels, and the triggers that set them off, share nothing with the power and networks an attack would take down?
The siren has its own power but is triggered through the network that failed. A.3.2.
If a warning channel went down, would you tell the public which channel was out and what replaced it?
People wait for a siren that will not sound. A.3.2.
Does your warning tell people what kind of threat is coming and what to do for it, and is that reviewed against how the threat changes?
One alert for every threat, read the same way for all of them. A.3.3.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Shorten the Signal, and Match the Reach

annex.p: Ukraine’s government reported cutting the signal from the Air Force Command to the regional authorities from several minutes to eight to fifteen seconds, divided warning below the region from January 2025 so that an alert sounds in the districts a threat approaches, and extended district alerting to every region but Donetsk and Luhansk in December 2025. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-1 and F-2: count the signal from the authority that detects to the authority that warns as part of the warning time; and match the reach of each true alert to the area actually threatened, since alerts that reach too far wear down response.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Make the Trigger Independent, and Say When a Channel Is Down

annex.p: When the attack on Kyivstar took the alert system out in Sumy on 12 December 2023, the city’s administration announced the outage and that police and rescue services would warn people. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-3 and F-4: make each warning channel independent of the networks an attack would take, its trigger included; and when a channel is down, tell the public so and name what replaces it.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Grade the Warning by Kind of Threat

annex.p: Ukraine announced in September 2026 a yellow alert for drones and a red one for missiles and massed attack, with criteria set by the military and civil authorities and reviewed weekly. This step adds the instrument’s own, from F-5: grade the instruction by the kinds of threat your area faces, and review it as the threat changes.

Since the full-scale Russian invasion of 24 February 2022, Ukraine has warned its population of air attack many thousands of times, by sirens, broadcast, messaging channels, a public application, and cell broadcast. The Air Force declares the threat and regional and, since 2025, district authorities warn their areas, and the signal between them was cut from minutes to seconds. Region-wide alerts for threats to a single district wore down people’s response until warning was divided by district. When an attack on the country’s largest mobile carrier took the alert system out in some areas, the authorities said so and police and rescuers warned people with loudspeakers. In 2026 Ukraine began grading alerts by kind of threat. The warning has held under sustained attack. The lessons are that every second between detecting a threat and warning people counts, that a warning that reaches too far loses its audience, and that a channel’s independence must reach its trigger. Any authority that must warn people while power and networks are under attack has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Shooting at the Route 91 Harvest Festival, October 2017
what: At 10:05 p.m. on 1 October 2017, a gunman firing from the thirty-second floor of a hotel in Las Vegas fired into a crowd of more than 22,000 at the Route 91 Harvest festival for about ten minutes, killing fifty-eight people that night. Thirteen agencies, several hundred police officers, and about 130 private ambulances responded, many without assignment, and about 800 patients reached hospitals by their own means. Because the gunman's position was not located for about an hour, fire and medical crews waited to enter, and command vetted sixteen reports of attacks elsewhere before sending anyone.
tier: A deliberate attack, not military action: the gunman aimed at the crowd, not at the response, and nothing shows the response forces were chosen or studied.

findings.title: Capacity was abundant and unaccounted.
findings.text: Command could not direct units it did not know were there.

findings.title: The class's account of the false reports needs correction.
findings.text: The reports of other attacks were vetted, and no source shows units drawn to false scenes.

findings.title: Self-dispatch is to be absorbed, not forbidden.
findings.text: Several hundred officers and dozens of ambulances arrived without assignment, and much of their work saved lives.

findings.title: The patient-transfer line presumes a transfer.
findings.text: About 800 patients reached hospitals without a transfer from a crew.

findings.title: A planned gathering is a known concentration.
findings.text: The festival's plan left out the fire service, and its medical supplies were sized for an ordinary night.

findings.title: The entry rule is needed outside military-action conditions.
findings.text: Crews faced the decision to enter a scene with an unlocated threat.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its forward reasoning about deliberate misdirection went to Project 9 as use-case material.

findings.title: Common accountability failed before any network did.
findings.text: No network failed, and accountability across agencies still broke down.

annex.p: This annex is for the police, fire, and emergency medical agencies of an area, the 911 centers that dispatch them, and the private ambulance companies an area’s plan relies on. It is also for the organizers and venues of large planned gatherings, whose obligations the Commercial Facilities series states. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
If a gunman’s position were elevated and concealed, do you have a stated rule for when fire and medical crews enter while the threat is unlocated?
Crews either wait without a rule or enter without one. A.3.2.

For a planned gathering of many thousands, does the plan join every discipline that would answer a mass-casualty incident there, with a dispatcher for the event and medical supplies sized for a surge?
The fire service learns of the event when the calls start. A.3.1.
Could your command track where each unit is, including off-duty officers and private ambulances that arrive without assignment?
Command has more help than it needs and cannot direct it. A.3.1.
Do you have check-in points on every approach where arriving units are recorded and assigned?
Self-dispatched units work where no one knows they are. A.3.1.
Would you know which hospitals received how many patients if most of them arrived by their own means?
Hospitals are overwhelmed before anyone knows who went where. A.3.3.
Would your command vet reports of other attacks before committing units to them?
Units are drawn to scenes where nothing is happening. A.3.2.
Have you exercised common accountability and mutual-aid channels under the strain of many units converging, not only under the loss of a network?
Accountability fails although every network still works. A.3.3.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Plan Planned Gatherings, and Absorb Self-Dispatch

annex.p: The 1 October After-Action Report, prepared by the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s National Exercise Division with the Clark County Fire Department and the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department, recommends that agencies recognize that off-duty personnel will respond and bring them to staging. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-1, F-3, and F-5: count a unit as available only when command knows its location and assignment; set check-in points on every approach, known in advance to every agency and to off-duty personnel; treat private ambulance companies the plan relies on as part of command from the start; and for a planned gathering above a size the area sets, join every discipline in the plan, staff a dispatch position for the event, and size medical supplies at the venue for a surge.

annex.h3: A.3.2 State the Entry Rule, and Vet Reports Before Committing

annex.p: The same report found that the unified commanders acted appropriately in vetting reports of other attacks before committing resources. This step is the instrument’s own, from F-6: state the rule for entering a scene where a threat is continuing or unlocated for any deliberate event, not only for war, with the delay it accepts decided in advance.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Track Patients, and Exercise Accountability Under Convergence

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-4 and F-8. Plan for patients who reach hospitals without a transfer from a crew, so that the distribution of patients is known; and exercise common accountability and mutual-aid channels under the convergence of many units, not only under the loss of links.

At 10:05 p.m. on 1 October 2017, a gunman on the thirty-second floor of a hotel in Las Vegas fired into a crowd of more than 22,000 at the Route 91 Harvest festival for about ten minutes, killing fifty-eight people that night. The response was large and fast, thirteen agencies, several hundred police officers, and about 130 private ambulances, but command could not see much of it: many officers and ambulances arrived without assignment, about 800 patients reached hospitals by their own means, and the plan for the festival had not included the fire service. Because the gunman’s position was not located for about an hour, fire and medical crews waited to enter, and command vetted sixteen reports of attacks elsewhere before sending anyone. The lessons are that a large planned gathering is a known concentration and should be planned by every discipline that would answer it, that help which command cannot track is not yet capacity, and that the rule for entering a scene with an unlocated threat must be stated in advance.
