Any area that hosts large gatherings has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this area does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: Repeat Strikes on Rescue Crews in Ukraine, 2022 to 2026
what: Since February 2022, Ukraine's rescue crews have been struck repeatedly, above all by second strikes timed to hit the responders who answer a first, in attacks that Ukrainian authorities and documenting organizations attribute to Russian forces. A documenting organization counted 401 attacks on responders to October 2025, rising each year, and its counts and the State Emergency Service's own differ by a factor of two to three. The Service adopted a wait before full entry, a small first team, airspace observers, body armor, and withdrawal on threat, and the share of attacks that killed someone fell from about fifteen percent to about three.
tier: Military action by a state, in which the responders themselves are the target, sustained for years.

findings.title: The hold-back rule exists, and its residual has been measured.
findings.text: The Service's entry rule cut deaths at the cost of slower rescue.

findings.title: A fixed wait is itself a pattern.
findings.text: Second strikes came anywhere from ten minutes to five hours after the first.

findings.title: An adversary who watches needs no plans.
findings.text: Drones confirmed responders were present before strikes.

findings.title: The warning at the scene is a protective function.
findings.text: Airspace observers and drone detectors did most to keep responders alive.

findings.title: Stations are targets, and some are also shelters.
findings.text: Stations were struck by the hundred, some with civilians sheltering in them.

findings.title: Under military action, the design duration is a campaign measured in years.
findings.text: The attacks have continued for more than four years.

findings.title: An agency must record its losses by cause.
findings.text: The counts differ by two to three times, and only the agency holds the full record.

findings.title: Against a persistent adversary, the design basis is re-validated.
findings.text: The attacker changed weapons and timing as the response adapted.

annex.p: This annex is for fire, rescue, and emergency medical agencies, and for the authorities that set the rules under which their crews enter a scene. It is also for any agency that may answer a deliberate attack in which the responders themselves could be the target. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Do you have a stated rule for entering a scene where a second attack on the responders is credible, with the delay it accepts decided in advance?
Each crew decides at the scene, or no one does. A.3.1.
If your rule is a fixed wait, could an attacker learn it and time a strike to it?
The rule tells the attacker when to strike. A.3.1.
Could your crews tell that a scene was being watched from the air, and withdraw on a detected threat?
Crews are struck by an attacker who watched them arrive. A.3.2.
Are your stations dispersed, free of single points, and separated from any role they play as shelters?
A strike on a station takes the response and the people sheltering there. A.3.2.
Do you record responders hurt and stations and vehicles damaged by cause?
You cannot show what the attacks cost, or whether your protections work. A.3.3.
Do you re-check your protective rules when an attacker’s weapons or timing change?
Last year’s rule becomes this year’s weakness. A.3.3.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Adopt an Entry Rule, and Vary It

annex.p: By 2025, by the published accounts the instrument cites, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service required a wait of thirty to forty minutes before full entry, a small first team and a later second, continuous observation of the airspace, helmets and body armor, and withdrawal on any detected threat; over the period in which it did so the share of attacks on responders that killed someone fell from about fifteen percent to about three. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-1 and F-2: adopt a stated entry rule, record what its delay costs in rescue and what it buys in lives, and avoid an interval so fixed and known that an attacker can time a strike to it.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Watch the Scene, and Separate Stations From Shelters

annex.p: The Service’s practice included airspace observers and drone detectors at the scene. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-3, F-4, and F-5: treat warning at the scene as a protective function, with awareness of the airspace, dispersal and cover, the smallest crew exposure the task allows, and lawful means to detect an observing drone; and separate a station’s response role from any role it plays as a shelter.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Record Losses by Cause, and Re-Validate

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-6, F-7, and F-8. Size depth of crews and equipment for a campaign of years where military action is the design event; record every responder hurt and every station and vehicle damaged by cause; and re-validate protective rules whenever an attacker’s weapons, interval, or targets change.

Since February 2022, Ukraine’s rescue crews have been struck again and again by what Ukrainian authorities and documenting organizations attribute to Russian forces, above all by second strikes timed to hit the responders who answer a first. The documenting organization counted 401 attacks on responders to October 2025, rising each year, and its figures and the State Emergency Service’s own differ by a factor of two to three. The Service changed how it works: a wait before full entry, a small first team, observers watching the sky, body armor, and withdrawal on any threat. The share of attacks that killed someone fell from about fifteen percent to about three, at the cost of slower rescue for people trapped. The lessons are that an entry rule for a scene where responders may be targeted must be decided in advance, that it must not become a pattern an attacker can learn, and that a watching adversary defeats secrecy of plans alone. A deliberate second strike needs no war, only an attacker who has seen the response arrive. The questions in this annex show management whether this agency is ready for one, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Ransomware Attack on the Irish Health Service Executive, May 2021
what: On 14 May 2021, ransomware was detonated across the national network of Ireland's Health Service Executive, eight weeks after the attacker entered through a phishing email and after several detections that were not acted on. About 80 percent of the estate was encrypted, 31 of 54 acute hospitals cancelled services on the first day, and care went to paper. Restoration took 130 days, and one hospital that cut itself off early kept its systems.
tier: A deliberate criminal attack, not military action: a crime for money, attributed to no state, in peacetime.

findings.title: An alert anywhere on a shared network is the system's.
findings.text: The attacker was detected several times and not stopped.

findings.title: The hold time is set by the restoration of the estate.
findings.text: Continuity plans did not envisage a total loss, and restoration took 130 days.

findings.title: The harm is measured while it happens.
findings.text: The effect on patient care was never measured.

findings.title: A hospital keeps its systems only if it can cut itself off.
findings.text: Every hospital on the flat network lost its systems, except one that blocked the attack.

findings.title: The restored record is reconciled with the paper.
findings.text: Some data was lost, and care during the outage was recorded on paper.

annex.p: This annex is for hospitals and health systems, especially those joined to a shared or national network, and for the technology and clinical leaders who would run care without computers. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Would a phishing email opened by one member of staff give an attacker a foothold on the network your hospitals share?
One click reaches the whole system. A.3.1.
Are your security tools set to block, and is every alert on the shared network acted on, wherever it arises?
The attacker is seen and not stopped for weeks. A.3.1.
Could each hospital cut itself off from the shared network and keep its own systems?
Every hospital loses its systems together. A.3.2.
Do your continuity plans assume the loss of all information technology, for months, with manual processes prepared in every hospital?
Some hospitals improvise while others cope. A.3.2.
Would you measure the harm to patients while care runs on paper?
No one can say afterward what the attack cost patients. A.3.3.
When systems return, will you reconcile the restored records with what was written on paper?
Care is given from records that are incomplete. A.3.3.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Act on Every Alert, and Block

annex.p: The independent post-incident review recorded several detections of the attacker’s activity in the eight weeks before the ransomware was detonated, none acted on, with antivirus in monitor mode, and the Executive estimated the cost of carrying out the review’s recommendations at almost 657 million euros over seven years. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-1: treat an alert anywhere on a shared network as the whole system’s, and set protective tools to block.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Let Each Hospital Stand Alone, and Plan for Months

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-2 and F-4. Make sure each hospital can cut itself off from the shared network and keep its systems, as one voluntary hospital did; and plan the manual mode for the full time to restore the estate, which here was 130 days.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Measure the Harm, and Reconcile the Record

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-3 and F-5. Measure the effect on patients while care runs by hand; and reconcile the restored record with the paper record of the manual period.

On 14 May 2021, ransomware was detonated across the network of Ireland’s Health Service Executive, which runs the country’s public health service and its acute hospitals over a single national network. The attacker had entered eight weeks earlier through a phishing email, and was detected several times without being stopped. About 80 percent of the estate was encrypted, and the Executive shut its systems down. On the first day 31 of 54 acute hospitals cancelled services, radiotherapy stopped at five centers, and care went to paper. One hospital that detected the attack early and cut itself off kept its own systems. Restoration took 130 days, some data could not be recovered, and the harm to patients was never measured. The attackers were criminals seeking money, attributed to no state. The lessons are that an alert anywhere on a shared network belongs to the whole system, that each hospital must be able to stand alone, and that plans must assume the loss of all computers for months. Any health system on a shared network has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this system does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Loss of Power at Memorial Medical Center, August and September 2005
what: Memorial Medical Center in New Orleans stood below sea level with its transfer switches near the ground. In Hurricane Katrina city power failed on 29 August, the flood rose the next day, and the emergency power failed early on 31 August. Ventilator batteries ran out, heat rose above 100 degrees, and patients were evacuated by boat and helicopter over three days. Forty-five bodies were recovered.
tier: Not an attack: a hurricane and flood took the hospital's power beyond its endurance.

findings.title: The plan covers the failure of the essential electrical system itself.
findings.text: The plan offered no guidance for a complete power failure.

findings.title: The site's height against the flood is stated, and a known warning is a departure.
findings.text: A 2004 recommendation to raise the electrical equipment was not carried out.

findings.title: The means of evacuation are part of the design basis.
findings.text: Patients left by boat and from an unlit helipad, carried by hand.

findings.title: A tenant's patients are inside the hospital's plan.
findings.text: A separate hospital's 52 patients were on the seventh floor.

annex.p: This annex is for hospitals, especially those in flood-prone places, their facilities engineers, and the tenant hospitals and care providers that share their buildings. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Are your generators, transfer switches, and distribution panels above the flood your site could see?
A little water disables the whole emergency electrical system. A.3.1.
Does your plan cover the failure of the emergency electrical system itself, not only of the grid?
When the generators stop, there is no plan. A.3.1.
How long would life-sustaining equipment run on its own batteries if all power were lost, and what then?
Ventilators stop within half an hour. A.3.1.
Could you evacuate every patient without power, elevators, or road access, and how long would it take?
Patients are carried by hand for days. A.3.2.
Are the patients of any tenant hospital in your building inside your plan?
A floor of patients falls outside everyone’s plan. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Protect the Emergency Electrical System, and Plan for Its Loss

annex.p: No authority has published an action for owners that this instrument reads. These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1 and F-2: state the site’s height against the flood and place the emergency electrical system above it, acting on any known warning; and plan for the failure of the emergency electrical system itself, with what life-sustaining care does when it is gone.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Make Evacuation Part of the Design, and Include Every Patient

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-3 and F-4. Plan the means of evacuation, by boat, helicopter, and stair, for a building without power or elevators; and bring the patients of every tenant hospital into the plan.

Memorial Medical Center in New Orleans stood three feet below sea level, with its main emergency-power transfer switches a few feet above the ground; a recommendation of 2004 to raise its electrical equipment had not been carried out. When Hurricane Katrina struck on 29 August 2005, city power failed and the generators took over; the next day the flood rose around the hospital, and early on 31 August the emergency power failed. The plan assumed backup power for at least three days and offered no guidance for its complete loss. Ventilator batteries ran out, the heat rose above 100 degrees, and patients were evacuated by boat and from an unlit helipad over three days, reached by one elevator and then by hand. A separate hospital with 52 patients occupied the seventh floor. Forty-five bodies were recovered, more than from any comparable hospital in the city. The lessons are that a hospital’s emergency power must stand above the flood, that the plan must cover its failure, and that evacuation without power is part of the design. Any hospital in a flood-prone place has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this hospital does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Strike on the Okhmatdyt Children's Hospital, July 2024
what: On 8 July 2024, during a mass missile attack on Ukraine, the national children's hospital in Kyiv was hit; the United Nations monitoring mission assessed a high likelihood of a direct hit, and the governments' statements on the weapon differ. Dialysis and intensive care were destroyed or badly damaged, a child was in surgery when the power failed, and 94 children were moved to other hospitals in the same city. The record is open.
tier: Military action, in an armed conflict during a mass missile attack, with each statement on the weapon its author's own.

findings.title: The patient who cannot be moved is sheltered where the care is.
findings.text: Children on dialysis and ventilators were in the buildings destroyed.

findings.title: A service that lives in one building is a single point.
findings.text: Dialysis and transplant services were lost with their buildings.

findings.title: The receiving hospitals are under the same attack.
findings.text: Patients were moved to hospitals in the same city under the same campaign.

findings.title: Power reaches the point of care after a strike.
findings.text: Power failed during surgery, and the elevators were out.

annex.p: This annex is for hospitals that could be struck in a war, especially tertiary and national hospitals whose services no other hospital can replace, and for the health authorities that plan where their patients would go. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Is care that cannot be interrupted, such as dialysis, ventilation, and surgery, given in protected space, or have you stated which patients you cannot protect in place?
The patients who cannot be moved are where the strike lands. A.3.1.
Does any service that no other hospital can replace depend on a single building?
One strike ends a national service for months. A.3.1.
Have you named receiving hospitals, at least one outside the area that could be struck together with yours?
Patients are moved to hospitals under the same attack. A.3.2.
Do operating rooms and intensive care keep power and light if the building’s distribution is lost, and is there an evacuation route without elevators?
Surgery continues in the dark and patients are carried down stairs. A.3.2.
Is discharge home planned as a protective action, with criteria and follow-up?
Hundreds of children go home without a plan. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Shelter the Patient Who Cannot Be Moved, and Give Each Irreplaceable Service a Second Place

annex.p: No authority has published an action for owners that this instrument reads. These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1 and F-2: give care that cannot be interrupted in protected space, or state the patients who cannot be protected in place with the warning time the region’s alerting gives; and give each service no other hospital can replace a second location or a declared residual.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Name Receiving Hospitals Beyond the Struck Area, and Keep Power at the Point of Care

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-3 and F-4. Name receiving hospitals for each group of patients, one outside the area a campaign may strike together; plan discharge as a protective action; let staff and supplies move with their patients; and keep power and light at the point of care, with an evacuation route that needs no elevators.

On 8 July 2024, during a mass missile attack on Ukraine, Okhmatdyt, the country’s national children’s hospital in Kyiv, was hit. The United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission assessed a high likelihood of a direct hit and factors suggesting a Russian missile, without making a determination; Ukraine’s Security Service said missile fragments were found and called it a war crime; Russia’s Ministry of Defence said the damage came from a Ukrainian air defense missile. Each statement is its author’s own, and the record is open. The toxicology building, where children received dialysis, was destroyed and intensive care was destroyed or badly damaged; a child was in surgery when the power failed, and patients were carried down stairs with the elevators out. Ninety-four children were moved to other hospitals in the same city, 465 were sent home, and national services such as transplants were lost for months. The counts of dead and wounded differ by publisher. The lessons are that care that cannot be interrupted must be given where it can be protected, that no irreplaceable service should live in one building, and that receiving hospitals must lie beyond the area struck. Any hospital that could be struck in a war has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this hospital is ready, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Flooding of Baxter's North Cove Plant in Hurricane Helene, September 2024
what: The remnants of Hurricane Helene flooded Baxter's North Cove plant in North Carolina, which the federal government said made about 60 percent of the nation's intravenous fluids. Production stopped, hospitals conserved, supply was allocated, and the regulator permitted temporary imports. The plant's highest-throughput line restarted in about a month, but the shortage lasted into early 2025.
tier: Not an attack: a flood. None of the four characteristics is present.

findings.title: One Plant Carried Most of What Every Hospital Uses.
findings.text: A plant carrying most of a first-band material has a second source or reserve, or declares the concentration.

annex.p: This annex is for makers of medical products, the distributors and group purchasers who supply hospitals, the hospitals themselves, and the regulators who plan for shortages. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to an organization. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an organization answers about its own supply (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an organization can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one organization. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the organization; it is that organization’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
What share of each critical material you make, or buy, comes from one plant, and what would supply it if that plant stopped for three months?
Your substitution may have to be built after the loss. A.3.2.
Is the plant’s flood and fire protection designed against the region’s worst hazards, and when was that last reviewed?
A regional storm may take the whole supply. A.3.1.
Is the rule by which supply is allocated in a shortage stated in advance and known to customers?
Allocation will be decided under pressure. A.3.1.
Are the permissions for importing or substituting a material arranged before a shortage?
Weeks pass while they are granted. A.3.1.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The class’s requirements (§4.5, §4.6, §5.1) state siting and flood protection against regional hazards, substitution with its permissions arranged in advance, allocation by a rule stated in advance, and a restart planned with the regulator. The Food and Drug Administration’s drug-shortage program and its temporary importation of products from abroad, and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s advisory to providers, were used in 2024. Each is its author’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Hold a Second Source or a Reserve for What One Plant Carries

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1. For each critical material most of which comes from one plant, arrange a qualified second source or a reserve held elsewhere, sized to how long that plant would take to restore, or say plainly that you carry the concentration and by when it will end.

In late September 2024 the remnants of Hurricane Helene flooded a plant in western North Carolina that, by the federal government’s account, made about 60 percent of the nation’s intravenous fluids, the salt-water bags used for almost every hospital patient. Production stopped. Hospitals were told to conserve, supplies were rationed, and the federal regulator allowed imports from the company’s plants abroad. The company restarted its biggest line in about a month, but the shortage lasted into early 2025. The lesson is that when most of a material every hospital needs comes from one plant, a second source or a reserve elsewhere has to exist before the plant is lost, not be arranged afterwards. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own supply, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Failure of the First Federal COVID-19 Test Kits, February 2020
date_full: 4 to 29 February 2020, read to December 2021 (record closed)
what: The only authorized test for COVID-19 in early February 2020 was the CDC's, sent to public-health laboratories from 6 February. Within days many laboratories reported inconclusive results; the agency's root-cause analysis found the kits released after a check had detected a high failure rate. Laboratories able to make their own tests could use them only from 29 February, when the FDA relaxed its rule as community spread was confirmed.
tier: Not an attack: a failure in making and design. None of the four characteristics is present.

findings.title: The Second Source Was Held Back by the Rule.
findings.text: The second source is usable under the authority's rules from the first days of an emergency.

annex.p: This annex is for public-health and clinical laboratories, the agencies that authorize tests in an emergency, and the officials who plan for the onset of an outbreak. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to a laboratory or agency. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an organization answers about its own testing (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an organization can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one organization. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the organization; it is that organization’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
If the first test for a new pathogen came from one source and failed, could you test by another method within days?
Detection will wait on the first source. A.3.2.
Does a test you receive pass a lot check before you put it into use, and who may release it if the check fails?
A failed check may be overridden. A.3.1.
Under the rules that govern you, could you use your own validated test in the first week of an emergency?
Your second source may be held back by the rule. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The class’s requirements (§4.2, §5.2) state validation and lot verification before use, a second method or source, and recall and notification within hours. The Food and Drug Administration’s guidance on testing in public health emergencies, first issued on 29 February 2020 and since revised, sets out how laboratories may validate and use their own tests. Each is its author’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Have a Second Way to Test, and the Permission to Use It

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1. Prepare a second method for detecting a new pathogen before you need it, and know under what rule you could use it in the first days of an emergency; if the rule does not allow it, say so to the authority now.

When COVID-19 reached the United States in early 2020, the only authorized test was one made by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and sent to state public-health laboratories in early February. Within days many laboratories found it gave inconclusive results; the agency later found that the kits had been released even though a quality check had shown a high failure rate. Laboratories that could have made their own tests needed federal authorization to use them, and the rule was not relaxed until 29 February, by which time the virus was already spreading in communities. The lessons are that a test must pass its checks before it is released, and that a second way to test, and the permission to use it, must exist before the first one fails. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own testing, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Ransomware Attack on Synnovis, June 2024
date_full: 3 June 2024 onward, read to June 2025 (record closed as to the disruption)
what: On 3 June 2024 ransomware disabled Synnovis, the pathology provider to hospitals across south-east London. Testing and blood matching ran at about a tenth of normal in the second week; more than ten thousand appointments and seventeen hundred procedures were postponed, and one trust later said the attack contributed to a death. Hospitals used O-type blood, and NHS Blood and Transplant issued an amber alert for O-negative in July. A criminal group claimed the attack.
tier: A criminal ransomware attack; not placed at the military-action tier: persistence and precision are not established and denial is absent.

findings.title: The Manual Mode Ran at a Tenth of Need.
findings.text: The manual mode is sized against urgent need, and the exercise shows it.

findings.title: The Substitution Drew Down the Nation's Universal Blood.
findings.text: The reserve a substitution draws on is counted, with the time it lasts.

annex.p: This annex is for hospitals and health systems that rely on a shared or outsourced laboratory, the laboratories themselves, and the blood services that supply them. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to a hospital or laboratory. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an organization answers about its own testing (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an organization can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one organization. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the organization; it is that organization’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
If your laboratory provider’s systems went down tonight, how much of your urgent testing and blood matching could you do by hand, and for how long?
Your manual mode may run at a tenth of need. A.3.2.
Has your manual mode been exercised at the rate your urgent patients need?
A procedure is not a capacity. A.3.2.
If you could not match blood, how much universal blood would you use per day, and does your blood service know?
You may spend a national reserve unseen. A.3.2.
Can your provider restore from systems and backups an attacker could not reach?
Restoration may restore the intrusion. A.3.1.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The class’s requirements (§3.3, §4.5, §5.3) state the share counted across every hospital served, a manual mode exercised in advance, results released only by a trusted path, and restoration from beyond the attack’s reach. NHS Blood and Transplant’s guidance on the use of O-negative blood and its amber-alert procedures set out how the blood supply is managed in a shortage. Each is its author’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Size Your Manual Mode, and Tell Your Blood Service What It Would Draw

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1 and F-2. Work out how much urgent testing and blood matching you must keep doing if your laboratory’s systems are lost, and exercise your manual mode at that rate. And tell your blood service how much universal blood you would use per day if you could not match, so that the reserve is planned and not discovered.

On 3 June 2024 a ransomware attack disabled Synnovis, the company that runs blood tests and blood matching for hospitals across south-east London. The hospitals fell back on manual methods that, in the second week, ran at about a tenth of normal. Thousands of operations and appointments were postponed, and one hospital trust later said the attack contributed to a patient’s death. Unable to match blood, the hospitals used universal type O blood, and a month later the national blood service declared a severe shortage of O-negative. The lessons are that a backup way of testing must be sized to what patients need, not just written down, and that a hospital’s fallback can quietly drain a national reserve unless it is planned with the blood service. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own testing, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Release of Foot-and-Mouth Disease Virus From the Pirbright Site, 2007
what: In August 2007 foot-and-mouth disease was confirmed on a farm near Guildford, and the strain was traced beyond reasonable doubt to the nearby Pirbright site, shared by a government institute and a vaccine maker. The Health and Safety Executive found live virus had most likely entered the site's cracked and root-damaged drains, that heavy rain may have increased the release, and that vehicle and people movements had not been adequately controlled; it could not say which occupant was the source.
tier: Not an attack: a decayed drain. None of the four characteristics is present.

findings.title: The Release Was Found by the Disease It Caused.
findings.text: What leaves a high-containment site is monitored by each route.

findings.title: Two Occupants Shared One Barrier, and No One Owned Its Condition.
findings.text: A shared barrier has one named owner.

annex.p: This annex is for operators of high-containment laboratories and of facilities that make vaccines or work with dangerous agents, the regulators who license them, and the animal-health and public-health authorities near them. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to a laboratory. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions a laboratory answers about its own site (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account a laboratory can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one laboratory. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the laboratory; it is that laboratory’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Are your drains and other passive barriers inspected and repaired on a schedule set by the consequence of a release, and when were they last inspected?
The oldest barrier may be the one that fails. A.3.1.
Do you monitor what leaves your site by each route, effluent above all, for the agents you hold?
A release may be found only by the disease it causes. A.3.2.
Are movements of people, vehicles, and contractors near your barriers controlled, especially during works?
A vehicle may carry the agent off site. A.3.1.
If you share a site, is one party named as owner of each shared barrier’s condition?
No one may own the drain. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The Health and Safety Executive’s final report of September 2007 set out the failures it found at the site, among them the condition of the drains and the control of movements, and the regulation of work with animal pathogens in Great Britain was reviewed afterwards. The class’s requirements (§4.6, §5.6) state barriers for each route, passive barriers maintained and inspected, control of movement, and a plan for a suspected release. Each is its author’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Watch What Leaves, and Give Each Shared Barrier One Owner

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1 and F-2. Monitor what leaves your site by each route, effluent above all, for the agents you hold, so that a breach is found by you and not by a farmer. And if you share a site, name one owner for each shared barrier’s condition, inspection, and repair.

In August 2007 foot-and-mouth disease broke out in cattle on a farm near Guildford in England. The government traced the virus to the nearby Pirbright site, where a government institute and a vaccine company worked with it. The Health and Safety Executive found that live virus had most likely leaked into the site’s drains, which were cracked and in poor condition, that heavy rain may have helped carry it out, and that vehicles and people moving near the drains had not been properly controlled. It could not say which of the two occupants was the source. Animals had to be culled and movements restricted. The lessons are that a laboratory’s oldest, simplest barriers need as much care as its newest, that a site should watch what leaves it rather than learn of a leak from a farmer, and that every shared barrier needs one owner. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own site, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Ransomware Attack on Change Healthcare, February 2024
date_full: 12 February 2024 onward, read to May 2024 (record closed as to the disruption)
what: On 12 February 2024 intruders used stolen credentials on a Change Healthcare remote access portal without multifactor authentication, moved laterally and took data, and deployed ransomware on 21 February. The exchange, through which a large share of the sector's claims and prescriptions pass, was severed; pharmacies and providers lost their usual path, and federal advance payments followed on 9 March. The ALPHV group claimed the attack; a $22 million ransom was paid, and about 192.7 million people's data was breached.
tier: A criminal ransomware attack; not placed at the military-action tier: precision is not established and denial is absent.

findings.title: One Password Opened the Sector's Exchange.
findings.text: Every remote path into a shared exchange has a second factor and is watched.

annex.p: This annex is for health-information exchanges, clearinghouses, and prescription networks, the hospitals, practices, and pharmacies that depend on them, and the payers and agencies that keep funds moving. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to an organization. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an organization answers about its own systems (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an organization can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one organization. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the organization; it is that organization’s finding, and the place to start. Because the event’s access ran through a remote access portal reachable from outside, the standing exposure item is asked first.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Before the questions below: have you listed every way your systems can be reached remotely, with the authentication each requires?
You cannot protect a door you have not counted. A.3.2.
Does every remote access path into your systems require a second factor, with no exceptions?
One stolen password may be enough. A.3.1, A.3.2.
Would you see an intruder moving inside your systems within days, not weeks?
Nine days may pass unseen. A.3.2.
If your clearinghouse stopped tomorrow, which transactions could you send another way, and have you tested it?
Your prescriptions and cash may stop with it. A.3.1.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The Department of Health and Human Services’ cybersecurity performance goals for the health sector, published in January 2024, list multifactor authentication among their essential goals. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services’ accelerated and advance payments of March 2024 are the payment mechanism used after the event. The class’s requirements (§4.1) state a dependency inventory and a tested alternative path. Each is its author’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Put a Second Factor on Every Remote Door, and Watch Them

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1. If your organization is a shared exchange, require a second factor on every remote path into it, keep an inventory of those paths, and watch them closely enough to see an unexpected use within days.

On 12 February 2024 criminals logged into a remote access portal at Change Healthcare, the clearinghouse through which a large share of America’s medical claims and prescriptions pass, using a stolen password; the portal did not require a second factor. Nine days later they deployed ransomware, and the parent company cut the exchange off. Pharmacies struggled to fill prescriptions and doctors and hospitals could not get paid, until the federal government advanced payments in March. The company paid a $22 million ransom, and the data of about 193 million people was breached. The lessons are that every remote door into a system the whole sector depends on needs a second factor and close watching, and that the facilities that depend on it need a tested way around it. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own systems, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Fire at the Diehl Plant in Berlin, May 2024
what: On 3 May 2024 a fire broke out in a production building at the Diehl group's metal-coating plant in Berlin-Lichterfelde, which made parts for other industries and, on the company's account, did not supply the group's defense unit. The building partly collapsed and was demolished. The insurers and the Berlin public prosecutor found a technical, electrotechnical cause; unnamed security officials told the press they suspected Russian sabotage, which is unproven.
tier: Not military action on the record: the case was closed as an accident, and the suspicion of sabotage is unproven. The instrument is revised if a deliberate act is later established and attributed.

findings.title: The protective response rests on the security assessment, not only the criminal finding.
findings.text: Officials' suspicion rested on intercepts not admissible in court.

findings.title: A defense group's other sites carry its reputation.
findings.text: A site making no defense product was reported as a target because of the group's name.

annex.p: This annex is for defense manufacturers and the groups they belong to, including sites that make no defense product but carry a defense group’s name, and for the security staff and local authorities who investigate incidents at them. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Do you treat every site that carries your group’s name as a possible target, whether or not it supplies defense work?
A site you think of as civilian is chosen for the name on the gate. A.3.2.
If a fire destroyed a production building, how long would it take to restore production?
You learn the recovery time after the loss. A.3.1.
When a fire’s cause is uncertain, do your protective steps follow the security assessment, or wait for a criminal finding?
Protection waits on a court that may never rule. A.3.1.
Do you compare incidents across your sites and your peers’ sites, to see a pattern no single investigation shows?
A campaign looks like a run of accidents. A.3.1.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Act on the Security Assessment, and Look for the Pattern

annex.p: No authority has published an action for owners that this instrument reads; the prosecutor closed the case as an electrotechnical accident, and officials’ suspicion of sabotage was reported unproven. These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1: base protective measures on the security assessment, not only on the criminal finding; know the recovery time of each production building; and compare incidents across sites for a pattern.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Protect the Group’s Other Sites

annex.p: This step is this instrument’s, from F-2. Treat a defense group’s other sites as within the threat its defense work attracts, whatever they make.

On 3 May 2024 a fire broke out in a production building at the Diehl group’s metal-coating plant in Berlin-Lichterfelde; the building partly collapsed and was demolished four days later. The site belongs to a defense group but, on the company’s account, made parts for other industries and did not supply its defense unit. The company’s insurers attributed the fire to technical problems, and the Berlin public prosecutor closed the case in December 2024, finding an electrotechnical cause and no sign of arson. Unnamed security officials told the press they believed Russian saboteurs were likely responsible, on intercepts not admissible in court; that suspicion is unproven. The record is open in the sense that a later finding would change this instrument. The lessons are that protection should follow the security assessment rather than wait for a criminal finding, and that every site carrying a defense group’s name can be chosen for it. Any defense group with sites in several places has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this group does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: Ukrainian Strikes on Russian Defense Production, 2024 and 2025
what: In April 2024 and April 2025, Ukraine's forces struck a drone plant in Russia's Alabuga special economic zone, more than 1,000 kilometers from Ukraine. In 2024 a light aircraft carrying explosives hit a workers' dormitory, while the production halls, fitted with anti-drone cages, were undamaged in imagery. The effect of the 2025 strike has not been established, and the two sides' accounts differ.
tier: Military action by a state's armed forces in an armed conflict, not placed at the military-action tier because denial is not established on the record.

findings.title: Protection is designed against the campaign's weapon.
findings.text: The anti-drone cages over the halls held.

findings.title: The workforce and its housing are within the campaign's reach.
findings.text: The strike hit the dormitory where workers live.

annex.p: This annex is for defense manufacturers whose plants could be struck at long range in a conflict, wherever they stand, and for the governments that set their protective requirements. It reads a campaign against one side’s plants for what any plant’s defenders can learn from it. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Does your protection plan assume your distance from any front keeps your plant safe?
A plant far from the front is struck anyway. A.3.1.
If your plant were struck once, have you planned for it to be struck again?
A repaired plant is the next target. A.3.1.
Are your main production buildings protected against the weapon a campaign would use, such as small drones?
A single light aircraft stops production. A.3.1.
Is your workforce, and any housing on or near the site, inside your protection plan?
The strike misses the halls and hits the people who work in them. A.3.2.
Do you know how long it would take to restore each part of the plant after a strike?
Recovery time is learned under fire. A.3.1.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Protect Against the Campaign’s Weapon, Wherever the Plant Stands

annex.p: No authority has published an action for owners that this instrument reads. These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1: give no credit for distance from a front; protect production buildings against the weapon a campaign would use, as the plant here fitted anti-drone cages over its main halls in 2023; plan for repeated strikes; and know the recovery time of each part of the plant.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Bring the Workforce Inside the Plan

annex.p: This step is this instrument’s, from F-2. Include the workforce, and any housing on or near the site, in the protection plan, since the strike of 2024 hit a dormitory and not the halls.

In April 2024 and again in April 2025, Ukraine’s forces struck a drone plant in Russia’s Alabuga special economic zone, more than 1,000 kilometers from Ukraine; the 2025 strike was claimed by Ukraine’s General Staff. The plant produces attack drones. In 2024 a single light aircraft carrying explosives hit a dormitory where students who work at the plant live; the main production halls, fitted the year before with anti-drone cages over their roofs, were undamaged in satellite imagery, and the dormitory was under repair within a week. The effect of the 2025 strike has not been established; Russia said it downed one drone. The two sides’ accounts differ, and each is stated as its own. The lessons are that distance from a front gives no protection, that a plant must be protected against the weapon a campaign uses, and that the workforce and its housing are within reach. Any defense plant that could be struck in a conflict has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this plant does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Theft of C-17 and Fighter Aircraft Data, 2008 to 2014
what: Between 2008 and 2014, on the United States government's account, a businessman conspired with two people in China to break into the networks of American defense contractors and steal data on the C-17 transport aircraft and on fighter aircraft. He chose the targets and, from directory listings sent to him, the files to steal. He pleaded guilty in 2016; the volume of data taken has not been established by the court.
tier: Military action under the author's ruling that a state's covert theft operation is military action, on the United States government's account, but not placed at the military-action tier because denial is not established on the record.

findings.title: The index of a holding is protected like its contents.
findings.text: The files to steal were chosen from directory listings.

findings.title: The people who hold the data are part of the holding.
findings.text: The targets were chosen by person, company, and technology.

annex.p: This annex is for defense contractors and their suppliers that hold controlled technical data, and for the security and information technology staff who protect it. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Could an intruder learn which of your people, programs, and technologies hold your most valuable data, from sources outside your network or inside it?
The attacker is guided to exactly what to take. A.3.1.
Are your directory listings and file indexes protected like the data they describe?
The attacker shops from your own catalog. A.3.1.
Would you detect an intrusion within a stated time, rather than years later?
Theft runs for years before anyone notices. A.3.2.
If data were taken, could you say how much, and what it would give an adversary?
You cannot tell what was lost or what it cost. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Protect the Index, and the People Who Hold the Data

annex.p: No authority has published an action for owners that this instrument reads; the plea and sentencing records are its record. These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1 and F-2: protect directory listings and indexes of controlled data as the data is protected; and treat the people who hold the data, and what can be learned about them, as part of the holding.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Detect Within a Stated Time, and Know What Was Taken

annex.p: This step is this instrument’s, drawn from the facility class’s requirement of detection within a stated time, which the event engages (element I-3) though no finding is cut on it: detect an intrusion into a holding of controlled data within a stated time, and keep the records that would show what was taken.

Between 2008 and 2014, on the United States government’s account, a businessman conspired with two people in China to break into the networks of American defense contractors and steal data on the C-17 transport aircraft and on fighter aircraft. He told them which people, companies, and technologies to target; they sent him directory listings from the victims’ computers, and he chose which files to steal. He pleaded guilty in 2016 and was sentenced. The volume of data taken has not been established by the court. The lessons are that an attacker who knows the industry needs only an index to choose what to take, that the people who hold controlled data are part of what must be protected, and that intrusions must be found within a stated time, not years later. Any company that holds controlled technical data has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this company does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: China's Export Controls on Critical Minerals, 2023 to 2025
date: 3 July 2023 to November 2025, suspensions to 27 November 2026 and 10 January 2027
date_full: 3 July 2023 to November 2025, suspensions to 27 November 2026 and 10 January 2027 (record open)
what: China licensed exports of gallium and germanium from August 2023, then graphite, antimony, and superhard materials; on 3 December 2024 prohibited in principle their export to the United States and of dual-use items to United States military users; and from 4 April 2025 licensed seven rare earths including samarium. The prohibition on exports to the United States was suspended to 27 November 2026; the military-user prohibition and rare-earth licensing were not.
tier: Met, on the author's ruling of 19 November 2026 that a state's export control used as an adversarial action against another state's defense may be counted as military action: each of the four characteristics is established on the record.

findings.title: A Suspension Is Not a Removal.
findings.text: Cover is measured against the day the suspension ends.

findings.title: A Denial Counted as Military Action Has an Answer Beyond the Supplier.
findings.text: A denial counted as military action is reported to those who can answer it diplomatically.

annex.p: This annex is for defense suppliers and their sub-tier suppliers, the program offices that buy from them, and those who oversee the industrial base. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to a supplier. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions a supplier answers about its own products (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account a supplier can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one supplier. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the supplier; it is that supplier’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Do you know which of your products depend, at any tier, on gallium, germanium, graphite, antimony, superhard materials, or the seven controlled rare earths?
You may not know you are exposed. A.3.1.
For each, how long would your stocks and qualified alternatives last if the input were denied to you tomorrow?
Production may stop when stocks run out. A.3.1.
Is that cover measured from the day the current suspension ends, not from today?
A suspension may be read as relief. A.3.2.
Is an alternative source qualified now, at the quality your products need?
Qualifying one after the denial may take longer than your stocks last. A.3.1.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The announcements themselves state the measures. The Department of Defense’s and the Department of Commerce’s guidance and programs on critical minerals and defense supply-chain resilience set out related practice. The class’s requirements (§4.5, §5.2) state foreign-input dependence as a quantity, a potential adversary’s supply as a first-tier exposure, and alternatives qualified before the denial. Each is its author’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Count From the Day the Suspension Ends

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1. Restate your dependence on each controlled input every time the controlling state announces, suspends, or extends a measure, and measure your cover from the date the suspension ends.

Since 2023, China, which refines most of the world’s supply of several minerals used in defense electronics, magnets, and munitions, has required export licenses for gallium, germanium, graphite, antimony, superhard materials, and seven rare earths, and in December 2024 banned exporting several of them to the United States and any dual-use items to the United States military. Some of these measures have since been suspended for set periods, one to 27 November 2026 and another to 10 January 2027, but the ban on supplying the United States military has not been lifted. The lessons are that a supplier must know which of its products depend on these materials, and that a suspension can end on a date another government chooses. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own products, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: Counterfeit Networking Equipment Sold Into Defense Systems, 2013 to 2022
date: about August 2013 to at least April 2022
date_full: about August 2013 to at least April 2022 (record closed)
what: A reseller operating through at least 19 companies and about 25 online storefronts imported tens of thousands of modified networking devices from China and Hong Kong and sold them, with counterfeit labels and documents, as new genuine products of a major manufacturer. They reached hospitals, schools, and government and military systems, including platforms supporting military aircraft. The operator was sentenced on 1 May 2024.
tier: Criminal fraud, below the tier: intentionality and persistence present, precision and denial absent; not a state's operation.

findings.title: The Marks Said Which Channel It Came From.
findings.text: A seller's own documents do not establish the channel.

annex.p: This annex is for defense suppliers, their buyers of electronic and networking equipment, the program offices that accept their systems, and those who oversee them. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to a supplier. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions a supplier answers about its own purchasing (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account a supplier can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one supplier. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the supplier; it is that supplier’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
For each networking or electronic device you bought, have you confirmed with the manufacturer that the seller was authorized?
You may be buying outside the authorized channel without knowing it. A.3.2.
Do you test and inspect any part from a seller you have not confirmed, to a stated standard, before it is accepted?
Counterfeit devices may be installed on the strength of their labels. A.3.1.
Does every lot you ship carry a record of where it came from and what was done to it?
Your customers may not be able to trace it. A.3.1.
If you learned a lot was counterfeit, could you find every system it reached, and would you report it?
Counterfeit parts may remain in systems no one lists. A.3.1.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The Department of Justice’s account sets out the scheme. The acquisition regulation’s requirements for the detection and avoidance of counterfeit electronic parts and the reporting of suspect counterfeits through the government’s reporting system set out related practice. The class’s requirements (§4.3, §5.4) state provenance records, testing of parts bought outside the authorized channel, and reporting. Each is its author’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Ask the Manufacturer, Not the Seller

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1. Before you accept equipment that claims a manufacturer’s brand, confirm with that manufacturer that the seller is one of its authorized distributors, and treat anything you cannot confirm as needing test and inspection.

For nearly nine years, from 2013 to 2022, a reseller operating through at least 19 companies and about 25 online stores sold tens of thousands of fake networking devices, made in China and Hong Kong and dressed up with forged labels and paperwork as new products of a major American manufacturer. They ended up in hospitals, schools, and government and military systems, including platforms that support fighter jets. The scheme was a fraud for profit, and its operator was sentenced in 2024 to more than six years in prison. The lessons are that labels and paperwork can be forged, and that a buyer should confirm with the manufacturer itself that a seller is authorized before trusting what it sells. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own purchasing, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: An Intelligence Officer's Attempt to Obtain Aerospace Design Data Through Engineers, 2013 to 2018
date_full: at least December 2013 to April 2018 (record closed)
what: On the United States government's account, a deputy division director of China's Ministry of State Security used aliases, front companies, and universities to recruit aerospace engineers to travel to China and then sought their companies' proprietary information, from 2017 seeking GE Aviation's composite fan-module design through an engineer, by then with the company and FBI cooperating. He was arrested in Belgium in 2018, convicted in 2021, and sentenced to 20 years in 2022.
tier: Recorded as military action below the tier: intentionality, persistence, and precision established, denial absent.

findings.title: The Design Sought Was Outside the Class.
findings.text: The human path is closed where the design is held.

annex.p: This annex is for defense and aerospace companies that hold design knowledge, their engineers and researchers, their security and counterintelligence staff, and those who oversee them. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to a company. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions a company answers about its own engineers (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account a company can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one company. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the company; it is that company’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Do you know which of your people hold knowledge of your most valuable designs and their test results?
You may not know who an adversary would approach. A.3.1.
Are your people told what an approach looks like, including an invitation to present at a university abroad?
An approach may look like ordinary research. A.3.1.
Are approaches, foreign travel, and outside contacts reported and assessed, and would an engineer carrying company documents to a presentation abroad be known to you?
An unreported approach may pass a design before you know it was sought. A.3.2.
Is an approach that seeks a design handled at once as an attempt on it, with your counterintelligence partners?
An attempt may run to completion. A.3.1.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The Department of Justice’s account and the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s guidance to industry on economic espionage and insider risk set out what was found and related practice. The class’s requirements (§4.3, §5.2) state knowing who holds the design, reporting and assessing approaches, travel, and contacts, and handling an approach as an attempt on the holding. Each is its author’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Know Who Holds the Design, Wherever It Is Held

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1. If your company holds a design with defense application, whether or not it is classified or under a defense contract, know who holds it and have their approaches reported and assessed as if it were.

From at least 2013 until his arrest in 2018, an officer of China’s Ministry of State Security, according to the United States government, used fake names, front companies, and universities to approach engineers at aviation and aerospace companies, often by inviting them to give a talk in China, and then asked them for their companies’ secrets. One target was a GE Aviation engineer who knew the design of a composite jet-engine fan that no other company has managed to copy. As reported, the engineer went to China with company documents without telling the company. The company and the FBI ended up running the conversation, and the officer was convicted and sentenced to 20 years. The lessons are that people are the way in, and that a company must know who holds its most valuable knowledge and hear about every approach to them. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own engineers, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Loss of Half the Nation's Ammonium Perchlorate Capacity at Henderson, Nevada, 4 May 1988
what: Fire and explosions destroyed the PEPCON ammonium perchlorate plant at Henderson, Nevada, killing two and injuring several hundred. It was one of two free-world producers; the other, about two miles away, closed briefly. About half the nation's capacity for the oxidizer of the Shuttle and of missiles was lost, and an advisory group allocated the remainder. The Fire Administration attributed ignition to a welding torch; the Department of Labor found it undetermined.
tier: Not an attack: a fire at a near-sole source. None of the four characteristics is present.

findings.title: Two Plants in One Town Were One Source.
findings.text: A second source counts only if one event cannot take both.

annex.p: This annex is for program offices, prime contractors, and their suppliers of energetics and other first-tier inputs, and those who plan the industrial base. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to a program. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions a program answers about its own inputs (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account a program can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one program office or supplier. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the program office or supplier; it is that program office or supplier’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
For each first-tier input your programs need, how many producers are there, and where are they?
You may count two sources where there is one. A.3.2.
Could one fire, explosion, flood, or strike reach more than one of them?
One event may take the whole supply. A.3.2.
Is it known now how much of each input your programs need and how much each producer makes?
An allocation may be made without the basis for it. A.3.1.
Is the authority to allocate what remains named, with its basis, before any loss?
The allocation may wait for a body to be formed. A.3.1.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The General Accounting Office’s report and the case study set out what was found. The Department of Defense’s industrial-base assessments and its authorities under the Defense Production Act to give priority, allocate, and build capacity set out related practice. The class’s requirements (§4.2, §6.2) state sole sources known, the authority to allocate named, and second sources qualified. Each is its author’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Count by What One Event Can Reach

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1. When you count the sources of a first-tier input, count as one any that a single fire, explosion, flood, or strike could reach together, and treat the input as sole-source until a source outside that reach is qualified.

On 4 May 1988, a fire and a series of explosions destroyed the PEPCON plant in Henderson, Nevada, killing two people and injuring several hundred. The plant was one of only two in the free world that made ammonium perchlorate, the oxidizer in the solid rocket fuel of the Space Shuttle and of many military missiles. The other plant was about two miles away in the same town and was briefly closed. The country lost half its supply overnight, and an advisory group had to divide what remained among the programs that needed it. The government had not known how much each program needed or how much each plant made. The lessons are that two suppliers next to each other are really one, and that we must know our needs and our sources before a loss. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own inputs, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Bombing of the Murrah Federal Building, April 1995
what: On the morning of 19 April 1995 a truck bomb was detonated at the curb beside the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building in Oklahoma City, destroying the columns under a transfer girder and bringing down about half the building. Of 175 people in the collapsed part, 153 died; of 186 elsewhere, 10 died. Nineteen of the dead were children, in a building that housed a day-care center.
tier: A deliberate domestic act of terrorism, not military action: no state was involved.

findings.title: Structural robustness is measured by the people it protects.
findings.text: Almost everyone in the collapsed part died; almost everyone elsewhere lived.

findings.title: Those who cannot escape unaided are placed, not only counted.
findings.text: Children in the building's day-care center were among the dead.

findings.title: A housed function continues from outside the building before it moves.
findings.text: The Social Security Administration kept serving the city from other offices and its central records, and opened a new office thirty-three days later.

annex.p: This annex is for owners, tenants, and security managers of government buildings, federal, state, and local, and for any public building that stands close to a street and holds many people, including those who cannot leave without help. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
How close can a vehicle get to your building’s structure, and is that distance stated against the explosive your facility’s security level assumes?
A truck at the curb is within reach of a column. A.3.1.
Would the loss of one or two columns bring down floors above them, or is your structure designed to resist progressive collapse?
A single blast brings down half the building. A.3.1.
Do you know how many people are in the building at its busiest hours, and where?
The building is full when the blast comes. A.3.2.
Where in the building are those who cannot escape unaided, such as children in a day-care center, and is that the safest place?
The most vulnerable are in the most exposed space. A.3.2.
If your building were lost this morning, which of your functions would be performed again today from elsewhere, from which records, and by whom?
The work stops until a new office opens. A.3.3.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Hold the Standoff, and Design Against Collapse
