annex.p: After the bombing, the Department of Justice’s assessment of 28 June 1995 sorted federal facilities into five security levels and set minimum standards for each, and Executive Order 12977 of 19 October 1995 established the Interagency Security Committee to set security standards for federal facilities, which it still does. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-1: require both standoff and structural robustness, and measure robustness by the people it protects.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Place the Vulnerable Where They Are Safest

annex.p: This step is this instrument’s, from F-2. State where in the building those who cannot escape unaided are placed, such as a day-care center, and put them where the building best protects them.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Carry the Work Before You Move the Office

annex.p: This step is this instrument’s, from F-3. Hold the records each function needs where the same event cannot reach them, name the offices that would take its work and its calls on the day, and plan for the staff you would draw from elsewhere if your own are among the casualties. On its own account, the Social Security Administration did all three in 1995 and kept serving the city while a new office was found.

At about nine in the morning on 19 April 1995 a truck bomb was detonated at the curb beside the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building in Oklahoma City. The blast destroyed the columns under a third-floor transfer girder, and the floors above collapsed, taking about half the building. Of 175 people in the part that collapsed, 153 died; of 186 in the part that stood, 10 died. Nineteen of the dead were children, in a building that housed a day-care center. It was a domestic act of terrorism; no state was involved. After it, the federal government set five security levels for its facilities and created the Interagency Security Committee to set their security standards. The Social Security Administration, which lost sixteen of its people, kept serving the city from its other offices and its central records and opened a new office thirty-three days later. The lessons are that distance from the street and a structure that resists collapse are both needed, that robustness is measured by the lives it saves, and that those who cannot escape on their own must be placed where the building protects them best. Any public building near a street has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this building does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Breach of the United States Capitol, January 2021
what: On 6 January 2021, during the joint session of Congress to count the electoral votes, a crowd overcame the police lines and entered the Capitol. The Senate recessed at 2:13 p.m., floor staff carried the states' certificates from the chamber, and about 140 officers were assaulted. The National Guard began arriving at 5:20 p.m., about three hours after the request was approved, and the count was completed in the night.
tier: A deliberate adversarial event, not military action: no state is alleged in any account to have acted.

findings.title: The reinforcement time is the sum of two chains.
findings.text: Approval of the request and the Guard's arrival each took time.

findings.title: The instruments of a time-bound act are records.
findings.text: The count rested on paper certificates carried from the floor.

annex.p: This annex is for the security leaders of legislatures, courts, election offices, and other government bodies that must complete acts scheduled by law, and for the police and military forces that would reinforce them. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Which of your acts must happen on a date set by law, and is security planned for each of them?
An act the law will not let you postpone is the day you are least prepared. A.3.1.
Do you prepare a full operational and staffing plan for each such act, with officers equipped and trained for it?
Front-line officers face a crowd without the equipment or training they need. A.3.1.
How long would reinforcement take, counting both the time to approve the request and the time for the reinforcing force to arrive?
Help arrives hours after it is asked for. A.3.2.
Are the physical instruments of the act, such as certificates or ballots, protected as records, so the act can resume if the room is lost?
The act cannot continue because its documents are lost. A.3.2.
Could your body resume and complete its act on time if it had to stop for hours?
The act misses its deadline. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Plan Each Time-Bound Act

annex.p: The Senate committees’ bipartisan report found failures of intelligence and of planning, found that the Capitol Police prepared no department-wide operational or staffing plan for the joint session and that its leadership did not give front-line officers effective protective equipment or training, and recommended that the Chief be empowered to request the National Guard’s assistance in an emergency. No step of this instrument’s is added here.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Shorten Reinforcement, and Protect the Act’s Records

annex.p: Public Law 117-77, of 22 December 2021, allows the Chief of the Capitol Police to request assistance without the Board’s prior approval when the Chief determines it necessary. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-1 and F-2: count reinforcement time as the sum of the time to approve the request and the time for the reinforcing force to arrive; and treat the physical instruments of a time-bound act as records, protected so the act can resume.

On 6 January 2021 Congress met in joint session to count the electoral votes of the 2020 presidential election, an act scheduled by the Constitution and by law. A crowd overcame the police lines and entered the Capitol; the Senate went into recess at 2:13 p.m., floor staff carried the states’ certificates from the chamber, and about 140 officers were assaulted. The Capitol Police Board approved a request for the National Guard at 2:10 p.m., and the Guard began arriving at 5:20 p.m. The Senate returned at 8:06 p.m., and the count was completed in the night. A bipartisan Senate report found failures of intelligence and planning, no department-wide plan for the session, and officers without the equipment or training they needed; Congress later let the Chief of the Capitol Police request help without the Board’s prior approval. The House select committee’s findings on the event’s cause are its own. The lessons are that an act the law schedules must be planned for as the most exposed day of the year, that reinforcement time counts both the approval and the arrival, and that the papers of the act are records to protect. Any body that must complete an act by a date set in law has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show leadership whether this body does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Ransomware Attack on the City of Atlanta, March 2018
date: 10 to 22 March 2018 and the months after
date_full: 10 to 22 March 2018 and the months after
what: In March 2018 ransomware encrypted about 3,789 of the City of Atlanta's computers, and its court, jail processing, water billing, and procurement went to paper, while police, fire, 911, and water treatment were unaffected. The city's estimate of the damage grew to a third of 424 programs by June, and years of dashcam video were lost. The Department of Justice indicted two foreign nationals for the wider campaign; no government role is alleged.
tier: A deliberate criminal attack, not military action: no government role is alleged.

findings.title: Payment is not a recovery path.
findings.text: The attackers' payment page disappeared within days.

findings.title: The inventory carries criticality and is the first assessment.
findings.text: The city's estimate of what was lost grew for three months.

annex.p: This annex is for cities, counties, and other local governments, and for the technology teams that run their courts, utilities billing, permits, records, and other services. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Have the vulnerabilities your own audits found been fixed, and is someone accountable for it?
The attacker enters through a gap you already knew about. A.3.2.
Are your records, such as video evidence and court files, backed up in copies an attacker could not encrypt?
Years of records are lost. A.3.1.
Could your courts, jails, billing, and procurement run on paper, and for how long?
Are your police, fire, 911, and water treatment systems separate from the city’s general network?
The attack reaches the functions people depend on most. A.3.2.
Do you keep an inventory of every program, marked by how critical it is, so you can tell at once what is lost?
Your estimate of the damage keeps growing for months. A.3.1.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Plan to Restore or Rebuild, Not to Pay, and Know Your Inventory

annex.p: No authority has published an action for owners that this instrument reads. These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1 and F-2: count only restoring from protected copies or rebuilding as recovery paths, since the attackers’ payment page disappeared within days; and keep an inventory of programs marked by criticality, as the first assessment after an attack.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Close Known Gaps, Separate Emergency Functions, and Prepare Paper

annex.p: These steps are the instrument’s, drawn from the facility class’s provisions the event confirms (elements I-1, E-1, and E-2), though no finding is cut on them: close the gaps your own audits find; keep emergency functions separate from the general network, as Atlanta’s police, fire, 911, and water treatment were; and prepare each service to run on paper.

In March 2018 ransomware encrypted about 3,789 of the City of Atlanta’s computers. Its municipal court could not take payments or validate warrants, its jail processed people by hand, and its water billing and procurement stopped; police, fire, 911, and water treatment were unaffected. The city’s own audit had found vulnerabilities two months before. The city’s estimate of the damage grew from a fifth of its programs, none critical, to a third of 424 by June, nearly thirty percent of them mission-critical, and years of police dashcam video were lost. The attackers’ page for arranging payment disappeared within days. The Department of Justice indicted two foreign nationals for a wider campaign of such attacks; no government role is alleged, and the charges are untried. The lessons are that paying is not a recovery plan, that a city must know which of its systems are critical before it loses them, and that its emergency functions must stand apart. Any local government has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show leadership whether this government does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Killings at the Fulton County Courthouse, Atlanta, 11 March 2005
what: A man on trial overpowered the deputy escorting him, took her gun from a lockbox, went to the presiding judge's chambers, whose door was by practice unlocked, and in the courtroom killed the judge and the court reporter; he killed a sheriff's sergeant outside and a federal agent elsewhere before surrendering the next day. One deputy escorted up to four by policy, and a chamber alarm was verified by four calls before dispatch.
tier: Non-military adversarial, the act of one person, below the tier: intentionality and precision established, persistence absent, denial not established.

findings.title: A Practice and a Policy Opened the Building.
findings.text: No protection is relaxed by practice without being assessed.

annex.p: This annex is for court administrators, sheriffs and court security officers, judges, and those who design and oversee courthouse security. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to a courthouse. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions a court answers about its own courthouse (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account a court can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one court or sheriff. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the court or sheriff; it is that court or sheriff’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Are the doors between the secure circulation and chambers and courtrooms locked in practice, every day, and does someone know their state?
The design may be open where it is meant to be closed. A.3.1.
Is a duress alarm from chambers or a courtroom answered at once, or verified first?
Help may wait on telephone calls. A.3.2.
Do indications of a defendant’s intent, such as weapons found, change his escort?
One escort may face a person known to be dangerous. A.3.1.
Has any change in your practices or policies, such as unlocked doors or alarm verification, been assessed against your security design before it was adopted?
Practice may have relaxed the design without anyone deciding to. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The commission on courthouse security’s recommendations, and the national guidance on courthouse security published by court-administration and judicial-security organizations, set out related practice. The class’s requirements (§3.3, §4.3, §5.2) state the escort, the locked doors, the duress alarm, and the control room. Each is its author’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Treat a Change in Practice as a Change in Design

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1. Before any practice or policy relaxes a protection your courthouse’s security relies on, a door left open for convenience, an alarm verified before it is answered, more prisoners per escort, have a named authority assess it against the security design and record the decision.

On 11 March 2005, a man on trial in Atlanta’s Fulton County Courthouse overpowered the deputy escorting him, took her gun, and went to the judge’s chambers, where the door, as had become the practice, was unlocked. He entered the courtroom and killed the judge and the court reporter, then killed a sheriff’s sergeant outside and a federal agent elsewhere in the city before he surrendered the next day. Under a new policy, the officer watching the alarms had made telephone calls before sending help. The lessons are that a courthouse’s protections only work if they are kept up every day, and that no one should relax them, for convenience or by policy, without checking what that does to the building’s safety. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own courthouse, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Attack at a Federal Judge's Home, New Jersey, 19 July 2020
what: A lawyer who had appeared before a federal district judge came to her New Jersey home posing as a delivery driver and opened fire when the door was opened, killing her son and seriously wounding her husband; he had found her address and photographs of her home and car online. The Inspector General found the Marshals Service's online threat detection and home intrusion systems inadequate, and the Judicial Security and Privacy Act of 2022 followed.
tier: Non-military adversarial, the act of one person, below the tier: intentionality and precision established, persistence and denial not established.

findings.title: The Door Was Opened to a Delivery.
findings.text: No door is opened to an unverified caller.

annex.p: This annex is for judges and others who serve courts in exposed roles, their families, the agencies that protect them, and court administrators. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to a court. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions a court answers about its own judges (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account a court can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one court or protecting agency. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the court or protecting agency; it is that court or protecting agency’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Can a judge’s home address, or photographs of the home or car, be found online today, and who is removing them?
An attacker may find the home in minutes. A.3.1.
Are threats against judges, including those posted online, assessed continuously, years after a decision?
A threat may go unseen. A.3.1.
Does each judge’s household know not to open the door to an unverified caller or delivery, and have a place away from home to receive deliveries?
The door may be opened to the attacker. A.3.2.
Is each judge’s home protected with intrusion detection the protecting agency monitors?
An attack may go unanswered. A.3.1.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The Judicial Security and Privacy Act of 2022, the Inspector General’s recommendations to the Marshals Service, and the judiciary’s and the Marshals Service’s guidance to judges on home security and personal information set out related practice. The class’s requirements (§4.4, §5.3) state continuous threat assessment, home protection, and removal of personal information. Each is its author’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Protect the Door, Not Only the House

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1. Give each judge’s household a way to verify any caller or delivery before the door is opened, and a place away from the home where packages can be received, and make sure everyone in the house knows both.

On 19 July 2020, a lawyer who had appeared before a federal judge in New Jersey went to her home disguised as a delivery driver. When the door was opened he started shooting, killing her twenty-year-old son and badly wounding her husband. He had found her address and photographs of her house and car on the internet. A federal watchdog later found that the Marshals Service could not adequately spot threats posted online and that its home alarm systems were outdated, and Congress passed a law in 2022 to keep federal judges’ personal information off the internet. The lessons are that a judge’s home must be protected as carefully as the courtroom, and that this includes who is allowed to come to the door. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own judges, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Theft of Background-Investigation Records From the Office of Personnel Management, 2014 to 2015
date: 2012 to 26 March 2015, disclosed June and July 2015
date_full: 2012 to 26 March 2015, disclosed June and July 2015 (record closed)
what: An adversary present on OPM's network from 2012 took the background-investigation records of 21.5 million people, including about 5.6 million fingerprints, and the personnel records of 4.2 million federal employees between July 2014 and March 2015. One intruder was removed in May 2014 while another, which had entered with a contractor's credentials, remained. The House Oversight majority staff found the breaches preventable.
tier: Met, recorded as military action at the tier on the congressional record's attribution: intentionality, persistence, and precision established, and denial established as denial of function on the author's ruling of 20 November 2026.

findings.title: One Intruder Was Removed and Another Stayed.
findings.text: A holding is not called clear while a second intruder can remain.

findings.title: Denial of a Holding's Function Without Its Destruction.
findings.text: Denial is read as denial of function, with a consequence limit.

annex.p: This annex is for agencies and organizations that hold vetting, personnel, or biometric records, their contractors, and those who oversee them. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to an agency. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an agency answers about its own records (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an agency can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one agency. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the agency; it is that agency’s finding, and the place to start. Because the event’s access ran through credentials used to reach the Office’s network from outside, the standing exposure item is asked first.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Are your vetting, personnel, and biometric records protected at the level of what they describe, not as an ordinary personnel system?
The records of everyone you trust may be held as office data. A.3.1.
Do you know where every copy is, including at other agencies or providers, and who can reach each?
Records may be taken from a place you do not watch. A.3.1.
Are the credentials you issue to contractors held to the same verification as your own staff’s?
A contractor’s credential may be the way in. A.3.1.
After you remove an intruder, does someone independent search for any related presence before you declare the network clear?
A second intruder may stay and take what the first could not. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The committee majority staff’s report and the Office’s Inspector General’s reports set out what they found and recommended. Federal requirements for the protection of high-value assets and for incident response set out related practice. The class’s requirements (§4.2, §4.6) state the vetting records as a first-tier holding, the custodian’s knowledge of them, detection and bounding in a stated time, and contractor credentials held to verification. Each is its author’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Search Again Before You Call It Clear

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1. When you remove an intruder from systems that hold your most sensitive records, have a party independent of your first response search those systems and everything that can reach them for any related presence, and treat the records as reached until that search is done.

Between 2014 and 2015, attackers whom a congressional report describes as state-sponsored stole the government’s background-investigation files on 21.5 million people, including the fingerprints of about 5.6 million, and the personnel records of 4.2 million federal employees from the Office of Personnel Management. These files describe the private lives, contacts, and vulnerabilities of the people the government trusts with its secrets, and they cannot be changed. The attackers were in the network for years; when one intruder was found and removed in 2014, another stayed and took the files. The lessons are that records like these must be protected as carefully as what they protect, and that removing one intruder does not mean the network is clean. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own records, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Intrusion Into the Illinois Voter Registration System, 2016
what: From 23 June 2016 an attacker exploited the online voter application of the Illinois State Board of Elections by structured-query injection; staff noticed on 12 July, the Board took the system offline on 13 July and restored it by 28 July, and notified about 76,000 voters. The Senate Intelligence Committee reported access to up to 200,000 records and no evidence of change. A July 2018 indictment charged Russian military intelligence officers.
tier: Recorded as military action below the tier on the indictment's attribution: intentionality, persistence, and precision established, denial absent.

findings.title: No Evidence of Change Is Not a Showing of None.
findings.text: The roll is shown unchanged, not inferred to be.

annex.p: This annex is for state and local election officials, the vendors of voter-registration systems, and those who oversee election security. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to an election office. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an election office answers about its own roll (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an election office can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one election office. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the election office; it is that election office’s finding, and the place to start. Because the event’s access ran through the system’s public online application, the standing exposure item is asked first.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Is every interface to your voter-registration system, including the public online application, inventoried with what it can read and change, and tested against injection?
The public application may open the whole roll. A.3.1.
How quickly would you notice an intruder reading the roll?
An intruder may read for weeks. A.3.1.
Do you keep regular copies of the roll that your own systems cannot reach, and could you compare every record against one after an intrusion?
You may be unable to show that nothing changed. A.3.2.
Can your poll books run on a copy taken before an incident, and on paper?
Voters may be turned away while the system is restored. A.3.1.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The Senate Committee’s recommendations, and the guidance of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and the Election Assistance Commission on securing voter-registration systems, set out related practice. The class’s requirements (§4.2, §5.2) state the roll as a first-tier holding, inventoried interfaces, a record of every change, detection in a stated time, and poll books on a prior copy and paper. Each is its author’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Keep a Copy the Intruder Cannot Reach

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1. Keep regular copies of your roll where your own systems and accounts cannot reach them, and after any intrusion compare every record against the last copy taken before it, resolving each difference before poll books are drawn.

From 23 June 2016, an attacker broke into the Illinois State Board of Elections’ voter-registration system through a flaw in its online voter application and read voters’ records for about three weeks before staff noticed. The Board took the system offline and notified about 76,000 voters; a Senate committee later said the intruder had access to up to 200,000 records, and a federal indictment in 2018 charged Russian military intelligence officers with stealing information on about 500,000. The Senate committee found no evidence that any record was changed, but said the intruder could have changed them. The lessons are that the public front door to the voter roll must be secured like the roll itself, and that an election office must be able to prove, not assume, that its records were not altered. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own roll, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Attack on Ukraine's Central Election Commission, May 2014
date_full: March to 25 May 2014 (record closed as to the event)
what: During the armed conflict of 2014, intruders in the network of Ukraine's Central Election Commission since March deleted files four days before the presidential election, disabling the tallying system, which the commission restored from backups. On election night the Security Service removed a program set to publish a false winner, by one account about forty minutes before a Russian state channel broadcast the false result as the commission's. The results website was attacked after the polls closed. The count stood.
tier: Adversarial, during an armed conflict, attributed by Ukraine's Security Service to attackers acting from Russia; not placed at the military-action tier: intentionality, persistence, and precision are present, and denial is not established, on the author's ruling of 20 November 2026 that an attempt at denial is not denial. A near miss on the tier: two barriers held, one by minutes.

findings.title: The Publication System Was the Adversary's for Two Months.
findings.text: The publication system is shown clean before election night.

findings.title: A Counterfeit Was Aired as the Commission's Own.
findings.text: Official results carry a mark that shows a counterfeit for what it is.

findings.title: Two Barriers Held, One by Minutes.
findings.text: The barriers that held are kept, and the minutes are widened.

annex.p: This annex is for election authorities at every level, the vendors who build and run their results and publication systems, and the officials who certify results. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to an election authority. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an election authority answers about its own systems (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an election authority can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one election authority. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the election authority; it is that election authority’s finding, and the place to start. Because the event’s access ran through systems reachable from outside the commission, the standing exposure item is asked first.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Before the questions below: have you listed every system of yours that can be reached from outside, the results website and its publishing system above all, with who can change each?
You cannot verify what you have not listed. A.3.2.
Is your election-night publication system restored or verified from a known-good state after its last change and before the polls close?
An intruder’s result may be waiting in it. A.3.2.
Are the backups you would restore from beyond the reach of anyone in your publication system?
Your restoration may restore the intruder. A.3.2.
If your tallying or publication system were destroyed tonight, how many days would you need to restore it from backups no one in it can reach, and how many days before the vote do you have?
The margin that held here was four days; yours may be less. A.3.2.
How long before results are published is your publication system checked for a planted result, and would a finding leave you time to restore?
The margin that held here was minutes. A.3.2.
If an image of your website showing a false result were broadcast tonight, could you show at once that it is not yours?
A counterfeit will stand until you can. A.3.2.
Is the unofficial result published on election night separated from the tabulation and the canvass, and checked against paper before certification?
A false publication may reach the count. A.3.1.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The Central Election Commission restored its systems from backups before the vote, and the Security Service removed the false-result program before publication; the class’s requirements for count assurance, reporting separation, and audit against paper (§4.4) state the protections that worked. The election-security guidance of national authorities, among them the United States’ Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, sets out practices for results reporting and its separation from tabulation. Each is its publisher’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Show the Publishing System Clean, and Make Your Results Recognizable

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1 to F-3. Before the polls close, restore or verify your results-publishing system from a known-good state, and keep its backups where no one in it can reach them. And publish official results in a way the public and the press can verify as yours, so that a counterfeit can be shown for what it is the moment it appears. Check the publication system early enough that, if you find a planted result, you still have time to restore.

In May 2014, during the conflict in eastern Ukraine, hackers who had been inside the computers of Ukraine’s Central Election Commission since March deleted files four days before the presidential election and disabled the vote-tallying system; the commission restored it from backups. On election night, government specialists found a program on the commission’s servers set to show a fringe candidate winning with 37 percent, and removed it shortly before results were published; he actually received about 1 percent. A Russian state television channel broadcast the false result anyway, presented as the commission’s website. The lessons are that the system that publishes results must be shown clean before election night, not checked in the last hour, and that official results should be published in a form the public can verify, so that a counterfeit can be shown to be one. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own systems, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Shooting at Robb Elementary School, Uvalde, 24 May 2022
what: An eighteen-year-old gunman killed nineteen students and two teachers in two adjoining classrooms, likely entering through a door whose lock the Texas House committee found was widely known to be faulty. The lockdown did not reach every teacher. Officers entered within minutes and withdrew; more than 370 came; the Justice Department recorded 77 minutes from the first officers' arrival to the tactical entry and found cascading failures of leadership and command.
tier: Non-military adversarial, the act of one person, below the tier: intentionality and precision established, persistence absent, denial not established.

findings.title: The Lock Everyone Knew Was Faulty.
findings.text: No room relies on a lock known to fail.

annex.p: This annex is for school districts, principals and teachers, school-district and local police, and those who oversee school safety. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to a school. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions a school answers about its own school (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account a school can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one school or district. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the school or district; it is that school or district’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Can every classroom door be locked from inside, at once, by the adult present, and is every lock checked regularly?
A room may not lock when it must. A.3.2.
If a lock is reported faulty, how quickly is it repaired, and what does that room do in a lockdown until then?
Children may shelter behind a door that does not hold. A.3.2.
Does your lockdown alarm reach every room by more than one means, including the intercom?
A teacher may not know there is a lockdown. A.3.1.
Have the police agencies that would answer your school agreed in advance who commands, how calls from inside reach them, and what they do on arrival?
Officers present may wait without command. A.3.1.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The committee’s report and the Justice Department’s review set out their findings and recommendations, among them on incident command, active-shooter training, and school security. State requirements on school safety audits and locked doors, and federal guidance on school security and active-shooter response, set out related practice. The class’s requirements (§4.2, §4.3, §5.2) state lockdown, the alarm, and the response time including command. Each is its author’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Find and Fix Every Lock That Fails

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1. Check every lock your lockdown relies on at set intervals, repair any defect within days, give any room with a faulty lock a stated alternative until it is fixed, and treat propping or defeating a lock as a change no one may make on their own.

On 24 May 2022, an eighteen-year-old gunman entered Robb Elementary School in Uvalde, Texas, and killed nineteen children and two teachers in two connected classrooms. A Texas House committee found that the lock on one of those classrooms was widely known to be faulty and had not been fixed, that staff often propped doors open, and that not every teacher was told of the lockdown. Officers arrived within minutes, but the Justice Department found that seventy-seven minutes passed before a team went into the classroom, with no one taking command as hundreds of officers gathered. The lessons are that a school’s locks and alarms must work every day, not only on paper, and that the police who would respond must agree in advance who is in charge and that they will go in. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own school, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Tornado at Plaza Towers Elementary School, Moore, 20 May 2013
what: A tornado of the highest rating crossed Moore, Oklahoma, killing 24 or 25 people as the sources count. At Plaza Towers Elementary seven children were killed sheltering, as practiced, in the designated safety area of a building with no safe room; at Briarwood Elementary, also without one, everyone survived the building's destruction. NIST studied the schools' performance, and the district rebuilt both with safe rooms.
tier: Not an attack: a natural hazard. None of the four characteristics is present.

findings.title: A School With No Refuge Has to Say So.
findings.text: No school drills its children into a space it has not said is not a refuge.

annex.p: This annex is for school districts and principals in regions of tornado, hurricane, earthquake, or tsunami hazard, emergency managers, and those who oversee school construction. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to a school. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions a school answers about its own school (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account a school can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one school or district. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the school or district; it is that school or district’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Does your school have a refuge built to withstand the storms of your region, with room for everyone in it?
Children may shelter where the building will not stand. A.3.1.
Is the space where your children drill an engineered refuge, or the safest available corridor?
The drill may lead children to a space that fails. A.3.2.
Can every child and adult reach the refuge within the warning the hazard gives?
Some may not reach it in time. A.3.1.
If you have no refuge yet, have you told families, and what do you do on days the hazard is forecast?
Families may believe the school is safer than it is. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The National Institute of Standards and Technology’s reconnaissance, the model building code’s storm-shelter requirement for new schools in the highest tornado-hazard region, the standard for storm shelters, and the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s guidance on safe rooms set out related practice. The class’s requirements (§4.4, §5.1) state a refuge built against the hazard for every occupant within the warning. Each is its author’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Say When There Is No Refuge, and Plan for the Day

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1. If your school has no refuge built for your region’s storms, tell your district and families plainly, and decide in advance, with a named person and set criteria, what you will do on days the hazard is forecast, such as moving children to a refuge elsewhere or dismissing early.

On the afternoon of 20 May 2013, a tornado of the most violent rating struck Moore, Oklahoma, killing at least 24 people. At Plaza Towers Elementary School, seven children were killed while sheltering exactly where they had practiced, in the school’s designated safe area; the school had no purpose-built storm shelter. A nearby school, Briarwood Elementary, was also destroyed and also had no shelter, but everyone there survived. Both schools were rebuilt with safe rooms. The lessons are that a drill does not make a hallway a shelter, and that a school without a real refuge must say so and plan for dangerous days until it has one. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own school, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The PowerSchool Breach, December 2024
date_full: from about 22 December 2024, discovered 28 December 2024 (record closed)
what: An intruder used stolen credentials to reach PowerSchool's student information system and, from about 22 December 2024, exported data with its own support tool, including for many districts all historical data and, in some cases, parents' access rights. The company paid a ransom for deletion; in May 2025 districts were extorted with the same data. A person pleaded guilty in June and was sentenced on 14 October 2025. Scale figures are the intruder's claim.
tier: Criminal extortion, attributed to no state, below the tier: only intentionality established.

findings.title: A Ransom Paid Did Not Make the Record Safe.
findings.text: No protected family learns last that its child's record is out.

annex.p: This annex is for school districts and their technology staff, the vendors of student information systems, and those who oversee student privacy and safety. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to a district. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions a district answers about its own student records (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account a district can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one district. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the district; it is that district’s finding, and the place to start. Because the event’s access ran through stolen credentials used to reach the vendor’s platform from outside, the standing exposure item is asked first.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Are the accounts your vendor’s staff and support tools use to reach your data protected by more than a password, and can you see when they are used?
A stolen credential may export your district’s whole record. A.3.1.
Could each school find a child’s guardians, custody restrictions, and medical alerts today if the platform were unavailable or untrustworthy?
A school may not know who may take a child. A.3.1.
If records showing who may not take a child were stolen, who would tell the protected families, and how fast?
A family a court has protected may learn last. A.3.2.
Would a change to who may take a child be confirmed by a path other than the system it was made in?
A child may be released to the wrong person. A.3.1.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The company’s and the districts’ notices set out what was taken and their responses. Federal guidance on student data privacy and on ransomware, and state breach-notification laws, set out related practice. The class’s requirements (§4.6, §5.5) state copies the attack did not reach, confirmation of changes to who may take a child, and restoration of the record. Each is its author’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Assume the Record Is Out and Tell Those It Protects

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1. If records showing custody restrictions or protected addresses are stolen, treat them as public whatever the vendor or the attacker says, and tell the affected families and the agencies protecting them within hours.

In December 2024, an intruder using stolen login details broke into PowerSchool, the student-records system used by thousands of schools across North America, and copied data using the company’s own support tool. For many districts, everything they held on the platform was taken, including in some cases records of which parents are allowed to pick up their children. The company paid a ransom to have the data deleted, but in May 2025 school districts received extortion demands using the same stolen data. The person responsible was sentenced in 2025 to four years in prison. The lessons are that one vendor’s system can expose many schools at once, that paying a ransom does not make stolen data safe, and that families whose children a court protects must be told quickly when their records are taken. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own student records, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Bombing at the Manchester Arena, May 2017
what: At 22:31 on 22 May 2017, as a concert audience was leaving, a bomb was detonated in the foyer linking the Manchester Arena to Manchester Victoria station, outside the screened perimeter. Twenty-two people were killed and many hundreds injured. The public inquiry found that the attacker had reconnoitered the venue, waited partly out of camera view, and was the subject of a concern that never reached senior security, and that no officer was in the foyer as the crowd came through.
tier: A deliberate attack, not military action: the inquiry found no state acted.

findings.title: The watch on the edge is confirmed when it is needed.
findings.text: No officer was in the foyer when the crowd came through it.

findings.title: A concern at the edge has a time to reach someone who acts.
findings.text: A member of the public's concern reached stewards and went no further.

annex.p: This annex is for arenas, stadiums, theaters, and other venues where large crowds gather, for the security contractors and transport police who share their approaches, and for the stewards who are often the first to see something wrong. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Would you notice someone carrying out reconnaissance of your venue on several occasions?
The attacker learns your venue and is never noticed. A.3.2.
Are the spaces just outside your screened perimeter, such as shared foyers and approaches, watched, including the places your cameras do not see?
The attacker waits where no one looks. A.3.1.
When a member of the public or a steward raises a concern, how long does it take to reach someone who can act?
A warning is heard and goes no further. A.3.2.
Where several organizations share responsibility for a space, is it settled who does what, and confirmed on the night?
Each thinks another has it covered. A.3.1.
Is the edge of your venue watched most closely when the crowd is densest, as people leave?
The space is empty of security when it is full of people. A.3.1.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Watch the Edge When the Crowd Passes, and Settle the Shared Space

annex.p: The Manchester Arena Inquiry found that the loss of life and injury would highly likely have been less had the attacker been confronted, and recommended a statutory duty on those responsible for premises to prepare for and protect against terrorist attack, with those who share a space bearing responsibility for its common areas in proportion to their use. The Terrorism (Protection of Premises) Act 2025 placed that duty on qualifying premises and events in the United Kingdom, with the Security Industry Authority as regulator. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-1: confirm on the night that the watch on the edge is in place when the crowd passes.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Give a Concern a Time to Reach Someone Who Acts

annex.p: This step is this instrument’s, from F-2. State how quickly a concern raised at the edge must reach someone with authority to act, and train stewards and staff to pass it on.

At 22:31 on 22 May 2017, as a concert audience was leaving the Manchester Arena, a man detonated a bomb in the foyer linking the arena to Manchester Victoria railway station, outside the arena’s screened perimeter. Twenty-two people were killed and many hundreds injured. The public inquiry found that he had carried out reconnaissance on at least three occasions, that he waited in the foyer partly where cameras did not see, that a member of the public’s concern about him reached stewards but not senior security management, and that the three organizations responsible for the foyer did not coordinate and no officer was there when the crowd came through. It found that had he been confronted, the loss would highly likely have been less, and the United Kingdom later enacted a duty on venues to prepare for and protect against terrorist attack. No state was involved. The lessons are that the edge of a venue must be watched when the crowd passes, that a concern must reach someone who acts in time, and that those who share a space must settle who covers it. Any venue that holds large crowds has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this venue does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Crowd Crush at the Astroworld Festival, November 2021
what: At the Astroworld festival in Houston on 5 November 2021, about fifty thousand people attended a site where no occupancy load had been issued, and the crowd pressed toward the stage. Warnings began at 9:00 p.m., a mass-casualty incident was declared at 9:38 p.m., and the show ended about 10:10 p.m. Ten people died of compression asphyxia; a grand jury declined to indict anyone.
tier: Not an attack: a crowd crush with no adversary.

findings.title: The stop has triggers, and the response's declaration is one.
findings.text: The show went on for half an hour after a mass-casualty declaration.

findings.title: The plan binds every authority that permits or answers.
findings.text: The county permitted the event and the city answered it.

annex.p: This annex is for promoters and producers of large festivals and concerts, the venues and sites that host them, and the county and city authorities that permit them and answer their emergencies. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Has an occupancy load been set for your event, and does the plan bind every authority that permits it or answers it?
No one knows how many people the site can hold, or who is in charge. A.3.1.
Would your perimeter hold against people without tickets, and would you count the crowd from the gate?
The crowd grows beyond the plan before the show begins. A.3.1.
Do you watch crowd density near the stage, where pressure builds?
The crowd is crushed before anyone sees it. A.3.2.
Are the triggers to pause or stop the show written down and agreed in advance, and does a declared emergency stop it?
The show goes on for half an hour after a mass-casualty declaration. A.3.2.
Does someone on site hold the authority to stop the show, and does the unified command include the local 911 agencies?
No one with authority acts on the warnings. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Permit Through One Plan That Binds Every Authority

annex.p: The Texas Task Force on Concert Safety found the permitting process inconsistent across the state, found that no occupancy load had been issued, and recommended a universal permitting template. This step adds the instrument’s own, from F-2: make the event plan bind every authority that permits or answers it, county and city alike.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Write the Stop Triggers in Advance, and Give Someone the Authority

annex.p: The task force recommended a unified command group on site that includes the local 911 agencies, with a production representative holding authority to stop the show; triggers for pausing or stopping the show written into the permit and agreed in advance; and event-specific training, walkthroughs, and tabletop exercises. This step adds the instrument’s own, from F-1: count the response’s own declaration of a mass-casualty incident as a trigger that stops the show.

On 5 November 2021, at the Astroworld festival in a parking lot at NRG Park in Houston, about fifty thousand people attended, and people without tickets had breached the perimeter hours before the headlining set. As the crowd pressed toward the stage, warnings reached the event’s staff from 9:00 p.m., a mass-casualty incident was declared at 9:38 p.m., and the show did not end until about 10:10 p.m. Ten people, aged nine to twenty-seven, died of compression asphyxia, and hundreds were injured. No occupancy load had been issued; the event was permitted by the county and answered by the city. A grand jury declined to indict anyone, and the state’s task force recommended a single permitting template, a unified command on site with authority to stop the show, and stop triggers agreed in advance. No one intended harm. The lessons are that an event must have one plan binding every authority, that the triggers to stop it must be written before the gates open, and that someone on site must hold the authority to act on them. Any large event has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this event does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Superdome as Refuge of Last Resort in Hurricane Katrina, 2005
what: In Hurricane Katrina the Louisiana Superdome, in the floodplain, served as New Orleans's refuge of last resort; the storm tore its roof covering and cut its power, and more than twenty thousand people were held there for nearly a week without working plumbing. When it was full, about nineteen thousand gathered at the Convention Center, never planned as a shelter. Buses promised on the Monday arrived from the Wednesday, and the last evacuees left on 3 September.
tier: Not an attack: a hurricane exceeded what the refuge could withstand.

findings.title: A refuge states where its overflow goes.
findings.text: Thousands were turned away to an unplanned building.

findings.title: The means of evacuation are committed before the refuge opens.
findings.text: Promised buses were ordered two days later.

annex.p: This annex is for owners and operators of stadiums, convention centers, and other large buildings that may be designated as refuges of last resort, and for the state and local emergency managers who designate and supply them. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Can your building withstand the hazard it would shelter people from, standing outside the floodplain or able to hold its people above the flood, and resisting the wind?
The refuge is in the hazard’s path. A.3.1.
Would your building keep power, plumbing, and communication with the people inside if the storm damaged it?
Thousands are held for days without working toilets. A.3.1.
How many people can your refuge hold, and where do the rest go when it is full?
Thousands gather at a building never planned or supplied as a shelter. A.3.2.
Are the buses and other means to evacuate the refuge committed before it opens?
People wait days for transport that was promised. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Designate Only a Refuge That Can Withstand the Hazard

annex.p: The House committee found that Louisiana’s plans required a shelter of last resort to be outside the floodplain, or able to place its people above the flood, and to resist hurricane winds, that the Superdome was used although it lay in the floodplain, and that state and local governments made inappropriate selections of shelters of last resort. This instrument adds no step of its own here.

annex.h3: A.3.2 State Where the Overflow Goes, and Commit the Buses First

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1 and F-2. State the refuge’s capacity and where its overflow goes, supplied; and commit the means of evacuation before the refuge opens.

When Hurricane Katrina struck New Orleans in August 2005, the Louisiana Superdome served as the refuge of last resort, although it lay in the floodplain and the state’s own plans called for a refuge that could withstand the storm. The storm tore the covering from its roof and cut its power, leaving its plumbing, air conditioning, and public address system useless, and more than twenty thousand people were held there for nearly a week. By the Tuesday it was overcrowded and people were turned away; about nineteen thousand gathered at the Convention Center, which was never planned as a shelter and received supplies only on the Friday. Buses promised on the Monday were ordered on the Wednesday, and the last evacuees left on Saturday 3 September. Congressional committees found that state and local governments chose shelters of last resort poorly. No one attacked anything. The lessons are that a refuge must be able to withstand the hazard, that it must say where its overflow goes, and that the means to evacuate it must be committed before it opens. Any building that may be named a refuge has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this building is ready, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Grenfell Tower Fire, London, 14 June 2017
date_full: 14 June 2017 (record open: charging decisions expected before 14 June 2027)
what: A fire in a fourth-floor kitchen of the 24-storey Grenfell Tower escaped into an external wall clad in 2016 with polyethylene-core aluminium composite panels and spread around the building. The stay-put strategy failed by 01:26 and was revoked at 02:47. Seventy-two people died. The inquiry found the deaths all avoidable; England's evacuation-plan regulations came into force on 6 April 2026.
tier: Not an attack: an accidental fire. None of the four characteristics is present.

findings.title: The Certificate Stood for the Wall.
findings.text: The wall's behavior is shown as built.

annex.p: This annex is for owners and managers of residential and lodging high-rise buildings, the fire and rescue services, and those who regulate building safety. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to a building. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an owner answers about its own buildings (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an owner can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one building owner or manager. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the building owner or manager; it is that building owner or manager’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Has your building’s external wall, doors, or layout changed since it was approved, and has its fire strategy been reassessed for each change?
Your strategy may rest on a building that no longer exists. A.3.1.
Is the fire performance of the wall as built shown by a test or assessment of the whole system, not only by the products’ certificates?
A wall of certified products may still carry fire. A.3.2.
Who decides to change a stay-put strategy to evacuation, on what signs, and how quickly, and has it been exercised?
The decision may come after the strategy has failed. A.3.1.
Can every resident be told to leave, and does every resident who cannot leave unaided have a plan the fire service knows?
Residents may stay or be trapped. A.3.1.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The inquiry’s recommendations, the Building Safety Act 2022, and the Fire Safety (Residential Evacuation Plans) (England) Regulations 2025 set out what is now required in England, and national fire-safety guidance elsewhere sets out related practice. The class’s requirements (§4.2 to §4.4, §5.1) state the strategy as a design-basis quantity, the authority and means to change it, and plans for residents who cannot leave unaided. Each is its author’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Know How the Wall Behaves as Built

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1. If your building’s external wall has been changed, have the fire performance of the wall as built assessed as a system, independently of the products’ manufacturers, and do not rely on residents staying in place until it has.

Shortly before one in the morning on 14 June 2017, a fire in a fourth-floor kitchen at Grenfell Tower, a 24-storey block of flats in West London, spread into the building’s outer cladding, added in a refurbishment the year before, and climbed the outside of the tower. Residents had been told to stay in their flats in a fire, but that advice failed within about half an hour and was not withdrawn until nearly two hours after the first call. Seventy-two people died, eighteen of them children. The public inquiry found that every death was avoidable and that many organizations, from government to manufacturers to the building’s managers, had failed the residents over years. The lessons are that any change to a building’s walls changes its fire safety, and that there must be a way to tell everyone to leave and a plan for those who cannot. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own buildings, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Attacks on the Mumbai Hotels, 26 to 29 November 2008
what: Ten attackers who came by sea struck Mumbai's railway terminus, a café, a hospital, a Jewish community center, and the Taj Mahal Palace and Oberoi Trident hotels, firing on guests, setting fires, and holding hostages; the last was killed in the Taj about sixty hours later. 166 people died. Handlers abroad directed the attackers from live television of the hotels. An enquiry found that security advice given after a September alert naming the Taj had not all been implemented.
tier: Non-military adversarial, below the tier: intentionality and precision established, persistence not determined, denial not established.

findings.title: The Broadcast Was the Attackers' Window.
findings.text: The attacker does not learn from the broadcast what the response is doing.

annex.p: This annex is for owners, managers, and security staff of large hotels and residential buildings, and the police and fire services that respond to them. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to a hotel. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions a hotel answers about its own hotels (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account a hotel can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one hotel. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the hotel; it is that hotel’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
When the police give you security advice after a warning, who decides whether it is carried out, and by when?
Advice may be left undone when the attack comes. A.3.1.
Can you tell, within minutes, how many guests and staff are in the building and where, without the attacker learning it?
Responders may not find the people they must protect. A.3.1.
Can you tell guests to stay hidden, barricade, or leave by a route, by a means the attacker does not see or hear?
Instructions may draw the attacker to the guests. A.3.1.
Have you agreed with the police in advance how the building, its plans, keys, and systems are handed to them, and how live broadcast of the response is handled?
The attacker may watch the response on television. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The committee’s report set out its findings and recommendations to the state. National guidance on armed attacks in crowded places and on hotel security, published by counterterrorism and police authorities, sets out related practice. The class’s requirements (§4.4, §4.5, §5.3, §7.2) state locating and instructing occupants, handing the building’s systems to the response, independent fire protection and escape, and acting on warnings. Each is its author’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Close the Window the Broadcast Opens

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1. Agree in advance with the police and the authorities responsible for broadcasting how live coverage of your building’s occupied floors and the response’s positions would be withheld or delayed during an attack, and make it part of how you hand the building over.

Over three nights from 26 November 2008, ten gunmen attacked Mumbai, among other places at two of its largest hotels, the Taj Mahal Palace and the Oberoi Trident. In the hotels they shot guests and staff, set fires, and held hostages, and the siege of the Taj lasted about sixty hours. In all, 166 people were killed. The attackers’ handlers, far away, watched live television of the hotels and told the gunmen by phone what the police were doing. An official inquiry found that the hotels had not carried out some of the security advice police gave them after a warning in September 2008 that named the Taj as a possible target. The lessons are that a hotel must be able to find and instruct its guests without the attacker learning where they are, and that warnings must be acted on. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own hotels, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Cyberattack on MGM Resorts, September 2023
what: MGM Resorts disclosed a cybersecurity issue on 11 September 2023 and shut systems down; slot machines, room keys, reservations, payments, and teller machines were unavailable or restricted for days. Its 8-K of 5 October estimated about $100 million of quarterly effect and reported customer data from before March 2019 taken. The filings do not state the entry; an ALPHV affiliate claimed it called the help desk.
tier: Criminal, below the tier: intentionality and denial established, persistence not established, precision not determined.

findings.title: One Entry Reached Years of Customers.
findings.text: One entry cannot reach years of customers' records.

annex.p: This annex is for chains and resort groups whose properties share enterprise systems, their help desks and support contractors, and those who oversee them. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to a property or group. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions a group answers about its own properties (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account a group can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one group. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the group; it is that group’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Which of your properties’ systems, payments, room keys, gaming, reservations, share one identity service and one help desk?
One entry may stop every property at once. A.3.1.
How long can each property sell, pay out, and admit guests by hand?
Commerce may stop when the systems stop. A.3.1.
Can a caller who knows an employee’s name and public profile get that employee’s administrative credential reset?
Your help desk may be the way in. A.3.1.
How far back does the customer data reachable from your shared systems go, and why?
One entry may take years of customers’ records. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The company’s filings set out what it disclosed. Federal guidance on social engineering of help desks and on ransomware, and the gaming regulators’ requirements for casino systems, set out related practice. The class’s requirements (§4.4, §5.5, §7.2) state enterprise reach and manual operation, verified credential resets, and life-safety independent of the enterprise. Each is its author’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Keep Old Customer Data Out of Reach

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1. State how long you keep customers’ personal data where your shared systems can reach it, and move or delete anything older so that a single break-in cannot take it.

In September 2023, MGM Resorts shut down many of its computer systems after a cyberattack. For days, slot machines, digital room keys, reservations, card payments, and cash machines at its casinos and hotels were out or limited, and staff worked on paper. The company estimated about $100 million in lost earnings for the quarter and reported that personal information of some customers from before March 2019 had been taken. A criminal group claimed it got in by phoning the company’s help desk and posing as an employee; the company has not said how the attackers entered. The lessons are that systems shared by every property can all fail together, that each property needs a way to keep operating by hand, and that old customer data should not be kept where one break-in can reach it. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own properties, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Crush at Hillsborough, Sheffield, 15 April 1989
date_full: 15 April 1989, read to the inquests' determinations of 26 April 2016 (record closed)
what: At an FA Cup semi-final, a dense crowd built up outside too few turnstiles. To relieve it, the police commander ordered an exit gate opened, and about two thousand people entered; many went down a tunnel into two pens behind the goal that were already full and fenced at the front against pitch incursion. The crush killed ninety-seven people. People reaching the track were first read as disorder, and the major incident and the ambulance response came late. The 2016 inquests found the dead unlawfully killed and that supporters' behavior did not contribute at the turnstiles.
tier: Not an attack: a crowd moved into a space no one was counting. None of the four characteristics is present.

findings.title: The Crush Was Read as Disorder.
findings.text: The signs of a crush are named in advance and answered as one.

findings.title: A Barrier Built Against One Hazard Held the Crowd in Another.
findings.text: Every barrier is assessed against the crush it can make.

annex.p: This annex is for the owners and operators of stadiums, arenas, and other places where crowds gather, the police and stewards who command crowds at events, and the safety officials who certify grounds. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to a venue. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions a venue answers about its own venues (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account a venue can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one venue. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the venue; it is that venue’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Before anyone opens a gate to relieve a crowd, does the person deciding know where the people will go and whether that space can take them?
You may relieve one crush by making another. A.3.1, A.3.2.
Is the number of people in each pen, terrace, or section counted as they enter, and is the way in closed when it is full?
A space judged full by eye fills past capacity. A.3.1.
For each fence, gate, or barrier in your crowd’s space, have you asked what it does in a crush, and who opens it?
A barrier against one hazard may hold the crowd in another. A.3.2.
Are your stewards, police, and ambulance crews told which signs mean a crush, and to treat them as one before working out whether it is disorder?
The response may hold back while the crush does its work. A.3.2.
Is one person named to declare a major incident at your venue, and on what signs?
The declaration may come late. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published
