annex.p: Lord Justice Taylor’s final report of January 1990 made recommendations on the safety of sports grounds, among them all-seated accommodation at the major grounds. The jury’s determinations of 26 April 2016 set out the errors in planning, in the opening of the gate, in the stadium’s design and certification, and in the emergency response that caused or contributed to the deaths. Each is its author’s. No step of this instrument’s is added here.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Name the Signs of a Crush, and Test Every Barrier Against One

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1 and F-2. Write down the signs your people are to read as a crush, people coming over a barrier above all, and tell every steward, officer, and medic to answer them as a crush first; name who declares the major incident. And for every fence, gate, and barrier in the spaces your crowd uses, ask what it does in a crush, how it is opened, and who opens it, and count, do not judge, how many each space holds.

On 15 April 1989, at an FA Cup semi-final in Sheffield, a large crowd built up outside the turnstiles at one end of the ground. To relieve it, the police commander ordered an exit gate opened. About two thousand people came in, and many went down a tunnel into two pens behind the goal that were already full. The pens were fenced at the front to keep fans off the pitch. The crush killed ninety-seven people. When people climbed out onto the track, police at first took it for a pitch invasion, and the major incident and the ambulance response were declared and sent late. Inquests in 2016 found the dead were unlawfully killed, found errors in planning, in the opening of the gate, in the stadium’s design and certification, and in the response, and found that the behavior of supporters did not contribute. The lessons are that whoever opens a way for a crowd must know where it leads and how full that space is, that a fence built against one danger can trap people in another, and that the signs of a crush must be treated as a crush first. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own venues, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Attacks at the Stade de France and the Bataclan, Paris, 13 November 2015
what: From 21:16 three attackers detonated explosive vests outside the Stade de France during a match attended by about 80,000 and the President; at least one had reportedly been turned away at a gate, and the crowd was kept inside. In the city attackers fired on café terraces, and three entered the Bataclan, killing 90 and holding hostages until after midnight. 130 died. The parliamentary commission found that soldiers nearby did not intervene, their rules not providing for it.
tier: Non-military adversarial, below the tier: intentionality and precision established, persistence not determined, denial not established.

findings.title: The Most Senior Person Present Decided.
findings.text: The hold decision has one known holder even when the head of state is present.

annex.p: This annex is for operators and security managers of stadiums, concert halls, and other gathering places, the police and armed forces that may respond to them, and the authorities who coordinate a city’s response. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to a venue. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions a venue answers about its own venue (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account a venue can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one venue. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the venue; it is that venue’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Who decides whether your crowd is held or released if an attack happens outside or nearby, on what basis, and has it been exercised?
The decision may be made on the night by whoever is present. A.3.1.
If a head of state or other senior official attends, does your plan say who then makes that decision?
The decision may pass without the venue’s information. A.3.2.
Is your screen placed so that someone turned away is turned away from the crowd, not into it?
An attacker turned away may strike the queue. A.3.1.
Do you know, before each event, which armed forces will be near your venue and whether their rules let them engage an attack inside it?
Armed forces present may not be able to act. A.3.1.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The commission’s recommendations set out what it asked of the state. National guidance on crowded places and on protecting venues against marauding attacks, published by counterterrorism authorities, sets out related practice. The class’s requirements (§4.3) state the hold-or-release decision with its holder, the screen placed away from the crowd, the armed forces’ rules known in advance, and means to tell the crowd. Each is its author’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Settle Who Decides Before the Dignitary Arrives

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1. When a head of state or other senior official will attend, agree with their protective detail beforehand whether the decision to hold or release the crowd stays with your named holder, passes to them, or is taken jointly, and how your information reaches whoever decides.

On the night of 13 November 2015, attackers struck several places in and around Paris. Outside the Stade de France, where about eighty thousand people, including the French President, were watching France play Germany, three suicide bombers blew themselves up; at least one had reportedly been turned away at a gate. The crowd was kept inside and the match finished. In the city, attackers shot at people on café terraces and three gunmen entered the Bataclan concert hall, killing ninety people there. In all, 130 people died. A parliamentary inquiry later found that soldiers near the Bataclan did not step in because their rules did not allow it. The lessons are that every venue needs a decision, made in advance, about holding or releasing its crowd, and must know who will be able to help it if armed attackers come in. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own venue, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The TRITON Attack on a Petrochemical Safety System, 2017
what: In 2017, on the accounts of the United States government and the investigators, an intruder spent almost a year in the networks of a petrochemical plant in the Middle East before reaching the engineering workstation of its Triconex safety controllers and installing malware designed to make the safety system unsafe while it appeared normal. An error in the malware tripped the plant to a safe shutdown twice, in June and August 2017; the first trip was taken for a mechanical glitch, and the second led to discovery. Nothing was released and no one was hurt.
tier: Not military action, though it is the nearest the record offers: the governments that attribute it describe a deliberate and persistent capability for physical harm, but it came in peacetime, alone, and ended in a safe shutdown.

findings.title: The safety system was not independent, and the class requires it to be.
findings.text: The safety system could be reached from the corporate and operations networks.

findings.title: A governed act left standing is not governed.
findings.text: The controller's key switch was left in PROGRAM.

findings.title: The firmware beneath the logic.
findings.text: The malware used a firmware flaw to run in the controller's memory regardless of the key switch.

findings.title: The design failed safe because the attacker erred.
findings.text: The shutdown came from a mistake in the malware, not from the design defeating it.

findings.title: The intrusion passed its first trip.
findings.text: The plant restarted after the first trip with the intruder still inside.

findings.title: The determinism exemption rests on the installed configuration.
findings.text: The function running was no longer the function tested as installed.

findings.title: The adversary behaved as the class expects.
findings.text: The actor stayed for months and chose the safety layer over the control system.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its qualification of the facility class's account of the event went to the class as an erratum.

annex.p: This annex is for owners and operators of chemical, petrochemical, and refining plants whose processes are protected by safety instrumented systems, and for the engineers who program and maintain those systems. It is also for any owner, in any sector, whose last protective layer is a programmable controller. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Can your safety engineering workstation, or your safety system itself, be reached from the corporate or operations networks?
An intruder who reaches the control network can reach the safety layer. A.3.1.
Is the key switch on every safety controller out of PROGRAM except during scheduled programming, and is its position alarmed at the operator station?
The controller accepts new code whenever someone sends it. A.3.1.
Are your safety controllers on firmware that corrects the published vulnerabilities, and do you know which older controllers you still run?
An implant in running firmware answers an attacker whatever the key switch says. A.3.2.
Could you tell whether the logic and firmware running in a safety controller are those you tested as installed?
You cannot know your safety function is the one you certified. A.3.2.
After an unexplained safety trip, do you investigate for intrusion before restarting?
The plant restarts with the intruder still inside. A.3.3.
Would you detect an actor who had been in your networks for months, working off-hours and covering tracks?
You learn of the intruder from the trip it causes. A.3.3.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Isolate the Safety System, and Govern the Key Switch

annex.p: The advisories published in December 2017, by the vendor, the government, and the investigators, converge: keep the key switch out of PROGRAM except during scheduled programming, alarm its state at operator stations, isolate the safety network, and connect the engineering workstation to no other network. This step adds the instrument’s own, from F-1 and F-2: treat each change of key-switch position as a deliberate, authenticated, and recorded act, never left standing.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Correct the Firmware, and Check What Is Running

annex.p: The government advisory ICSA-18-107-02 identifies the controller vulnerabilities the malware used, and the Federal Bureau of Investigation reports that the vendor corrected them in firmware released in June 2018 and that older controllers remain in use and vulnerable. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-3 and F-6: bring safety controllers to corrected firmware, and verify periodically that the firmware and logic running are those tested as installed.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Treat an Unexplained Trip as a Possible Intrusion

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-4, F-5, and F-7. Investigate an unexplained safety trip for intrusion before restarting; do not count on an attacker’s error to make the design fail safe; and look for an actor that stays for months, works off-hours, and returns to learn how the plant responds.

In 2017, on the accounts of the United States government and the investigators, an intruder spent almost a year in the networks of a petrochemical plant in the Middle East before reaching the engineering workstation of its Triconex safety controllers, the last automated layer that shuts the process down when it becomes dangerous. The malware was designed to make the safety system unsafe while it appeared normal. It failed: an error in it tripped the plant to a safe shutdown twice, and the first trip was taken for a mechanical glitch, so the plant restarted with the intruder inside. The United States and the United Kingdom attribute the attack to a Russian government research institute; that is their attribution. Nothing was released and no one was hurt, but the governments state the capability was for an explosion, a toxic release, and loss of life. The lessons are that the safety system must be isolated from every other network, that its programming switch must never be left open, and that an unexplained trip may be an intrusion. Any plant protected by a programmable safety system has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this plant does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Organic Peroxide Fires at Arkema's Crosby Plant, August and September 2017
what: When Hurricane Harvey stalled over Texas in August 2017, floodwater at the Arkema plant in Crosby rose more than two feet above the 500-year flood elevation and took every layer that kept more than 350,000 pounds of organic peroxides cold: refrigeration, generators, liquid nitrogen, and the means of moving the product. Trailers burned on 31 August and 1 September, and the rest were burned on purpose on 3 September. Twenty-one emergency responders sought medical attention, and about 205 residents were evacuated for about a week.
tier: Not an attack: the hazard was a flood beyond the plant's design, though it denied power, backups, and access as an adversary might.

findings.title: One flood took every layer.
findings.text: Every layer of protection failed to the same flood.

findings.title: The grace period was days, and the decision fell before the flood.
findings.text: Moving the product off site would have needed a decision possibly before landfall.

findings.title: The class names no design-basis hazard.
findings.text: The plant had no single flood design basis.

findings.title: The plant's worst case was not the event.
findings.text: The plant's worst-case planning covered other chemicals, not the organic peroxides that burned.

findings.title: The fire reaches the next inventory.
findings.text: The safety zone had to account for the fire reaching other hazardous tanks on site.

findings.title: The zone was enforced from a road through it.
findings.text: Responders on a highway through the zone were exposed.

findings.title: The abandoned plant was seen in part.
findings.text: After the crew left, only some trailers were monitored, and the monitors measured air, not product.

findings.title: A flood reached the residual the class declares for war.
findings.text: A natural hazard reached the outcome the class expects only from sustained attack.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its qualification of the facility class's account of the event went to the class as an erratum.

annex.p: This annex is for owners and operators of chemical plants and warehouses that hold temperature-controlled or reactive inventory, and for the county and state agencies that plan the response around them. It is also for any owner, in any sector, whose backups could all be lost to one flood. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Have you set a flood design basis for your site, and does it exceed the flood your safeguards are sized for?
Your protection is sized for a flood smaller than the one that may come. A.3.1.
Could one flood take your primary and backup power, cooling, and the vehicles that would move your inventory, all at once?
Do you know how long your inventory holds without cooling, and when you must decide to move it off site, possibly before the storm arrives?
By the time you decide, the roads and drivers are gone. A.3.2.
Does your worst-case planning cover the inventory most likely to fail in a flood, not only the chemicals your regulatory plan names?
The event you prepared for is not the one that happens. A.3.1.
If your crew left the site, could you still see the state of every container, measuring the product rather than the air around it?
The container that fails first is the one you cannot see. A.3.3.
Is the public safety zone sized for a fire that reaches your next inventory, and would roads through it be closed?
Responders enforcing the zone are exposed inside it. A.3.3.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Set a Flood Design Basis Above the Safeguards

annex.p: The Chemical Safety Board made five recommendations, to the plant, its company, the Center for Chemical Process Safety, and Harris County; all are closed as acceptable action, and the plant now meets the county’s revised 500-year flood elevation standard. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-1, F-3, and F-4: state the flood your site must withstand; place backup power, cooling, and the means of moving inventory so that one flood cannot take them all; and plan the worst case around the inventory a flood would fail, not only the chemicals a regulatory plan names.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Know the Grace Period, and Decide Early

annex.p: This step is this instrument’s, from F-2 and F-8. Know how long temperature-controlled inventory holds without cooling, and set in advance the point, which may fall before landfall, at which it is moved off site, while roads, vehicles, and drivers are still available.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Watch the Abandoned Site, and Size the Zone to the Next Inventory

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-5, F-6, and F-7. Monitor every container of temperature-controlled product after the crew withdraws, measuring the product; size the public zone for a fire that reaches the next hazardous inventory on site; and close roads through the zone once decomposition is reported.

When Hurricane Harvey stalled over Texas in August 2017, floodwater at the Arkema plant in Crosby rose more than two feet above the 500-year flood elevation. The plant held more than 350,000 pounds of organic peroxides that decompose and burn if they warm. One flood took every layer that kept them cold: the refrigeration, the emergency generators, the liquid nitrogen system, and the trucks and roads needed to move the product away. The crew was evacuated, and trailers of product burned on 31 August and 1 September, and the rest were burned on purpose on 3 September. No one died, but twenty-one emergency responders sought medical attention after exposures on a highway through the safety zone, and about 205 residents were evacuated for about a week. The Chemical Safety Board, whose report is the record, found that every layer failed in common. The lessons are that a plant must set the flood it will withstand, that backups must not share the flood that takes the primary, and that the decision to move dangerous inventory may need to come before the storm. Any plant with inventory that depends on power and cooling has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this plant does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Chlorine Release at Graniteville, January 2005
what: At about 2:39 a.m. on 6 January 2005, a freight train running through Graniteville, South Carolina, was diverted by a main-line switch a local crew had left lined for an industry track, and struck a standing train. A chlorine tank car was punctured and about 120,000 pounds of chlorine escaped within minutes into a valley holding houses and a mill running a night shift. Nine people died, among them six mill workers and the train's engineer.
tier: Not an attack: the cause, on the National Transportation Safety Board's determination, was a switch left misaligned, and the switch showed no evidence of tampering.

findings.title: Movement protection must know the switch.
findings.text: Nothing detected the switch's position, and the train could not stop in the distance its banner could be seen.

findings.title: The movement authority rested on one person's memory.
findings.text: The train was cleared on a crew member's belief that the switch was restored.

findings.title: The strongest car was punctured by its neighbor.
findings.text: A car among the strongest in service was punctured by another car's coupler.

findings.title: A deliberate diversion needs no weapon.
findings.text: The same consequence could be reached on purpose through an unmonitored switch.

findings.title: The ground, the night shift, and the building's air set the exposure.
findings.text: The cloud settled in the valley and was drawn into the mill by its ventilation.

findings.title: The first decisions are made before the cargo is known.
findings.text: Responders learned what the train carried only after their first decisions.

findings.title: The crew and the trackside facility stood in the footprint.
findings.text: The engineer survived the collision and died in the cloud.

findings.title: Who held each decision on the cargo is not on the record.
findings.text: Twelve days of handling the damaged car included a failed patch and a second release.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its qualification of the facility class's account of the event went to the class as an erratum.

annex.p: This annex is for railroads that carry inhalation-hazard chemicals, the shippers that load them, and the plants and communities that stand beside the track. It is also for the fire departments and emergency managers who would answer a release. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
On lines that carry inhalation-hazard cars, does anything report the position of hand-operated main-line switches, or does the crew’s report stand alone?
A switch left wrong is found by the next train. A.3.1.
Before a movement authority is issued, is there an independent indication that the switches are restored, beyond one person’s memory?
The authority rests on one person’s belief. A.3.1.
Can trains carrying these cars stop short of a misaligned switch at the speed they run?
The warning comes inside the stopping distance. A.3.1.
Where are inhalation-hazard cars placed in your trains, and are they in a position where a derailment is least likely to puncture them?
The strongest car is punctured by its neighbor. A.3.2.
Do plants beside the track know how to shut their ventilation and shelter their night shift if a cloud arrives?
Building fans draw the gas inside. A.3.2.
Would your first responders know within minutes what the train carries, and do crews carry escape breathing apparatus?
The first decisions are made blind, and the crew walks into the cloud. A.3.3.
For the days of handling a damaged car, is it settled who decides each step?
A patch fails and the release recurs with no clear holder. A.3.3.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Know the Switch, Independently of the Crew

annex.p: The National Transportation Safety Board did not believe rules and forms were sufficient to prevent such errors, and recommended a device conveying switch status independent of the switch banner and train speeds that allow a stop short of a misaligned switch. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-1, F-2, and F-4: on lines carrying inhalation-hazard cars, give the movement authority an independent indication of switch position; and treat a hand-operated switch in such territory as a deliberate route to release, not only an accidental one.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Place the Cars, and Prepare the Neighbors

annex.p: The Board found that placing such cars toward the rear of a train would reduce their exposure in a derailment. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-3 and F-5: place inhalation-hazard cars where they are least exposed; and make sure plants beside the track can stop their ventilation and shelter their workers, the night shift especially.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Equip the Crew, Inform the Responders, and Name the Holders

annex.p: The federal rule of 2024 now requires escape breathing apparatus for train crews carrying such cargo. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-6, F-7, and F-8: give responders the train’s cargo within minutes; prepare first decisions that can be made before the cargo is known; and name who holds each decision in the days of handling a damaged car.

At about 2:39 a.m. on 6 January 2005, a Norfolk Southern freight train running through Graniteville, South Carolina, was diverted by a main-line switch that a local crew had left lined for a mill’s industry track the evening before, and struck a standing train. A chlorine tank car, among the strongest in service, was punctured by the coupler of another car, and about 120,000 pounds of chlorine escaped within minutes into a valley holding houses and a mill that ran through the night. Nine people died, among them six mill workers and the train’s engineer, and thousands were evacuated. Nothing reported the switch’s position; the train could not stop in the distance at which the switch’s banner could be seen; and responders learned what the train carried only after their first decisions. The National Transportation Safety Board, whose report is the record, found that rules and forms alone were not enough. The lessons are that on lines carrying such cargo the position of a switch must be known independently of the crew, and that the plants and responders beside the track must be ready for a cloud. Any railroad or plant along a hazardous-materials route has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Derailment at East Palestine, February 2023
what: On the night of 3 February 2023, a Norfolk Southern freight train derailed at East Palestine, Ohio, after a bearing failed on a car carrying nothing hazardous, and a fire spread among thirty-eight derailed cars. On 6 February, with the evacuation enlarged, the railroad's contractors opened and burned the vinyl chloride in five pressure cars the derailment had not breached. The National Transportation Safety Board found the cars were not undergoing the reaction the decision assumed. No one was killed or injured, and released liquids reached two streams.
tier: Not an attack: the cause was a mechanical failure, and no actor was involved.

findings.title: The defect that started it is not in the event categories.
findings.text: A failing bearing on a non-hazardous car was read by detectors, and one alert was not seen.

findings.title: The weakest car sets the fire.
findings.text: Older tank cars released lading and fed the fire around the pressure cars.

findings.title: The relief devices relieved, and their behavior became an indication.
findings.text: The devices' venting was read as a sign of reaction that was not occurring.

findings.title: The basis was corrupted more widely than the class says.
findings.text: The incident commander was given a threshold found in no guidance and minutes to decide.

findings.title: The shipper's knowledge must reach the decider by a channel the carrier does not control.
findings.text: The shipper, who believed the reaction was not occurring, was not in the room.

findings.title: The response made the largest release, and the model does not count it.
findings.text: The vent and burn released the contents of five unbreached cars.

findings.title: Responders lacked the consist when the placards burned.
findings.text: The consist reached the incident commander on paper five hours after the derailment.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its qualification of the facility class's account of the event went to the class as an erratum.

annex.p: This annex is for railroads that carry hazardous materials, the shippers whose products they carry, and the fire departments and incident commanders who decide what to do with damaged cars. It is also for any owner, in any sector, whose emergency decisions rest on information supplied by a party with its own interest in the outcome. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Would an alert from a wayside detector on a car carrying nothing hazardous be seen and acted on before the next detector?
A failing bearing on an ordinary car derails the hazardous ones. A.3.1.
Are the cars most likely to breach and start a fire, such as older tank cars, placed and phased out with that in mind?
The weakest car sets the fire that exposes the strongest. A.3.1.
Would your incident commander have the train’s consist within the hour, and a common radio with the railroad?
Responders work blind while the placards burn. A.3.2.
Does the shipper’s knowledge of its product reach the person deciding on the cargo directly, not only through the carrier or its contractors?
The decider hears only one party’s account. A.3.3.
Is the basis for a decision such as a vent and burn checked against the measured trend and the published guidance, with time to decide?
An irreversible decision is made in minutes on a threshold no guidance contains. A.3.3.
Does your planning count the release a response itself would make?
The response makes the largest release of the event. A.3.3.

annex.h3: A.3.1 See the Alert, and Retire the Weak Cars

annex.p: On the National Transportation Safety Board’s account, wayside detectors remain voluntary. These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1 and F-2: treat the alerts of wayside detectors as safety indications on every car of a train carrying hazardous materials, whatever the car itself carries; and account in train makeup and fleet replacement for the cars most likely to breach and feed a fire.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Give Responders the Consist

annex.p: This step is this instrument’s, from F-7. Make sure the incident commander has the consist within the hour by a means that does not depend on placards or paper, and that responders and the railroad share a radio.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Protect the Basis of the Decision

annex.p: The consent decree that settled the United States’ case with the railroad requires a coordination procedure before any vent and burn the railroad proposes. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-3, F-4, F-5, and F-6: bring the shipper’s knowledge to the decider by a channel the carrier does not control; check the basis of an irreversible decision against the measured trend and published guidance; read relief-device behavior with care before taking it as a sign of reaction; and count the release a response would make.

On the night of 3 February 2023, a Norfolk Southern freight train derailed at East Palestine, Ohio, after a bearing failed on a car that carried nothing hazardous; the bearing’s rising heat had been read by wayside detectors, but the alert at one was not seen. Thirty-eight cars derailed and a fire spread among them. Three days later, with the evacuation enlarged, the railroad’s contractors opened and burned the vinyl chloride in five pressure cars that the derailment had not breached. The National Transportation Safety Board, whose report is the record, found that the cars were not undergoing the reaction the decision assumed, that the incident commander was given minutes to decide, and that the shipper, who believed the reaction was not occurring, was not in the room. No one was killed or injured, and the released liquids and firefighting water reached two streams. The lessons are that every detector alert matters on a hazardous train, and that the person deciding on dangerous cargo must hear the shipper directly and have time to check the basis. Any operation whose emergency decisions rest on others’ information has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Fire and Explosion at West Fertilizer, April 2013
what: On the evening of 17 April 2013, a fire at the West Fertilizer Company in West, Texas, reached about forty to sixty tons of ammonium nitrate stored in wooden bins in a wood-framed building, and about twenty minutes after the fire was reported the pile detonated. Fifteen people died, twelve of them responders, more than 260 were injured, and schools, a nursing home, and apartments nearby were destroyed or damaged. The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives determined that the fire was intentionally set, and its investigation is open.
tier: Not military action: whatever lit the fire, the explosion and its reach followed, on the Chemical Safety Board's analysis, from how and where the material was stored and how the response unfolded.

findings.title: What makes a store detonable in a burning building.
findings.text: Combustible construction, nearby combustibles, and no detection or sprinklers likely contributed to the detonation.

findings.title: The distance is held by two parties.
findings.text: Schools, a nursing home, and apartments were built near the facility over the years.

findings.title: In advance means a plan, for everyone who comes.
findings.text: There was no plan, incident command, or public alert, and twelve of the dead were responders.

findings.title: The ammonia beside the nitrate.
findings.text: Ammonia vessels nearby were damaged and leaked, a near-miss.

findings.title: The source term, the railcar, and what stood near.
findings.text: A nearby railcar of the same material overturned without detonating.

findings.title: A fire whatever its cause.
findings.text: The fire's cause is contested, and the consequence did not depend on it.

findings.title: In the deliberate analog, the response is part of the consequence.
findings.text: A set fire draws responders and onlookers toward the store before it detonates.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its completion of the facility class's regulatory statement went to the class as an erratum.

findings.title: Who holds the design basis for a small retailer.
findings.text: No outside party checked the facility's storage against a standard.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its qualification of the facility class's account of the event went to the class as an erratum.

findings.title: Material awaiting disposal belongs to the class.
findings.text: Carried from the withdrawn Beirut instrument: a cargo held for years by no facility fell under no one's design basis.

findings.title: The disposition decision had no holder.
findings.text: Carried from the withdrawn Beirut instrument: many authorities held part of the decision and none the whole.

annex.p: This annex is for retailers, blenders, and distributors that store ammonium nitrate or other materials that can detonate, the fire departments that would answer a fire there, and the local governments that decide what may be built nearby. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Is your ammonium nitrate stored in a noncombustible building, away from other combustibles, with detection or sprinklers?
A fire in the building can contaminate and detonate the pile. A.3.1.
Is there water within reach of your store, at the pressure a fire would need?
Responders arrive and cannot fight the fire. A.3.2.
Do your fire department and every neighboring department have a plan for a fire at your store, including when to stand back and when to withdraw?
Responders move toward the fire in the minutes before it detonates. A.3.2.
Do you know what stands within the blast distance of your store, schools, homes, a nursing home, and are both you and the local government holding that distance?
A detonation reaches buildings full of people. A.3.3.
Are other hazards on your site, such as ammonia vessels or a railcar of the same material, sited so a blast cannot spread to them?
One explosion becomes two releases. A.3.1.
Does anyone outside your business, an insurer, a supplier, or a regulator, check that your storage meets a standard?
No one knows the store is dangerous until it explodes. A.3.3.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Store It So a Fire Cannot Detonate It

annex.p: After the event, Texas adopted rules in 2014 and a statute in 2015, and the 2016 edition of NFPA 400 prohibited combustible construction for new ammonium nitrate storage. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-1, F-4, and F-5: store ammonium nitrate in noncombustible construction, apart from other combustibles, with detection or sprinklers; and site other hazards on the property so that a blast cannot reach them.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Plan the Response, Including the Withdrawal

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-3, F-6, and F-7. Prepare a plan with every department that would come, covering incident command, water supply, a public alert, and when to stand back and withdraw from a fire that may detonate, whatever caused the fire; and plan for onlookers drawn to the scene.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Hold the Distance, and Name Who Checks

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-2 and F-9. Treat the distance between the store and schools, homes, and care facilities as held by the business and the local government together; and make sure some party outside the business, a producer’s certification as one producer adopted after the event, an insurer, or a regulator, checks the store against a standard.

On the evening of 17 April 2013, a fire at the West Fertilizer Company in West, Texas, reached about forty to sixty tons of ammonium nitrate stored in wooden bins in a wood-framed building, and about twenty minutes after the fire was reported the pile detonated. Fifteen people died, twelve of them responders, and more than 260 were injured. Two schools, a nursing home, and apartments built near the facility over the years were destroyed or damaged. The building had no detection or sprinklers, the nearest hydrant was too far, and there was no plan for a fire there. The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives determined in 2016 that the fire was intentionally set, and its investigation remains open; the Chemical Safety Board, whose report is the record, found that storage and siting set the consequence, whatever lit the fire. The lessons are that such material must be stored so that a fire cannot detonate it, that responders must have a plan that includes withdrawal, and that the distance to schools and homes must be held. Any business that stores material that can explode has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this business does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The LockerGoga Ransomware Attacks, March 2019
what: In March 2019, LockerGoga ransomware struck two related chemical companies in the United States, Hexion and Momentive, and the Norwegian aluminum producer Norsk Hydro within days of each other. At Hydro the attackers had entered months earlier and pushed the ransomware from the company's own domain controllers to every joined machine. Business systems were lost at all three companies; the chemical plants, on separate networks, ran safely, and Hydro worked by hand, restored from backups, and paid no ransom.
tier: A deliberate criminal attack, not military action: no government has attributed it to a state, and no safety incident at any site was reported.

findings.title: Fleet reach runs through the domain.
findings.text: The ransomware was pushed from the company's own domain controllers to every joined machine.

findings.title: The plants that stopped were waiting on production systems.
findings.text: Some plants stopped only because they lost connection to production systems.

findings.title: Manual fallback and the response outward took people, stock, channels, and notice.
findings.text: Manual operation took stock, paper, retirees, and new channels to customers.

findings.title: A compromise found at the center starts the same response.
findings.text: Hydro isolated every plant and verified containment before recovering.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its substance is carried by F-3.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its substance is carried by F-3.

findings.title: Restoration rested on backups beyond the attack.
findings.text: Hydro rebuilt from backups the attack had not reached.

findings.title: Two companies sharing services share reach.
findings.text: The two chemical companies shared technology services.

findings.title: Withdrawn.
findings.text: Its qualification of the facility class's account of the event went to the class as an erratum.

annex.p: This annex is for chemical and process companies that run many sites from a shared enterprise network, and for the technology teams that administer their domains. It is also for any owner, in any sector, whose plants could be reached by a change pushed from the center. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Which machines at your plants are joined to, or reachable from, your enterprise domain, and could a change pushed from your domain controllers reach them?
One compromised administrator account reaches every plant. A.3.1.
Would you detect an intruder holding administrative credentials for months before acting?
You learn of the intruder when every screen goes dark. A.3.1.
Could your plants keep running if they lost connection to the enterprise’s production and business systems?
Plants stop although nothing at them was attacked. A.3.2.
Have you planned a manual fallback, with the people, stock, paper, and channels of communication it would take for weeks?
Orders, shipping, and payments stop with the network. A.3.2.
Do you have backups the attacker could not reach, and a plan to isolate every site and verify containment before you restore?
Restoration reinfects the network or has nothing clean to restore. A.3.3.
If you share technology services with another company, do you know what that connection lets an attacker reach?
An attack on one company reaches the other. A.3.3.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Separate the Plants From the Domain

annex.p: No authority has published an action for owners that this instrument reads; Microsoft’s and the companies’ accounts are its record. These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1: learn which plant machines are joined to or reachable from the enterprise domain, separate those that bear on the process, and watch for an intruder who holds administrative credentials for months.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Let the Plants Run Alone, and Prepare the Manual Fallback

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-2 and F-3. Make sure plants can run safely without the enterprise’s production systems; and plan the manual fallback in people, stock, paper, and channels outward to customers and authorities, for weeks.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Isolate, Verify, and Restore From Backups Beyond Reach

annex.p: Norsk Hydro isolated all its plants, disconnected every server and PC, verified containment before recovery, rebuilt from backups, and paid no ransom. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-4, F-7, and F-8: treat a compromise found at the center as starting the same isolation; keep backups beyond the attacker’s reach; and know what a shared services agreement with another company lets an attacker reach.

In March 2019, LockerGoga ransomware struck two related chemical companies in the United States, Hexion and Momentive, and the Norwegian aluminum producer Norsk Hydro within days of each other. At Hydro, on Microsoft’s account, the attackers had entered in December 2018 through an infected attachment, captured administrative credentials, and pushed the ransomware from the company’s own domain controllers to every joined machine at once. Email, computers, and business systems were lost at all three companies. The chemical companies’ plants, on separate networks, ran safely; some of Hydro’s plants stopped for lack of connection to production systems, and the company worked by hand, from paper and stock, with retirees who knew the old ways. Hydro isolated every plant, restored from backups, and paid no ransom. The attackers were criminals acting for payment, and law enforcement in several countries has investigated them. The lessons are that an enterprise domain can reach every plant at once, that plants must be able to run without the center, and that backups must be beyond an attacker’s reach. Any company that runs many sites from one network has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this company does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Destruction of the Kakhovka Dam, June 2023
what: Russian forces took the Kakhovka dam on Ukraine's Dnipro River in February 2022 and held it for some fifteen months, during which its owner could neither operate nor inspect it. The reservoir was drawn low and then raised high, water poured over the spillway for six weeks, and the dam was breached in the early hours of 6 June 2023. About 620 square kilometers flooded, about 100,000 residents were directly affected, and about 700,000 people lost access to drinking water.
tier: Placed at the military-action tier, on the author's ruling of 17 November 2026. Military action by a party to an armed conflict that held the dam, against the dam and the reservoir it impounds. Precision is read from the pattern of what was reached and kept from restoration: the one structure whose breach floods the valley and empties the reservoir others depend on, its pool driven to a three-decade low and then over the spillway, its damage left unrepaired, and its breach at the high pool. Ukraine and Russia each say the other destroyed the dam; no finding is made between them.

findings.title: A held dam's pool is the holder's, not the permit's.
findings.text: The party holding the dam set its pool for months.

findings.title: Persistence acts through operation, and a denied structure is still observed.
findings.text: Damage was visible from satellites days before the breach.

findings.title: The design basis does not wait on attribution.
findings.text: The cause is disputed, and the people downstream needed a warning anyway.

findings.title: The warning must reach a valley under another authority.
findings.text: Most of the flooded area lay in territory held by the party that held the dam.

findings.title: A dependent's margin is its reserve and the time to build another.
findings.text: The Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant lost the reservoir it drew from.

findings.title: When the dam is held, the owner's lever is upstream.
findings.text: The owner could act only through the dams above.

findings.title: The consequence is validated on the footprint, not the count of the dead.
findings.text: Counts of the dead differ by an order of magnitude.

annex.p: This annex is for owners and operators of dams with large reservoirs, the authorities that warn the valleys below them, and the facilities that depend on their pools, among them nuclear plants and water systems. It is also for any owner whose structure could be held or denied by another party in war. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
If you lost control of your dam for months, do you know who would set the pool, and what pool would make a breach worst?
The holder sets the pool, and the pool sets the flood. A.3.1.
Could you watch your dam from outside it, by satellite or from the reservoir, if you could not inspect it?
Damage builds for weeks with no one to warn. A.3.1.
Does your downstream warning reach every community in the footprint, including any under another authority?
Part of the valley gets no warning and no help. A.3.2.
For facilities that draw on your pool, do you know how long their reserve lasts once it falls and how long it would take to build another source?
A nuclear plant or a city loses its water with the reservoir. A.3.3.
Is your warning plan set to act on the condition of the dam, without waiting to know who caused it?
The warning waits on a question no one can answer in time. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Plan for a Held Dam, and Watch It From Outside

annex.p: No authority has published an action for owners that this instrument reads. These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1, F-2, and F-6: plan for the case in which a dam is held by another party, naming the pool that would make a breach worst and the levers upstream that the owner still holds; and watch a denied structure from outside it.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Warn the Whole Valley, Whatever the Cause

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-3, F-4, and F-7. Act on the condition of the dam without waiting for attribution; make the warning reach every community in the footprint, including any under another authority; and validate the consequence on the footprint flooded, not on the count of the dead.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Know the Dependents’ Margins

annex.p: This step is this instrument’s, from F-5. For each facility that draws on the pool, know its reserve and the time to build another source, so that the margin is stated before it is needed.

Russian forces took the Kakhovka dam on Ukraine’s Dnipro River in the first days of the full-scale invasion of February 2022 and held it for some fifteen months, during which its owner could neither operate nor inspect it. The reservoir was drawn to a three-decade low and then raised to a three-decade high, water poured over the spillway for six weeks, and damage was visible on satellite images days before the dam was breached in the early hours of 6 June 2023. About 620 square kilometers flooded and about 100,000 residents were directly affected; about 700,000 people lost access to drinking water, and the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant upstream lost the reservoir it drew from and was cooled from its own pond. Ukraine and Russia each say the other destroyed the dam, and no court has ruled; this instrument makes no finding between them. The count of the dead differs by an order of magnitude among publishers. The lessons are that a dam held by another party is a dam whose pool and condition the owner must still plan for and watch, and that the warning must reach the whole valley whoever caused the breach. Any owner of a dam that could be held or denied has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this dam does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Oroville Spillway Incident, February 2017
what: In February 2017, the concrete chute of the main spillway at California's Oroville Dam broke apart while passing a large flood, and on 11 February the lake rose over the emergency spillway, which had never been used. As erosion advanced toward its crest, about 188,000 people downstream were ordered to evacuate. The dam did not fail.
tier: Not an attack: a spillway failed while passing a flood, and the dam held.

findings.title: The dam's safety comes before the served function, and the order is written down.
findings.text: Releases were limited partly to protect the powerhouse.

findings.title: A never-used path's showing yields a time for the warning.
findings.text: The emergency spillway's first use showed how much warning its erosion left.

findings.title: The evacuation trigger is an observable condition stated in advance.
findings.text: The order for 188,000 people was given on an observation made in the moment.

findings.title: A release path is shown from its ground, not from its record.
findings.text: Every review had mischaracterized the chute's foundation.

findings.title: Compliance is not sufficient.
findings.text: The investigators found that meeting regulation did not manage the risk.

annex.p: This annex is for owners and operators of dams whose spillways must pass large floods, the engineers who review them, and the authorities that order evacuations below them. It is also for any owner whose structure serves a function, such as power or water supply, that could be weighed against its safety. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Has your spillway’s foundation been examined from the ground itself, or does your confidence rest on past reviews?
A weakness every review missed fails under flow. A.3.1.
In an emergency, is it written down that the dam’s safety comes before the power or water it serves?
Releases are held back to protect a powerhouse while the dam is at risk. A.3.2.
If you had to use a release path that has never passed water, do you know how fast it could erode and how much warning that leaves?
The warning comes when the erosion is already advancing. A.3.2.
Is the condition that triggers an evacuation stated in advance and observable?
An order for many thousands is given in minutes on an unplanned judgment. A.3.2.
Beyond meeting regulatory requirements, do you have a comprehensive assessment of how your dam could fail?
A dam in compliance fails anyway. A.3.1.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Know the Ground, and Go Beyond Compliance

annex.p: The independent forensic team found the incident caused by a long-term systemic failure of the owner, regulatory practice, and industry practice to recognize spillway design and construction weaknesses, and found that compliance with regulatory requirements is not sufficient to manage risk. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s Order No. 880 provides for comprehensive assessments of the dams it regulates. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-4 and F-5: show a release path from its ground, not from its record.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Put Safety First in Writing, and State the Trigger

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1, F-2, and F-3. Write down that the dam’s safety comes before its served function; for a path that has never passed water, derive the warning time from how it could fail; and state in advance the observable condition that triggers an evacuation.

In February 2017, the concrete chute of the main spillway at California’s Oroville Dam, which holds the largest reservoir of the State Water Project, broke apart while passing a large flood. Releases were limited, partly to protect the hydroelectric powerhouse, and on 11 February the lake rose over the emergency spillway, which had never been used. The next afternoon, as erosion advanced toward its crest, about 188,000 people downstream were ordered to evacuate. The dam did not fail, and the flood passed. The independent forensic team, whose report is the record, found a long-term systemic failure of the owner, regulators, and industry to recognize weaknesses in the spillway’s design and foundation, and found that compliance with regulation was not enough. The lessons are that a spillway must be known from its ground, that the dam’s safety must come before the power or water it serves, and that the trigger for an evacuation must be stated before it is needed. Any owner of a dam has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this dam does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Failures of the Edenville and Sanford Dams, May 2020
what: On 19 May 2020, after heavy rain, the Edenville Dam on Michigan's Tittabawassee River failed, and its flood overwhelmed the Sanford Dam downstream, which failed in turn. Edenville's federal license had been revoked in 2018 over its spillway capacity, and its regulation had passed to the state. About 11,000 people were evacuated and about 1,000 structures were severely damaged or destroyed; no one died.
tier: Not an attack: an embankment failed at a high pool, and the flood took the dam below it.

findings.title: The cascade's analysis and warning survive a change of regulator.
findings.text: The four dams in series were not analyzed and warned as one.

findings.title: The downstream authority warns on its own trigger.
findings.text: The county ordered evacuation before the owner activated its plan.

findings.title: A gate is credited only as far as people can safely work it.
findings.text: Edenville's gates could be opened only part of the way.

findings.title: A dam's record moves with its regulation.
findings.text: The state received little information about the dam when regulation passed to it.

findings.title: An event's footprint is recorded for the model.
findings.text: The flood's extent was not recorded below the confluence.

annex.p: This annex is for owners of dams in a series on one river, the state and federal regulators that oversee them, and the county emergency managers and facilities in the valley below. It is also for any owner whose dam changes regulator or ownership. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
If your dam is one of several in series, does one analysis and one warning plan cover the whole cascade, whoever regulates each dam?
A failure upstream overwhelms a dam downstream that planned alone. A.3.1.
Can your gates actually be opened to their full height, safely, by the people who would open them?
Capacity on paper is not capacity in a flood. A.3.2.
If your dam changed regulator, did its full record move with it?
The new regulator does not know the dam. A.3.1.
Does the county below act on its own trigger, without waiting for the owner?
The valley waits on an owner who is not there. A.3.3.
Do facilities in the footprint, such as a chemical plant, know when to shut down and move hazardous material?
A flood becomes a chemical release. A.3.3.
Is the flood’s extent recorded during the event, so models can be checked afterward?
The next model repeats this one’s errors. A.3.3.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Analyze and Warn the Cascade as One

annex.p: The independent forensic team found the failures foreseeable and preventable, the result of decisions and inactions over the dams’ history by the owners, regulators, and others. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-1 and F-4: keep one analysis and one warning for a cascade, surviving any change of regulator; and move a dam’s whole record with its regulation.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Credit Only the Gate People Can Safely Work

annex.p: This step is this instrument’s, from F-3. Credit a gate’s capacity only as far as people can safely open it in the conditions of a flood.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Let the County Act, and Record the Flood

annex.p: Midland County ordered evacuation about midnight, before the owners activated their emergency plan, and the incident response review calls for data collected before an event to support inundation modeling. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-2 and F-5: give the downstream authority its own trigger; prepare facilities in the footprint to shut down ahead of a flood; and record the flood’s observed extent.

On 19 May 2020, after heavy rain, the Edenville Dam on Michigan’s Tittabawassee River failed and its flood overwhelmed the Sanford Dam downstream, which failed in turn. The two were among four dams of one owner built in series in the 1920s. Edenville’s federal license had been revoked in 2018 because its spillways could not pass the largest flood its design required, and regulation passed to the state, which had little information about the dam. Its gates could be opened only part of the way. About 11,000 people were evacuated, the county having ordered evacuation before the owner activated the emergency plan; about 1,000 structures were severely damaged or destroyed, and no one died. A chemical plant downstream shut down ahead of the flood. The independent forensic team, whose report is the record, found the failures foreseeable and preventable. The lessons are that a cascade of dams must be analyzed and warned as one, that a gate counts only as far as people can safely open it, and that a dam’s record must follow it when its regulator changes. Any owner of a dam in a series has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this dam does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Intrusion Into the Bowman Avenue Dam, 2013
what: In August and September 2013, on the United States Attorney's account, an intruder repeatedly reached the control system of the Bowman Avenue Dam, a small flood-control structure in Rye Brook, New York, and read its water levels and the status of its sluice gate. The gate could not be moved only because it had been disconnected for maintenance. The county's emergency managers learned of the intrusion from the press more than two years later.
tier: Not military action: it occurred in peacetime, and the United States Government, which links it to a state, proceeded by criminal indictment, whose charges are untried.

findings.title: Read access to a gate's controls is a compromise of the gate.
findings.text: The intruder read the gate's status through the system that commands it.

findings.title: An intrusion into a gate's controls is reported to those who warn the valley.
findings.text: Emergency managers learned of it from the press.

findings.title: No federal security requirement reached this dam.
findings.text: The dam is a municipal structure outside federal jurisdiction.

annex.p: This annex is for owners of small dams and other water-control works whose gates are operated by computer, the municipal and county agencies that own and oversee them, and the emergency managers who warn the valleys below. It is also for any owner of a control system that can be reached from a network. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known

Before the questions below: have you listed every part of the gate’s control system that talks to the outside world, with the network it does so through (your own, a cellular carrier’s, or a vendor’s or integrator’s remote-support path) and the address it actually uses?
You cannot look at an exposure you have not listed, and a search of your own addresses can come back clean while equipment at someone else’s is open. A.3.3.
Do you know every path by which your gate’s control system can be reached from outside, including any cellular modem?
An intruder enters by a path you did not know was there. A.3.1.
Would you detect someone reading your control system’s data for weeks?
An intruder learns your dam before acting. A.3.1.
Is remote operation of your gate a governed act, rather than prevented only by chance, such as a maintenance disconnection?
Nothing stands between the intruder and the gate. A.3.1.
If your control system were breached, would the people who warn the valley be told?
Emergency managers learn of the breach from the press. A.3.2.
Does your dam have an emergency action plan?
No one knows what to do if the gate is moved. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Know Every Path, and Treat Reading as Compromise

annex.p: A Department of Homeland Security bulletin of 2014, as the instrument cites it, described a control system reached by cellular modem as directly connected to the internet. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-1: record and verify every remote path to a gate’s controls; treat read access to them as a compromise of the gate; and make remote operation a governed act, not one prevented by chance.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Tell Those Who Warn, and Have a Plan

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-2 and F-3. Report an intrusion into a gate’s controls to the emergency managers who warn the valley; and keep an emergency action plan for the dam, whether or not a federal requirement reaches it.

annex.h3: A.3.3 List What Talks to the Outside, Then Look as an Attacker Would

annex.p: List first, then look. The inventory comes first because exposed equipment often sits outside your own address space: the intrusion on this record came through a cellular modem, which takes its address from the carrier, not from the dam’s owner. Then look at each address on the list as an attacker would, by any of three routes, each its provider’s. Shodan and Censys each offer a search of the devices they have found answering on the internet, and a search limited to your own address blocks and the addresses on your list shows you what it would show anyone. In the United States, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency offers Cyber Hygiene Vulnerability Scanning, which scans the internet-facing assets an organization names and reports weekly, at no cost to governments and critical infrastructure organizations (cisa.gov, Cyber Hygiene Services). Your integrator and vendors can tell you what they can reach remotely, if you ask them. Whatever the look finds that is not on your list goes on it, and whatever need not talk to the outside should stop. The inventory and the look are a standing item in every annex whose event turned on equipment reachable from the internet, on the author’s direction of 15 November 2026; here they rest on element I-1 and F-1.

Between 28 August and 18 September 2013, on the United States Attorney’s account, an intruder repeatedly reached the control system of the Bowman Avenue Dam, a small flood-control structure in Rye Brook, New York, and read its water levels, temperature, and the status of its sluice gate. Remote operation of the gate would have been possible had it not been disconnected for maintenance. The city was told soon after; the county’s emergency managers learned of it from the press more than two years later. In 2016 the Justice Department indicted the person charged with the intrusion as part of a group it said acted on behalf of the government of Iran; that is the United States Government’s statement, and the charges are untried. The dam was reported in 2022 to have no emergency plan. The lessons are that every path into a gate’s controls must be known, that reading the controls is a compromise of the gate, and that the people who warn the valley must be told. Any owner of a computer-operated gate has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this dam does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Overfilling and Breach of the Taum Sauk Upper Reservoir, December 2005
date_full: 14 December 2005, read to the Commission's order of 2 October 2006 (record closed)
what: Before dawn on 14 December 2005 the upper reservoir of the Taum Sauk pumped-storage project in Missouri, which had no spillway and was run from a control room more than a hundred miles away, was pumped over its parapet. Its three level transducers hung on one support that had come loose and read about two feet low; the backup probes had been raised after an overtopping in September, their alarm hung on one probe, and a programming error had disconnected them from one pump. The remote operator did not know the backup was ineffective, and the regulator had not been told. The rockfill crest eroded, the reservoir emptied in minutes through Johnson's Shut-Ins State Park, and the park superintendent's family was swept away in their house and survived.
tier: Not an attack: an overfill on instruments that read wrong and a protection changed without anyone deciding the fill knowing. None of the four characteristics is present.

findings.title: The reading was adjusted to look right.
findings.text: Any offset to a reading or change to a protection is a governed act, recorded and tested.

findings.title: The person deciding the fill did not know the protection was gone.
findings.text: Show the protection's state to whoever decides the fill.

findings.title: The backup had never been shown to work.
findings.text: Test the protection end to end, as installed and after every change.

findings.title: Nothing passive stood between the pumps and the crest.
findings.text: A reservoir filled by pumps carries an overflow sized to them, or declares its absence.

findings.title: The precursor did not reach the regulator.
findings.text: Report an overtopping or a protection found out of service, and restrict the fill until it is shown in service.

findings.title: Erratum: why the probes were too high.
findings.text: They were moved on 1 October 2005, on the Commission's order.

annex.p: This annex is for the owners and operators of pumped-storage projects and of any reservoir filled or drawn by pumps or gates under remote control, for the contractors who maintain their instruments and controls, and for the dam-safety regulators who oversee them. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility classes; this annex is addressed to a reservoir. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an owner answers about its own reservoir (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an owner can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one reservoir. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the owner; it is that owner’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Do your level instruments share a mounting, a pipe, a power supply, or a controller, so that one failure takes them all?
Your redundancy may be one instrument counted three times. A.3.1, A.3.2.
Is any offset or correction applied to a level reading in your controller, and who approved it, when, and on what basis?
Your reading may have been made to agree rather than shown to be right. A.3.2.
When was your high-level shutdown last tested from the water to the trip of every pump, and does its signal pass through a controller or a timer?
The backup may not work, and no one would know until it had to. A.3.1, A.3.2.
Does the person who decides the fill, wherever they sit, see whether the high-level protection is in service?
The fill may run on a protection everyone else knows is gone. A.3.2.
If your reservoir is filled by pumps, does it have an overflow that can pass what the pumps deliver, and how much freeboard do you hold against the rim as surveyed?
A foot of freeboard is the whole of your margin. A.3.1, A.3.2.
When your reservoir overtops, or a protection is found out of service, is the regulator told before the next fill?
The check on your operation cannot act on what it does not know. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s letter of 13 January 2006 required every pumped-storage licensee to review the effectiveness of its instrumentation and monitoring, its operating procedures, a fault-tree analysis, its operator training, and its Emergency Action Plan. The over-pumping protection criteria presented to the Commission’s pumped-storage meeting of November 2006 call for a protection separate from level control and held to stricter requirements, fail-safe, hardwired so that its shutdown does not pass through computers, controllers, or timers, and tested periodically, and warn that redundancy without independence gives a false sense of security. The first is the Commission’s; the second is its consultant’s, and this instrument does not find that it became a requirement. No step of this instrument’s is added here.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Govern Every Change, Show the Protection, and Give the Water a Way Out

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1 to F-5. Treat any offset, recalibration, or change to a level reading or a high-level protection as a change to the protection, approved, recorded, and followed by a test. Test the protection from the water at its level to the trip of every pump, as installed and after every change. Show the person who decides the fill whether the protection is in service, and do not fill near the top while it is not. If the reservoir is filled by pumps and has no overflow that can pass what they deliver, say so in its safety case, with the date the condition ends.
