And report an overtopping, or a protection found out of service, to the regulator before the next fill.

Before dawn on 14 December 2005, the upper reservoir of a pumped-storage plant in the Missouri Ozarks was pumped over the top of its wall, and the wall gave way. A billion gallons and more ran down the mountain in minutes, through a state park; the park superintendent’s family was swept away in their house and survived. The reservoir had no spillway. Its level gauges had come loose from their mounts the year before, all three together, and read about two feet low. The backup sensors meant to stop the pumps had been raised after a smaller overflow in September, and a programming error had disconnected them from one pump. The operator running the plant from a hundred miles away did not know the backup was not working, and the regulator was not told of the September overflow or the changes until after the breach. The company paid the largest penalty the federal regulator had then imposed in a hydroelectric case and rebuilt the reservoir with an overflow. The lessons are that three gauges on one mount are one gauge, that a reading adjusted until it looks right is not a reading shown to be right, that a backup nobody has tested is not a backup, and that the person deciding must know when the protection is gone. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own reservoirs, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Vajont Landslide and Displacement Wave, October 1963
date_full: 9 October 1963, read from first filling in 1960 (record closed)
what: Monte Toc's flank above the Vajont reservoir, identified as an ancient landslide, cracked and partly slid in 1960 and crept faster as the level rose. On 9 October 1963, during a drawdown, some 240 to 270 million cubic meters slid into the reservoir in under a minute, sending a wave over the almost intact dam into the Piave Valley that killed between about 1,900 and 2,500 people. The expected movement had been described as minor and the valley was not evacuated.
tier: Not an attack: a slope failing under the reservoir's operation. None of the four characteristics is present.

findings.title: The Valley Was Left in Place on an Estimate.
findings.text: The valley is warned against the largest credible slide, not the expected one.

annex.p: This annex is for owners and operators of reservoirs in steep valleys, the dam-safety regulators who oversee them, and the emergency managers of the communities below. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to a reservoir. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an owner answers about its own reservoirs (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an owner can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one reservoir owner. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the reservoir owner; it is that reservoir owner’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Have you identified every slope around your reservoir that could slide into it and raise a wave that reaches the crest?
The wave may come from the rim, not the dam. A.3.1.
Is the movement of each such slope watched against the reservoir’s level and the rate you change it?
You may be driving the slope with the level. A.3.1.
Is the movement at which you warn the valley set against the largest slide the slope could produce, not the one you expect?
The valley may be left in place on an estimate. A.3.2.
Do the people below and around the reservoir know a wave can come from a slide even if the dam holds?
They may think the dam is their protection. A.3.1.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The class’s requirements (§4.3, §5.2) state the identification and monitoring of slopes against level and rate of change, a bounded rate of change where the slope depends on it, and a movement stated in advance at which the reservoir is drawn down and the valley warned. National dam-safety guidance on reservoir-rim stability and on Emergency Action Plans sets out related practice. Each is its author’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Warn Against the Worst Slide, Not the Expected One

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1. Set the movement at which you warn and evacuate the valley against the largest slide your rim could credibly produce and the fastest it could move, and do not let an estimate of a smaller one keep people in place once that movement is reached.

On the night of 9 October 1963, part of a mountain in the Italian Alps, some 250 million cubic meters of rock, slid into the reservoir behind the Vajont Dam. The water it pushed out rose over the dam in a wave hundreds of meters high and swept through the valley below, destroying the town of Longarone and killing about two thousand people. The dam itself hardly cracked. The slope had been known to be an old landslide, had partly slid in 1960, and had been moving faster as the reservoir was filled; engineers were lowering the water when it failed, expecting a smaller, slower slide, and the valley was not evacuated. The lessons are that a reservoir can flood a valley without its dam failing, and that the warning must be set against the worst slide the slope could produce, not the one expected. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own reservoirs, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Failure of the New Orleans Hurricane Protection System in Hurricane Katrina, August 2005
impacted: Healthcare and Public Health, Emergency Services
what: Katrina's surge exceeded the New Orleans system's design in places, and many reaches were overtopped and eroded. At four breaches on the 17th Street, London Avenue, and Inner Harbor Navigation canals, I-walls failed through their foundations before water reached their tops. Most of the city flooded for weeks. The task force found the system incomplete, inconsistent, and not performing as a system; the independent team traced the failures to engineering errors and the interactions among its federal and local keepers.
tier: Not an attack: a line failing to a storm. None of the four characteristics is present.

findings.title: The Line Had Many Keepers and No Owner of Its Level.
findings.text: A line of many keepers has one owner of its level.

annex.p: This annex is for the owners and keepers of levees, floodwalls, and flood gates, the communities they protect, and the agencies that build and inspect them. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to a line of protection. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an owner answers about its own line (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an owner can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one owner. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the owner; it is that owner’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Do you know the level of protection of every reach of your line, and is the lowest stated as the line’s level?
The city is protected only to its weakest reach. A.3.1.
Has every floodwall been shown to hold until water reaches its top, foundations included?
A wall may fail before it is overtopped. A.3.1.
Is one party accountable for the level of the whole line, across every builder and keeper?
No one may know where the line is weakest. A.3.2.
Where will your line be overtopped first, and will it hold while overtopped?
Water beyond design may enter by breach. A.3.1.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The task force’s and the independent team’s reports set out the failures they found. The class’s requirements (§4.2, §4.3, §5.1) state the line as one system with its lowest reach as its level, floodwalls shown to hold to their tops, armored overtopping, and the evacuation margin. The National Levee Safety Program and the levee database kept by the Army Corps of Engineers with the Federal Emergency Management Agency set out related practice. Each is its author’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Make One Party Answer for the Whole Line

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1. Name one party accountable for the level of your whole line of protection, every reach, wall, gate, and pump, whoever built or keeps each part, and give it the authority to require each keeper to bring its reach up to that level.

When Hurricane Katrina’s storm surge reached New Orleans on 29 August 2005, the system of levees and floodwalls meant to protect the city failed. In places the surge was higher than the system was designed for, but at four places floodwalls along the city’s canals collapsed before the water reached their tops, because their foundations gave way. Most of the city flooded and stayed flooded for weeks. Investigators found that the system had been built and kept by several agencies and boards, that its height and strength varied from reach to reach, and that no one held the whole system to one standard. The lessons are that a city is protected only as well as the weakest reach of its line, and that one party must answer for the whole of it. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own line, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Kelly Barnes Dam Failure at Toccoa Falls, November 1977
date_full: 6 November 1977, read from the National Dam Inspection Act of 1972 (record closed)
what: The small, privately owned Kelly Barnes Dam above Toccoa Falls Bible College, unmaintained and overgrown, failed at about 1:30 in the morning during intensive rain; its flood passed over the 186-foot falls and killed 39 people on the campus. A national inspection program authorized in 1972 had never been funded for inspections. In December 1977 the President directed the inspection of more than 9,000 high-hazard non-federal dams.
tier: Not an attack: a dam failing in a storm. None of the four characteristics is present.

findings.title: Coverage on Paper Is Not Coverage.
findings.text: Coverage is counted as achieved, not as authorized.

annex.p: This annex is for owners of small and private dams, the state dam-safety programs that oversee them, and the emergency managers of the communities below. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to a dam. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an owner answers about its own dam (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an owner can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one dam owner. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the dam owner; it is that dam owner’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Is your dam in the state’s inventory, with a hazard-potential classification that reflects who now lives, works, or studies below it?
The program may not know your dam is dangerous. A.3.1.
When was your dam last inspected, and was it at the frequency its classification requires?
Coverage on paper may not be coverage. A.3.2.
Do you hold an Emergency Action Plan, and has it been exercised with the people below?
A failure at night may meet them unwarned. A.3.1.
Is the dam maintained, with trees and woody growth kept off the embankment?
The dam may fail in the next large storm. A.3.1.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The class’s requirements (§3.3, §4.1) state program coverage for every hazard-potential class and the bringing of high and significant hazard dams into a program. State dam-safety programs, the National Inventory of Dams kept by the Army Corps of Engineers, and the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s guidance on Emergency Action Plans and on the maintenance of embankment dams set out related practice. Each is its author’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Count Coverage by What Has Been Done

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1. Count your program’s coverage from inspections actually made and plans actually exercised, by hazard-potential class, and report any class your program is authorized to cover but cannot as uncovered until it can.

At about 1:30 in the morning of 6 November 1977, in heavy rain, the small, privately owned Kelly Barnes Dam in Georgia failed. Its flood went over Toccoa Falls and through the campus of Toccoa Falls Bible College below, killing 39 people. The dam had not been maintained for years and was overgrown with trees. Congress had passed a law in 1972 to inspect dams like it, but no money had been provided for inspections, and none had been made; there was no warning. Within weeks the President ordered the inspection of more than 9,000 high-hazard dams. The lessons are that a dam above people must be in a program that actually inspects it, and that a program counts only what it has done. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own dam, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Compromise of the SolarWinds Orion Platform, 2019 and 2020
what: Between 2019 and 2020 an intruder in SolarWinds' environment planted an implant on the build server for its Orion network-management platform that swapped a source file during each build and restored it afterward. The signed, backdoored update reached fewer than 18,000 installations, and was used against a chosen few, among them nine federal agencies, moving into cloud identity and email. The United States government attributed the campaign to the Russian Foreign Intelligence Service.
tier: Recorded as military action on the United States government's attribution, but not placed at the military-action tier because denial is not established on the record.

findings.title: The independent build is independent of the build.
findings.text: The implant left the repository clean and changed only what was built.

findings.title: A product's reach includes the credentials it holds.
findings.text: The platform's broad credentials carried the actor into cloud identity and email.

findings.title: A privileged product speaks only to what it declares.
findings.text: The backdoor disguised its traffic as the platform's own.

findings.title: The exposed population is known from a record.
findings.text: Agencies had to find their own affected instances.

annex.p: This annex is for software vendors who build and sign the products their customers install, and for the operators who run privileged management and monitoring products inside their own networks. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
As a vendor, would you detect an intruder who had been inside your build environment for months, testing an insertion?
Your next release carries the attacker’s code. A.3.2.
Is your build checked by a process independent of the build server itself, so that a file swapped during the build and restored afterward would be caught?
The repository is clean while the shipped product is not. A.3.2.
As a customer, do you treat a vendor’s signature as proof of origin only, not of integrity?
A signed update installs the backdoor. A.3.1.
How much does your monitoring or management product reach, and what credentials does it hold?
One compromised product reaches every system and your cloud identity. A.3.1.
Does each privileged product speak only to the destinations it declares, and would you see if it began to speak elsewhere?
The backdoor’s traffic looks like the product’s own. A.3.1.
Could you say at once which of your systems run an affected version, and disconnect them?
You cannot find what you must disconnect. A.3.1.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Disconnect, Hunt, and Rebuild as Directed, and Limit the Product’s Reach

annex.p: The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency directed federal civilian agencies on 13 December 2020 to disconnect or power down the affected Orion versions immediately; its supplemental guidance held them from rebuilding until directed, required forensic investigation or an indicator search, and required instances still connected to be updated to a corrected version by 31 December 2020. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-2, F-3, and F-4: count the credentials a product holds as part of its reach and limit them; let a privileged product speak only to the destinations it declares; and keep a record from which affected installations can be found at once.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Check the Build Independently

annex.p: This step is this instrument’s, from F-1. As a vendor, verify each build by a process independent of the build server, so that what ships is shown to be what the repository holds.

Between 2019 and 2020 an intruder inside SolarWinds’ environment planted an implant on the build server for its Orion network-management platform. During each build it swapped one source file for a backdoored version and restored the original afterward, so the code repository stayed clean. The backdoored component was signed by the vendor and delivered as an ordinary update to fewer than 18,000 installations. It lay dormant for two weeks, disguised its traffic as the platform’s own, and was used against a chosen few, among them nine federal agencies and about a hundred companies, moving from the platform into cloud identity and email. It was found in December 2020 by a security firm investigating its own intrusion. The United States government attributed the campaign to the Russian Foreign Intelligence Service; that is its attribution. The lessons are that a signature proves origin and not integrity, that a privileged product’s credentials are part of its reach, and that a build must be checked independently of itself. Any organization that runs privileged software from a vendor, or builds it, has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this organization does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Faulty Content Update of 19 July 2024
what: On 19 July 2024 CrowdStrike released a content update to its kernel-level Falcon sensor to all customers at once, and a latent defect crashed about 8.5 million Windows hosts in seventy-eight minutes. Many had to be repaired by hand; about 99 percent of sensors were back in ten days, but one airline took five days to recover and 911 centers handled calls by hand.
tier: Not an attack: a defective update from the vendor.

findings.title: A facility that cannot wait is not in the first ring by default.
findings.text: The update reached 911 centers in the same session as everyone else.

findings.title: Recovery is measured to the service, not the host.
findings.text: Sensors returned in ten days while some services took longer.

findings.title: Privilege is a parameter the design can lower.
findings.text: Kernel privilege is why each host had to be repaired by hand.

annex.p: This annex is for operators who run endpoint security or other software that runs with kernel privilege and is updated by its vendor, especially 911 centers, hospitals, airlines, and other facilities that cannot wait, and for the vendors who push those updates. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Do your version policies govern every channel through which a vendor can change the software, including content updates?
An update you never approved reaches every host. A.3.1.
Is a facility that cannot wait, such as a 911 center, kept out of the first group to receive an update?
The most critical hosts get the faulty update first. A.3.1.
If a kernel-level update crashed your hosts at boot, could you recover them without visiting each one, and do you have the recovery keys at hand?
Every host must be repaired by hand, one at a time. A.3.2.
Is your recovery measured to the service, such as dispatch or flight operations, and not only to hosts back online?
Hosts return while the service stays down for days. A.3.2.
Could your facility operate by hand while its computers were down?
Calls and patients wait while systems restart. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Govern Every Channel, and Keep Critical Facilities Out of the First Ring

annex.p: The vendor committed to a staggered deployment of rapid response content beginning with a canary, to give customers control over where and when it is deployed, and to independent third-party review of its code and processes, and its root-cause analysis added field-count and bounds checks and tests with non-wildcard values. This step adds the instrument’s own, from F-1: place a facility that cannot wait outside the first ring of any update, by default.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Recover to the Service, and Lower the Privilege

annex.p: On 19 November 2024 the operating-system vendor announced a recovery feature to apply fixes to machines that cannot boot, and capabilities to let security products run outside the kernel. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-2 and F-3: measure recovery to the service, not the host; and lower the privilege of a product wherever the design allows, since kernel privilege is what made each host a hand repair.

At 04:09 UTC on 19 July 2024, CrowdStrike released a content update to its Falcon security sensor, which runs in the Windows kernel, to all customers at once. A latent defect, a template expecting twenty-one inputs where the sensor supplied twenty, crashed about 8.5 million Windows hosts in seventy-eight minutes, and many could not restart long enough to receive the correction; they had to be repaired by hand, often with recovery keys. About 99 percent of sensors were back online within ten days, but some services took much longer: one airline cancelled about 7,000 flights over five days, and 911 centers handled calls by hand. Customers’ policies for holding the sensor at a version did not govern content. No one attacked anything. The vendor committed to staged releases and customer control, and the operating system’s vendor announced ways to fix machines that cannot boot and to run security products outside the kernel. The lessons are that every channel that can change a product must be governed, that facilities that cannot wait should not receive an update first, and that recovery is measured by the service, not the host. Any organization running vendor-updated software with deep privilege has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this organization does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Backdoor in the XZ Utils Compression Library, 2024
what: In 2024 a backdoor was found in XZ Utils, a compression library linked by remote-login servers on many Linux systems. A contributor had gained release authority from the project's single unpaid maintainer, hid the code in unused binary test files, and put its activation only in the release package. It reached development and rolling releases but not stable ones, and was found by chance from a slowdown in logins.
tier: A deliberate supply-chain compromise, not placed at the military-action tier: the actor is unidentified and no government has attributed it.

findings.title: Reviewed means readable, and the release is generated from the repository.
findings.text: The payload sat in binary files, and its activation only in the release package.

findings.title: The pace of intake is part of the defense.
findings.text: Accounts pressed distributions to take the new versions quickly.

findings.title: A change in who can release is a change to the product.
findings.text: The contributor gained release authority over about a year.

annex.p: This annex is for maintainers of open-source components, the operating-system distributions that package them, and the organizations that build products and systems on them. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
For each open-source component you depend on, do you know who can release it, and would you notice if that changed?
A new maintainer with bad intent releases your next version. A.3.2.
Is everything in the source you build from readable and reviewed, including binary test files?
The payload hides in files no one reads. A.3.1.
Is your release generated from the repository, or can it carry files the repository does not?
The release contains code the repository never showed. A.3.1.
Do you take new upstream versions at a measured pace, and resist pressure to take them quickly?
Requests to hurry bring the backdoor in. A.3.2.
Would you notice a small change in your systems’ behavior, such as logins taking longer?
The backdoor is found only by chance. A.3.2.
Could you downgrade or roll back a component the same day an advisory is issued?
You cannot remove what you have shipped. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Review What Is Readable, and Generate the Release

annex.p: No authority has published an action for maintainers that this instrument reads beyond the advisory below. This step is this instrument’s, from F-1: require that reviewed source be readable, and that the release be generated from the repository, not carry files of its own.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Govern the Pace of Intake and the Right to Release

annex.p: On 29 March 2024 the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency advised users to downgrade to an uncompromised version, and Debian rolled back the same day. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-2 and F-3: take upstream versions at a pace that leaves time for review; and treat a change in who can release a component as a change to the product.

In 2024 a backdoor was found in XZ Utils, a compression library that Linux distributions package and that many programs, including remote-login servers, link against. The project had one unpaid maintainer, who over about two years was pressed by accounts, probably fake, to hand it on, and a contributor gained the authority to release it. The contributor hid the backdoor’s code in binary test files that no test used and put the step that activated it only in the release package, not in the repository. Other accounts then pressed distributions to take the new versions. It reached development, beta, and rolling releases but not stable ones. An engineer at Microsoft noticed that failed logins were taking about half a second longer, traced it, and reported it on 29 March 2024; the government advised downgrading that day, and distributions rolled back. No use of it is recorded, and no government has attributed it. The lessons are that reviewed code must be readable, that a release must be built from what was reviewed, and that a change in who can release a component is a change to the product. Any organization that builds on open source has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this organization does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Compromise of Eight eMudhra Intermediate Certificate Authorities, 2025 and 2026
what: In April 2025 eMudhra created eight intermediate signing keys whose private keys, through a script error on its account, anyone could recover from the public certificates, allowing forgery of website and Windows code-signing identities. An outside researcher reported it on 17 October 2026; browsers blocked the intermediates within hours, and the root was distrusted. No misuse is recorded, but unattended clients without transparency or revocation checking stay exposed until their trust stores refresh.
tier: Not an attack: a defect in a key ceremony, with no misuse recorded.

findings.title: Two paths on one anchor are not independent.
findings.text: Paths through two roots rested on the same compromised keys.

findings.title: Exposure is set by the client's architecture, and the classes do not state it.
findings.text: Browsers were protected in hours; unattended clients were not.

findings.title: The browser's containment does not reach the infrastructure client.
findings.text: Infrastructure clients seldom check revocation or transparency.

findings.title: The blast radius of a trust anchor is bounded by its consumers' containment.
findings.text: One defect reached clients in every sector.

findings.title: The origin evidence rests on an authority the vendor does not hold.
findings.text: Code signed under the recoverable keys would be accepted as a vendor's.

findings.title: Trust-store refresh is the residual-risk variable.
findings.text: Offline and embedded clients carry the exposure longest.

annex.p: This annex is for operators of systems that trust certificates, especially unattended and embedded clients in industrial, utility, and other infrastructure that do not check certificate transparency or revocation, and for the certificate authorities whose ceremonies create the keys. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Before the questions below: have you listed every unattended, offline, or embedded client you run, the trust store it uses, how that store is refreshed, and the roots and intermediates in it?
No internet search can see which issuers a device trusts, so this exposure is found only by listing it. A.3.3.
Do the systems you rely on trust more than one certificate path that leads back to the same anchor?
Two paths you think independent fail together. A.3.1.
Do your clients check certificate transparency or revocation, or only that a signature chains to a trusted root?
A forged certificate is accepted without question. A.3.1.
Do you trust code signed under a root whose keys could be recovered by anyone, and could you tell?
Malicious code is accepted as signed by a trusted vendor. A.3.2.
How quickly are the trust stores of your unattended, offline, or embedded clients refreshed?
Your clients keep trusting a compromised anchor for months. A.3.2.
If your certificates had to be replaced quickly, could you replace them?
Services stop while certificates are reissued. A.3.2.
As an issuer, would an anomaly such as an invalid signature be traced to its cause rather than closed?
A weak key goes unnoticed for months. A.3.1.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Contain at the Client, and Count Shared Anchors as One

annex.p: On the root programs’ records, Chrome blocked the six TLS intermediates within hours of the report on 17 October 2026, Mozilla blocked all eight the same day, the issuer revoked them the next morning, Apple added protections on 19 October, and Microsoft blocked the certificates on 20 October through its certificate trust list updates. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-1, F-2, F-3, and F-4: count two certificate paths that rest on one anchor as one; and give infrastructure clients the containment browsers have, revocation and transparency checking, or state that they lack it.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Refresh Trust Stores, and Know Who Holds the Origin

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-5 and F-6. Treat the time to refresh each client’s trust store as the residual-risk variable, and shorten it most for offline, air-gapped, and embedded clients; and know which authority your code-signing evidence rests on, since a vendor does not hold the root its signatures chain to.

annex.h3: A.3.3 List What Your Unattended Clients Trust

annex.p: The exposure in this event was not a service anyone could scan for. It was the set of certificates an unattended device trusts, which no search of the internet can see, so the inventory here is of trust stores, not addresses. List each unattended, offline, or embedded client, the trust store it uses, how and when that store is refreshed, and the roots and intermediates in it. Mark each anchor the client does not need, and ask the device’s vendor how it can be removed and how fast a revocation reaches the device. The inventory is the form the standing exposure item takes in this annex, on the author’s direction of 15 November 2026; here it rests on element E-3 and F-5.

In April 2025 a certificate authority, eMudhra, created eight intermediate signing keys whose private keys, on the issuer’s account through a script error, were small numbers anyone could recover from the public certificates. Six could vouch for any website’s identity and two for any Windows software publisher’s, through roots widely trusted. Invalid signatures in 2025 were attributed to another cause and the matter closed. An outside researcher found the weakness on 17 October 2026 and reported it; browsers blocked the intermediates within hours, the issuer revoked them the next day, operating-system vendors followed within days, and the root was distrusted, leaving about 30,000 certificates to be replaced. No misuse is recorded, and browsers that check public transparency logs can show none occurred against them. But unattended clients that do not check transparency or revocation, common in infrastructure, stay exposed until their trust stores are refreshed, and there is no public record either way for them. No one attacked anything. The lessons are that two certificate paths to one anchor are one path, that the containment browsers have does not reach most infrastructure clients, and that the time to refresh a trust store is the time a client stays exposed. Any operator of systems that trust certificates has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Disruption of Amazon Web Services' Northern Virginia Region, 19 and 20 October 2025
what: A race between two enactors of the name-record automation for a database service's regional endpoint removed every address for it at 11:48 PM Pacific time. Restoring it sent the server lease manager into congestive collapse with no recovery procedure, impairing new launches until 1:50 PM; health checks on an incomplete network view removed healthy load-balancer capacity until 2:09 PM. Running work largely kept running.
tier: Not an attack: a provider's automation failing of its own sequence. None of the four characteristics is present.

findings.title: The Order That Was Never Enforced.
findings.text: If an order matters, it is identified, enforced, and tested.

findings.title: A Rate Limit Is Not a Check on the Measurement.
findings.text: Capacity is not removed on a measurement known to be incomplete.

annex.p: This annex is for organizations that run first- or second-tier services on a cloud provider, the providers themselves, and those who oversee them. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to an organization. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an organization answers about its own systems (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an organization can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one organization. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the organization; it is that organization’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Do you know which of your services need the provider’s control plane in one region to start, scale, or recover?
A regional control-plane loss may stop all new work. A.3.1.
Can your essential service be restored outside the region, and outside the provider, and has that been exercised?
You may wait on the provider’s recovery. A.3.1.
Does any automation you run remove capacity or records on what it measures, and does it stop when its view is incomplete?
Your own automation may take healthy work out. A.3.2.

Has your concurrent automation had every order of execution its correct result depends on identified, and is each enforced at the moment of action or made impossible by construction, and tested as enforced?
An order that matters but is not enforced may remove what you need most. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The provider’s summary sets out its own commitments, to fix the race, to protect against incorrect plans, and to limit the capacity a load balancer can remove. The class’s requirements (§4.2, §4.3, §4.6, §5.1) state fault domains and dependencies, staging of changes, limits on capacity removal, exercised recovery of control-plane services, and the tenant’s restoration outside the region and the provider. Each is its author’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Check the Measurement and Test the Timing

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s. From F-2: make any automation that removes capacity or records on a measurement stop and keep what is running when its view is incomplete or stale. From F-1: test your concurrent automation under delays and out-of-order actions, and do not treat it as proven until you have.

Late on 19 October 2025, an automated system inside Amazon Web Services’ largest region, in Northern Virginia, removed the network addresses of one of its own core database services. Two parts of the automation had acted in an order no one had tested, and one cleaned up the very record that was in use. Restoring the database set off a second failure in the system that manages the region’s servers, which had no rehearsed way back, and a third system, checking servers before their network setup was complete, took healthy capacity out of service. Work already running mostly kept going, but starting or scaling anything in the region was impaired for most of the next day, and many organizations’ services went with it. The lessons are that well-built automation can fail in orders of events never tested, and that automation which removes capacity must check that what it sees is complete. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own systems, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Deletion of UniSuper's Private Cloud, May 2024
date_full: May 2024, read from provisioning in early 2023 (record closed)
what: Provisioning the fund's private cloud in early 2023, operators left one parameter blank and the system assigned an unknown one-year term. At its end the provider's systems deleted the private cloud, without notice, across both geographies the fund had duplicated it in. Backups the fund held with another provider minimized its loss, and members could use its services again by mid-May. The provider retired the tool.
tier: Not an attack: a provider's process acting on an unseen default. None of the four characteristics is present.

findings.title: A Blank Became a Deletion.
findings.text: No destructive default is set by an omission.

annex.p: This annex is for organizations whose essential services run in a provider’s cloud, the providers, and those who oversee them. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to an organization. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an organization answers about its own systems (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an organization can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one organization. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the organization; it is that organization’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Do you know every term, retention period, or setting under which your provider’s systems could delete your environment, and have you seen each value?
A deletion may be set that no one knows of. A.3.2.
Would your provider notify you, and wait, before any deletion it did not get from you?
Your environment may go without notice. A.3.1.
Is your duplicate held somewhere your provider’s control plane cannot reach?
One act may remove both copies. A.3.1.
Is a copy of your essential state held with another party, beyond any account that reaches the original, and have you restored from it?
You may be recovered only on the provider’s timetable, or not at all. A.3.1.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The joint statement of the fund and the provider and the provider’s account set out what happened and the provider’s own corrections. The class’s requirements (§4.4, §4.6, §5.2) state notice, delay, and approval on any provider deletion, a statement of the processes that can delete, no credit for duplication within one provider, and a copy recoverable without the provider and exercised. Each is its author’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Leave Nothing Blank That Can Delete

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1. Ask your provider for every parameter that can set the deletion, retention, or term of your environment and the value each holds today, and require that none can be left unset or defaulted when your environment is provisioned or changed.

In May 2024, UniSuper, an Australian pension fund with hundreds of thousands of members, lost its entire cloud environment for about two weeks. Its provider’s own systems deleted it, in both of the regions where the fund had kept copies. A year earlier, when the environment was set up, a staff member had left one setting blank, and the system filled in a one-year expiry that no one knew about; when the year ran out, it deleted everything without telling anyone. The fund recovered because it also kept a backup with a different company. The lessons are that a copy kept with the same provider is not protection against that provider’s own mistake, and that a setting able to delete our systems should never be left to a default. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own systems, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Campaign Through Managed Service Providers, 2014 to 2018
date_full: about 2014 to 2018, read to the indictment of 20 December 2018 (record closed as to the event)
what: On the United States Department of Justice's account, from about 2014 a group acting in association with China's Ministry of State Security reached managed service providers and used their standing access into clients to take data from companies in at least twelve countries and many sectors. The clients could not tell the adversary's use of the access from their provider's, and the campaign ran for years before private researchers described it in 2017.
tier: A campaign of theft charged by the United States, and attributed also by allied governments, as a state's operation; not placed at the military-action tier: precision is not established and denial is absent.

findings.title: Access That Stands Is Open to Whoever Holds It.
findings.text: Provider access is opened by the customer for a task, and closed after it.

findings.title: The Watch Was Kept by the Party Whose Access Was the Route.
findings.text: The watch on a provider's access is not kept by the provider.

annex.p: This annex is for organizations whose systems are run in whole or part by a managed service provider, and for the providers themselves. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to an organization. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an organization answers about its own systems (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an organization can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one organization. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the organization; it is that organization’s finding, and the place to start. Because the event’s access ran through a provider’s remote connections into its customers, the standing exposure item is asked first.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Before the questions below: have you listed every outside party that can reach your systems, your managed service provider above all, with the accounts and tools each uses and what each can reach?
You cannot watch or cut access you have not listed. A.3.2.
Is your provider’s administrative access open all the time, or opened by you for a task and closed afterwards?
Access that stands is open to whoever holds it. A.3.2.
Is your provider’s access to one customer separate from its access to every other?
One customer’s compromise reaches the next. A.3.1.
Who reads the record of your provider’s use of its access, and is that party independent of the provider?
The route may be watching itself. A.3.2.
Could you cut your provider’s access today without its help, and keep running?
You may not be able to close the door. A.3.1.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The United States Computer Emergency Readiness Team’s alerts of 2017 and 2018 and the joint advisory of May 2022 by cybersecurity authorities of several governments set out practices for managed service providers and their customers, among them least privilege, separation of each customer’s access, logging, and the customer’s ability to manage the provider’s access. Each is its publisher’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Open the Door for the Task, and Watch It Yourself

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1 and F-2. Have your provider’s administrative access to your critical systems opened by you for each task and closed afterwards. And make sure the record of what your provider does with that access is read by you or by someone independent of the provider.

From about 2014, on the United States Department of Justice’s account, a hacking group working with China’s state security service broke into managed service providers, the firms that run computer systems for other companies, and used the access those firms held into their clients to steal data from businesses in at least twelve countries and many industries. The clients could not tell the hackers’ use of that access from their provider’s, and the campaign ran for years before it was publicly described. The United States charged two people in December 2018, and several allied governments joined in attributing the campaign. The lessons are that access an outside firm holds into your systems should be opened for a task and closed afterwards, not left standing, and that someone other than that firm should be watching how it is used. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own systems, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Attack on Dyn's Managed Name Service, 21 October 2016
what: Two distributed denial-of-service attacks, from about 11:10 to 13:20 and 15:50 to 17:00 UTC, flooded Dyn's managed name platform from a Mirai botnet of up to 100,000 internet-of-things devices on the provider's estimate. The names of many large services could not be resolved by users without held answers; holders with a second provider rode through. No government attribution is recorded.
tier: Adversarial, below the tier: intentionality and denial established, persistence not established, precision not determined.

findings.title: A Single Point of Failure No Holder Chose.
findings.text: The sector knows where its names are concentrated.

annex.p: This annex is for organizations whose essential services or operations depend on public names, the providers that answer for them, and those who oversee them. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to an organization. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an organization answers about its own names (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an organization can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one organization. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the organization; it is that organization’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Are your critical names answered by more than one provider, sharing no network, platform, or management?
One provider’s loss may take your names with it. A.3.1.
Are your names’ answers set to be held long enough for resolvers to ride through a provider’s loss for a stated period?
Users may lose you the moment the provider stops answering. A.3.1.
Does any control or protective path at your facility need a public name resolved at the moment it acts?
A naming outage may stop a protective act. A.3.1.
Do you know how many of the services you depend on share one name provider with each other?
A shared point of failure may be invisible to you. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The provider’s analysis sets out the attacks and its own response. The class’s requirements (§4.6, §5.3, §6.4) state names answered by more than one provider, answers held for a ride-through period, more than one resolver, and no control or protective path that needs a public name as it acts. Each is its author’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Find Out Who Answers for the Names You Depend On

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1. Find out which provider answers for your names and for the names of the services you depend on, and where many share one provider alone, treat it as a single point of failure in your own plan, whether or not any one of them chose it.

On 21 October 2016, a company called Dyn, which runs the internet’s address lookup for many large websites and services, was flooded with traffic from tens of thousands of hacked household devices such as cameras and recorders. For several hours that day, people across the United States and Europe could not reach many well-known sites, because their computers could not look up where those sites were. The sites themselves were working. Companies that used a second lookup provider, and computers that had remembered the answers, were not affected. The lessons are that many organizations relying on the same provider can share a weakness none of them chose, and that every critical service should have more than one way to be found. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own names, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Forging of Identity Tokens With a Stolen Microsoft Signing Key, 2023
date_full: May and June 2023, read from the key's creation in 2016 (record open in part)
what: Using tokens signed with a 2016 Microsoft consumer signing key that a flaw let work for enterprise accounts, an actor the Cyber Safety Review Board and Microsoft assess to be affiliated with the People's Republic of China reached the Exchange Online mailboxes of 22 organizations and more than 500 individuals. The Department of State found it through records not all customers held. Microsoft did not know how or when the key was obtained.
tier: Met, recorded as military action at the tier on the Board's record: intentionality, persistence, and precision established, and denial established as denial of function on the signing key, on the author's ruling of 20 November 2026.

findings.title: A Valid Signature on a Token No One Issued.
findings.text: A forged token is evident whatever the key's history.

findings.title: The Key's Function Was Denied Though Nothing Was Stopped.
findings.text: Denial is established on the key, not on the mail.

annex.p: This annex is for organizations that rely on a cloud identity provider for their people’s and services’ sign-in, the providers themselves, and those who oversee them. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to an organization. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an organization answers about its own identity services (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an organization can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one organization. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the organization; it is that organization’s finding, and the place to start. Because the event’s access ran through a service reachable from the internet, the standing exposure item is asked first.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Can you see, without paying more, the records of who signed in to your mail and other cloud services and from where?
A forged sign-in may go unseen by you. A.3.1.
Do the services you run check that a token was issued for your identities, rather than trusting the provider to have checked?
A key for another population may be accepted for yours. A.3.1.
Could you revoke your trust in your provider’s keys, and move your critical sign-in elsewhere, and in how long?
You may be unable to stop a forged key’s use. A.3.2.
Has your identity provider told you how its keys are held, rotated, and retired, and could it tell you when one left its control?
You may not know how long you have been exposed. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The Board’s review set out its findings and its recommendations to Microsoft and to cloud providers, and federal guidance on the logging available to tenants of cloud services followed. The class’s requirements (§4.5, §5.5) state protected, rotated, and scoped keys, relying services that check scope, tenant access to the records, and the ability to revoke trust and move authentication in a stated time. Each is its author’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Ask How a Forged Token Would Be Told From a Real One

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1. Ask your identity provider how a token it did not issue would be told from one it did, at the moment it is presented, and do not rest your critical services on a signature alone if the answer is that it cannot.

In the summer of 2023, an espionage group that the United States government’s Cyber Safety Review Board and Microsoft assess to be affiliated with China read the email of 22 organizations and more than 500 people, including senior United States officials. It did so by using a Microsoft signing key, the digital stamp that tells online services a sign-in is genuine, created in 2016 for consumer accounts. A flaw let that key work for business and government accounts too. The intrusion was found by the State Department, which had paid for records most customers did not have, and Microsoft could not say how or when the key had been taken. The lessons are that a single key at a large provider can open doors across every sector, and that we should ask our providers how a forged sign-in would be detected. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own identity services, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Disclosure of and Response to the Log4j Vulnerability, December 2021
date_full: 24 November to 17 December 2021 (record of the event closed; remediation open)
what: A flaw in the Log4j library reported to the Apache Software Foundation on 24 November 2021 was discussed publicly and disclosed on 9 December; the correction was brought forward to 10 December, and widespread exploitation followed at once. Defenders could not readily find where the library ran. The Cyber Safety Review Board found the vulnerability endemic, with instances likely to remain for a decade or longer.
tier: Not an attack in the event read: a disclosure and response. No characteristic is established.

findings.title: The Leak Set the Timeline.
findings.text: A leak starts the defenders' clock with the adversaries'.

annex.p: This annex is for every organization that runs software built from shared components, the maintainers and coordinators of those components, and those who oversee them. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to an organization. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an organization answers about its own software (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an organization can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one organization. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the organization; it is that organization’s finding, and the place to start. Because the flaw was exploited through applications reachable from the internet, the standing exposure item is asked first.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Could you list, from a record and not a scan, every system you run that carries a named library, within hours of a disclosure?
You may be searching while adversaries are exploiting. A.3.1.
Do your suppliers give you a record of the components in what they sell you?
You may not be able to find the flaw in their products. A.3.1.
Do you receive disclosures and corrections by more than one path, as fast as they become public?
You may learn of a flaw after the adversary. A.3.2.
Have you found and corrected every Log4j instance, including those inside products you bought?
An old flaw may still be open in your systems. A.3.1.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The Board’s review set out its findings and recommendations, among them that organizations be able to find vulnerable software through records of their components. Emergency Directive 22-02 and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s guidance on Log4j set out the actions for federal agencies and others. The class’s requirements (§3.3, §4.2, §4.3) state finding a named component from a record and sharing paths that reach defenders in time. Each is its author’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Ask the Coordinator How Fast a Leak Becomes a Correction

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1. Where you maintain or coordinate a widely used component, hold a correction or containment and the defenders’ indications ready to publish from the day a flaw is reported, and state how fast you would publish them if the flaw leaked.

In December 2021, a serious flaw was found in Log4j, a small, free piece of software used for record-keeping inside an enormous number of applications, from cloud services to industrial software. It was reported privately to its volunteer maintainers in late November, but it leaked on 9 December before the fix was ready, and attackers began trying to use it within hours. Most organizations could not quickly tell where they were using Log4j, because it was buried inside other products, and had to search for it. The government’s Cyber Safety Review Board expects vulnerable copies to remain in use for a decade or longer. The lessons are that every organization needs a record of the components inside its software, and that those coordinating a fix must be ready for it to leak. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own software, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Exploitation of Exchange Server Vulnerabilities and the Court-Authorized Removal of Web Shells, 2021
date_full: January to April 2021, read to the attribution of 19 July 2021 (record closed)
what: Through January and February 2021, hacking groups exploited unknown flaws in on-premises Exchange Server to place web shells. After Microsoft's disclosure and updates of 2 March, other groups followed. Patching closed the flaws but left web shells in place, and by the end of March hundreds remained on servers whose owners appeared unable to remove them. In April the FBI, under a court's authorization, deleted the remaining web shells of one group by a command through each, without patching or searching further, and then tried to notify each owner.
tier: An espionage campaign the United States and its allies attributed to actors affiliated with a state's intelligence service, not placed at the military-action tier: precision is not established and denial is absent.

findings.title: The Last Population Was the One That Could Not Defend Itself.
findings.text: The owners who cannot act are planned for before the race.

findings.title: A Bounded Act Leaves Everything Else.
findings.text: The notice of a bounded act says what it did not do, and the system stays counted as exposed.

annex.p: This annex is for the owners of servers reachable from the internet, above all organizations without a security operations center of their own, for the managed service providers who support them, and for the agencies that coordinate the response to a disclosed flaw. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to an organization. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an organization answers about its own systems (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an organization can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one organization. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the organization; it is that organization’s finding, and the place to start. Because the event’s access ran through servers reachable from the internet, the standing exposure item is asked first.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Before the questions below: have you listed every system of yours that can be reached from the internet, with the software and version each runs and who would patch it?
You cannot patch or search what you have not listed. A.3.2.
When a flaw in software you run is disclosed, do you search for signs that it was used against you before the patch, as well as apply the patch?
A patch closes the door and leaves anyone already inside. A.3.1.
If you could not find or remove an intrusion yourself, whom would you call, and is that arranged in advance?
You may be the last owner standing when the race ends. A.3.2.
If you were told that an agency had removed something from your server, would you know what it had not done and what you must still do?
A removal is not a clearance. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: Microsoft’s remediation guidance of March 2021 and the joint advisory of the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency of 10 March 2021 set out how to patch Exchange Server and how to search for and remove signs of compromise, and the Department of Justice’s announcement of 13 April 2021 urged every defender to follow them. Emergency Directive 21-02 required federal agencies to act. Each is its publisher’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Arrange Your Help Before You Need It, and Read a Removal Notice as What It Is

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1 and F-2. If you have no one who could find and remove an intrusion on your servers, arrange that help now, with a managed provider, an association, or an agency, and know whom you would call the day a flaw is disclosed. And if you are told that someone has removed something from your systems, treat the system as still exposed until you have patched it, searched it, and cleared it yourself.

In early 2021 hackers used unknown flaws in Microsoft’s Exchange mail server to break into organizations and leave hidden back doors. When Microsoft announced the flaws and the fixes on 2 March, other groups rushed to use them too. The fixes closed the flaws but did not remove back doors already left behind. Most organizations cleaned their servers, but by the end of March hundreds had not, often because they could not find what had been left. In April the FBI, with a court’s permission, sent a command through each remaining back door that deleted it, and then told the owners. It did not patch their servers or look for anything else. The United States and its allies later attributed the first break-ins to a state’s intelligence service. The lessons are that an organization should know, before it needs it, who would help if it could not clean up an intrusion itself, and that a notice that something was removed is not a clean bill of health. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own systems, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Theft From Bangladesh Bank's Account, February 2016
what: In February 2016 attackers inside Bangladesh Bank's network used its own payment terminals to send thirty-five instructions, for about $951 million, to its account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, and malware hid them by altering the bank's records and printed confirmations. Five, for about $101 million, were paid automatically; $20 million was stopped, and of $81 million drained through the Philippines about $15 million has been recovered. The United States Department of Justice attributes the theft to a group it describes as sponsored by North Korea.
tier: Recorded as military action on the United States government's attribution, but not placed at the military-action tier because denial is not established on the record.

findings.title: A stop reaches every party through which the money can still move.
findings.text: Stop requests went unanswered across weekends and a holiday.

findings.title: The receiving system's own check stands before finality.
findings.text: Five instructions were paid automatically before review flagged the rest.

findings.title: A failure of the endpoint's own reporting is a sign.
findings.text: A missing printout and software that would not start were taken as routine faults.

annex.p: This annex is for banks, central banks, and other institutions that send high-value payment instructions over an interbank messaging network, and for the operators of the systems that receive and settle them. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Could an intruder in your network reach the terminals that send your payment instructions?
An authenticated message is sent by someone who is not authorized. A.3.1.
Do you reconcile sent payments by a path an intruder in your terminals could not alter?
The record you check has been doctored. A.3.1.
Would a failed printer or software that will not start on a payment terminal be treated as a possible attack?
The sign is taken for a routine fault. A.3.2.
Could you stop a payment at any hour, including your weekend and holidays and those of every party it passes through?
Stop requests go unanswered while the money moves. A.3.2.
As a receiving system, do you check unusual instructions before they become final, not after?
Payments are paid automatically before the review that would catch them. A.3.3.
Once a payment is final, could you recover the money?
Most of what is stolen is gone for good. A.3.3.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Protect the Endpoint, and Reconcile Independently

annex.p: The messaging cooperative stated that the attack depended on the compromise of a local terminal, not on a flaw in its network, and in 2016 launched a customer security programme whose mandatory controls for users’ endpoints, with annual attestation, have applied since 2017. This step adds the instrument’s own, from F-3: reconcile what was sent by a path the endpoint cannot alter, since the malware doctored the endpoint’s own records.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Treat the Endpoint’s Own Failures as Signs, and Reach Every Party at Any Hour

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1 and F-3. Treat a failure of the endpoint’s own reporting, a confirmation that does not print or software that will not start, as a sign of attack; and make sure a stop can reach every party through which the money can still move, at any hour of any party’s week.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Check Before Finality

annex.p: This step is this instrument’s, from F-2. Where you receive and settle instructions, check unusual instructions before they become final.

In February 2016 attackers inside Bangladesh Bank’s network used its own payment terminals to send thirty-five instructions, for about $951 million, to its account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. They sent them late on the last day of the bank’s week, and malware hid them by altering the bank’s records and printed confirmations. Five instructions, about $101 million, were paid automatically before manual review flagged the rest. $20 million was stopped on a misspelling; $81 million was withdrawn through the Philippines, and only about $15 million has been recovered. In Dhaka a missing printout was taken for a printer fault, and the bank’s stop requests went unanswered across weekends and a holiday. The United States Department of Justice attributes the theft to a group it describes as sponsored by North Korea; that is its attribution. The lessons are that a payment terminal must be protected as the money itself, that its own failures may be signs of attack, and that a stop must be able to reach every party at any hour. Any institution that sends high-value payments has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this institution does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Bank of England RTGS Outage, October 2014
what: On 20 October 2014 the Bank of England's real-time gross settlement system stopped two minutes after opening, when a weekend change woke latent defects. Reconciliation before restart took 165 minutes against an estimate of 60 to 90, the Bank chose to keep fixing rather than switch to its contingency, and settlement resumed about nine hours late. Every payment settled in an extended day, though some house purchases completed late.
tier: Not an attack: a change triggered latent software defects.

findings.title: The verification time is prepared, not estimated.
findings.text: The reconciliation had no prepared scripts and took twice its estimate.

findings.title: The deciding authority knows the deadlines before it decides.
findings.text: Decisions were taken without full understanding of the effect on house purchases.

findings.title: The decision to keep fixing expires at a stated hour.
findings.text: The contingency needed hours to take over, and the decision to keep fixing had no stated limit.

annex.p: This annex is for operators of settlement and other critical financial systems, the teams that change them, and the senior officials who decide during an outage whether to fix or switch to the contingency. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Is every change to your system judged for whether it puts the system into a configuration you have not tested, however routine it seems?
A routine change wakes a latent defect. A.3.1.
Have you exercised your contingency system, including switching back?
The contingency is not used because no one trusts it. A.3.2.
If you had to verify the integrity of your data before restarting, do you have prepared scripts and a measured time?
Verification takes twice as long as estimated. A.3.1.
Are your criteria for switching to the contingency stated in advance, with an hour after which fixing forward must stop?
The team keeps fixing until switching is no longer possible. A.3.2.
Do those deciding know the deadlines downstream, such as house purchases, before they decide?
Decisions are made without knowing who is hurt by the delay. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Govern Changes, and Prepare Verification

annex.p: The Bank of England accepted every recommendation of the independent review: it deferred functional and non-routine changes, put changes under a delivery board, and added a loss-of-integrity scenario to its contingency manual. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-1: prepare the integrity verification needed before restart, with scripts and a measured time, rather than estimating it on the day.

annex.h3: A.3.2 State the Switch Criteria, the Deadline, and the Downstream Impact

annex.p: The Bank undertook to set out its criteria for invoking its contingency and to assess reverting from it within the week. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-2 and F-3: give the decision to keep fixing a stated expiry hour, set by the contingency’s switchover time; and make sure the deciding authority knows the deadlines downstream before it decides.
