On 20 October 2014 the Bank of England’s real-time gross settlement system, which settles the United Kingdom’s high-value CHAPS payments, stopped two minutes after opening. A weekend change the Bank had considered routine had woken defects left by earlier changes. Because the failure might have compromised account positions, the system had to be reconciled before it restarted; that took 165 minutes against an estimate of 60 to 90, without prepared scripts. The Bank chose to keep fixing rather than switch to its contingency, which needed up to two and a half hours to take over, and settlement resumed at 15:15, about nine hours late. The day was extended and every payment settled, but some house purchases completed late. The independent review found the decisions taken without full understanding of the effect on the wider economy, and the Bank accepted every recommendation. No one attacked anything. The lessons are that no change is routine until it is shown to be, that the time to verify integrity must be prepared in advance, and that the decision to keep fixing must expire at a stated hour. Any operator of a critical system with a contingency has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: Ukraine's Payment System Through the War, 2022 Onward
what: From the first day of the full-scale invasion in February 2022, the National Bank of Ukraine kept the country's payment system running without disruption, on plans drawn up in 2014, with its backup on reserve sites and banks' data allowed abroad. From October 2022, in a campaign of strikes on the grid that the International Criminal Court's warrants attribute to the Russian armed forces, the National Bank and the banks kept the public's access through more than 2,370 branches with their own power and communications.
tier: Military action by a state's armed forces against the grid the payment system depends on, sustained for years; the system held.

findings.title: The assured finality condition reaches the edge.
findings.text: Branches with their own power kept cash and banking within the public's reach.

findings.title: The permissions continuity needs are granted before the war.
findings.text: Permission to hold data abroad was granted only in the first weeks of the war.

annex.p: This annex is for central banks, payment system operators, and commercial banks that must keep payments and cash available to the public through a sustained attack on power and communications. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Do you have contingency plans, prepared in advance, for operating through an armed conflict or sustained attack?
Plans are written during the crisis. A.3.2.
Are your backup sites, and your participants’ data, outside the reach of the attack you plan for, with the legal permissions already granted?
Recovery waits on permission that should have been given before. A.3.2.
Could your system extend its hours, or run around the clock, when people and businesses need it?
Payments queue while the system keeps office hours. A.3.1.
When the grid fails, can the public still reach cash and banking through branches with their own power and communications?
The system settles, but people cannot get their money. A.3.1.
Can you show, at each resumption, that your records have not been altered?
Trust in the records is lost with the power. A.3.1.
Are you ready for attacks on your banks’ online services alongside the physical campaign?
Online banking fails at the moment people need it. A.3.1.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Keep Settlement and the Public’s Access Running

annex.p: The National Bank of Ukraine kept its payment system running twenty-four hours a day from the first day of the invasion, deploying its backup on reserve sites; with the banks it formed the Power Banking network of branches with alternative energy, backup communications, and enhanced cash collection, more than 2,370 of them by July 2023; and in April 2023 it launched a new generation of the system open around the clock. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-1: carry the assurance of finality to the edge, where the public reaches cash and banking, and verify the integrity of records at each resumption.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Prepare Plans and Permissions Before the War

annex.p: The National Bank and the banks drew up contingency plans in 2014 and activated them in February 2022, and banks were authorized in the first weeks of the war to process and store data in cloud services abroad. This step adds the instrument’s own, from F-2: grant the permissions continuity needs, such as data held abroad, before the conflict, not in its first weeks.

From the first day of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the National Bank of Ukraine kept the country’s payment system running without disruption, on contingency plans drawn up after the annexation of Crimea in 2014. It moved its backup to reserve sites, and banks were authorized in the first weeks to keep their data in cloud services abroad. From October 2022, in a campaign the International Criminal Court’s warrants cover and attribute to the Russian armed forces, missile strikes on power plants and substations brought long blackouts. The National Bank and the banks answered with more than 2,370 branches with their own power and communications, so the public could still reach cash and banking, and in 2023 the system began to run around the clock. Attacks on banks’ websites before the invasion were attributed by the United States and the United Kingdom to Russia; those are their attributions. The lessons are that payments can be kept running through a sustained attack if plans and permissions are ready before it, and that the public’s access at the edge matters as much as settlement at the center. Any payment system or bank has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this institution is ready, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Ransomware Attack on ICBC Financial Services, November 2023
what: A ransomware attack, claimed by the group the security community calls LockBit, disrupted systems at the United States broker-dealer of the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China. Counterparties disconnected; it cleared trades by other means, carrying settlement information by hand on a portable drive, and, as reported, briefly owed its settlement bank $9 billion, met by its parent's capital, during a thirty-year Treasury auction.
tier: Adversarial, below the tier: intentionality and denial established, persistence not established, precision not determined.

findings.title: A Parent's Capital No Design Basis Named.
findings.text: A disconnected member's means of paying is known before it is needed.

annex.p: This annex is for clearing members and broker-dealers, the clearing utilities and settlement banks they deal with, and those who oversee them. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to a firm. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions a firm answers about its own clearing operations (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account a firm can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one firm. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the firm; it is that firm’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
If your systems were encrypted tonight, how would your trade and position records reach the utility and your counterparties tomorrow, and on what authentication?
Your records may travel on a drive no one agreed to accept. A.3.1.
Who decides whether you disconnect from a compromised counterparty, and when you reconnect, and on what basis?
Disconnection may be decided ad hoc, firm by firm. A.3.1.
How much could a day’s disconnection leave you owing, and where would the money come from?
You may be driven toward default by the loss of your means of paying. A.3.2.
If that money is a parent’s, is the commitment written, sized, and known to your settlement bank?
Your counterparties may not know you can pay. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The class’s requirements (§4.3, §5.2) state an out-of-band records path agreed in advance, a basis for clearing by hand, named authorities for disconnection and reconnection, and the member’s liquidity for the time it states. The sector’s regulators and its information-sharing organization have published guidance on ransomware and on third-party and counterparty connections. Each is its author’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Know Where the Money Comes From If You Are Cut Off

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1. Size what a day or more of your own disconnection could leave you owing, name the source that would meet it, and if that source is a parent or affiliate, get its commitment in writing, sized and timed, and make it known to your settlement bank and the utility.

In November 2023, a ransomware attack shut down systems at ICBC Financial Services, the New York broker-dealer of China’s largest bank, which helps clear trades in United States Treasury bonds. Other firms cut their connections to it to protect themselves, which also cut off its normal way of settling, and it ended up sending trade information to counterparties by hand on a portable drive. As reported, it briefly owed its settlement bank about $9 billion, far more than its own capital, until its parent bank stepped in. The lessons are that being cut off can push a firm toward default even if it has done nothing wrong, and that a firm must know in advance how it would settle and where the money would come from. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own clearing operations, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Erroneous Orders From Knight Capital’s Router, August 2012
date_full: 1 August 2012, read to the Commission's order of 16 October 2013 (record closed)
what: On 1 August 2012 a trading firm deployed new code to seven of the eight servers of its equity order router. The eighth still held a function retired in 2003, and the new code reused the flag that switched it on. In the first forty-five minutes of trading it sent more than four million orders while filling 212 customer orders, and the firm lost more than $460 million. Ninety-seven e-mails had named the error before the open and were not read as alerts. The firm stayed connected while it diagnosed, and one fix spread the fault to the healthy servers.
tier: Not an attack: a deployment error and retired code. None of the four characteristics is present.

findings.title: The Firm Diagnosed While Connected, and the Fix Spread the Fault.
findings.text: A stop of all order flow comes before any diagnosis, and a repair waits on a confirmed one.

findings.title: Retired Code Was Left Live and Its Switch Reused.
findings.text: Remove retired code, retire its switches, and verify every server before trading.

annex.p: This annex is for broker-dealers and other firms that send orders to markets through automated systems, for the venues and clearing houses that receive them, and for their regulators. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to a firm. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions a firm answers about its own trading systems (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account a firm can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one firm. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the firm; it is that firm’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Is every function you no longer use removed from every production server, and is no flag or message type that once called it reused?
An old switch may wake old code. A.3.2.
Is each deployment verified complete on every server before the system trades?
One missed server is an untested configuration. A.3.2.
Do your systems’ error messages before and during trading stop the system until someone clears them, or do they arrive as mail?
The warning may be read after the loss. A.3.1, A.3.2.
Are your order limits between your systems and the market, and do they count outstanding orders as well as fills?
A limit that blocks nothing is not a limit. A.3.1.
Who may disconnect your order flow from the market, on what sign, and have they done it in an exercise?
You will stay connected while you look for the cause. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The Securities and Exchange Commission’s market access rule requires a broker or dealer with market access to maintain risk-management controls and supervisory procedures reasonably designed to prevent the entry of erroneous orders and of orders that exceed pre-set credit or capital thresholds. The Commission’s order of 16 October 2013 required the firm to have an independent consultant review its software development and deployment, its routers, firm-wide thresholds linked to pre-trade controls, and its incident response. Each is the Commission’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Stop First, and Leave No Old Switch Live

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1 and F-2. Name in advance who disconnects your order flow and on what sign, and have them do it before anyone diagnoses or repairs; make a repair during an incident wait on a confirmed diagnosis. Remove every retired function from every production server, do not reuse an identifier that once called it, and verify each deployment on every server before trading.

On the morning of 1 August 2012, a trading firm’s order router began sending orders to the stock market without end. New software had been installed on seven of the router’s eight servers; the eighth still held a function retired nine years before, and the new software reused the switch that turned it on. Ninety-seven warning e-mails had gone out before the open, but they were not treated as alerts. In forty-five minutes the router sent more than four million orders, and the firm lost more than $460 million. Its staff stayed connected to the market while they looked for the cause, and one fix they tried, removing the new software from the healthy servers, spread the fault. The lessons are that when a trading system misbehaves, the first act is to stop it, not to fix it; that a warning must stop the system, not sit in an inbox; and that old code left on a production machine is a fault waiting for a switch. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own trading systems, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Failed Migration of TSB's Customer Accounts, April 2018
what: Over a weekend in April 2018 TSB moved every customer's records to a new platform built and run by its parent's technology subsidiary, which had not been properly tested. Nearly 1.9 million customers were locked out, some for weeks, and some were affected until December 2018. The bank paid £32.7 million in redress, and in December 2022 its regulators fined it £48.65 million over the migration and its outsourcing.
tier: Not an attack: a change to the core failing of itself. None of the four characteristics is present.

findings.title: The Bank Could Know Only What the Builder Told It.
findings.text: The authority that decides knows what has been tested from evidence it holds.

annex.p: This annex is for banks and building societies, the parties that build and run their core platforms, and those who oversee them. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to an institution. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an institution answers about its own core platform (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an institution can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one institution. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the institution; it is that institution’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Will your next change to the core reach a small population first, so that its failure is bounded before it reaches every customer?
A failed change may reach every customer at once. A.3.1.
Has the change been tested in the configuration in which it will run, at its real volumes?
The platform may fail the first time it carries the real load. A.3.1.
If another party builds or runs your platform, does your board see testing evidence verified independently of that party?
Your board may be told only what the builder reports. A.3.2.
Can you go back to the previous ledger, and for how long?
Customers may be locked out until the new platform is fixed. A.3.1.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The review’s recommendations and the regulators’ final notices set out what they found and expect. The United Kingdom’s regulators’ requirements on operational resilience and on outsourcing and third-party risk set out related practice. The class’s requirements (§4.3, §5.1) state the change as a governed act, staged, tested as it will run, with a path back, and decided by an authority told what is untested. Each is its author’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 See the Testing for Yourself

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1. Where another party, your own affiliate included, builds or runs your core platform, require evidence that each major change was tested as it will run, verified by someone independent of the builder, before your board or named authority decides to go live.

Over a weekend in April 2018, the British bank TSB moved all of its customers’ accounts to a new computer system built and run by a technology company owned by its parent. The new system had not been properly tested, and when it went live, nearly two million customers were locked out of their accounts, some for weeks, and problems for some lasted until December. The bank paid £32.7 million to customers, and in 2022 its regulators fined it £48.65 million for failing to control the move and to manage the risks of relying on an outside supplier. The lessons are that a change should never reach every customer at once, and that a board must see real evidence, not the supplier’s assurance, that a system has been tested. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own core platform, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Denial-of-Service Attacks on United States Banks, 2011 to 2013
date_full: December 2011 to May 2013, read to the indictment of 24 March 2016 (record closed as to the event)
what: From late 2011 to mid-2013, floods of traffic at up to 140 gigabits per second struck forty-six major companies, mostly United States banks, on more than 176 days. On some days hundreds of thousands of customers could not reach their accounts online; the ledgers were untouched and branches and cash machines stayed open. A group claiming the attacks announced its targets in advance. The United States charged seven people it said worked on behalf of the Iranian government.
tier: A campaign charged by the United States as work on behalf of a state; not placed at the military-action tier and not recorded as military action: precision and denial are not established, on the author's confirmation of 19 November 2026.

findings.title: The Capacity Was Set Against a Flood the Adversary Chose.
findings.text: Channel capacity is set against the largest flood shown and brought into force on an announcement.

annex.p: This annex is for banks and credit unions, the mitigation providers and network carriers that protect their online channels, and their regulators. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to an institution. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an institution answers about its own channels (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an institution can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one institution. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the institution; it is that institution’s finding, and the place to start. Because the event’s attack ran against channels reachable from the internet, the standing exposure item is asked first.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Before the questions below: have you listed every channel and service of yours reachable from the internet, with the mitigation in front of each and the provider that runs it?
You cannot protect a door you have not counted. A.3.2.
What is the largest flood your online channels can absorb, and how does it compare with the largest flood shown against your sector?
Your capacity may be set below what has already been used. A.3.2.
If a group named your institution and a date, what would you do before that date, and who decides?
The warning may pass while the flood arrives. A.3.2.
If your online channels were down for a day, could your customers reach their balances and cash another way that shares nothing with them?
The public will experience it as the loss of their money. A.3.1.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The Department of Justice’s announcement of 24 March 2016 describes the campaign. The financial regulators and the sector’s information-sharing bodies issued guidance during and after the campaign on preparing for and responding to distributed denial-of-service attacks, among them mitigation capacity and alternative channels. Each is its publisher’s. No step of this instrument’s is added here.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Set Your Capacity Against What Has Been Shown, and Act on a Warning

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1. Set the flood your online channels can absorb against the largest shown against your sector, and review it when a larger one appears. And when a group names your institution and a date, bring your mitigation into force before that date, on a decision named in advance.

From late 2011 to mid-2013, attackers flooded the websites and online banking of forty-six major companies, most of them United States banks, on more than 176 days. On some days, hundreds of thousands of customers could not reach their accounts online, though no account data was touched and branches and cash machines stayed open. The group that claimed the attacks announced its targets in advance, and the floods still overwhelmed the sites. In 2016, the United States charged seven people it said worked for companies acting on behalf of the Iranian government. The banks built their defenses during the campaign. The lessons are that online capacity must be set against the largest attack already seen, not the last one planned for, and that a public warning naming your institution is a reason to act before the day it names. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own channels, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Ledger Shortfall at Synapse Financial Technologies, 2024
what: Synapse kept the ledger of end users' shares of pooled accounts at several partner banks. It filed for bankruptcy on 22 April 2024; in May the banks froze end users' funds when the accounts could not be reconciled, and the court-appointed trustee reported a shortfall of $65 million to $96 million, later $65 million to $95 million, against the funds the banks held. The FDIC proposed a recordkeeping rule in September 2024.
tier: Not an attack: an intermediary's ledger failing. None of the four characteristics is present.

findings.title: Every Bank Could Balance and the Total Not.
findings.text: A difference that no one bank can see is found the day it arises.

annex.p: This annex is for banks that hold pooled or custodial accounts for financial-technology firms, the firms and intermediaries themselves, and those who oversee them. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to an institution. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an institution answers about its own custodial accounts (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an institution can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one institution. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the institution; it is that institution’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Can you read, without the intermediary, the record of each end user’s share of the pooled accounts you hold?
You may be unable to say whose money it is. A.3.1.
Do you reconcile that record with what you hold every business day?
A shortfall may grow unseen. A.3.1.
If the intermediary also places end users’ money at other banks, does anyone reconcile each end user’s total across all of them?
Every bank may balance while the total does not. A.3.2.
Could end users reach their reconciled share while a difference is resolved?
Every end user may be frozen for months. A.3.1.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation’s proposed rule on recordkeeping for custodial accounts and the banking agencies’ guidance on bank arrangements with third parties and financial-technology firms set out related practice. The class’s requirements (§4.2, §5.3) state a record the bank can read without the intermediary, daily reconciliation, a difference raised to a named authority, and continued access to the reconciled share. Each is its author’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Reconcile Across Every Bank, Not Only Your Own

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1. Where an intermediary spreads its end users’ money across your bank and others, agree with the other banks on a party that reconciles each end user’s total across all of you every business day, and on what happens when it finds a difference.

In April 2024, Synapse, a company that connected consumer finance apps to the banks holding their customers’ money, went bankrupt. The money sat in pooled accounts at several banks, but only Synapse kept the record of how much belonged to each person. When it failed, the banks could not tell who owned what and froze the accounts, leaving many people without access to their savings for months. The court-appointed trustee found a gap of tens of millions of dollars between Synapse’s records and the money the banks actually held. The lessons are that a bank must be able to read, by itself, the record of whose money it holds, and that when money is spread across several banks, someone must check the total for each customer across all of them. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own custodial accounts, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Ransomware Attack on JBS, May and June 2021
what: On 30 May 2021 criminals attacked servers supporting JBS's North American and Australian systems, and by 1 June every one of its United States beef plants had stopped, with national cattle slaughter down 22 percent. Most plants were back within two days, because encrypted backups and core systems had not been reached. The Federal Bureau of Investigation attributed the attack to a criminal ransomware group.
tier: A deliberate criminal attack, not military action: a crime for money, attributed to no state.

findings.title: The supply share is counted across the shared system.
findings.text: One attack on shared servers stopped every United States beef plant of the company.

findings.title: Restoration is credited only from what the attack cannot reach.
findings.text: The company returned fast because its backups were not reached.

annex.p: This annex is for food processors, especially those running many plants from shared business systems, and for the technology and operations leaders who would decide to stop and restart them. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Do your plants depend on business systems served from a central or shared set of servers?
An attack on the center stops every plant at once. A.3.1.
Have you planned an orderly stop of your systems and plants as a protective action, and who decides it?
Plants stop in disorder, with animals and product in the line. A.3.1.
Are your backups kept where an attacker inside your network could not reach them?
There is nothing clean to restore from. A.3.2.
How much of the national supply of your product do your plants carry together, counted across the systems they share?
Your stop is a national shortage. A.3.1.
How long would it take to restart your plants, and could other processors take up your volume meanwhile?
Perishable inflow backs up with nowhere to go. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Count Your Share Across the Shared System, and Plan the Stop

annex.p: No authority has published an action for owners that this instrument reads; the company’s statements and the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s attribution are its record. These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1: count the share of supply your plants carry together across the systems they share, and plan an orderly stop as a protective action.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Credit Restoration Only From What the Attack Cannot Reach

annex.p: This step is this instrument’s, from F-2. Credit a fast restart only to backups and core systems kept beyond the attacker’s reach, as the company’s encrypted backups were.

On 30 May 2021 JBS, among the largest meat processors in the world, found that criminals had attacked servers supporting its North American and Australian information systems, and it suspended all affected systems. By 1 June every one of its United States beef plants had stopped or cancelled shifts, and national cattle slaughter fell 22 percent and hog slaughter 20 percent. Most plants were back within two days, because the company’s encrypted backups had not been reached and its core systems were never accessed; it said it lost less than one day’s production. The company later stated that it paid the equivalent of $11 million. The Federal Bureau of Investigation attributed the attack to a criminal ransomware group; no state was involved. The lessons are that plants sharing one set of business systems share one exposure, that an orderly stop is a protective action to plan, and that a fast restart depends on backups the attacker cannot reach. Any processor running many plants from shared systems has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this company does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Abbott Sturgis Shutdown and the Infant Formula Shortage, 2022
what: On 17 February 2022 Abbott Nutrition recalled powdered infant formula and stopped its Sturgis, Michigan, plant after infant infections and the finding of Cronobacter in the plant's environment; a causal link was not established. The plant was the only source of some specialty formulas, whistleblower complaints had gone unaddressed for months, and by mid-May the national in-stock rate had fallen to about 80 percent before imports were admitted.
tier: Not an attack: a contamination and safety stop at a plant on which a dependent population relied.

findings.title: A report from inside the plant reaches the release decision.
findings.text: Whistleblower complaints were not acted on for months.

findings.title: The permissions substitution needs are in hand before the stop.
findings.text: Imports were admitted three months after the plant stopped.

annex.p: This annex is for makers of infant formula, medical foods, and other products a dependent population cannot do without, and for the regulators who inspect them and would admit substitutes in a shortage. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Does a report from inside your plant, such as a whistleblower complaint, reach the people who decide whether product is released?
A warning sits for months while product ships. A.3.1.
Does your release decision rest on the plant’s environment as well as on finished product tests?
Product passes its tests while the plant harbors the pathogen. A.3.1.
Is any product, such as a specialty formula, made only at one of your sites?
A single plant’s stop leaves some infants with nothing. A.3.2.
If your plant stopped, are the permissions to bring in substitutes, such as imports, in hand before you stop?
Shelves empty for months while permissions are arranged. A.3.2.
Is your restart planned, including against the hazards your site faces, such as flooding?
The restarted plant stops again within days. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Bring Inside Reports to the Release Decision

annex.p: The Inspector General of the Department of Health and Human Services found that the agency had no policies setting timeframes for mission-critical inspections, had not established the structure or responsibilities to handle whistleblower complaints efficiently, and lacked sufficient policies for initiating an infant-formula recall, and made nine recommendations. This step adds the instrument’s own, from F-1: route a report from inside the plant to the release decision.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Have Substitution in Hand Before the Stop

annex.p: This step is this instrument’s, from F-2. Arrange in advance the permissions a substitute supply needs, such as imports admitted under enforcement discretion, so that they take effect when the plant stops, not months after.

On 17 February 2022 Abbott Nutrition recalled powdered infant formula and stopped its plant in Sturgis, Michigan, after infant infections were reported and the pathogen Cronobacter was found in the plant’s environment; its finished product tested negative, and a causal link to the illnesses was not established. The company held the largest share of the United States market, and the plant was the only source of some specialty formulas. Whistleblower complaints had been received months before and not acted on promptly. By mid-May the national in-stock rate for formula had fallen to about 80 percent, and only then did the federal government fly in formula and admit products not otherwise permitted. The plant restarted under a consent decree in June and was stopped again by flooding nine days later. The Inspector General, whose report is the record, found gaps in the agency’s handling of inspections, complaints, and recalls. The lessons are that a report from inside the plant must reach the release decision, and that permissions for substitutes must be ready before the stop. Any maker of a product a dependent population cannot do without has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this company does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Melamine Adulteration of Milk in China, 2008
what: In 2008 raw milk in China was diluted and laced with melamine at collection stations to pass tests that measured nitrogen as a stand-in for protein, and tainted products reached twenty-two makers of infant formula. About 294,000 children were diagnosed, more than 50,000 hospitalized, and six died. China then tested every batch of raw milk for melamine and prosecuted those responsible.
tier: A deliberate crime for profit, not military action: attributed to no state.

findings.title: Test the property, not the proxy.
findings.text: The tests measured nitrogen and could not tell melamine from protein.

findings.title: Someone watches the dependent population's health.
findings.text: Months passed between the first kidney stones and the link to formula.

findings.title: The stretch between farm and plant belongs to a design basis.
findings.text: No single agency held the collection stations where milk was adulterated.

annex.p: This annex is for food processors and dairies that buy raw materials through collectors and intermediaries, especially for infant and other first-band products, and for the public health authorities that watch the health of dependent populations. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Do your acceptance tests measure the property you need, such as protein, or a proxy for it that an adulterant could fool?
Adulterated material passes your tests. A.3.1.
Does anyone hold responsibility for the stretch between the farm and your plant, such as collection stations?
The adulteration happens where no one is looking. A.3.2.
Do you control the protein and other raw materials your suppliers sell you, not only the milk?
A tainted ingredient enters through a supplier. A.3.1.
Would a rise in illness among the population that eats your product be noticed and linked to you quickly?
Months pass between the first cases and the cause. A.3.2.
If an adulterant were found, could you test every batch for it at once?
Testing waits while tainted product ships. A.3.1.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Test the Property, Not the Proxy

annex.p: After the event, China stationed inspectors at the major dairy manufacturers, tested every batch of raw milk for melamine, and set interim limits for melamine in infant formula and other foods, and an expert meeting of the World Health Organization set a tolerable daily intake. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-1: test what you receive for the property you need, not a proxy an adulterant can fool, and control the raw materials your suppliers sell you.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Hold the Stretch Between Farm and Plant, and Watch the Population

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-2 and F-3. Make someone responsible for the stretch between farm and plant; and make sure someone watches the health of the population that depends on your product, so that a rise in illness is linked to its cause quickly.

In 2008, in China, raw milk was diluted with water at collection stations and melamine, an industrial chemical rich in nitrogen, was added to make it pass tests that measured nitrogen as a stand-in for protein; melamine-laced protein materials were also sold to formula makers. Tainted products were found at twenty-two makers of infant formula. Pediatricians noticed rising numbers of infants with kidney stones in the spring, and the link to formula took months to confirm. About 294,000 children were diagnosed, more than 50,000 were hospitalized, and six died. China then tested every batch of raw milk for melamine, set limits, examined more than 20 million children free of charge, and prosecuted those responsible. It was a crime for profit, attributed to no state. The lessons are that tests must measure the property needed and not a proxy that can be fooled, that someone must hold the stretch between farm and plant, and that someone must watch the health of those who depend on the product. Any processor that buys raw materials through intermediaries has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this company does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Defrost Attacks on Supermarket Refrigeration, October and November 2026
what: On the night of 11 October 2026, refrigerated cases and freezers in about 700 French supermarkets were set into defrost through remotely managed controllers reachable from the internet, many past their manufacturers' support, and temperatures rose to as much as 50°C. A second wave struck stores in several more countries on 1 and 2 November. Stock was discarded, equipment was damaged, and in some stores the heaters started fires; no shortage or illness was reported.
tier: A deliberate and repeated attack, not placed at the military-action tier: no government has attributed it to a state, it came in peacetime, and it removed stock rather than supply. The European Union's statement is recorded as one of intent, not attribution.

findings.title: A distributed tier is concentrated by what its facilities share.
findings.text: Hundreds of stores failed in one night because they ran the same controllers.

findings.title: The cold chain's protective function is independent of the controller it protects.
findings.text: The controller the attackers held also held the limit, the alarm, and the display.

findings.title: Temperature abuse is a safety-axis event.
findings.text: The controllers can be made to hide a warming as well as cause one.

findings.title: Building equipment driven by a digital command is a fire initiator in occupied retail space.
findings.text: Defrost heaters run without limit started fires in stores.

findings.title: Equipment past its support is a design-basis condition.
findings.text: Most of the controllers named receive no updates.

annex.p: This annex is for supermarkets, food retailers, and cold-storage operators, for the refrigeration contractors who manage their controllers remotely, and for any operator of building equipment a contractor can reach over a network. It recasts the interim actions of v0.4 into the three-part form, carrying each of them into A.3. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known

Before the questions below: have you listed every refrigeration controller in every store that talks to the outside world, with the network it does so through (your own, a cellular carrier’s, or a vendor’s or integrator’s remote-support path) and the address it actually uses?
You cannot look at an exposure you have not listed, and a search of your own addresses can come back clean while equipment at someone else’s is open. A.3.6.
Can your refrigeration controllers be reached from the internet, and do you know which are past their manufacturer’s support?
Your cold chain is open to anyone who scans for it. A.3.1, A.3.3.
Do you know every path to your controllers, including your contractor’s link and any cellular modem on the unit itself?
You close the store’s connection and leave another open. A.3.1.
If a controller were compromised, would you reset it, patch it, and review its configuration and defrost schedules before returning it to service?
The attacker stays on the unit after you think it is clean. A.3.2.
Is there a temperature limit on each case or cold room that ends heating whatever the controller commands, with an alarm that does not depend on the controller?
Food spoils before anyone is told, and the controller says all is well. A.3.4.
How many of your stores share the same make of controller or the same contractor, so that one attack reaches them all in a night?
A distributed chain fails like a single site. A.3.1.
Could heaters driven without limit start a fire in an occupied store?
A digital command becomes a fire. A.3.4.
Do you know whom to report a compromise to?
Others are attacked the same way while you stay silent. A.3.5.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Remove the Exposure, Including the Routes Around It

annex.p: The French government’s computer emergency response team told operators to take affected units, and any unit reachable at a public address, off the internet; to restore remote access only through a secured private network or protected connection; to treat filtering by source address as a short-term measure only; and to check insurance conditions before cutting a refrigeration contractor’s data link. Coop’s report that some of its fridges sat on a 4G mobile link shows a route the alert does not name. This step adds the instrument’s own, from F-1: treat every path to the controller, the contractor’s and any cellular one included, as part of the exposure, and count the stores that share one make or one contractor as one exposure.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Patch, Harden, and Reset

annex.p: The alert told operators to update firmware, set Danfoss devices to their strict security mode, change default passwords, review the whole configuration and especially the defrost schedules, and, where a unit is compromised, reboot it, as Danfoss advises, or reset it to factory settings and reconfigure it before returning it to service, a reset alone not sufficing if the unit stays exposed or unpatched. Danfoss fixed the flaws in the supported AK-SM 800A at firmware 4.2 and 4.3.1, installed by hand, and Sabcobel’s account of the second wave in Belgium is the evidence that patching after the first reduced the harm.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Retire or Isolate Unsupported Units

annex.p: Danfoss declared the AK-SC 355 end of life in 2016 and the AK-SM 800 in 2021, and has long advised migration; the alert states that keeping an unpatched end-of-life device exposed carries a very high probability of compromise. This step adds the instrument’s own, from F-5: replace or isolate each such unit, and set the date by which it is done.

annex.h3: A.3.4 Put a Limit on the Heat the Controller Cannot Override

annex.p: No authority has yet published this action; it is this instrument’s, from F-2 and F-4. Fit a thermostat or high-temperature cutout on the case or cold room itself, acting on its own measurement, that ends heating and raises an alarm whatever the supervisory controller commands. It bounds both the spoiled stock and the fire.

annex.h3: A.3.5 Report and Coordinate

annex.p: The alert asks that compromises be reported to the national computer emergency response team. Sweden’s national cybersecurity center is responding to incidents, and British retailers are working with the National Cyber Security Centre to secure their refrigeration. This instrument adds no step of its own here.

annex.h3: A.3.6 List What Talks to the Outside, Then Look as an Attacker Would

annex.p: List first, then look. The inventory comes first because exposed equipment often sits outside your own address space: the units on this record were reached at public addresses, and some sat behind a contractor’s link or on a 4G mobile link, so a store’s own address space may not hold them. Then look at each address on the list as an attacker would, by any of three routes, each its provider’s. Shodan and Censys each offer a search of the devices they have found answering on the internet, and a search limited to your own address blocks and the addresses on your list shows you what it would show anyone. In the United States, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency offers Cyber Hygiene Vulnerability Scanning, which scans the internet-facing assets an organization names and reports weekly, at no cost to governments and critical infrastructure organizations (cisa.gov, Cyber Hygiene Services). Your integrator and vendors can tell you what they can reach remotely, if you ask them. Whatever the look finds that is not on your list goes on it, and whatever need not talk to the outside should stop. The inventory and the look are a standing item in every annex whose event turned on equipment reachable from the internet, on the author’s direction of 15 November 2026; here they rest on elements A-1 and A-2 and F-1.

On the night of 11 October 2026, refrigerated cases and freezers in about 700 French supermarkets, of every chain, were set into defrost through their remotely managed controllers, and temperatures rose to as much as 50°C within hours. On the night of 1 November it happened again in several more countries. The controllers, of several makes and many past their manufacturers’ support, were reachable from the internet, directly, through contractors, or over cellular links on the units. Stock was discarded, equipment damaged, and in some French stores the heaters started fires that the sprinklers answered; where alarms sounded, the food was already spoiled. No shortage and no illness were reported. No government has attributed the attacks to a state; the European Union called the second wave a deliberate attempt to disrupt the food supply chain, which is its statement of intent, not an attribution. The lessons are that stores sharing one make of controller or one contractor share one exposure, that every path to a controller must be closed, and that a limit on the heat must act on the case itself whatever the controller commands. Any operator of remotely managed building equipment has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this operation does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Ammonia Release at Millard Refrigerated Services, August 2010
date_full: 23 August 2010, read to the settlement of 2 June 2015 (record closed)
what: On 22 August 2010 a cold-storage terminal near Mobile, Alabama, lost power for more than seven hours. During the restart an operator cleared an alarm, which interrupted a blast freezer's defrost, and a programming error let four coils grouped to one valve set go straight back to refrigeration full of hot gas. On the morning of 23 August the hydraulic shock ruptured a 12-inch suction pipe on the roof and released about 32,000 pounds of anhydrous ammonia. The cloud crossed a canal to contractors working on the Deepwater Horizon response; about 150 people reported exposure, 32 were hospitalized and four placed in intensive care. The emergency shutdown was not used, and the release ran about four hours.
tier: Not an attack: a latent control-logic error opened by an ordinary command during recovery from a power outage. None of the four characteristics is present.

findings.title: The shutdown was available and not ordered.
findings.text: Name in advance who orders the emergency shutdown and on what detected release.

findings.title: A local command took tested logic outside what was tested.
findings.text: The determinism showing must cover every command the controller accepts, local resets and overrides included.

findings.title: The release was set by what one command could release.
findings.text: Postulate the release at the largest inventory one valve set or command can bring into play.

findings.title: Erratum: the earlier releases.
findings.text: The agency attributes the 2007 release to hydraulic shock and identifies no root cause for January 2010.

annex.p: This annex is for the owners and operators of cold-storage warehouses and other facilities with ammonia refrigeration, for the contractors who program and service their controls, and for the emergency planners of the communities around them. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to a facility. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions a facility answers about its own plant (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account a facility can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one facility. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the facility; it is that facility’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Has your defrost and restart logic been tested, as installed, for a restart after a long outage and for a defrost interrupted by hand?
The transition that ruptured Millard’s piping may be in your logic too. A.3.1, A.3.2.
Who can change your refrigeration controls or clear an alarm that interrupts a defrost, and is that access restricted and recorded?
Anyone at the panel can open the transition. A.3.2.
How many evaporator coils share one set of control valves, and how much hot gas can one valve opening release?
Your worst release may be several times what you planned for. A.3.1, A.3.2.
Is it written down who presses the emergency shutdown, and on what sign of a release, before anyone goes to isolate it?
The shutdown may wait while the release grows. A.3.1, A.3.2.
Do your neighbors, and the people working next door, know your release would reach them and what to do?
The people most exposed at Millard were not Millard’s. A.3.1.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Lessons and Requirements Already Published

annex.p: The Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board’s bulletin gives five lessons: avoid grouping several large evaporators to one set of control valves; program the defrost sequence to depressurize or bleed the coil automatically on restart; avoid interrupting evaporators by hand while in defrost; run pump-out long enough to remove all liquid from the coils; and use the emergency shutdown to de-energize pumps, compressors, and valves in a release. The Environmental Protection Agency’s settlement records the Clean Air Act’s general duty to identify the hazard of hydraulic shock and design against it, and the risk-management program rule for plants above its threshold. Each is its publisher’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Name the Shutdown, Lock the Logic, and Count the Largest Release

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1 to F-3. Write down who orders the emergency shutdown and on what detected release, so that it is pressed before anyone climbs to the roof. Test the defrost and restart logic for every command the controller accepts, an alarm reset and a manual override included, in every state it can be in after an outage, and restrict and record who can change it, at the panel as well as remotely. And size your release planning to the most hot gas and liquid that one valve set or one command can put into a line at once.

On the morning of 23 August 2010, the refrigeration plant of a cold-storage terminal near Mobile, Alabama, ruptured and released about 32,000 pounds of ammonia. The plant had lost power for more than seven hours the day before. During the restart, an operator cleared an alarm, which interrupted the defrost of a blast freezer, and a programming error in the control system let the freezer’s coils go straight back to cooling while still full of hot gas. The shock that followed broke a large pipe on the roof. The cloud drifted across a canal to where contractors were working on the Gulf oil spill; about 150 people reported being exposed and 32 were hospitalized. The plant’s emergency shutdown was not used while staff tried to close valves by hand, and the release ran for about four hours. The lessons are that control logic is only as safe as the situations it has been tested in, a restart after an outage above all; that pressing the shutdown must be a decision made in advance, not in the cloud; and that how a plant is piped decides how bad its worst day is. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own plant, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Cyberattack on United Natural Foods, June 2025
date_full: 5 June to 16 July 2025 (record closed as to the disruption)
what: On 5 June 2025, United Natural Foods, a wholesaler supplying about 30,000 grocery locations and the primary distributor to Whole Foods, found unauthorized activity on its systems and took systems offline to contain it. Ordering and distribution stopped and customers' shelves emptied. Core ordering was restored in about ten days, and operations were reported normal by mid-July, with $350 to $400 million in lost sales. No food was made unsafe; the attacker and method are undisclosed.
tier: A deliberate intrusion attributed to no one; not placed at the military-action tier: persistence and precision are not established and denial is absent.

findings.title: The Containment Decision Was the Supply Consequence.
findings.text: The decision to take a distributor's systems offline is prepared in advance.

annex.p: This annex is for grocery wholesalers and distributors, the retailers and institutions that depend on one of them for most of what they sell or serve, and the authorities who plan for a region’s food supply. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to a distributor or its customer. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an organization answers about its own supply (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an organization can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one organization. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the organization; it is that organization’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
If you had to take your ordering and warehouse systems offline tonight, is it written down who decides, on what sign, and what each of your largest customers would be told?
The decision will be made in the hour, and your customers will learn from their shelves. A.3.2.
Can you receive, pick, and dispatch for a stated period without your systems, and have you exercised it?
Your workarounds will be invented during the outage. A.3.1.
If you are a store, hospital, or institution, what would supply you if your main distributor stopped for two weeks?
Your substitution is someone else’s spare capacity, not yet arranged. A.3.1.
Can you restore from systems and backups the intruder could not reach?
You may restore the intrusion. A.3.1.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The company’s report of 9 June 2025 records that it activated its incident response plan and implemented workarounds under its business continuity plans. The class’s requirements (§4.5, §4.6, §5.6) state a manual mode exercised in advance, records that survive the loss of the systems, restoration from beyond the attack’s reach, and a first-band customer’s substitution stated before the event. Each is its author’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Decide in Advance Who Takes the Systems Down, and Tell Your Customers

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1. Write down who may take your ordering and warehouse systems offline, on what signs, what it costs each of your largest customers, and how and when they are told and supplied, so that the decision that protects your systems does not leave your customers to find out from their shelves.

On 5 June 2025, United Natural Foods, a wholesaler supplying about 30,000 grocery stores in the United States and Canada and the main distributor to Whole Foods, found intruders in its computer systems and took systems offline to contain them. Its ability to take and deliver orders stopped, and shelves emptied at stores across its customer base. No food was made unsafe. The company restored its core ordering within about ten days and said operations were back to normal by mid-July, estimating the loss at $350 to $400 million in sales. It has not said who attacked it or how. The lesson is that taking a distributor’s systems offline is itself the event’s biggest consequence, so the decision of who takes it, on what sign, and how customers are told and supplied, should be prepared before it is needed. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own supply, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza in Poultry and Dairy Cattle, 2022 Onward
date_full: February 2022 onward, read to April 2025 (record open)
what: H5N1 carried by wild birds reached commercial poultry in February 2022 and has been confirmed in every state; by April 2025 about 169 million birds had been lost, three-quarters of them layers, and reinfected premises had drawn a third of the indemnity. From March 2024 it was found in dairy cattle, first as an unexplained drop in milk; national milk testing began in December 2024. Seventy people, most of them farm workers, were infected by April 2025, and one died.
tier: Not an attack: a disease carried by wild birds. None of the four characteristics is present.

findings.title: The New Host Was Under National Surveillance Eight Months After the First Confirmation.
findings.text: A new host is put under surveillance within a stated time.

findings.title: The People Who Worked With the Animals Were Infected.
findings.text: The people who work with infected animals are protected as part of the response.

annex.p: This annex is for poultry and dairy producers, the veterinarians and state animal-health officials who serve them, and the public-health officials who look after the people who work with animals. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to an operation. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operation answers about its own operation (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operation can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operation; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Is the biosecurity of your operation stated for every path by which a disease can enter wild birds, people, vehicles, and equipment, and audited?
The disease will find the path you have not closed. A.3.1.
If your animals showed an unexplained illness or drop in production, who would you call, and how fast?
A new host is found by the farmer who reports it first. A.3.1.
If your premises were depopulated, what failure would you correct before restocking, and who would confirm it?
You may restock into the same exposure. A.3.1.
Do the people who handle your animals, and who would cull them, have protection and a way to be tested if they fall ill?
The disease may reach your workers before anyone looks. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service conditions indemnity, from December 2024, on a passing biosecurity audit before a previously infected premises, or one in the buffer zone around it, is restocked, and publishes biosecurity guidance for poultry and dairy operations. The Department of Agriculture’s federal orders require testing before the interstate movement of lactating dairy cattle and national testing of raw milk. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention publish guidance on protecting and monitoring people who work with infected animals. Each is its publisher’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Report the Unexplained, and Protect the People Who Handle the Animals

annex.p: These steps are from this instrument, F-1 and F-2. Report any unexplained illness or drop in production in your animals at once, whatever the species, because a new host is found by the first person who reports it. And make sure the people who work with your animals, and those who would cull them, have protection and a way to be tested and treated.

Since February 2022, a highly contagious strain of bird flu, carried by wild birds, has spread through United States poultry, costing about 169 million birds by April 2025, most of them egg-laying hens, and more than a billion dollars in federal response and indemnity. Some farms were infected more than once, and since December 2024 indemnity has depended on passing a biosecurity audit before restocking. In March 2024, the virus was found in dairy cattle, first noticed as an unexplained drop in milk; national testing of milk began in December. Seventy people, most of them farm workers, were infected by April 2025, and one person died. The lessons are that a farm’s biosecurity must close every path of entry, that an unexplained illness in any animal must be reported at once, and that the people who handle sick animals are part of what the response must protect. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own operation, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Contamination of Michigan Livestock Feed With PBB, 1973 and 1974
date_full: 1973 to 1974 (record closed as to the contamination, open as to its human consequence)
what: In 1973, a Michigan plant shipped bags of a PBB flame retardant in place of a look-alike feed supplement. Mixed into feed and sent across the state, it reached cattle and other livestock and their milk, meat, and eggs. The animals were tested for infections, and PBB was identified about nine months later by a farmer's own testing. Over 500 farms were quarantined and many thousands of animals destroyed, but contaminated products had been sold statewide, and the federal action level was lowered a year on. Exposed residents and their children are still followed.
tier: Not an attack: a substitution of bags. None of the four characteristics is present.

findings.title: The Signs Were Taken for Disease for Most of a Year.
findings.text: An unexplained sign leads, within a stated time, to the testing of the inputs.

findings.title: The Threshold That Decided What Was Held Moved After the Product Was Sold.
findings.text: Products of a persistent contaminant are held until tested, against lifetime exposure.

annex.p: This annex is for feed mills and other suppliers of agricultural inputs, the farms and ranches that use them, and the state and federal authorities for animal health and food safety. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to an operation. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operation answers about its own operation (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operation can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operation; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Do you check what you receive by testing the property of an input, or only by its label and paperwork?
Two products in the same bag look the same. A.3.1.
Could you tell, from your records, every farm that received a given batch of your feed or input within hours?
A contaminated batch will be found farm by farm. A.3.1.
If your animals show a sign the first tests do not explain, whom do you ask to test their feed for chemicals, and how fast?
The sign may be taken for disease for most of a year. A.3.2.
If an input you used were found contaminated with a persistent chemical, would your products be held until tested, whatever the current action level?
What you sell below a provisional level may be carried for a generation. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The class’s requirements (§4.2, §4.3, §4.4) state receiving checks that test the property and not the label, traceability from batch to operation, detection on the first unexplained sign, and the hold of products from every operation reached. The Food and Drug Administration’s rules on current good manufacturing practice and hazard analysis for animal food, under the Food Safety Modernization Act, set requirements for feed mills. Each is its author’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Test the Feed When the Sign Is Unexplained, and Hold What It Reached

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1 and F-2. If your animals show a sign the first tests do not explain, have their feed and inputs tested for chemicals within a set time, and ask the authority to do it. And if an input you used is found contaminated with a chemical that persists, hold your products until they are tested, whatever the action level of the day.

In 1973, a Michigan chemical plant that made both a flame retardant and a cattle-feed supplement shipped bags of the retardant, PBB, in place of the supplement because it had run short of printed bags; the two looked alike. The retardant was mixed into feed and sent to farms across the state. Cattle sickened and milk production fell, but the animals were tested for infections, and it was nine months before a farmer trained as a chemist had the feed analyzed, and PBB was found. More than 500 farms were quarantined and many thousands of animals destroyed, but by then contaminated milk, meat, and eggs had been sold across Michigan, and researchers estimate most of the state’s people were exposed. PBB stays in the body for decades and passes to children, and a registry still follows the exposed families. The lessons are that a label is not a test, that a sickness the first tests do not explain should lead quickly to testing the feed, and that products of a contaminated input should be held until tested. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own operation, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Salmonella Saintpaul Outbreak and the Tomato Warning, 2008
what: An uncommon strain of Salmonella Saintpaul was reported from New Mexico on 22 May 2008. Interviews associated illness with raw tomatoes, and on 7 June the Food and Drug Administration warned the nation against certain raw tomatoes. The trace did not reach a source and illness continued. Restaurant cluster studies from late June pointed to raw jalapeño peppers, and the strain was found on peppers from Mexico in July. The tomato warning was lifted on 17 July after about 1,220 illnesses; in all 1,442 people were reported ill and at least 286 hospitalized.
tier: Not an attack: contamination not shown to be deliberate. None of the four characteristics is present.

findings.title: The Advisory Did Not Say What Would Show It Wrong.
findings.text: An advisory says when issued what would show it wrong, and is reviewed when that happens.

findings.title: The Path From Those Who Find Illness to Those Who Act Was Not Measured.
findings.text: The path from those who find illness to those who act is a parameter, sized and timed.

annex.p: This annex is for growers, packers, distributors, and retailers of fresh produce, and the public-health and food-safety agencies that investigate outbreaks and issue advisories. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to an organization. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an organization answers about its own operation (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an organization can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one organization. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the organization; it is that organization’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
If your product were named in a warning tomorrow, could you show within hours where each lot came from and went?
The trace will stop at you, and the warning will stand. A.3.1.
If you issue or advise on a warning, have you said what result would show it was aimed at the wrong food?
The warning will stand while illness continues. A.3.2.
When illness keeps occurring after a named food is off the shelves, who in your agency or company raises it, and to whom?
The evidence against the warning may sit in the counts. A.3.2.
Do the people who find illness and the people who act on it share data on a path whose speed is known?
The cluster that points to the true source may arrive late. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The Food and Drug Administration’s rule on additional traceability records for listed foods, under section 204 of the Food Safety Modernization Act, will require records of where listed foods came from and went; Congress has barred its enforcement before 20 July 2028. The agencies’ report of 29 August 2008 describes how the outbreak was traced. Each is its publisher’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Say What Would Prove the Warning Wrong, and Measure the Path

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1 and F-2. When a warning is issued on an association, write down with it the result that would show it was aimed at the wrong food, and review it the moment that result appears. And know how illness data move from those who find it to those who act, and how long that takes.

In May 2008, health officials in New Mexico found an unusual strain of Salmonella. Sick people interviewed often named raw tomatoes, and on 7 June the Food and Drug Administration warned the nation against certain raw tomatoes. Tracing the tomatoes back through packers and distributors did not find a source, and people kept getting sick. At the end of June, a state investigation of a restaurant cluster found illness linked to salsa with canned tomatoes and raw jalapeño peppers, and in July the strain was found on peppers from Mexico. The tomato warning was lifted on 17 July. In all, 1,442 people were reported ill and at least 286 hospitalized. The agencies concluded that peppers were a major source and tomatoes possibly a source early on. The lessons are that a warning should say, when it is issued, what would show it was aimed at the wrong food, and that the speed with which data move between agencies decides how long a wrong warning stands.
