The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own operation, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Denial of Large Transformer Replacement in Ukraine, 2022 Onward
what: From October 2022 Ukraine's power system was struck in repeated waves, in a campaign the International Criminal Court's warrants cover and that the court, Ukraine, and its partners attribute to the Russian armed forces, with large autotransformers named as key targets. By January 2023 the transmission operator said it needed fifty-nine; each can take up to two years to buy and deliver, and Europe's largest transformer plant, in Zaporizhzhia, had closed. Substations were struck again and again, and later strikes fell on the crews restoring them. The first donor-funded replacements arrived in October 2023.
tier: Military action by a state's armed forces against the installed transformers and their replacement path together, sustained for years.

findings.title: Repair capacity is part of the replacement path.
findings.text: More than half of the damaged units were struck repeatedly, which blocked their repair.

findings.title: The emergency order path includes the buyer and the funds.
findings.text: The first replacements came through a United Nations agency acting as buyer with donor funds.

findings.title: Each replacement should leave the adversary less to take.
findings.text: Replacements put back where the originals stood were struck again; each should move the grid toward a topology nearer the loads, toward microgrids, and over more corridors at voltage classes whose transformers are easier to source.

annex.p: This annex is for electric utilities and transmission operators that depend on large power transformers, for the manufacturers and repair shops that build and mend them, and for the governments and agencies that would buy them in an emergency. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
If your domestic transformer source were closed or struck, how many qualified sources would remain, and where are they?
Your replacement path ends with one plant. A.3.1.
Have you planned for a campaign that strikes the installed transformer and its replacement together?
Spares are lost with the units they were meant to replace. A.3.2.
Do you know how many large transformers you would need after a campaign, and how many reserve units you hold?
The count of what is needed outruns the reserve. A.3.2.
Is repair capacity, including crews, shops, and the ability to repair a unit struck more than once, part of your replacement plan?
Damaged units wait for repair that cannot be done. A.3.1.
Do you know how long it takes to buy, build, and deliver a large transformer, and who would buy one in an emergency and with what funds?
Replacement takes years because no one can place the order. A.3.1.
Are some reserve units held beyond the reach of an attack on your territory?
The reserve is destroyed where it is stored. A.3.2.
Does your restoration plan assume that crews and replacement units can work at a struck site without being struck again?
The restoration becomes the next target. A.3.3.

If a large transformer at one of your substations were destroyed, would you replace it only where it stood and at the same voltage, or also consider a site nearer the loads or a voltage class with more units available?
Each replacement restores the target the adversary already knows. A.3.3.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Plan Repair and the Emergency Order

annex.p: No authority has published an action for owners that this instrument reads. These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1 and F-2: make repair capacity part of the replacement path; and arrange in advance who buys a large transformer in an emergency and with what funds, as the United Nations Development Programme did for Ukraine’s transmission operator with funds from Japan.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Hold a Reserve Beyond the Campaign’s Reach

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, drawn from the facility class’s governing scenario as the event characterizes it. Count the transformers a campaign could take and the reserve that would answer it; and hold part of the reserve beyond the campaign’s reach, as Ukraine’s foreign-built units were to be held in Poland and Romania until needed.

annex.h3: A.3.3 Protect the Restoration and Place the Replacement

annex.p: Ukraine’s Ministry of Energy has withdrawn repair crews for a time where the risk of repeated attacks made the work unsafe, as it stated on 8 November 2025, and the practices Ukraine’s State Emergency Service adopted against second strikes on its rescuers are recorded in Repeat Strikes on Rescue Crews in Ukraine. UA Grid Defense: Cyber-Kinetic (Eclectic Technologies) recommends that each replacement be placed as close to the critical loads as transmission permits, along load paths put in priority in advance, and planned to reduce the megawatts lost per weapon. Each is its publisher’s. The remaining steps are this instrument’s, from F-1 and F-3: plan restoration on the assumption that the crew and the unit may be struck again, and protect them before crediting them; and decide, before a loss, where and at what specification each critical transformer would be replaced, so that its replacement can leave the adversary less to take.

From October 2022 Ukraine’s power system was struck in repeated waves, in a campaign the International Criminal Court’s warrants cover and that the court, Ukraine, and its partners attribute to the Russian armed forces. Large autotransformers were named as key targets. By January 2023 the transmission operator said it needed fifty-nine of them; each costs about $2 million, weighs hundreds of tons, and can take up to two years to buy and deliver. Europe’s largest transformer plant, in Zaporizhzhia, had closed in March 2022, and later attacks on Ukrainian factories slowed domestic production. More than half of the damaged units were struck more than once, which blocked their repair, and later strikes fell on the crews sent to repair them. The first new autotransformers bought with donor funds arrived in October 2023, through a United Nations agency acting as buyer. The lessons are that repair capacity is part of the replacement path, that someone must be ready to buy in an emergency, that a reserve must be held beyond the reach of the attack, and that a replacement put back where the original stood is put back where the attacker already knows to strike. Any utility that depends on large transformers has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this utility does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Shortage of Transformers in the United States, 2021 Onward
what: Since 2021 average transformer lead times in the United States have risen from about 50 weeks to about 120, and large units to as much as four years, as new loads, an aging fleet, and constrained manufacturing outran supply. Imports supply about 80 percent of power transformers. The National Infrastructure Advisory Council recommended in 2024 support for domestic capacity, a virtual reserve, and standardized designs.
tier: Not an attack: demand outran supply over a condition of years.

findings.title: The national queue is measured by someone with a duty to watch it.
findings.text: Every lead-time figure read came from analysts and an advisory council, not from a body charged to watch.

findings.title: The source count is stated with its trade exposure.
findings.text: Imports supply about 80 percent of power transformers, and tariffs raised their cost.

annex.p: This annex is for electric utilities, developers, and large industrial customers that buy power and distribution transformers, for the manufacturers that make them, and for the agencies that watch the national supply. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Do you know the current lead time for each transformer type you depend on, and does anyone with a duty to watch the national queue measure it?
You learn the lead time when you place an order you need now. A.3.1.
How many of your transformers come from abroad, and what would tariffs or a trade decision do to their cost and supply?
A trade decision lengthens your queue. A.3.2.
Could you take a standardized design rather than a custom one, to shorten the wait?
Every unit is built to order and waits in line. A.3.1.
Do you hold, or share in, a reserve of spare units for your most critical substations?
A single failure waits years for a replacement. A.3.1.
Have you forecast your own demand from new load, renewables, and the aging of your fleet?
Demand you did not forecast joins the queue ahead of you. A.3.1.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Watch the Queue, Standardize, and Share a Reserve

annex.p: The National Infrastructure Advisory Council recommended in June 2024 federal support for domestic capacity, a strategic virtual reserve of transformers with the government as buyer of last resort, and standardization of designs. These steps add the instrument’s own, from F-1: track the lead time of each type you depend on, forecast your own demand, and take part in a shared reserve or standard design where you can.

annex.h3: A.3.2 State Your Source Count With Its Trade Exposure

annex.p: This step is this instrument’s, from F-2. Know how many qualified sources you have for each type and how many lie abroad, and what tariffs or trade decisions would do to them.

Since 2021 the United States has been short of transformers. Average lead times rose from about 50 weeks in 2021 to about 120 weeks in 2024, and large units ran up to four years. The National Infrastructure Advisory Council reported in June 2024 that the causes include supply-chain disruption, an aging fleet whose average large power transformer is about 38 years old, new loads such as data centers, and an industry that holds capacity back through its cycles, with little standardization of designs. Imports supply about 80 percent of power transformers, and an analyst projected a 30 percent shortfall for 2025, with constraints into the 2030s. The Council recommended federal support for domestic manufacturing, a virtual reserve with the government as buyer of last resort, and standardized designs. No one attacked anything; demand simply outran supply. The lessons are that someone must watch the national queue, that the dependence on imports must be stated, and that a utility must plan for waits of years. Any utility or large customer that needs transformers has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this organization does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Cyberattack on a German Steel Mill, Reported 2014
what: In December 2014 Germany's Federal Office for Information Security reported that attackers had reached a steel mill's office network through spear-phishing and moved step by step into its production networks. Control components and then whole systems failed more and more often, a blast furnace could not be shut down in a controlled way, and the plant suffered massive damage. No government has attributed the attack.
tier: A deliberate cyberattack, not placed at the military-action tier: the actor is unidentified, and precision and denial are not established on the record.

findings.title: Unexplained control failures are treated as a possible attack.
findings.text: Control failures multiplied before the furnace could not be shut down.

findings.title: What the plant knows about its process is protected like the process.
findings.text: The attackers had extensive knowledge of the plant's control systems and process.

annex.p: This annex is for steel mills and other heavy manufacturers whose process control systems run furnaces, presses, and other equipment that takes long to repair or replace. It is also for any owner whose business network connects to its production network. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the framework; this annex is addressed to an operator. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions an operator answers about the operator’s own system (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account an operator can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one operation. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the operator; it is that operation’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Could a phishing message to a member of your staff give an attacker a way from your office network toward your production network?
One email starts the path to the plant. A.3.1.
Is every connection between your business and production networks controlled and monitored?
The attacker moves step by step without being seen. A.3.1.
When control components begin failing without explanation, do you consider an attack before you assume a fault?
Failures multiply while you treat them as maintenance. A.3.2.
Can your furnaces and other heavy equipment be brought to a safe stop by means an attacker in the control network cannot reach?
The equipment cannot be shut down when it must be. A.3.2.
Do you protect your knowledge of your own process and control systems as carefully as the systems themselves?
The attacker learns your process from your own documents. A.3.1.
Do you know how long it would take to repair or replace your heaviest equipment?
Damage that takes minutes to cause takes months to undo. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Guard the Path, and the Knowledge

annex.p: The Federal Office for Information Security reported the event in December 2014; no action for owners from it is read here. These steps are this instrument’s, from F-2: control and monitor every path from the business network into production, and protect what the plant knows about its process and control systems as the process itself is protected.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Treat Unexplained Failures as a Possible Attack, and Keep a Safe Stop Out of Reach

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1. Treat control failures that multiply without explanation as a possible attack; give heavy equipment a safe shutdown independent of systems an attacker could reach; and know the time to restore it.

In December 2014 Germany’s Federal Office for Information Security reported that attackers had reached the control systems of a steel mill in Germany. They gained access to the plant’s office network through spear-phishing and social engineering aimed at its staff, and worked their way step by step into the production networks. Control components and then whole systems began to fail more and more often, a blast furnace could not be shut down in a controlled way, and the plant suffered massive damage. The Office described the attackers as highly skilled, with deep knowledge of industrial control systems and of the production process. No government has attributed the attack, and the Office’s account is brief; this instrument does not extend it. The lessons are that every path from the office into the plant must be controlled, that unexplained failures may be an attack, and that heavy equipment needs a way to stop safely that an attacker cannot reach. Any plant whose business network touches its production network has the same exposure. The questions in this annex show management whether this plant does, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Ransomware Attack on Norsk Hydro, March 2019
what: LockerGoga ransomware spread across Norsk Hydro's information-technology systems from the evening of 18 March 2019, affecting operations in about forty countries. Smelters in Norway went largely to manual operation and several extrusion and rolled-products plants shut. The company did not pay, restored from backups, and put the 2019 impact at 650 to 750 million kroner, mainly lost sales from reduced production and impaired order handling.
tier: Criminal, below the tier: intentionality and denial established, persistence not established, precision not determined.

findings.title: The Plants Could Run but Not Ship.
findings.text: A plant that can still make can still deliver.

annex.p: This annex is for producers of metals and materials with plants on a shared enterprise network, their customers, and those who oversee them. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to a producer. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions a producer answers about its own plants (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account a producer can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one producer. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the producer; it is that producer’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Can each plant’s network be cut off from the enterprise and from the other plants in minutes?
One intrusion may reach every plant at once. A.3.1.
How long can each plant’s process be held or run by hand?
A process may be lost when its systems are. A.3.1.
Could you take, schedule, and ship customers’ orders by hand, or from systems an intrusion could not reach, for that same time?
Plants that can run may still deliver nothing. A.3.2.
Are the backups and systems you would restore from held where an intrusion cannot reach them, and have you restored from them?
You may have nothing clean to restore from. A.3.1.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The company’s own published account of its response is widely cited as practice. National guidance on ransomware and on the separation of operational technology from enterprise networks sets out related practice. The class’s requirements (§4.4, §5.5) state manual operation for a stated time, plant networks isolable from the enterprise and each other, and systems for restoration held beyond an intrusion’s reach. Each is its author’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Keep the Order Book Running Too

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1. Make sure you can receive, schedule, and ship your customers’ orders by hand, or from systems an intrusion into your enterprise could not reach, for as long as your plants can run by hand.

On the evening of 18 March 2019, ransomware spread through the computer systems of Norsk Hydro, one of the world’s largest aluminum producers, reaching its operations in about forty countries. The company switched its smelters to manual control and shut or slowed many of the plants that turn aluminum into parts for cars and buildings. It did not pay the ransom and rebuilt its systems from backups, and the attack cost it 650 to 750 million Norwegian kroner, mostly in lost sales because it could not produce or handle orders normally. The lessons are that a producer’s plants must be able to run without its office systems, and that it must also be able to take and ship orders when those systems are down. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own plants, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Loss of the Mariupol Steelworks, 2022
date_full: February to May 2022, read to August 2022 (record open)
what: At the outbreak of the full-scale invasion in February 2022, the Azovstal and Ilyich works in Mariupol, about two-fifths of Ukraine's crude steel and all of its slab exports, were put into hot conservation and stopped. The city was besieged; Azovstal became the defenders' last stronghold and was largely destroyed, and both works came under occupation by May. The owner said they would never operate under occupation, and by August one was reported cut for scrap.
tier: An event in an armed conflict, not placed at the military-action tier on this reading: persistence and denial are present and precision is supportable, but intentionality in the class's form is not established, as the author confirmed on 19 November 2026.

findings.title: The Plants Were Conserved in Hours, on a Decision No One Had Stated in Advance.
findings.text: The conservation of a plant under threat is decided in advance.

annex.p: This annex is for producers of steel and other primary materials, the governments that plan for their supply in a crisis, and the manufacturers and grid operators who depend on them. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to a producer. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions a producer answers about its own plants (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account a producer can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one producer. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the producer; it is that producer’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
If a plant of yours fell within reach of a campaign, is it written down who orders its conservation, on what sign, and what state it is left in?
The decision will be composed in the hours you have. A.3.2.
How much of your country’s output of your material comes from plants within reach of a single campaign or a single city?
The loss may be the nation’s, not only yours. A.3.1.
Do your customers abroad know how they would be supplied if your plants were lost at once?
Their mills stop with yours. A.3.1.
How long would it take to restart each plant from conservation, and what would it need that a campaign could take?
A plant conserved may not be a plant restarted. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The class’s requirements (§4.2, §4.3, §6.3) state that plants within a campaign’s reach are counted as absent in a material’s source concentration, that stock is held beyond that reach and sized for a campaign, and that the energy of surviving plants is stated. Governments’ and industry bodies’ supply-security planning for primary materials sets out practices to the same end. Each is its author’s. No step of this instrument’s is added here.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Decide the Conservation Before the Campaign

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1. For each plant that could fall within reach of a campaign, write down who orders its conservation, on what sign, the state it is left in, and the time and inputs it needs to restart.

When Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022, the owner of Mariupol’s two great steelworks, which together made about two-fifths of Ukraine’s crude steel, put them into a protective shutdown to save their equipment. The city was besieged; one works, Azovstal, became the defenders’ last stronghold and was largely destroyed, and both came under occupation in May. Ukraine lost about two-fifths of its steelmaking in weeks, and mills abroad that relied on the works’ steel slab lost their supply. The owner said its plants would never operate under occupation, and later reports said one was being cut up for scrap. The lesson for a producer is that a plant within reach of a war should have its shutdown decided and planned in advance, and that a nation’s supply of a basic material should not depend on works that one campaign can take. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own plants, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Fire at the Renesas Naka Plant, March 2021
what: A fire in plating equipment in the N3 building, which houses the Naka plant's 300-millimeter line, damaged twenty-three units of equipment. Production restarted on 17 April at under ten percent, reached about 88 percent at the end of May after the last replacement tool arrived, and returned to its pre-fire level on 24 June, during a worldwide shortage of the automotive microcontrollers the line makes.
tier: Not an attack: an accidental fire. None of the four characteristics is present.

findings.title: The Last Tool Set the Recovery.
findings.text: The line comes back within what its customers can wait.

annex.p: This annex is for semiconductor and electronics manufacturers, the automotive and industrial firms that buy their chips, and those who oversee supply-chain resilience. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to a fab. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions a manufacturer answers about its own lines (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account a manufacturer can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one manufacturer. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the manufacturer; it is that manufacturer’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
How long would your line take to restart after a fire in one tool, and is that time stated?
Your customers may not know how long to plan for. A.3.1.
Is your cleanroom protected against the smoke and water from a fire in one tool?
One tool’s fire may take the whole line. A.3.1.
How long would your critical replacement tools take to arrive during a sector-wide shortage, not in ordinary times?
Recovery may wait for tools the whole industry wants. A.3.2.
Can your output be moved to another qualified line within the time your customers’ inventory covers?
Your customers’ lines may stop before yours restarts. A.3.1.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The company’s announcements set out its recovery. Industry guidance on semiconductor business continuity and on cleanroom fire protection sets out related practice. The class’s requirements (§4.2, §5.1) state the fab restart time, cleanroom protection, critical tool lead times, and qualified alternative production. Each is its author’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Count the Tool Lead Time in a Shortage

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1. Find out how long your critical tools would take to replace during an industry-wide shortage, and where that is longer than your customers can wait, hold spares or reserve them with the tool makers.

On 19 March 2021, a fire broke out in a piece of plating equipment at Renesas’s Naka plant in Japan, on the production line that makes many of the microcontroller chips used in cars. Twenty-three machines were damaged. Production restarted a month later at under ten percent and did not return to normal until late June, largely because replacement machines took time to arrive. The fire came during a worldwide chip shortage, so carmakers already short of chips lost more. The lessons are that a single small fire can stop a critical production line for months, and that recovery plans must assume replacement equipment will be hardest to get exactly when it is needed most. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own lines, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Attack on a Toyota Supplier, February 2022
what: Kojima Industries, a supplier of plastic and electronic parts to Toyota, found an error on a file server on 26 February 2022 and later confirmed ransomware. Toyota announced that, owing to the supplier's system failure, it would suspend 28 lines at its 14 plants in Japan on 1 March, reported to cost about 13,000 vehicles; affiliates' plants also stopped. Production resumed on 2 March.
tier: Criminal, below the tier: intentionality and denial established, persistence not established, precision not determined.

findings.title: The Parts Were There; the Orders Were Not.
findings.text: A supplier's systems lost is not its parts lost.

annex.p: This annex is for manufacturers that run just-in-time lines, their critical suppliers, and those who oversee manufacturing resilience. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to a manufacturer. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions a manufacturer answers about its own lines (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account a manufacturer can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one manufacturer. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the manufacturer; it is that manufacturer’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
Which suppliers would stop your lines within a day if their systems went down?
You may not know which supplier stops you. A.3.1.
How long can each line run on the stock it holds of each such supplier’s parts?
The line may stop before the supplier recovers. A.3.1.
If a critical supplier’s systems were down tomorrow, how would orders and deliveries pass between you?
Parts may sit at the supplier with no way to order them. A.3.2.
Have you and that supplier exercised that path?
The path may fail when first used. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The companies’ announcements set out what happened. National guidance on ransomware and on supply-chain risk management for manufacturers sets out related practice. The class’s requirements (§4.3, §5.5) state the critical supplier known to the owner, the time the line can run without it, the supplier’s continuity of ordering and shipping, and inventory coverage. Each is its author’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Agree How You Will Order When the Systems Are Down

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1. With each supplier whose loss would stop your lines, agree a way to pass orders and delivery schedules that does not rely on either company’s business systems, and practice it.

In late February 2022, Kojima Industries, a Japanese supplier of plastic and electronic parts to Toyota, was hit by ransomware. Because Toyota’s factories hold very little stock and their orders to the supplier ran through its computer systems, Toyota stopped all 28 production lines at its 14 plants in Japan for a day, losing about 13,000 vehicles. Production resumed the next day. The lessons are that one supplier’s computer problem can stop a whole manufacturer, and that a company and its critical suppliers need an agreed way to keep orders and deliveries moving when their computers are down. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own lines, and most of the answers cost little to find.

title: The Nexperia Measures, 2025
date_full: 29 September to 19 November 2025, read to November 2026 (record open)
what: After the United States extended its Entity List to majority-owned affiliates on 29 September 2025, the Dutch minister invoked the Goods Availability Act over Nexperia on 30 September, announced 12 October. China banned exports from Nexperia's operations in China on 4 October; European automakers warned they were days from stopping. The Dutch order was suspended on 19 November 2025; the United States suspension runs to 10 January 2027.
tier: Governments' exercise of law, below the tier: persistence not established; independent of the ruling sought on DBA-DIB-RE-5.

findings.title: The Customers Learned Where the Parts Were Made When They Ran Short.
findings.text: The customer knows which governments can stop its parts before one does.

annex.p: This annex is for manufacturers that buy chips and other first-tier parts, the makers and distributors that sell them, and those who oversee supply-chain resilience. It is not a finding and states no requirement. The recommendations of Section 8 are addressed to the facility class; this annex is addressed to a manufacturer. It has three parts, each drawn from a section of the instrument: a self-check that turns the event’s elements (Table 4-1) into questions a manufacturer answers about its own parts (A.2); the actions published, each stated as its publisher’s, with this instrument’s own marked and tied to a finding (A.3); and a plain-language account a manufacturer can give a board (A.4).

The instrument reads the event against the design basis. The self-check reads the same event against one manufacturer. Each question is keyed to the element of Table 4-1 it comes from. A “no” or an “I don’t know” is not a failure of the manufacturer; it is that manufacturer’s finding, and the place to start.

table: If the answer is no, or not known
For each critical chip you buy, do you know where it is made, packaged, and tested?
Most of a part’s capacity may sit where one decision can stop it. A.3.2.
Do you know every government whose law could stop any of those steps, allied or not?
A measure you did not foresee may stop your supply. A.3.2.
How long would your stock cover if one of those governments stopped exports tomorrow, and how long would requalifying another source take?
Your lines may stop before another source is qualified. A.3.1.
Does your supplier tell you when any of that changes?
You may learn of a change when the parts stop. A.3.2.

annex.h3: A.3.1 Follow the Guidance Already Published

annex.p: The governments’ announcements set out their measures. Industry and government guidance on semiconductor supply-chain resilience and on dual sourcing sets out related practice. The class’s requirements (§4.3, §6.4) state the place of each step, every government whose law can stop it, and coverage sized for a decision as long as such decisions last. Each is its author’s.

annex.h3: A.3.2 Ask Where Every Step Is Done

annex.p: These steps are this instrument’s, from F-1. Ask each maker of your critical chips, directly or through your distributor, where each step of making, packaging, and testing is done and which governments could stop it, require them to tell you of changes, and size your stock and second sources on the answer.

In the autumn of 2025, the Dutch government used an emergency law for the first time to take control of key decisions at Nexperia, a chipmaker based in the Netherlands but owned by a Chinese company, citing concerns about governance and the transfer of technology. China answered by banning exports from Nexperia’s factories in China, where by one account about eighty percent of its finished chips are made. Car makers in Europe warned they were days from halting production. The measures were eased within weeks, but the dispute is not fully settled. The lessons are that governments, friendly or not, can stop the supply of parts by decision, and that a company must know where its critical parts are made and finished, and which governments could stop them, before it happens. The questions in this annex show management whether the same exposure is present in its own parts, and most of the answers cost little to find.
